Executive Summary
This paper presents a new theoretical framework for simultaneous QED and QCD resummation (QED⊗QCD resummation) applied to precision LHC physics. The central goal is to address the requirement for a theoretical precision tag of approximately 0.67% on LHC luminosity processes, given that experimental luminosity precision is at the 2% level. The QED⊗QCD framework is built upon the Yennie-Frautschi-Suura (YFS) exponentiation formalism, extended from QCD to include simultaneous exponentiation of both gluon and photon infrared divergent contributions. The framework provides an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series, free of double-counting between QCD and QED effects, in principle to all orders in both αs and α. The theory is applied to single heavy gauge boson production (W ± and Z → ℓℓ') at the LHC and Tevatron to quantify threshold corrections. Semi-analytical computations yield ratio values r_exp = σ_exp / σ_Born of 1.1901 (QCED) vs 1.1872 (QCD) at the LHC, and 1.1911 (QCED) vs 1.1879 (QCD) at the Tevatron, quantifying the QED effect at approximately 0.3%. This effect is found to be stable under scale variations and consistent with structure function evolution results. The paper also develops a prescription for shower/matrix element matching, combining the exact YFS calculus with HERWIG or PYTHIA parton showers via a pT-matching or shower-subtracted residual approach, to avoid double-counting of emissions. The authors demonstrate that both approaches have been partially realized for the exact O(α) Bhabha process at DAPHNE, and the W production analysis is in progress. The framework provides a firm theoretical basis for the complete O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) results required for future LHC, FNAL, RHIC, and ILC physics programs.

Research Context
The LHC experimental luminosity precision tag is at the 2% level. The required theoretical precision tag on corresponding luminosity processes must be at 0.67%. This precision requirement dictates that multiple gluon and photon radiative effects must be controlled. The QCD resummation theory in Ref. [3] is the starting point. QED contributions in structure function evolution lead to effects at the ∼0.3% level. These effects account for nearly half of the total error budget. The need for extension to QED⊗QCD was suggested by Refs. [9–14]. Threshold QED effects in heavy gauge boson production are also expected to be of similar size. All effects must be taken into account for a ∼1.0% theoretical precision tag.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a simultaneous QED⊗QCD resummation framework be realized without double-counting of effects? The theory is expected to extend to all orders in both αs and α. The QED effects in heavy gauge boson production are hypothesized to be of similar magnitude to those in structure functions. An exact rearrangement of the perturbative series is claimed, rather than an approximate resummation. The QED component of the threshold effect is predicted to be approximately 0.3%. The framework should be applicable to an exact treatment of the phase space in MC methods. A consistent shower/ME matching prescription is required to combine the resummation with parton showers. The QED effect is expected to be stable under scale variations.

Methodological Details
The study considers parton-level single heavy boson production: q + ¯q′ →V + n(g) + X →¯ℓℓ′ + n(g) + X. Vector bosons V include W ± and Z; leptons ℓ include e, μ, νe, νμ. The QCD resummation is based on Ref. [3], an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series. The resummation is based on the N=1 term in the exponent in the eikonal approximation. The exponential is augmented with a sum of residuals to all orders in αs. The new QED⊗QCD theory is obtained by simultaneously exponentiating QCD and QED infrared divergent terms. The YFS residuals are defined in Ref. [2] and represent successive application first for QCD then for QED. Semi-analytical methods are used with structure functions from Ref. [23]. Structure functions are evaluated from Ref. [23] without narrow resonance approximation. The cross section is constructed via the usual formula with structure functions Fi(xi). The ratio rexp = σexp/σBorn is computed for LHC and Tevatron. The parton-level Born cross section uses well-known results for the respective processes. The QED⊗QCD exponent is γQCED = (2Qf² α / π + 2CF αs / π) Lnls.

Procedures And Architectures
The QCD residuals ˜¯βn are free of all infrared divergences to all orders in αs(Q). The new QCED residuals ˜¯βn,m are free of all infrared singularities. The substitution rules link SUMIR(QCED) to SUMIR(QCD) via additive combination of QED terms. The QED component of γQCED is proportional to Qf² α / π; the QCD component is to CF αs / π. F_YFS and δ_YFS functions are well-known from Ref. [22] involving the Gamma function and Riemann zeta function. The QED⊗QCD threshold correction is computed using the ratio rexp at LHC and Tevatron scales. Two shower/ME matching approaches are described: pT matching and shower-subtracted residuals. pT matching: restrict pT of gluon emission below the factorization scale µ to avoid double counting. Shower-subtracted residuals: expand shower formula and residuals in αns to match exact order-by-order. Both approaches were partially realized for exact O(α) Bhabha at DAPHNE in Ref. [31].

Key Results
At the LHC, rexp = 1.1901 for QCED (QCD+QED) and 1.1872 for QCD alone. At the Tevatron, rexp = 1.1911 for QCED and 1.1879 for QCD alone. The QED effect is at the .3% level at both LHC and FNAL. The result is stable under scale variations. The QED effect size agrees with Refs. [15,16,18–20] on both QCD and QED effects. The QED effect size is similar to structure function results in Refs. [9–13]. QCD dominant corrections happen an order of magnitude earlier than QED due to average Bjorken x values. The leading ˜¯β0,0-level already gives a good estimate of the interplay between higher-order QED and QCD effects.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The QED effect of .3% is needed for LHC theory predictions at ≲1%. The framework provides a firm theoretical basis for complete O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) results. The exactness to all orders in αs and α is a key distinction from approximate resummation theories. The QCED exponent does not show explicitly an ordered exponential, leading to some confusion.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper presents semi-analytical results; a full Monte Carlo realization will appear elsewhere. The analysis of W production is still in progress. Some confusion seems to exist because the QCED expression does not explicitly show an ordered exponential. The QED component of γQCED is derived from Ref. [3] structure function results, and full MC is not presented. The shower/ME matching is under investigation, with only partial realization for O(α) Bhabha at DAPHNE.

Claims
The QED⊗QCD resummation theory provides an exact, all-orders rearrangement of the perturbative series valid over the entire phase space. The residuals are free of all infrared singularities to all orders in αs and α. The substitution rules ensure exact combination of QCD and QED terms. The theory is an exact rearrangement rather than an approximate resummation. The QCED exponent does not explicitly show an ordered exponential, leading to some confusion. The framework can be used to make contact with parton shower MCs without double counting. It provides the theoretical precision required for LHC luminosity determinations.
QED threshold corrections to heavy gauge boson production at the LHC are approximately 0.3% and stable under scale variations. LHC QCED = 1.1901 vs QCD = 1.1872 gives a ~0.3% QED difference. The result is stable under scale variations. The value is consistent with Refs. [15,16,18–20] and structure function results [9–13]. The W production analysis is still in progress and not reported here. QED effects are necessary for LHC predictions at the sub-1% level. The effect is large enough to be non-negligible in precision LHC measurements.
A consistent shower/ME matching prescription can combine exact YFS resummation with HERWIG or PYTHIA parton showers without double counting. Two approaches (pT matching and shower-subtracted residuals) are described. The shower-subtracted approach matches the perturbative expansion order-by-order. Only O(α) Bhabha at DAPHNE has been realized so far. A full MC realization is not presented in this paper. This enables the construction of full event generators with exact resummed kinematics. It opens the way to O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) calculations for LHC physics.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The QED⊗QCD ratio rexp is stable under scale variations. The QED effect is consistent across LHC and Tevatron scales and with independent structure function calculations.

Key Figures Tables
Equation (8) presents the central numerical results: LHC (QCED=1.1901, QCD=1.1872) and Tevatron (QCED=1.1911, QCD=1.1879). Equation (6) gives the explicit formula for γQCED. Equations (7) define the F_YFS and δ_YFS functions using Riemann zeta and Euler constants.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first QED⊗QCD resummation theory providing simultaneous, all-orders exponentiation of QCD and QED infrared effects without double counting, applicable to LHC precision measurements. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantification of the QED threshold effect at approximately 0.3% for both LHC and Tevatron, confirmed by agreement with independent structure function calculations and stability under scale variations. 3. The future path includes full Monte Carlo realization, completion of the W production analysis, and extension to the complete O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) results for LHC, RHIC, and ILC physics programs.

summary.authors: A.M. Mathai, H.J. Haubold
summary.field_subfield: Mathematics and Statistics / Entropy and Information Theory

The central thesis is that the recursivity postulate—a core characterization assumption—automatically determines the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy, which in turn gives rise to additivity when the product probability property (PPP) holds. Executive Summary
This theoretical paper by Mathai and Haubold examines the origins of additivity in Shannon entropy and introduces generalized entropy measures that exhibit non-additive behavior when applied to joint probability distributions. The central thesis is that the recursivity postulate—a core characterization assumption—automatically determines the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy, which in turn gives rise to additivity when the product probability property (PPP) holds. Conversely, for generalized entropies such as Rényi, Havrda-Charvát, Tsallis, and Mathai entropy, the absence of a logarithmic structure leads to non-additive joint entropy relations where the joint entropy equals the sum of marginal entropies plus a non-additive term proportional to the product of marginal entropies. The authors demonstrate that the term 'independence' is a misnomer; the product probability property alone does not guarantee additivity, but rather the logarithmic structure of the entropy measure itself does. Under the maximum entropy principle applied via the calculus of variations, the authors derive explicit probability density functions for continuous populations subject to various constraints. Mathai entropy, in particular, unifies exponential, power-law, and extended exponential densities in its pathway model, producing generalized type-1 and type-2 beta, Tsallis statistics, Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, and Weibull distributions from a single functional form. The pathway model further satisfies a first-order linear differential equation, connecting entropy maximization to differential structures. Finally, Mathai entropy is identified as a type of directed divergence or inaccuracy measure, linked to Kerridge's concept of inaccuracy. The paper serves to clarify the theoretical underpinnings of entropy additivity and to demonstrate the unifying power of Mathai's generalized entropy for diverse physical and statistical models, while noting that for specific small sample spaces, no independent events can exist under the product probability definition.

Research Context
Mathai and Rathie (1975, 1976) first considered various generalizations of Shannon entropy, called entropies of order α, including additivity properties and characterization theorems. The term 'independence' in the definition P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) has been widely used but the authors argue it is a misnomer that produces inconsistent results for trivial events. It has been conventionally emphasized that Shannon entropy satisfies the additivity property, leading to extensivity in thermodynamic and statistical contexts. The paper addresses a gap in understanding why Shannon entropy exhibits additivity while generalized entropies do not, even when the product probability property holds for the underlying distributions. The connection between entropy measures, Kerridge's measure of inaccuracy, and pathway models has not been fully elucidated prior to this work. Prior work established that Shannon entropy's logarithmic form is tied to a recursivity postulate, but the general consequences for all entropy types were not systematically examined.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the recursivity postulate automatically determines the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy and thereby gives rise to additivity under the product probability property. The hypothesis is that the nature of the recursivity postulate, rather than the product probability property itself, is what mandates the logarithmic structure of Shannon entropy. It is hypothesized that non-additivity is the natural process in statistical mechanics, even in product probability situations, and additivity only holds due to the involvement of a recursivity postulate. The paper investigates whether different generalized entropies of order α, derived from different functional forms, yield different non-additive joint entropy relations and different probability models under the maximum entropy principle. The authors predict that Mathai's entropy, with its unique functional form, will be convenient for obtaining various probability models through entropy maximization under different constraints. It is hypothesized that the pathway model satisfied by Mathai's entropy can be expressed as a first-order differential equation, linking information-theoretic entropy to differential structures.

Methodological Details
The paper is a purely theoretical mathematical treatise; no human subjects, participants, data splits, or experimental procedures are involved. The discrete case considers a multinomial population P = (p1, ..., pk) where pi > 0 and p1 + ... + pk = 1, defining the entropy measure Hk(P). The continuous case considers a real random variable x with density function f(x), where entropy measures are defined as integrals over the real line. Five discrete entropy measures are defined: Rényi entropy of order α, Havrda-Charvát entropy of order α, Tsallis entropy of order α, Mathai entropy of order α, and Mathai’s additive entropy. The continuous analogues of all five entropy measures are derived as integral functionals of the density function f(x). The maximum entropy principle is applied via the calculus of variation procedure, considering functionals of the form U = [f(x)]α − λ[f(x)] subject to normalization. The normalization condition is R f(x)dx = 1 and the constraint f(x) ≥ 0 for all x. The first moment constraint E(x) = R xf(x)dx is assumed fixed for all functionals, which generates the power-law form of the density. In the joint distribution analysis, the product probability property (Pij = piqj) is assumed to hold for bivariate and trivariate discrete populations. For the pathway model, the boundary conditions are specified with f(a) and f(b) fixed for all functionals for some limits a and b.

Procedures And Architectures
The characterization of Shannon entropy begins with the recursivity postulate: Hn(p1, ..., pm−1, pmq1, .., pmqn−m+1) = Hm(p1, ..., pm) + pmHn−m+1(q1, ..., qn−m+1), which implies a weighted sum when PPP holds. This postulate, along with continuity, symmetry, zero-indifference, and normalization, automatically yields the logarithmic form: Sk = −A Σ pi ln pi. For generalized entropies, the joint entropy relation is derived as Fm,n,α(P, Q) = Fm,α(P) + Fn,α(Q) + a(α)Fm,α(P)Fn,α(Q), where a(α) takes specific values: 0 for Rényi, 2^(1-α)⁻¹ for Havrda-Charvát, 1−α for Tsallis, α−1 for Mathai, and 0 for Mathai’s additive entropy. The maximum entropy procedure for continuous populations involves constructing a Lagrangian U = [f(x)]α − λ1[f(x)] − λ2xf(x) and solving the Euler equation ∂U/∂f = 0. For Havrda-Charvát and Tsallis entropies, an escort density µ[f(x)]α is introduced to make the first moment constraint tractable, yielding the Tsallis q-exponential form. For Mathai entropy, the first moment of f(x) itself is taken as fixed, bypassing the need for escort distributions and yielding Tsallis statistics directly. The pathway model is derived by setting the Euler equation (2−α)f^(1−α) − λ1 − λ2xδ = 0, with the parameter δ > 0 introduced. The functional form of the pathway model is f(x) = c x^(γ-1) [1 - s(1 − α)x^δ]^(1/(1−α)), which unifies various special cases. A first-order linear differential equation is derived by taking the derivative of the pathway model functional: x d/dx g(x) = (γ−1)g(x) − sδ[g(x)]α. The continuous joint entropy relations are stated as parallel to the discrete case, with identical non-additive terms.

Key Results
The recursivity postulate automatically determines the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy, making it a mathematical consequence of the postulate rather than a property of independence. The definition P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) is inconsistent with common sense: for n=3, 5, 7 there are no independent events among the non-trivial outcomes. The term 'independence' is a misnomer; the property should be called product probability property, and PPP alone does not imply additivity of entropy. In the bivariate joint distribution with PPP, the joint entropy is Mm,n,α(P, Q) = Mm,α(P) + Mn,α(Q) + (α −1)Mm,α(P)Mn,α(Q), demonstrating non-additivity. For the trivariate case, the joint entropy includes all pairwise non-additive terms and a trinomial term with coefficient (α −1)^2. The value of a(α) in the non-additive relation Fm,n,α(P, Q) = Fm,α(P) + Fn,α(Q) + a(α)Fm,α(P)Fn,α(Q) is: 0 for Rényi, 2^(1-α)⁻¹ for Havrda-Charvát, 1−α for Tsallis, α−1 for Mathai, and 0 for Mathai’s additive entropy. Maximizing Havrda-Charvát or Tsallis entropy under a standard first-moment constraint makes it difficult to produce valid density functions; the escort distribution is required for Tsallis. Maximizing Mathai entropy under the standard first-moment constraint directly yields Tsallis statistics: f = λ*[1 + (α −1)x]^(−1/(α−1)) for α > 1 and f = λ*[1 + (1−α)x]^(−1/(1−α)) for α < 1. The pathway model f(x) = c x^(γ-1) [1 − s(1 − α)x^δ]^(1/(1−α)) yields: Maxwell-Boltzmann for δ=2, γ=3, α→1; Gaussian for δ=2, γ=1, α→1; Weibull for γ=δ, α→1; Wigner function for γ=1, δ=2, 1 < q < 3; and superstatistics of Beck for α > 1. The pathway model satisfies the first-order linear differential equation x d/dx g(x) = (γ−1)g(x) − sδ[g(x)]α, a power law form coming from Tsallis statistics. The special case of the pathway model for δ=1 corresponds to Tsallis statistics (Gell-Mann and Tsallis, 2004). Mathai entropy Mα(f) = (1/(α−1)) [E[f(x)]^(1−α) − 1] matches the form of Kerridge's directed divergence with the same functional dependence on the density.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The logarithmic form of Shannon entropy is not a property of independence but a mathematical consequence of the recursivity postulate, which assumes a weighted sum over product probability situations. Additivity in Shannon entropy is a structural artifact of the logarithm rather than a fundamental property of statistical independence, implying that non-additivity is the natural process in statistical mechanics. Different entropy measures generate different non-additive behaviors, meaning the choice of entropy measure determines the non-extensivity of the resulting statistical model, even when PPP holds. Mathai's pathway model unifies exponential, power-law, and stretched exponential distributions in a single parameter space, suggesting a unified structural framework for diverse statistical forms. The connection between entropy maximization and first-order linear differential equations suggests that information-theoretic constraints on probability densities may be fundamentally linked to differential dynamics. Mathai entropy's interpretation as a directed divergence or inaccuracy measure aligns it with information-geometric interpretations of entropy as a distance measure between distributions.

Contradictions And Limitations
The definition of independence P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) is shown to be inconsistent with common sense and mathematically impossible for certain finite sample spaces (n=3, 5, 7), rendering the standard terminology 'independent events' a misnomer. Havrda-Charvát and Tsallis entropies are noted as being 'diﬃcult to produce densities' under standard maximum entropy constraints, requiring the introduction of escort distributions as a workaround. The parameter ranges for Mathai's entropy vary across different special cases (α < 1, α > 1, α → 1), and the pathway model requires specific combinations of γ, δ, and α to reproduce known distributions, limiting its practical applicability without fine-tuning. The derivation of continuous joint entropy relations is noted as parallel to the discrete case and a 'separate derivation is not given here', limiting the explicit verification of continuous non-additivity. The paper is a purely theoretical mathematical work and does not include empirical verification, data analysis, numerical simulations, or code availability, limiting its applicability in practical statistical applications. No mention of random seeds, specific numerical experiments, convergence rates, or sensitivity analyses is provided, as the work is entirely formal and analytical.

Claims
The recursivity postulate automatically determines the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy, thereby naturally giving rise to additivity when the product probability property holds. The recursivity postulate (2) imposes that the entropy of a partition must be a weighted sum of the sub-partition entropies, which only a logarithmic functional can satisfy. The authors show that if PPP holds then a logarithmic function can give a sum and enters Shannon entropy due to the assumption through a certain type of recursivity postulate. The characterization theorem with the recursivity postulate as the main assumption yields Sk = −A Σ pi ln pi, the unique logarithmic form. The authors acknowledge that this is an assumption introduced through a postulate, not a fundamental property of the product probability property itself. The fact that the recursivity postulate is an added postulate rather than a derived property suggests additivity is a choice, not a necessity. This implies that non-additive entropies are not 'incorrect' generalizations but rather alternative characterizations that do not impose a logarithmic structure. The distinction between Shannon additivity and general non-additivity has important consequences for statistical mechanics applications.
Mathai's pathway model unifies various probability distributions (Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, Weibull, Tsallis, Wigner function, superstatistics) within a single functional form under the maximum entropy principle. Setting δ=2, γ=3, α→1 recovers the Maxwell-Boltzmann density. Setting δ=2, γ=1, α→1 recovers the Gaussian density. Setting γ=δ, α→1 recovers the Weibull density. Setting γ=1, δ=2, 1 < q < 3 recovers the Wigner function W(p) in the Fokker-Planck framework. Setting γ=1, δ=1 recovers Tsallis statistics. Each special case requires a specific combination of the three parameters γ, δ, and α, limiting the model's universality to well-known known distributions. The superstatistics result is only available for α > 1, and other forms require α < 1 or α → 1, fragmenting the parameter space. The pathway model provides a unified framework for multiple physical distributions arising from different statistical and thermodynamic problems. The unifying structure suggests that diverse physical models may share a common entropic origin through entropy maximization.
Mathai entropy can be viewed as a type of directed divergence or inaccuracy measure, connected to Kerridge's concept of inaccuracy. Mα(f) matches the form of Kerridge's inaccuracy Hα(f:q) with q replaced by f, sharing the same functional structure. The paper explicitly states Mα(f) can also be looked upon as a type of directed divergence or inaccuracy measure. The connection to Kerridge's (1961) concept is stated as an extension of Mathai's work with Haubold. The normalization constant in Kerridge's form (2^1-α)⁻¹ differs from the constant in Mathai's form (1/(α−1)), meaning they are not identical measures. The equivalence is in functional form only; the exact numerical values of the measures differ by a constant factor. This identifies entropy not just as a measure of uncertainty but as a geometric distance between a candidate density and a true density. It bridges information-theoretic entropy with the concept of error or inaccuracy in statistical inference.
The pathway model satisfies a first-order linear differential equation, linking entropy maximization to differential structures. The pathway model g(x) satisfies x d/dx g(x) = (γ−1)g(x) − sδ[g(x)]α for the general case. For β=1 and γ≠1, the equation becomes x d/dx g(x) = (γ−1)g(x) − sδ[g(x)]^(α-1), a first-order linear equation. The differential equation applies only to the functional part of the pathway model, not the full normalized density. This connects the maximum entropy principle to the theory of differential equations, opening potential applications in dynamical systems. The linear structure suggests that entropy-constrained distributions may admit closed-form solutions via standard differential methods.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the proof that the recursivity postulate, rather than statistical independence, is what mathematically mandates the logarithmic functional form of Shannon entropy and its consequent additivity under the product probability property, while generalized entropies without the logarithmic form produce non-additive joint entropy relations. 2. The strongest evidence is the derivation of the non-additive joint entropy relation Fm,n,α(P,Q) = Fm,α(P) + Fn,α(Q) + a(α)Fm,α(P)Fn,α(Q) with explicit coefficients a(α) for all five entropy types, and the recovery of Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, Weibull, Tsallis, Wigner, and superstatistics densities from a single pathway model under entropy maximization. 3. The future path lies in applying the pathway model to multivariate systems, exploring its implications for statistical mechanics where non-additivity is expected, and developing the continuous joint entropy framework for practical statistical applications where product probability property holds.

Executive Summary
This theoretical paper by Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer argues that as the current ΛCDM (Lambda Cold Dark Matter) universe extrapolates forward in time, all observational evidence of the Hubble expansion will eventually disappear from the perspective of a local observer. The authors demonstrate that within a timescale comparable to the lifetime of the longest-lived main sequence stars, the observable universe will contract to a single gravitationally bound system (the merger product of the Milky Way and Andromeda and other Local Group remnants), rendering the universe effectively static. This 'island universe' perspective eliminates the three pillars of modern cosmology: the observed Hubble expansion, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation, and the primordial abundance of light elements. Specifically, the authors show that: (1) all structures beyond the Local Group will be driven outside the de Sitter event horizon on a timescale of approximately 100 billion years, and light from them will be exponentially redshifted until they become invisible; (2) the CMB peak will redshift to wavelengths exceeding 1 meter and become screened below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium (at roughly 300 MHz / 1 kHz) within less than 50 times the present age of the universe; and (3) stellar evolution and nucleosynthesis will contaminate the helium-4 abundance to a mass fraction of approximately 0.6, while the primordial deuterium will be destroyed, rendering BBN-based inference impossible. Furthermore, the authors argue that general relativity itself does not mandate an expanding or contracting universe interpretation for a non-expanding, non-singular local system, as the cosmological hypothesis of isotropy and homogeneity is violated for the far-future observer. The paper concludes that our current epoch is a unique 'cosmic coincidence' wherein the dark energy and dark matter densities are comparable, allowing us to simultaneously observe both the cosmological expansion and the dark energy that drives it—a window that will close as the universe ages. The epoch will mark the end of cosmology and the return of a static universe coordinate system, analogous to the de Sitter model originally presented in the early 20th century.

Research Context
Shortly after Einstein developed general relativity, Willem de Sitter proposed a static model of the universe containing no matter, which he thought might approximate a low-density universe. The de Sitter metric was originally understood to contain Einstein's cosmological constant, later equated to a vacuum energy density with a redshift proportional to distance. The de Sitter model languished for much of the last century once the Hubble expansion was discovered and the cosmological term abandoned. All present observational evidence is consistent with a ΛCDM flat universe consisting of roughly 30% matter and 70% dark energy with a constant density. All cosmological models with a non-zero cosmological constant will approach a de Sitter universe in the far future, a fact explored in multiple prior works. The authors identify a gap in previous work by pointing out a new eschatological physical consequence regarding the perspective of an observer within a bound gravitational system in the far future. Prior to this, it had not been fully analyzed that the static version of de Sitter space outside a local system would eventually become the appropriate physical coordinate system.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is: What will observers in the far future, within a bound gravitational system, be able to conclude about the true nature of the universe? The authors hypothesize that all evidence of the Hubble expansion will disappear, so observers will be fundamentally incapable of determining the true nature of the universe. The prediction is that observers will not be able to infer the existence of the highly dominant vacuum energy, the existence of the CMB, or the primordial origin of light elements. The hypothesis states that this epoch will mark the end of cosmology and the return of a static universe. The authors predict that observers will conclude the existence of a static 'island universe', precisely the standard model of the universe as conceived circa 1900. A further prediction is that this conclusion will hold despite the fact that the dominant energy in this universe will not be due to matter, but due to dark energy, with ρM/ρΛ ∼ 10⁻¹². The authors anticipate that dark energy will be undetectable in the far future, not only when ρΛ ≪ ρM but also when ρΛ ≫ ρM.

Methodological Details
The paper employs a theoretical framework extrapolating the current ΛCDM universe forward in time to the far future. The authors reference analytic calculations by reference [7] and numerical calculations by reference [10] concerning the fate of bound structures. The study identifies the Local Group as the only remaining gravitationally bound structure in the face of accelerated Hubble expansion. All more distant structures are predicted to be driven outside of the de Sitter event horizon. The time frame for this process is on the order of 100 billion years. The authors analyze the three observational pillars of modern cosmology: the Hubble expansion, the cosmic microwave background, and the abundance of elements produced in the early universe. For the CMB analysis, they use the plasma frequency formula νₚ = (n_e e² / πm_e)^(1/2) and observations of pulsar signal dispersion. The electron number density in the interstellar medium is taken as n_e ≈ 0.03 cm⁻³. The plasma frequency is given as ν_p ≈ 1 kHz, corresponding to a wavelength of λ_p ≈ 3 × 10⁷ cm. The authors reference the work of Gamow and collaborators [16] on Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and the fully developed BBN theory of reference [15]. For the BBN analysis, they cite a mass fraction of helium given by Y = 0.6 as the ultimate extrapolation of light elemental abundances. The primordial helium mass fraction is taken as Y = 0.25. They reference Lyman-α absorption systems back-lit by QSOs as the current method for determining deuterium abundance. For the GR analysis, they consider observations of planetary dynamics and ground-based tests such as gravitational time dilation. They reference Lemaitre's inference of a Big Bang singularity from general relativity.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors first establish the static form of the de Sitter metric in a coordinate system that embeds de Sitter spacetime with a cosmological constant Λ as a four-dimensional hyperboloid in a 5d Minkowski spacetime. The de Sitter metric in static form is given as ds² = (1 − r²/R²) dt² − dr² / (1 − r²/R²) − r² dΩ², with R² = 3Λ⁻¹. The authors note that de Sitter's original model was not globally static but eternally expanding, with the scale factor R(t) = exp(Ht). The static coordinate system corresponds only to the section of de Sitter space within a cosmological horizon at R = r_s. In the analysis of the Hubble expansion, the authors identify that galaxies and galaxy clusters have dropped out of the Hubble flow due to gravitational binding. They conclude that light from distant objects will be exponentially redshifted, making them invisible within the lifetime of the longest-lived main sequence stars. For the CMB analysis, they calculate that at t ≈ 100 Gyr, the peak wavelength will be redshifted to approximately λ ≈ 1 m, or a frequency of roughly 300 MHz. The intensity of the CMB is redshifted by about 12 orders of magnitude. The CMB becomes unobservable even in principle when the peak wavelength exceeds the horizon. The authors also compute that the CMB peak will redshift below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium, which they estimate at an expansion factor of ∼10⁸ relative to the present-day peak. They estimate this expansion factor will be reached when the universe is less than 50 times its present age, well below the lifetime of the longest-lived main sequence stars. For the GR analysis, the authors examine whether a static universe is inconsistent with general relativity, concluding it is not. They argue that the inference of expansion or contraction depends on the cosmological hypothesis of an isotropic and homogeneous universe, which is violated in the far future. For the BBN analysis, they extrapolate stellar nucleosynthesis to a helium mass fraction of 0.6 and predict destruction of relic deuterium. They note that QSOs and Lyman-α systems will have redshifted outside of the horizon, removing the current means of deuterium detection.

Key Results
All more distant structures beyond the Local Group will be driven outside of the de Sitter event horizon on a timescale on the order of 100 billion years. Light from objects outside the Local Group will be exponentially redshifted until they become truly invisible within a time frame comparable to the longest lived main sequence stars. The remaining visible objects will be gravitationally bound and decoupled from the Hubble expansion, leaving a single galaxy as the merger product of the Milky Way and Andromeda. At t ≈ 100 Gyr, the peak wavelength of the CMB will be redshifted to approximately 1 m, with a frequency of roughly 300 MHz. The intensity of the CMB will be redshifted by approximately 12 orders of magnitude. The CMB peak will redshift below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium (ν_p ≈ 1 kHz) at an expansion factor of ∼10⁸ relative to the present day. The expansion factor of ∼10⁸ will be reached when the universe is less than 50 times its present age, well below the lifetime of the longest-lived main sequence stars. After this time, the CMB becomes unobservable even in principle as the peak wavelength is driven to a length larger than the horizon. A static universe can prevail outside of a non-singular isolated self-gravitating object, and general relativity imposes no inconsistency with such a configuration. For BBN, extrapolating light elemental abundances forward by 100 Gyr leads to a mass fraction of helium given by Y = 0.6. The primordial helium mass fraction of Y = 0.25 will be a relatively small fraction of the stellar-produced abundance. The current 'smoking gun' deuterium abundance from Lyman-α absorption systems back-lit by QSOs will be unavailable as both the QSOs and the systems redshift outside the horizon. The cosmic coincidence that we live at the only time when dark energy and dark matter densities are comparable allows us to infer both the expansion and dark energy. At the time when the universe is an order of magnitude younger, no effects of dark energy on the expansion can be discerned. When the universe is more than an order of magnitude older, observers will be hard pressed to know they live in an expanding universe or that the expansion is dominated by dark energy.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors interpret the far-future universe as a static 'island universe', where the coordinate system appropriate for observers will resemble the static coordinate system in which de Sitter space was first presented. The theoretical implication is that dark energy is undetectable not only in the limit ρ_Λ ≪ ρ_M but also when ρ_Λ ≫ ρ_M, because future observers will have no probes of the length scales over which Λ dominates. The inference that the universe must expand or contract is dependent on the cosmological hypothesis of an isotropic and homogeneous universe, which ceases to hold in the far future. Physicists in the island universe will conclude their local system has a finite future but cannot determine whether it had a finite beginning. The authors argue that we live in a very special time in the evolution of the universe: the time at which we can observationally verify that we live in a very special time in the evolution of the universe. By the time the longest lived main sequence stars are nearing the end of their lives, all evidence that now forms the basis of modern cosmology will have disappeared. The return of the static universe marks the end of cosmology as a discipline capable of inferring the history and nature of the universe from a local perspective.

Contradictions And Limitations
The argument assumes the stability of the Local Group as the only remaining bound structure, which depends on the specific gravitational dynamics of the ΛCDM model. The extrapolation to a helium mass fraction of Y = 0.6 for BBN is a theoretical prediction [17] and may not be fully verified in the far future. The paper notes that the plasma frequency value ν_p ≈ 1 kHz depends on the electron number density of the interstellar medium, which may vary. The argument that dark energy is undetectable when ρ_Λ ≫ ρ_M is a theoretical claim that would need further validation. The authors acknowledge that the CMB becomes unobservable even in principle only at much later times when its peak wavelength exceeds the horizon. The assertion that the island universe is static depends on the absence of cosmological perturbations at the largest scales, which may still persist in some form.

Claims
All observational evidence of the Hubble expansion will disappear from the perspective of a local observer in the far future. The Local Group remains gravitationally bound while all more distant structures are driven outside the de Sitter event horizon. Light from distant objects will be exponentially redshifted until they become truly invisible. The only remaining visible objects will be gravitationally bound and decoupled from the Hubble expansion. The paper acknowledges that the CMB becomes unobservable even in principle only when its peak wavelength exceeds the horizon, which may take much longer than the lifetime of main sequence stars. A local observer will conclude the existence of a static island universe, the standard model from circa 1900.
The cosmic microwave background will become unobservable to far-future observers within approximately 50 times the present age of the universe. The peak wavelength redshifts to approximately 1 m or 300 MHz at t ≈ 100 Gyr. The intensity redshifts by about 12 orders of magnitude. The CMB peak redshifts below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium, producing an expansion factor of ∼10⁸. This expansion factor is reached when the universe is less than 50 times its present age. The CMB remains observable in principle until the peak wavelength exceeds the horizon. The wealth of information about early universe cosmology from CMB fluctuations will be out of reach.
Primordial light element abundances cannot be inferred in the far future due to stellar contamination and destruction of relic deuterium. The helium-4 mass fraction is expected to reach Y = 0.6, dwarfing the primordial Y = 0.25. Relic deuterium will be destroyed by multiple generations of stellar evolution. QSOs and Lyman-α absorption systems will have redshifted outside the horizon, removing the current detection method. Astute observers could still determine a lower limit on the age of their system using stellar evolution analyses of local stars. Inferring original BBN abundances will be difficult and probably not well motivated for far-future physicists.
A static universe is not inconsistent with general relativity, so far-future observers need not infer an expanding or contracting universe. The inference of expansion depends on the cosmological hypothesis of isotropy and homogeneity. Nothing is inconsistent with a non-singular isolated self-gravitating object in a static universe governed by general relativity. Physicists in the island universe will conclude their island has a finite future, but not a finite beginning. The paper notes that outside the local cluster, the universe will appear to be empty and static. The question of whether the island had a finite beginning will arise naturally but cannot be answered.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors cite analytic [7] and numerical [10] calculations as supporting the gravitational stability of the Local Group. Sensitivity is discussed regarding the plasma frequency threshold: even before the CMB becomes unobservable in principle, it is screened below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium. The BBN prediction of Y = 0.6 is cited as an extrapolation from reference [17] and may vary with different nucleosynthesis models.

Key Figures Tables
The paper contains no figures or tables; it is a theoretical exposition with analytic and numerical derivations described in the text.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the theoretical demonstration that in the far future of the ΛCDM universe, all observational pillars of modern cosmology (Hubble expansion, CMB, BBN) will disappear from the perspective of a local observer, rendering the universe effectively static. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative calculation showing that the CMB peak redshifts below the interstellar plasma frequency (requiring an expansion factor of ∼10⁸) in less than 50 times the current age of the universe, well within the lifetime of the longest-lived main sequence stars. 3. The future path is the recognition of our current epoch as a unique cosmic coincidence—the only time in the history of the universe when both the expansion and the dark energy driving it can be observationally verified simultaneously.

summary.title: Fermi-liquid eﬀects in the transresistivity in quantum Hall double layers near ν = 1/2
summary.authors: Natalya A. Zimbovskaya
summary.field_subfield: condensed matter physics; quantum Hall effect and Fermi-liquid theory
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a theoretical calculation of the temperature and magnetic field dependence of Coulomb drag transresistivity between two parallel two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) layers in the quantum Hall regime near filling factor ν = 1/2 for both layers. The author employs the Composite Fermion (CF) framework within the Random Phase Approximation to derive the density-density response functions and the resulting transresistivity expression. At ν = 1/2, the transresistivity follows a T⁴/³ temperature dependence (consistent with prior theoretical and experimental results). Away from ν = 1/2, a correction term appears that enhances transresistivity nearly quadratically with the deviation Δν = ν − 1/2, with a curvature coefficient β that shows a strong temperature dependence consistent with experimental measurements. A striking feature in the experimental data is the near independence of transresistivity on interlayer spacing at the reported values (dA = 10 nm, dB = 22.5 nm). The author demonstrates that under the Random Phase Approximation alone, the condition for spacing independence (α > 1) is not met (α ≈ 0.44), but Fermi-liquid renormalization of the CF effective mass and compressibility resolves this: with Fermi-liquid parameters A0 ≈ 15 and A1 ≈ 3, the renormalized compressibility drops sufficiently such that α > 1 is satisfied, explaining the observed spacing independence. The best-fit parameters (A0 = 15, A1 = 3, m* = 4mb) reproduce the experimental scaled drag resistivity versus Δν at T = 0.6 and the temperature dependence of the curvature coefficient β⁻¹. The work establishes Coulomb drag near ν = 1/2 as a sensitive probe of Fermi-liquid interactions in the CF system.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a theoretical calculation of the temperature and magnetic field dependence of Coulomb drag transresistivity between two parallel two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) layers in the quantum Hall regime near filling factor ν = 1/2 for both layers. The author employs the Composite Fermion (CF) framework within the Random Phase Approximation to derive the density-density response functions and the resulting transresistivity expression. At ν = 1/2, the transresistivity follows a T⁴/³ temperature dependence (consistent with prior theoretical and experimental results). Away from ν = 1/2, a correction term appears that enhances transresistivity nearly quadratically with the deviation Δν = ν − 1/2, with a curvature coefficient β that shows a strong temperature dependence consistent with experimental measurements. A striking feature in the experimental data is the near independence of transresistivity on interlayer spacing at the reported values (dA = 10 nm, dB = 22.5 nm). The author demonstrates that under the Random Phase Approximation alone, the condition for spacing independence (α > 1) is not met (α ≈ 0.44), but Fermi-liquid renormalization of the CF effective mass and compressibility resolves this: with Fermi-liquid parameters A0 ≈ 15 and A1 ≈ 3, the renormalized compressibility drops sufficiently such that α > 1 is satisfied, explaining the observed spacing independence. The best-fit parameters (A0 = 15, A1 = 3, m* = 4mb) reproduce the experimental scaled drag resistivity versus Δν at T = 0.6 and the temperature dependence of the curvature coefficient β⁻¹. The work establishes Coulomb drag near ν = 1/2 as a sensitive probe of Fermi-liquid interactions in the CF system.

Research Context
In Coulomb drag experiments, two 2DEGs are arranged close to each other so they interact via Coulomb forces. A current is applied to one layer and the voltage in the other nearby layer is measured to find transresistivity ρD. Theoretical work has established that at one half filling of the lowest Landau level for both layers, transresistivity is proportional to T⁴/³. This T⁴/³ dependence originates from the ballistic contribution where wave vectors ql ≫ 1 and frequencies ωτ ≫ 1. Experimental results showed drag enhanced quadratically with Δν = ν − 1/2, with curvature dependent on temperature but insensitive to sign of Δν and distance d. The present work is motivated by these experiments of reference [7] regarding Coulomb drag near ν = 1/2.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to calculate the temperature and magnetic field dependence of Coulomb drag transresistivity between two parallel 2DEGs in the quantum Hall regime near ν = 1/2 for both layers. The hypothesis is that Fermi-liquid interactions between the relevant quasiparticles (Composite Fermions) could give a significant effect on the transresistivity. Specifically, the author predicts that Fermi-liquid effects provide the independence of transresistivity on interlayer spacing for spacings reported in experiments. The transresistivity is expected to enhance nearly quadratically with Δν away from ν = 1/2. The curvature coefficient of this enhancement is predicted to depend strongly on temperature, matching the experimental observation. The predicted results are expected to agree with the experimental evidence from reference [7].

Methodological Details
The study considers two parallel layers of two-dimensional electron gases subject to a strong magnetic field providing ν close to 1/2 for both layers. The starting point is the well-known expression relating Coulomb drag transresistivity to density-density components of the polarization in both layers. Electron densities in the two layers are assumed equal (n1 = n2 = n). The Composite Fermion (CF) approach is used, where a single-layer polarizability describes the irreducible density-current response. The Random Phase Approximation (RPA) is adopted for the 2 × 2 polarizability matrix calculation. The Chern-Simons interaction matrix C is explicitly defined in terms of the wave vector q and magnetic length. The CF conductivity tensor components are derived from the standard solution of the Boltzmann transport equation for the CF distribution function. The CF velocity components are expanded in Fourier series to facilitate integration. The collisionless limit 1/τ → 0 is considered for the ballistic regime, with asymptotics in powers of the small parameter (qR)⁻¹. The screened interlayer potential U(q,ω) is given by the standard form involving bare Coulomb potentials Vb and Ub with dielectric constant ϵ. The compressibility dn/dµ of the ν = 1/2 state is defined as 3m*/8π¯h², differing from the noninteracting value N. The analysis is restricted to two identical layers Π(1) = Π(2) ≡ Π.

Procedures And Architectures
The RPA polarizability matrix is inverted to find the density-density response function Π00(q,ω). The CF conductivity tensor components ˜σ are derived using the Boltzmann transport equation approach of references [9] and [10]. A formal transformation introduces a new variable η related to the integration variable θ. The asymptotic expression for qvx(ψ + Ωθ) in powers of Ωθ leads to the collisionless limit forms for ˜σxx, ˜σyy, and ˜σxy. The integral over ω in the transresistivity formula is dominated by ω ∼ T, and the q-integral by q ∼ kF(T/T0)¹/³. The parameter δ = ω/qvF is found to be small compared to unity at low temperatures (T ∼ 1 K) for T0 of the order of room temperature. The screened interlayer potential U(q,ω) is substituted into the transresistivity integral. The Fermi-liquid correction enters via the renormalized polarizability Π*⁻¹ = Π⁻¹ + F(0) + F(1), keeping only the first two terms in the Legendre expansion. The effective mass m* is related to the bare mass mb via 1/mb = 1/m* + f1/2π¯h², with f1 characterizing the Fermi-liquid shift. Best-fit parameters are determined by comparing the theoretical curve to experimental data from reference [7] at T = 0.6. The Fermi-liquid parameters A0 and A1 are adjusted to achieve agreement with the experimental data.

Key Results
At ν = 1/2, the transresistivity ρD0 follows the T⁴/³ temperature dependence predicted by prior theory: ρD0 = h e² Γ(7/3)ζ(4/3) (T/T0)⁴/³ with T0 dependent on interlayer spacing. The correction δρD at low temperatures (T/T0) ≪ 1 includes terms proportional to (kF R)⁻¹ at (T/T0)⁴/³ and (T/T₀)²/³ in (kF R)⁻². The dominant term at low temperature is proportional to (T/T₀)²/³, causing the linear Δν term to be smaller than the last term in Eq. (22). The transresistivity enhances nearly quadratically with Δν, with the leading correction δρD ≈ 4/3 ρD0 Δν [1 + 3/4 Δν] + 4 a² h e² (2T/T₀)²/³ (Δν)². The ratio ρD/ρD0 is expressed in the approximate form 4β(Δν)² + 1, where β is the curvature coefficient. The curvature coefficient β is proportional to Γ(7/3)ζ(4/3) (2T₀/T)²/³ and its inverse shows the temperature dependence observed in experiments. Without Fermi-liquid corrections, the spacing-independence parameter α ≈ 0.44, which is too small to explain the experimental insensitivity to d. Including Fermi-liquid corrections with A0 = 15 and A1 = 3 (m* = 4mb) produces a renormalized compressibility dn*/dµ low enough for α > 1 to be satisfied. The best-fit T0 values are 487 K for dA = 10 nm and 587 K for dB = 22.5 nm, with the upper curve in Fig. 2 corresponding to dA = 10 nm. The theoretical curve (Eq. 22) with m* = 4mb, A0 = 15, and A1 = 3 shows good agreement with experimental data from reference [7]. The curvature β is found to be proportional to the second Fermi-liquid parameter A0 ≡ f0/2π¯h², with values of the order of 10 − 100.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The T⁴/³ temperature dependence of transresistivity at ν = 1/2 is a hallmark of the ballistic regime of Composite Fermions. The quadratic enhancement with Δν confirms that the transresistivity is sensitive to the Fermi-surface geometry of CF quasiparticles. The independence of transresistivity on interlayer spacing is interpreted as the dominance of intralayer screening over interlayer interactions when α > 1. The parameter α characterizes the ratio of the Thomas–Fermi screening length in a single 2DEG to the separation between the layers. The required α > 1 is only achieved by Fermi-liquid renormalization, indicating strong quasiparticle interactions in the CF system. The result provides one more evidence of strong Fermi-liquid interaction in the CF system near ν = 1/2. The Fermi-liquid renormalization reduces the CF compressibility and enhances the screening length in individual layers, suppressing interlayer coupling. The author notes that at larger interlayer distances, the d-dependence should eventually be revealed in experiments. The results enable estimation of the Fermi-liquid interaction strength between CF quasiparticles at ν = 1/2.

Contradictions And Limitations
The RPA without Fermi-liquid corrections fails to explain the experimental spacing independence, giving α ≈ 0.44 instead of α > 1. The expression for the coefficient a² cannot be used in the limit T → 0; it requires (T kF l/µ)¹/³ ≥ 1.5 for validity. Using the estimated mean free path of 1.0 μm and n = 1.4 × 10¹⁵ m⁻², the approximation for a² holds when T/µ is no less than 10⁻². The analysis is restricted to two identical layers; asymmetric interlayer properties would modify the results. The two T0 values (487 K and 587 K) for d = 10 nm and d = 22.5 nm do not coincide exactly, reflecting residual d-dependence. No random seed or explicit error bars on the best-fit parameters A0 and A1 are reported. The approximation for δ ≈ (T/µ)(T0/T)¹/³ assumes T0 is of the order of room temperature, which is a heuristic estimate. The linear Δν term in the correction causes an asymmetric shape of the plot relative to Δν = 0, though the asymmetry is not very significant.

Claims
Fermi-liquid interactions among Composite Fermion quasiparticles at ν = 1/2 explain the experimental insensitivity of Coulomb drag transresistivity to interlayer spacing at reported values. The RPA-only calculation yields α ≈ 0.44, failing to explain spacing independence. Including Fermi-liquid corrections with A0 = 15 and A1 = 3 gives α > 1, where intralayer screening predominates. The best-fit curve with A0 = 15 and A1 = 3 agrees with experimental data from Lilly et al. The renormalized compressibility dn*/dµ is low enough for the spacing-independence condition to be satisfied. The T0 values for dA = 10 nm and dB = 22.5 nm (487 K and 587 K) do not coincide, indicating some residual spacing dependence. The curves in Fig. 2 do not coincide but are arranged rather close to each other. The approximation for a² requires (T kF l/µ)¹/³ ≥ 1.5, which may not hold for all experimental conditions. The results confirm strong Fermi-liquid interactions in the CF system at ν = 1/2. Coulomb drag serves as a sensitive probe of quasiparticle interactions in the quantum Hall regime. Future experiments at larger interlayer distances could reveal the d-dependence of transresistivity.
Transresistivity at ν = 1/2 follows a T⁴/³ temperature dependence, and away from ν = 1/2 it enhances nearly quadratically with Δν. At ν = 1/2, ρD0 ∝ (T/T0)⁴/³ from Eq. (20). The correction δρD has a quadratic term 4/3 ρD0 Δν [1 + 3/4 Δν] + 4 a² (2T/T₀)²/³ (Δν)². The curvature β of the quadratic fit shows the predicted temperature dependence matching experiments. The collisionless limit derivation confirms the T⁴/³ form at ν = 1/2. The linear Δν term causes an asymmetric shape relative to Δν = 0, deviating from a pure quadratic. The a² approximation is not valid as T → 0, limiting the T⁴/³ to T²/³ crossover regime. The T⁴/³ law is a hallmark of the ballistic CF regime and validates the CF framework. The quadratic enhancement provides a quantitative test of CF Fermi-surface geometry.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The CF conductivity components in earlier works [8] were not used because they lacked a smooth passage to the Beff → 0 limit at finite q. The Fermi-liquid correction retains only the first two terms in the Legendre polynomial expansion to avoid overly lengthy calculations. The analysis compares two experimental datasets from Lilly et al. (dA = 10 nm and dB = 22.5 nm) against the theoretical curve at T = 0.6. The quadratic form ρD/ρD0 = 4β(Δν)² + 1 is presented after keeping only the greatest term in the correction expression.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the scaled drag resistivity versus Δν at T = 0.6; the lowest dashed curve is the theoretical plot (m* = 4mb, A0 = 15) and remaining curves are experimental data from reference [7]. Figure 2 shows the temperature dependence of the curvature coefficient β⁻¹ for two interlayer distances (dA = 10 nm and dB = 22.5 nm) compared to experimental curvature data from reference [7]. summary.title: Einstein vs Maxwell: Is gravitation a curvature of space, a field in flat space, or both?
summary.authors: Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical physics: General relativity, gravitational field theory, cosmology
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical derivation with new analytic solution and cosmological application
summary.executive_summary: This paper by Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen presents a field-theoretic formulation of general relativity in which the gravitational energy-momentum tensor is derived in a straightforward manner starting from a Minkowski background space-time. The metric tensor is defined as a non-linear coding of distances in flat space, analogous to optical thickness in cloudy media. Using Rosen's bimetric framework and Logunov's relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG), the author breaks general coordinate invariance by introducing a bimetric coupling between the Riemann and Minkowski metrics. This approach allows the Einstein equations to be rewritten in a Newton-like shape (acceleration = mass−1 × force), where the total energy-momentum tensor of gravitation and matter is conserved. For flat space cosmology (FLRW with k = 0), the gravitational energy density is negative and exactly cancels the material energy density, leading to a universe with no overall energy. The paper further develops the RTG with a positive cosmological constant, producing a singularity-free Schwarzschild-like black hole solution. In this interior solution, metric components remain positive and do not change sign, preserving the role of time, while the gravitational field dies out quickly. The corresponding cosmological evolution reproduces the ΛCDM model with an additional positive curvature-type term from the bimetric coupling and predicts a form of inflation at early times without a separate inflaton field. A brick-wall transition layer of width ∼ 0.977 × 10−9 for solar-mass black holes is identified, and the test particle motion confirms that in-falling matter penetrates the horizon rather than being reflected. The author concludes that the field-theoretic and curved-space descriptions are equivalent perspectives, but RTG favors Maxwell's view of gravitation as a field in flat space, with implications for quantum gravity where fields rather than space itself would be quantized.

The author concludes that the field-theoretic and curved-space descriptions are equivalent perspectives, but RTG favors Maxwell's view of gravitation as a field in flat space, with implications for quantum gravity where fields rather than space itself would be quantized.

Einstein's step from flat to curved space, as described by Lorentz and Poincaré, left the issue of the quasi energy-momentum tensor unresolved in general relativity. The proper energy-momentum tensor of gravitation was recently derived by Babak and Grishchuk using a field-theoretic approach in a Minkowski background space-time. Nathan Rosen's bimetric theory, involving both the Minkowski and Riemann metrics, naturally bridges particle physics and cosmology by assigning ηµν to particle physics and gµν to cosmology. Logunov and coworkers extended this into the relativistic theory of gravitation, introducing an extra gauge-transformation-related action that introduces a bimetric term coupling the two metrics. The debate over whether gravitation is a curvature of space or a field in flat space remains a fundamental tension between the Maxwell and Einstein viewpoints. Previous attempts to modify general relativity with a positive cosmological constant encountered deep troubles with established properties of the theory.

Can the Einstein equations be reformulated into a field-theoretic Newtonian shape (acceleration = mass−1 × force) with a proper, conserved energy-momentum tensor in Minkowski space? A positive cosmological constant, when combined with a bimetric coupling in the RTG framework, can resolve the singularity of the Schwarzschild black hole. In flat space cosmology, the gravitational energy must exactly cancel the material energy, leading to a universe with zero overall energy. The RTG with positive ρΛ produces a black hole solution where metric components remain positive in the interior, thus preserving the role of time. The cosmological equations derived from the RTG should reproduce the ΛCDM model while accommodating positive curvature and predicting early inflation without a separate inflaton field. The RTG action is constructed by discarding a total derivative of the Hilbert-Einstein action and using Rosen's bimetric coupling between the Riemann and Minkowski metrics. Curvature is reinterpreted as a geometric description of the gravitational field in flat space, not as a property of empty space itself, echoing Maxwell's view. The separation of curved space into flat space and gravitational field implies that the quantum version of RTG would involve quantization of fields rather than space. The cosmic speed of light changes with cosmic time, while the conformal speed dr/dτ = c/a(τ) remains the standard value, providing a purely kinematic explanation for redshift. The RTG with positive ρΛ does not produce true black holes with horizons; the solutions are instead termed grey holes, lacking an event horizon. The approach is quantitatively applicable only for M > 10³ M⊙, as the brick wall width otherwise reaches the Planck scale, where quantum gravity effects dominate. Logunov's theory with ρbi < 0 has self-repulsive properties for matter falling onto a black hole and limits the scale factor to a minimal and maximal size. The combination τµν = (c⁴/8πG) [γ/g Aµν − (Rµν − 1/2gµνR)] yields a bilinear form in first-order covariant derivatives, eliminating all second-order terms. In Cartesian coordinates, τµν coincides with the Landau-Lifshitz quasi-tensor, extending a previously known result to arbitrary coordinate systems. The derivation relies on Rosen's assumption that Rµν remains unchanged when replacing partial derivatives with Minkowski covariant ones, which may not be universally valid. A proper energy-momentum tensor enables a clear transfer of energy from gravitational waves to detectors, addressing a fundamental difficulty in GTR. The metric components U and V die out but remain positive in the interior, confirming that time keeps its usual role as a temporal coordinate. For the extreme case βi = 0 at ri = ∞, the particle velocity |dℓ/dτ| remains less than c for all r, ensuring causal motion through the horizon. No true black hole with a horizon exists; the solutions are termed grey holes, and the horizon radius rh equals half the Schwarzschild radius. The approach is physically meaningful only for M > 10³ M⊙, as the brick wall width otherwise reaches the Planck scale. The interior is regularized, and the singularity at r = 0 is removed by the bimetric coupling term, resolving a fundamental GTR problem. The finite time T = rh/c¯µ² = 2.74 × 10³² M/M⊙ yr to reach the center confirms the solution's global structure and observability.

(26) yields an initial expansion a = (a²∗cτ/√(3Λbi/2))^(1/3), constituting an inflation scenario starting at t = −∞. At large times, the universe enters exponential growth a(τ) = C exp(H∞τ) with H∞ = c sqrt(Λ/3), and a(t) = a²∗/3 [3H∞(t₀ − t)]^(−1/3) in cosmic time. The positive curvature term ρ² = −3ρbi/2a² is of order O(Λbi/a²), which may not match observations for all cosmological eras. summary.title: Enhanced sensitivity to variation of me/mp in molecular spectra
summary.authors: D. DeMille, S. Sainis, J. Sage, T. Bergeman, S. Kotochigova, and E. Tiesinga
summary.field_subfield: Atomic and Molecular Physics / Fundamental Constants
summary.type_of_paper: Research article with experimental data and theoretical proposal
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a new laboratory experiment to search for spatial or temporal variations of the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ ≡ me/mp with enhanced sensitivity, leveraging nearly-degenerate molecular vibrational levels in Cs2. The authors demonstrate that the energy of molecular vibrational levels is highly sensitive to changes in µ, and that pairs of closely-spaced levels associated with different electronic potentials can amplify this sensitivity relative to the level splitting. The sensitivity is governed by the absolute energy shift ∂µΩ of the splitting with respect to fractional change ∆µ/µ and the relative shift ∂µΩ/Ω, the latter important for comparison with reference clocks and systematic effects. The authors verify the existence of such near-degenerate pairs in the ground vibronic levels of Cs2, showing spectroscopic data for the a3Σ+_u and X1Σ+_g states with binding energies around 449 and 523 GHz (tentatively assigned to va = 37 and va = 38). They demonstrate that the vibrational levels at intermediate excitation (near 3D/4) maximize energy sensitivity, with ∂µEv approximately half the harmonic value. For the specific near-degenerate a3Σ+_u (va = 37) and X1Σ+_g (vX = 138) pair, the splitting sensitivity ∂µΩ is approximately 5 × 10¹² Hz. By assuming one measurement every 2 seconds with signal-to-noise S=100, a statistical uncertainty δ(∆µ/µ) ∼10⁻¹⁷ in µ/µ could be achieved in approximately one day of integration, requiring only about 10⁻¹⁴ relative splitting accuracy. The system's narrow spectral lines (achievable with ultracold Cs2) and long radiative lifetimes (>1 s) make it promising for future searches. The authors also identify two forbidden transitions (microwave at 6.3 GHz and E1 at 9.8 GHz) that could be exploited, and note that the method requires less accuracy than the best atomic clocks. The work was supported by DOE, ONR, ARO, and NSF grants, and acknowledges experimental assistance from P. Hamilton and S.B. Cahn, plus comments from E.R. Hudson.

claims.description: A fractional change ∆µ/µ ≲10⁻¹⁷ in the electron-to-proton mass ratio can be detected with one day of integration in the Cs2 system.
The WKB-derived energy sensitivity formula ∂µEv = (v+1/2)2ρ(Ev) provides a general mechanism for amplifying the absolute size of ∂µΩ.
Cs2 is an attractive system for implementing the near-degeneracy scheme due to its overlapping a3Σ+_u and X1Σ+_g potentials and long radiative lifetimes.

top_influential_citations.C. Chin and V.V. Flambaum, Phys. Rev. top_influential_citations.N. Vanhaecke et al., Eur. Phys. J. D 28,: This paper provides the foundational long-range potentials for the a3Σ+ u state of Cs2, upon which the entire near-degeneracy analysis and the observed spectroscopic levels are built.

top_influential_citations.C. Samuelis et al., Phys. Rev. A 63, 012: The Hannover analytic form developed in this paper is used as the fallback potential model in regions of the Cs2 spectrum with insufficient data, directly influencing the fit and resulting level assignments.
