A theoretical scaling law ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ with exponent n = 0.35 predicts the transition boundary between the two bouncing modes in the film boiling regime and agrees well with experimental data.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates droplet impact on heated surfaces and identifies a new bouncing mode, 'bouncing-with-spray,' where vapor bubble burst at random sites in the liquid film creates holes, reducing the recoiling distance and dramatically shortening the droplet's residence time. The authors demonstrate this mode across three boiling regimes—nucleate, transition, and film boiling—using water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures with varying viscosities. Key findings include: the bouncing-with-spray mode reduces residence time by approximately 40% relative to the conventional retraction-bouncing mode; the reduction is independent of liquid viscosity; and a theoretical scaling law with exponent n = 0.35 predicts the transition boundary between the two modes in the film boiling regime. The mechanism is physically analogous to droplet fragmentation on superhydrophobic surfaces with ridges, but here fragmentation is induced by internal vapor generation rather than external geometry. The authors propose a scaling law based on energy conservation, equating heat transfer from the substrate to vaporization energy, and determine the critical condition at bubble radius equal to minimum film thickness (b ∼ Re⁻²⁵). The resulting dimensionless scaling relationship (Gr* Prv)¹/⁴ Fo* Ja³/⁴ ∼ Weⁿ Re⁻¹.¹ yields a transition boundary ∆T ∼ V⁻¹, which fits experimental data well. This approach induced by heat is characterized as simple and reliable, avoiding surface degradation and complex fabrication of surface microstructures or surface modification. The authors conclude with a regime map showing the transition boundary between the two bouncing modes as a function of substrate temperature and impact speed, and they note that the model also explains the transition in the transition boiling regime.

Research Context
Droplet impact is a ubiquitous phenomenon in nature and industrial applications including spray cooling, painting, inkjet printing, and fuel-spray impingement in internal combustion engines. Early studies focused on impact morphologies using high-speed imaging and analysis of ejected secondary droplets using phase Doppler anemometry. When the droplet impacts a heated surface, the boiling process includes nucleate boiling, transition boiling, and film boiling regimes. At high temperatures, the Leidenfrost effect generates a vapor layer underneath the droplet, acting as a thermal insulation layer that reduces vaporization rate. The contact time of a bouncing droplet is bounded by the Rayleigh time scale for an inviscid droplet on a superhydrophobic surface. Numerous strategies have been explored to reduce contact time, including superhydrophobic surfaces with ridges, pancake bouncing on lattices of submillimeter posts, asymmetric bouncing on curved surfaces, and egg-shaped droplets. In the film boiling regime, a vapor layer forms and the droplet, if it has sufficient kinetic energy, may bounce from the substrate after recoil, with residence time approximated as the period of a freely oscillating droplet. Previous theoretical models have predicted contact time in the nucleate boiling regime where the droplet can stick to the hot surface and evaporate.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a droplet bouncing mode caused by the burst of vapor bubbles can contribute to a dramatic reduction of the droplet residence time on a heated surface. The authors hypothesize that the bouncing-with-spray mode, induced by heat, will reduce residence time significantly compared with the traditional retraction-bouncing mode and will be simple and reliable compared to surface-modification strategies. A second research question concerns the physical mechanism by which bubble burst reduces residence time, specifically through hole formation in the liquid film and subsequent recoiling. The authors predict that the reduction in recoiling distance leads to a reduction in recoiling time, thereby shortening the residence time significantly. A third objective is to derive a theoretical scaling law for the transition boundary between the retraction-bouncing and bouncing-with-spray modes in the film boiling regime. The authors further hypothesize that the proposed scaling law will agree well with experimental data and can also explain the mode transition in the transition boiling regime.

Different droplet liquids (water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures) were pushed through an injection tube at a speed of approximately 4 µl/s by a syringe pump. The syringe pump was a Harvard Apparatus, Pump 11 elite Pico plus model. Droplets formed at the tip of a blunt syringe needle and detached when the gravitational force exceeded the surface tension force. The droplet impacted on a polished silicon substrate (silicon wafers) with roughness less than 0.5 nm. The substrate was heated by a copper holder with two K-type thermocouples placed 1 cm beside the point of impact. The temperature was controlled with an accuracy of ±1°C by a PID controller. A high-speed camera (Photron Fastcam SA1.1) captured both side-view and aerial-view images of the droplet impact evolution. The impact process was illuminated by an LED light source. The droplet size was typically D0 = 2.8 mm for water/glycerol mixtures, 2.2 to 3.4 mm for water, and 1.6 mm for ethanol. The impact speed ranged from 0.9 to 2.1 m/s. The Weber number was varied from 10 to 180 for different liquids. The Jakob number was defined as the ratio of sensible heat to latent heat of the liquid, Ja = cp(Tw − Ts)/ℓ. The liquid properties, including density, surface tension, dynamic viscosity, and latent heat, are summarized in Table 1. The droplet size, impact speed, and shape evolution were measured from high-speed images using a customized Matlab program. The roughness of the silicon wafer was less than 0.5 nm, ensuring a smooth substrate. Two K-type thermocouples were placed 1 cm from the impact point to monitor and control the substrate temperature. The experimental setup included a heated copper plate, silicon wafer, PID temperature controller, computer, syringe, syringe needle, high-speed camera, LED light source, height gauge, and optical fibre.

Procedures And Architectures
Droplets were generated at a blunt syringe needle tip and impacted the heated silicon wafer after detachment. The liquid film thickness b at the moment of maximum expansion scales as b ≈ Re⁻²⁵, derived from existing literature. The heat transfer from the substrate to the droplet was modeled by equating the heat flux times the heat transfer area to the vaporization enthalpy of the bubble. The time interval for heat transfer was approximated by the time for the droplet to reach its maximum lateral expansion τ0, which is independent of the impact speed and depends on the droplet oscillation period. The vapor layer was assumed to have a uniform thickness δ, with heat transfer dominated by conduction, and the heat flux per unit area approximated as λv∆T/δ. The radial vapor velocity was derived from mass conservation at a radial position r: πr² λv∆T / (δℓ) = 2πr u(r) δρv. The flow in the vapor layer was treated as Poiseuille flow, yielding the mean velocity u(r) = −δ² / (12µv) dp/dr. The pressure distribution in the vapor layer was obtained by integrating the velocity equation: p(r) = pa + 3λvµv∆T / (δ⁴) [R² − r²]. The vapor layer thickness δ was derived by equating the lift force from the vapor layer to the difference between the weight and buoyancy force of the droplet disk: δ = [3λvµv∆TR² / (2ρv(ρl − ρv)bℓg)]¹/⁴. The average heat transfer coefficient was then expressed as h = λv / δ, which simplifies to a ratio of thermal properties and geometry. In the critical condition for the transition, the liquid disk radius R was approximated by the maximum expansion diameter Rmax/R0 ∼ Weⁿ, with n = 0.35. Substituting all expressions into the energy balance equation yielded the dimensionless scaling: (cpv/cpl)³/⁴ (Gr* Prv)¹/⁴ Fo* Ja³/⁴ ∼ Weⁿ Re⁻¹.¹. A modified Grashof number Gr* = gρv(ρl − ρv)R⁰ / µ²v, the Prandtl number Prv = cpvµv/λv, and a modified Fourier number Fo* = λvτ0A / (ρvcρvR⁴) were defined. For the same liquid and same initial droplet size, physical properties and τ0 are treated as constants, leading to the transition boundary ∆T ∼ V⁻¹ for n = 0.35. The theoretical model uses the condition rv ≈ bmin at the moment of maximum expansion as the transition boundary between modes.

Key Results
In the nucleate boiling regime (We = 37, T = 260°C), the droplet contacts the surface directly, vapor bubbles form immediately, rise through the droplet, and break at the free surface, with the bottom liquid still sticking to the surface. In the transition boiling regime at low impact speed (We = 37, T = 380°C), the droplet recoils and bounces with spray-like ejection of tiny droplets, named the retraction-bouncing mode. At a higher impact speed (We = 69, T = 380°C) in the transition boiling regime, the droplet bounces without obvious retraction, accompanied by spray-like ejection, named the bouncing-with-spray mode. The residence time in the bouncing-with-spray mode is 6.5 ms compared to 12.0 ms in the retraction-bouncing mode at the same temperature (T = 380°C). Further increasing the impact speed (We = 105, T = 380°C) leads to liquid fingers at the rim and splashing, but the central region still bounces without obvious retraction, with a residence time of 6.3 ms versus 12.0 ms in the RB mode. In the film boiling regime at relatively low surface temperature (We = 25, T = 400°C), the retraction-bouncing mode is observed, and as temperature increases to 440°C, tiny droplet ejection becomes more uniform. At We = 60, T = 440°C in the film boiling regime, the bouncing-with-spray mode is observed; at We = 129, T = 440°C, splashing and the bouncing-with-spray mode both occur. The residence time of the bouncing-with-spray mode is consistently smaller than that of the retraction-bouncing mode in both transition and film boiling regimes. By normalizing the residence time with the Rayleigh time scale, past experiments show values from 2.2 to 3.2, while the retraction-bouncing mode in this study yields approximately 2.3. The bouncing-with-spray mode residence time, normalized, is about 1.4, indicating a reduction of approximately 40% compared to the retraction-bouncing mode. The residence time of the bouncing-with-spray mode was found to be independent of the liquid viscosity when droplet viscosity was varied by changing glycerol concentration at fixed V and D0. The scaling law ∆T ∼ V⁻¹ obtained from the theoretical model, with n = 0.35, agrees well with the experimental data in the film boiling regime as shown in Figure 6d. The theoretical model also explains why the transition temperature between the two modes increases with Weber number in the transition boiling regime. In the transition boiling regime, the critical Weber number increases with substrate temperature because the heat flux decreases, requiring a thinner liquid film for bubble burst. The experimental residence times for the retraction-bouncing mode in the film boiling regime range from approximately 2.8 ms to 11 ms depending on We and T. The experimental residence times for the bouncing-with-spray mode in the film boiling regime range from approximately 2.9 ms to 10.3 ms. At the lowest film boiling conditions (We = 129, T = 440°C), the residence times are 1.0 ms, 2.4 ms, and 6.7 ms, showing dramatic reduction.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The mechanism of residence time reduction is attributed to the burst of vapor bubbles at random sites in the liquid film, which produces holes that cause the liquid film to recoil from the holes. The holes expand rapidly and the liquid film recoils to several fragments, reducing the recoiling distance and consequently the recoiling time. This mechanism is physically analogous to the reduction in residence time during droplet bouncing on superhydrophobic surfaces with ridges, where ridges cause droplet fragmentation and decrease the recoiling distance. In the current study, the fragmentation of the droplet is induced by the internal burst of vapor bubbles rather than external surface microstructures. The reduction is always accompanied by a spray of tiny droplets during bubble bursting. The mode of droplet bouncing and the consequent residence time reduction were observed for all liquid types used in the experiments. The independence of residence time on viscosity indicates that the viscous force does not play an important role in this process. The theoretical model establishes that the critical condition for the transition boundary corresponds to the bubble radius being approximately equal to the minimum film thickness at maximum droplet expansion. The proposed scaling law ∆T ∼ V⁻¹ provides a quantitative prediction of the mode transition that fits experimental data and extends across boiling regimes. The approach is characterized as reliable by avoiding surface degradation and easy to achieve by avoiding complex fabrication of surface microstructures or surface modification.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors state that detailed numerical simulations and experimental measurements of the bursting bubbles in the bouncing-with-spray mode will be helpful for a better understanding of the impact process. The scaling exponent n = 0.35 was adopted, but the authors note that the exponent can be different for different surface structures, with other studies reporting values such as n = 0.39. The theoretical model assumes the heat transfer area A to the vapor bubble can be regarded as a constant for different liquids, which may not hold in all conditions. The vapor layer is assumed to have uniform thickness δ, which may not be strictly accurate in a radially developing flow. The paper does not report a random seed, explicit train/test split equivalent, or detailed demographics of the experimental conditions beyond the parameters described. The paper notes that there are many open questions in this area of droplet impact on heated surfaces and its residence time. The study does not report error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests for the experimental residence time measurements beyond the ±1°C temperature accuracy.

A bouncing-with-spray mode of droplet impact on heated surfaces, induced by vapor bubble burst, reduces residence time by approximately 40% compared to the retraction-bouncing mode. In the transition boiling regime, the residence time drops from 12.0 ms in the retraction-bouncing mode to 6.5 ms in the bouncing-with-spray mode at the same temperature. The normalized residence time drops from about 2.3 in the retraction-bouncing mode to about 1.4 in the bouncing-with-spray mode, yielding approximately 40% reduction. The reduction was observed across all liquid types: water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures at different viscosities. The bouncing-with-spray mode is characterized by the fragmentation of the liquid film into several fragments due to bubble burst holes, reducing recoiling distance. At the lowest film boiling conditions (We = 129, T = 440°C), the splashing behavior and the bouncing-with-spray mode still occur, indicating the mode is not universally applicable without some degree of fragmentation. The residence time in the film boiling regime with We = 129, T = 440°C shows values of 1.0 ms, 2.4 ms, and 6.7 ms, suggesting variability rather than a single reduction value. This heat-induced approach is reliable by avoiding surface degradation and easy to achieve without complex surface fabrication. The reduction can be applied to anti-icing, self-cleaning, corrosion-resistance, and maintaining surface dryness applications.
The residence time of the bouncing-with-spray mode is independent of liquid viscosity, indicating viscous forces do not significantly affect the mechanism. By using droplet fluids with different viscosities while fixing V and D0, the residence time of the bouncing-with-spray mode was found to be independent of viscosity. Figure 4 shows the effect of liquid viscosity on the residence time with multiple glycerol concentrations, and the curves overlap, confirming independence. The viscosity values ranged from 1.00 to 42.47 mPa·s across the water/glycerol mixtures tested in Table 1. The paper does not report the exact numerical value of the variation in residence time across viscosity changes, leaving the quantitative stability unquantified. The mechanism is governed by inertial, capillary, and vapor-dynamic forces rather than viscous dissipation, simplifying the design space for application.
A theoretical scaling law ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ with exponent n = 0.35 predicts the transition boundary between the two bouncing modes in the film boiling regime and agrees well with experimental data. The experimental data in the film boiling regime, plotted on a logarithm scale, agree well with the scaling ∆T ∼ V⁻¹. The scaling law is derived from energy conservation, bubble burst condition rv ≈ bmin, and the film thickness scaling b ∼ Re⁻²⁵. The model also explains why the transition temperature increases with We in the transition boiling regime, consistent with the regime map in Figure 6e. The authors note that the scaling exponent n can be different for different surface structures, with other studies reporting values such as n = 0.39. The theory relies on assumptions such as uniform vapor layer thickness and constant heat transfer area to the bubble, which may not hold perfectly. The model provides a predictive framework for determining the impact conditions under which the residence time reduction will be achieved.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The viscosity independence was tested by varying glycerol concentration from 28% to 75% in water/glycerol mixtures at fixed D0 = 2.8 mm and V = 1.2 m/s. The Weber number was varied from 10 to 180 across different liquids to explore the full impact regime, covering all three boiling modes. The temperature was varied from 260°C to 440°C to span nucleate, transition, and film boiling regimes. Different liquids with varying densities, surface tensions, viscosities, and latent heats were used to test the robustness of the observed mode. The regime map in Figure 6e shows the transition boundary for D0 = 2.2 mm, indicating a single parameter sweep for a fixed droplet size. The authors note that detailed numerical simulations and experimental measurements of the bursting bubbles would further validate the mechanism.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the bouncing-with-spray mode, where vapor bubble burst at random sites in the liquid film creates holes that fragment the film and reduce the recoiling distance, thereby cutting the droplet residence time by approximately 40% relative to the traditional retraction-bouncing mode. 2. summary.authors: TAKAO YAMAZAKI AND YIFAN YANG
summary.field_subfield: Number Theory / Arithmetic Geometry
summary.executive_summary: This paper constructs a geometrically maximal abelian covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of the modular curve X0(p) over Q unramified outside cusps, which is cyclic of degree 2Np where Np = (p − 1)/ gcd(p − 1, 12). The authors build on Mazur's theorem, which established that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np is the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering. The new covering is cyclic of degree 2Np and its restriction to Y0(p) (the open subscheme of X0(p) obtained by removing the two cusps) is a geometrically maximal unramified covering over Q. The covering factors as f′p = f p ◦ πp, where πp : X′2(p) → X2(p) is a degree two covering unramified outside cusps. The construction is achieved by adjoining a square root of a modular function F2h ∈ Q(X2(p)) to the function field of X2(p), where Fh is a product of six generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions). The authors prove that the resulting curve X′2(p) admits a geometrically integral model over Q and that the covering ramiﬁes precisely at each cusp. For p = 2 or 3, the construction is given directly via the map G_m → G_m sending x to x^2. For p ≥ 5, the proof proceeds by checking Fourier expansions of the constructed modular functions to verify the ramification behavior. The paper also establishes that the function field Q(X′2(p)) is a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by the square root of F2h, and that Q is algebraically closed in Q(X′2(p)). The result provides a complete description of the maximal abelian extension of X0(p) unramified outside cusps, extending the classical theory of the Shimura covering to the open curve Y0(p).

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper constructs a geometrically maximal abelian covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of the modular curve X0(p) over Q unramified outside cusps, which is cyclic of degree 2Np where Np = (p − 1)/ gcd(p − 1, 12). The authors build on Mazur's theorem, which established that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np is the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering. The new covering is cyclic of degree 2Np and its restriction to Y0(p) (the open subscheme of X0(p) obtained by removing the two cusps) is a geometrically maximal unramified covering over Q. The covering factors as f′p = f p ◦ πp, where πp : X′2(p) → X2(p) is a degree two covering unramified outside cusps. The construction is achieved by adjoining a square root of a modular function F2h ∈ Q(X2(p)) to the function field of X2(p), where Fh is a product of six generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions). The authors prove that the resulting curve X′2(p) admits a geometrically integral model over Q and that the covering ramiﬁes precisely at each cusp. For p = 2 or 3, the construction is given directly via the map G_m → G_m sending x to x^2. For p ≥ 5, the proof proceeds by checking Fourier expansions of the constructed modular functions to verify the ramification behavior. The paper also establishes that the function field Q(X′2(p)) is a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by the square root of F2h, and that Q is algebraically closed in Q(X′2(p)). The result provides a complete description of the maximal abelian extension of X0(p) unramified outside cusps, extending the classical theory of the Shimura covering to the open curve Y0(p).

Research Context
Mazur established that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np is the geometrically maximal unramiﬁed abelian covering over Q. The Shimura covering is the unique subcovering of X1(p) → X0(p) of degree Np = (p − 1)/ gcd(p − 1, 12). When a curve Y admits a degree one divisor, there exists a geometrically maximal unramiﬁed abelian covering. However, there is no such description if no Q-rational point is available. The goal is to find a geometrically maximal unramiﬁed abelian covering of Y0(p), the open curve obtained by removing the cusps from X0(p). The Shimura covering is the maximal unramiﬁed subcovering of fp : X1(p) → X0(p).

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether there exists a geometrically maximal unramiﬁed abelian covering of Y0(p) over Q that extends the Shimura covering. The authors hypothesize that such a covering exists as a cyclic covering of X0(p) of degree 2Np. Specifically, the covering is predicted to be unramiﬁed outside the two cusps of X0(p). The covering is further predicted to factor as a degree two unramiﬁed-outside-cusps covering of X2(p) composed with the Shimura covering. The construction is expected to be realized by adjoining a square root of a modular function in Q(X2(p)) to the function field of X2(p). The key ingredient for this construction is the generalized Dedekind eta functions. The paper does not hypothesize a specific bound on p; the result is stated for a general prime p.

Methodological Details
The paper considers the modular curves X0(p) and X1(p) as geometrically integral smooth proper curves over Q. A model of X1(p) over Q is chosen such that the cusp at inﬁnity splits completely in a finite cyclic covering fp : X1(p) → X0(p) of degree (p − 1)/2. The Shimura covering f p : X2(p) → X0(p) is the unique unramiﬁed subcovering of fp of degree Np = (p − 1)/ gcd(p − 1, 12). The open subscheme Y0(p) ⊂ X0(p) is defined such that X0(p) \ Y0(p) consists of all (two) cusps. The generalized Dedekind eta functions Eg(τ) are defined as products of q-series using the second Bernoulli polynomial B(x) = x^2 − x + 1/6. For p = 2 or 3, the covering is given by the map G_m → G_m sending x to x^2 under the identification Y0(p) ∼ G_m = P^1 \{0, ∞\}. For p ≥ 5, the authors assume p is an odd prime and work over the field k = Q. The divisor D = X0(p) \ Y0(p) consists of two Q-rational points (the 0 and ∞ cusps). The character group LD of GD is Z with trivial G_Q-action, and (LD ⊗ Q/Z)µ(−1) ∼ Z/2Z. An odd generator g of (Z/pZ)× is chosen to define the functions Fh. The function Fh(τ) is defined as a product of ℓ − 1 generalized Dedekind eta functions raised to the 6/ℓ power. The case is split into p ∝ 11 mod 12 and p ≡ 11 mod 12. In the case p ≡ 11 mod 12, Γ2(p) = Γ1(p) and a different construction using triplets of integers h1, h2, h3 is employed.

Procedures And Architectures
The covering X′2(p) is constructed as a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of the modular function F2h ∈ Q(X2(p)). The function Fh is defined as Fh(τ) = ∏_{j=0}^{ℓ−1} Eg^{jk}h(τ)^(6/ℓ). The character ψ of order 2 of SL(2, Z) is defined by its values on matrices based on parity of c and b. If ℓ is even (p ≡ 1 mod 4), a unique character χ of order 2 of Γ2(p) with Γ1(p) ⊂ ker χ is also defined. The subgroup Γ′2(p) is defined as the kernel of the character (ψχ if p ≡ 1 mod 4, ψ if p ≡ 3 mod 4) on Γ2(p). Lemma 3.3.2 proves that Γ′2(p) is a normal subgroup of Γ0(p) and Γ0(p)/Γ′2(p) is cyclic of order 2k. Proposition 3.3.3 asserts that X′2(p) associated to Γ2(p) admits a geometrically integral model over Q and the covering ramiﬁes precisely at each cusp. For p ∝ 11 mod 12, the proof uses the Fourier expansion of Eg to calculate the order of F2h at cusps. The order of F2h at a cusp with p∤c is shown to be 1, and at a cusp with p|c it is shown to be odd. In the case p ≡ 11 mod 12, the function Gh = (Eh1Eh2Eh3)^2 is used as the generating modular function. A remark notes that if p ∝ 1 mod 8, z(τ) = (η(τ)/η(pτ))^12/(p−1,12) is also a modular function on Γ′2(p). The function field Q(X′2(p)) is shown to be a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of F2h.

Key Results
The covering f′p : X′2(p) → X0(p) is a cyclic covering of degree 2Np. The covering f′p is a cyclic covering of degree 2Np, extending the Shimura covering of degree Np. The restriction of f′p to Y′2(p) : Y′2(p) → Y0(p) is a geometrically maximal unramiﬁed covering of Y0(p) over Q. The covering factors as f′p = f p ◦ πp, where πp : X′2(p) → X2(p) is a degree two covering unramiﬁed outside cusps. The curve X′2(p) admits a geometrically integral model over Q. The covering f′p ramiﬁes precisely at each cusp of X2(p). The function field Q(X′2(p)) of X′2(p) is a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of the explicitly constructed rational function F2h. Q is algebraically closed in Q(X′2(p)). For p = 2 or 3, the covering is the map x → x^2 on G_m. The order of F2h at any cusp of X2(p) with p∤c is exactly 1, and at cusps with p|c it is odd. The group Γ0(p)/Γ′2(p) is cyclic of order 2k. The result holds for all primes p; the construction handles p=2,3 separately and p≥5 for odd primes. The covering is unramiﬁed at all non-cusp points of X2(p).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result completes the description of the maximal abelian extension of X0(p) unramiﬁed outside cusps by providing a cyclic covering of degree 2Np. The construction demonstrates that generalizing the Shimura covering to the open curve Y0(p) requires extending the degree from Np to 2Np. The use of generalized Dedekind eta functions as modular functions highlights the power of these Siegel functions in constructing abelian coverings of modular curves. The quadratic extension structure suggests that the Galois group of the extension is a cyclic group of order 2Np, which is the minimal degree for a maximal extension. The result is consistent with the theory of the generalized Jacobian, as the covering corresponds to an extension whose conductor is supported at the cusps.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a short note and does not provide a full proof with all details; it states that general facts are prepared in §2 and the proof in §3. The construction for p = 2 or 3 is much simpler (the map x → x^2) and does not involve modular functions in the same way as the p ≥ 5 case. The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 requires a different construction (using triplets of integers) than the general p ∝ 11 mod 12 case. The remark about z(τ) being a modular function on Γ′2(p) but not on Γ2(p) when p ∝ 1 mod 8 suggests alternative generating functions exist. The paper does not explicitly prove that the covering is minimal in some sense, only that it is geometrically maximal. The full bibliography is not provided in the paper text, so specific reference details cannot be verified.

Claims
A geometrically maximal abelian covering X′2(p) → X0(p) over Q unramified outside cusps exists and is cyclic of degree 2Np. The theorem states there exists a cyclic covering of degree 2Np such that its restriction to Y0(p) is geometrically maximal. The covering factors as a degree two covering unramified outside cusps over the Shimura covering. The curve X′2(p) admits a geometrically integral model over Q and the covering ramiﬁes only at cusps. The function field is a quadratic extension generated by a square root of a modular function. For p = 2 or 3, the construction is trivial and does not involve the same modular function machinery. The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 requires a separate construction using triplets of integers. The maximal abelian extension of X0(p) unramified outside cusps is cyclic of degree 2Np. The Galois group is cyclic of order 2Np.
The covering f′p factors as f′p = f p ◦ πp, where πp is unramified outside cusps. Proposition 3.3.3 states the covering ramiﬁes precisely at each cusp. The order of F2h at any cusp is odd, ensuring the quadratic extension is unramified outside cusps. The Fourier expansion computation confirms the ramification behavior at cusps. The proof is split into cases (p ∝ 11 mod 12 and p ≡ 11 mod 12) with different function constructions. The Shimura covering is the intermediate covering in the cyclic tower X′2(p) → X2(p) → X0(p).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 is handled with a separate construction, showing the general approach needs adaptation in some cases. A remark notes that if p ∝ 1 mod 8, z(τ) can also generate the function field extension.

Key Figures Tables
The diagram showing the factorization of f′p through f p and πp illustrates the relationship between the coverings.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the construction of a cyclic degree 2Np geometrically maximal abelian covering of X0(p) unramified outside cusps, extending Mazur's result for the Shimura covering. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit construction of the modular function Fh using generalized Dedekind eta functions and the verification of its ramification behavior via Fourier expansion. 3. The future path lies in describing maximal abelian coverings for other modular curves, higher-dimensional analogues, or curves with more ramification allowed.

summary.title: Design of Real-time Semantic Segmentation Decoder for Automated Driving
summary.authors: Arindam Das, Saranya Kandan, Senthil Yogamani, Pavel Křížek
summary.field_subfield: Computer Vision / Semantic Segmentation and Efficient Neural Network Design
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses the computational expense of decoders in semantic segmentation for embedded deployments in automated driving. Unlike encoders, which have received extensive design research, decoders remain computationally heavy and less studied. The authors assume an efficient, task-independent encoder (VGG10) is available and focus on designing an efficient decoder architecture. They propose a novel non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning with multiple skip connections, containing both 1D and 3D kernels of various sizes (3x3, 5x5, 1x1) fused together. They design a family of decoder variants using VGG10 as the encoder, with four deconvolution layers interleaved with non-bottleneck blocks. The encoder reduces feature maps from 256 to 4 channels for 4 classes (lanes, curb, road, void). Using their own dataset (1280x384 images, 3016 train, 981 validation, 1002 test), they train end-to-end with the Adam optimizer, weight decay 0.9, batch size 4, learning rate 0.0005 with polynomial decay over 350K iterations on an NVIDIA Ti-tan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. The optimal decoder achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441 (74.41%), a 10% improvement over the baseline (D1 at 0.7255), with specific class improvements: 12% for lanes (0.5304 vs 0.4943) and 18% for curb (0.4696 vs 0.4296). The runtime increase is less than 2ms. The work demonstrates that decoder design can cover a significant portion of overall computation in segmentation tasks and proposes future systematic family of meta-architectures with fixed runtime budget learned via meta-learning.

The work demonstrates that decoder design can cover a significant portion of overall computation in segmentation tasks and proposes future systematic family of meta-architectures with fixed runtime budget learned via meta-learning.

Research Context
Semantic segmentation assigns class labels to each pixel in an image, making it critical for automated driving, augmented reality, and medical image processing. However, there is a computational bound for industrial applications due to limited resources on embedded platforms. Most prior research has focused on efficient encoders that are mostly task agnostic, leaving decoder design less explored. Early architectures like FCN (Long et al., 2015), SegNet (Badrinarayanan et al., 2015), and UNet (Ronneberger et al., 2015) used decoders that were mirror images of encoders with same complexity. Techniques including dilated convolution, spatial pyramid pooling (DeepLabv2), multi-path refinement (RefineNet), and multi-scale input processing have been extensively studied. None of these methods use a task-independent lightweight encoder model as employed in this work, nor do they support multi-task learning practice. The authors identify that decoders are computationally expensive as well for semantic segmentation tasks, motivating the focus on efficient decoder design.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether an efficient decoder design, using a novel non-bottleneck layer and a task-independent encoder, can achieve real-time performance on embedded platforms for semantic segmentation. The authors propose that a non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning with multiple skip connections can recover semantic information lost by a generic encoder. The specific hypothesis is that by cascading skip connections, the non-bottleneck layer can handle high gradient flow and be suitable for embedded platforms running in real-time with a lightweight encoder. They further hypothesize that experimentation with various design choices within a family of decoders will yield measurable improvement over a baseline configuration. Dropout is not used in the model. All experiments use an NVIDIA Ti-tan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. summary.title: Lusin characterisation of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators
summary.authors: Tan Duc Do, Trong Ngoc Nguyen, Truong Xuan Le
summary.field_subfield: harmonic analysis; Hardy spaces, Hermite operators, Lusin integrals
summary.executive_summary:
This paper establishes a complete Lusin area integral characterisation of Hardy spaces associated with the Hermite operator L = -∆ + |x|^2 on R^d, where d ≥ 3 and p ∈(0, 1]. The authors prove that the Hardy space H^p_L(Rd), defined via the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup associated with L, coincides with the space H^p_S(Rd) defined via the Lusin integral S_f(x) = (∫ Γ(x) t^(1-d) |∇_L P^t f(y)|^2 dy dt)^(1/2), where ∇_L = (∂_t, ∂_1 + x_1, ..., ∂_d + x_d) is the adapted gradient specific to Hermite operators, introduced by Thangavelu in 1990. The main result (Theorem 1.1) asserts equality between H^p_L(Rd) and H^p_S(Rd) as quasi-norm spaces. Furthermore, Theorem 1.2 establishes that the Riesz transforms R_L^j = (∂_j + x_j) L^(-1/2) are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j = 1, 2, ... .

The proof strategy is structured into several stages: First, the authors establish the embedding H^p_L(Rd) ⊂ H^p_{L,max}(Rd) using heat kernel and Poisson kernel estimates and atom-level estimates (Proposition 3.1). Second, they characterise H^p_L(Rd) as the intersection of H^p_A(Rd) (defined via a tent-space-like operator) and L^2(Rd), using tent space techniques and (p, 2, M)-atom decompositions (Section 4). Third, the Lusin integral S is approximated by truncated versions S^(ε, R), and a multi-scale analysis (Lemmas 5.1-5.4) shows that the maximal function can be controlled by the Lusin integral norm. Finally, the proof of Theorem 1.1 is completed by combining these intermediate characterisations.

The Riesz transform boundedness is proved through a density argument: since Riesz transforms are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd) (reduced to a comparison with the Lusin integral via the adapted gradient), and L^2_c(Rd) is dense in both spaces, the boundedness extends to all of H^p_L(Rd). The work extends Jiz12's p=1 result to the full range p ∈(0, 1], and the use of the adapted gradient ∂_j + x_j, first suggested by Thangavelu, is central to the characterisation.

Executive Summary
This paper establishes a complete Lusin area integral characterisation of Hardy spaces associated with the Hermite operator L = -∆ + |x|^2 on R^d, where d ≥ 3 and p ∈(0, 1]. The authors prove that the Hardy space H^p_L(Rd), defined via the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup associated with L, coincides with the space H^p_S(Rd) defined via the Lusin integral S_f(x) = (∫ Γ(x) t^(1-d) |∇_L P^t f(y)|^2 dy dt)^(1/2), where ∇_L = (∂_t, ∂_1 + x_1, ..., ∂_d + x_d) is the adapted gradient specific to Hermite operators, introduced by Thangavelu in 1990. The main result (Theorem 1.1) asserts equality between H^p_L(Rd) and H^p_S(Rd) as quasi-norm spaces. Furthermore, Theorem 1.2 establishes that the Riesz transforms R_L^j = (∂_j + x_j) L^(-1/2) are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j = 1, 2, ... .

The proof strategy is structured into several stages: First, the authors establish the embedding H^p_L(Rd) ⊂ H^p_{L,max}(Rd) using heat kernel and Poisson kernel estimates and atom-level estimates (Proposition 3.1). Second, they characterise H^p_L(Rd) as the intersection of H^p_A(Rd) (defined via a tent-space-like operator) and L^2(Rd), using tent space techniques and (p, 2, M)-atom decompositions (Section 4). Third, the Lusin integral S is approximated by truncated versions S^(ε, R), and a multi-scale analysis (Lemmas 5.1-5.4) shows that the maximal function can be controlled by the Lusin integral norm. Finally, the proof of Theorem 1.1 is completed by combining these intermediate characterisations.

The Riesz transform boundedness is proved through a density argument: since Riesz transforms are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd) (reduced to a comparison with the Lusin integral via the adapted gradient), and L^2_c(Rd) is dense in both spaces, the boundedness extends to all of H^p_L(Rd). The work extends Jiz12's p=1 result to the full range p ∈(0, 1], and the use of the adapted gradient ∂_j + x_j, first suggested by Thangavelu, is central to the characterisation.

Research Context
Hermite operators have been studied over the years due to their significant role in the harmonic oscillator. Hardy spaces with their rich structures are of fundamental interest in harmonic analysis. This paper will examine Hardy spaces with index p ∈(0, 1] associated with Hermite operators. The authors aim to characterise these spaces in terms of Lusin area integrals, following similar results in the literature. The approach differs in that the Lusin area integrals use derivatives of the form ∂j + xj, first suggested by Thangavelu in 1990, which are specific to Hermite operators. The work is motivated by Jiz12, whose results were for Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators only with index p = 1.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the Hardy space H^p_L(Rd) can be characterised in terms of the Lusin integral associated with the adapted gradient for the Hermite operator. The authors formulate the problem for d ≥ 3 and p ∈(0, 1], extending prior results for p=1 to the full range of p. The main hypothesis is that the space defined via the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup coincides with the space defined via the Lusin integral, as quasi-norm spaces. A secondary hypothesis is that the Riesz transforms R_L^j associated with the adapted gradient are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j = 1, 2, 3, ... The authors predict that the characterisation holds for all d ≥ 3 and all p ∈(0, 1], and that the Riesz transform boundedness is a direct consequence of the Lusin characterisation.

Methodological Details
The operator L is defined as the Hermite operator L = -∆ + |x|^2 on its maximal domain in L2(Rd). The sesquilinear form a0(u, v) = ∫ Rd Du · Dv + |x|^2 u v is defined on D(a0) = C∞ c (Rd), and it is shown to be positive and closable. The operator L is associated with the closure of a0 in the sense of Kato's First Representation Theorem. L generates a contraction C0-semigroup T on L2(Rd) with kernel g_t satisfying Gaussian-type upper bounds. The Poisson semigroup P is defined as P^t = e^(-t L^(1/2)), and it is also a contraction C0-semigroup on L2(Rd). The Hardy space H^p_L(Rd) is the completion of {f ∈ L2(Rd) : MLf ∈ L^p(Rd)} under the quasi-norm ∥f∥_H^p_L = ∥MLf∥_{L^p}, where MLf(x) = sup t>0 |Ttf(x)|. The adapted gradient is defined as ∇_L = (∂_t, ∂_1 + x_1, ..., ∂_d + x_d). The Lusin integral S_f(x) is defined as (∫ Γ(x) t^(1-d) |∇_L P^t f(y)|^2 dy dt)^(1/2), where Γ(x) = {(y, t) : |x −y| < t}. The Riesz transforms are defined as R_L^j = (∂_j + x_j) L^(-1/2) for j = 1, 2, ... A further space H^p_L,max(Rd) is defined via the maximal function f* ∈ L^p(Rd) of the Poisson semigroup. An intermediate operator A is defined as A f(x) = (∫ |x −y| < t t^(1-d) |∂_t P^t f(y)|^2 dy dt)^(1/2).

Procedures And Architectures
The proof of Theorem 1.1 proceeds in three stages, establishing a sequence of inclusions: H^p_L ⊂ H^p_{L,max} ⊂ H^p_S and H^p_S ⊂ H^p_A ∩ L^2 ⊂ H^p_L. The inclusion H^p_L ⊂ H^p_{L,max} is proved using atom estimates (Proposition 3.1) that require the condition d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, where δ comes from heat kernel regularity. The space H^p_A(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd) is defined via a tent-space-like operator and characterised using (p, 2, M)-atoms with M > d/2(1/p - 1/2). The reverse inclusion H^p_S ⊂ H^p_A ∩ L^2(Rd) is proved using tent space techniques, including a Calderón reproducing formula and a weakly convergent integral of the operator π_{Ψ,L}. The multi-scale analysis uses truncated Lusin integrals S^(ε,R) and a decomposition into ε,R regions, combined with a weak-type inequality (Lemma 5.2) and interpolation arguments. The Poisson semigroup is expressed via a spectral decomposition: P^t f = ∑ e^(-t(2n+d)^(1/2)) f_n, where f_n are Hermite expansions. Heat kernel estimates from JPY16 are used to establish Gaussian-type bounds for g_t and their gradient regularity.

Key Results
Theorem 1.1 states that H^p_L(Rd) coincides with H^p_S(Rd) as quasi-norm spaces for all d ≥ 3 and p ∈(0, 1]. Proposition 3.1 establishes the embedding H^p_L(Rd) ⊂ H^p_{L,max}(Rd) under the condition d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1. Proposition 4.9 proves H^p_A(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd) = H^p_{L,at,M}(Rd) for M > d/2(1/p - 1/2) ∨ 1. Proposition 4.10 proves H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_{L,at,M}(Rd) for M ≥ d/2(1/p - 1), completing the chain of equivalences. Theorem 1.2 states that each Riesz transform R_L^j = (∂_j + x_j) L^(-1/2) is bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j = 1, 2, ... The Riesz transform boundedness is reduced to showing boundedness on H^p_L(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd), then extended by density of L^2_c(Rd). The boundedness proof uses the fact that R_L^j f = (∂_t e^(-t L^(1/2)) L^(-1/2) f) and applies the Lusin characterisation. Proposition 2.5 provides an atomic decomposition of H^p_L(Rd) for d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, with atoms satisfying a support, size, and moment condition. Lemma 6.2 establishes that H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_{L+2}(Rd), allowing the Riesz transform analysis to proceed on the L^2(Rd) intersection.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results complete the Lusin area integral characterisation for all p ∈(0, 1], extending Jiz12's p=1 result to the full range. The adapted gradient ∂_j + x_j, first suggested by Thangavelu, is proved to be the correct object for characterising Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators. The equivalence of spaces links the Poisson semigroup's maximal function to the Lusin area integral, providing two alternative characterisations of the same Hardy space. The Riesz transform boundedness shows that the adapted gradient operators act as multipliers on these Hardy spaces, analogous to the classical Riesz transforms. The atomic decomposition result (Proposition 2.5) provides a concrete representation of H^p_L functions as sums of atoms, useful for further harmonic analysis.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dimension must satisfy d ≥ 3, so the results do not extend to d = 1 and d = 2. The atomic decomposition requires d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, so the characterisation does not hold for all p > d/(d+δ). The proof relies on several intermediate spaces (H^p_{L,max}, H^p_A, H^p_{L,at,M}) and a chain of inclusions, rather than a direct single-step equivalence. The characterisation requires d ≥ 3, but the paper does not investigate the case d < 3 explicitly. Some constants are implicit and their explicit values are not determined; the paper uses C as a generic positive constant.

Claims
Theorem 1.1: The Hardy space H^p_L(Rd) defined via the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup coincides with the space H^p_S(Rd) defined via the Lusin integral associated with the adapted gradient for all d ≥ 3 and p ∈(0, 1]. Proposition 5.4 establishes that ∥Sf∥_{L^p} ≤ C ∥f*∥_{L^p}, linking the Lusin integral to the maximal function. The proof of Theorem 1.1 (⊃) follows from Proposition 4.11 and the fact that ∥·∥_H^p_A ≤ ∥·∥_H^p_S. The proof of Theorem 1.1 (⊂) follows directly from Propositions 3.1 and 5.4. The inclusion H^p_L ⊂ H^p_{L,max} requires the condition d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, so the equivalence is not established for all p. The equivalence is proved via a chain of intermediate spaces (H^p_{L,max}, H^p_A, H^p_{L,at,M}), not by a direct comparison of norms. The Lusin integral can replace the maximal function in characterising Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators. The result extends Jiz12's p=1 characterisation to the full range p ∈(0, 1].
Theorem 1.2: The Riesz transforms R_L^j = (∂_j + x_j) L^(-1/2) are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j = 1, 2, 3, ... and all p ∈(0, 1]. The boundedness on H^p_L(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd) reduces to ∥R_L^j f∥_{H^p_{L+2}} ≤ C ∥S_{L+2} R_L^j f∥_{L^p} ≤ C ∥S_L f∥_{L^p} ≤ C ∥f∥_{H^p_L}. The density of L^2_c(Rd) in both H^p_L(Rd) and H^p_{L+2}(Rd) extends the boundedness to the full space. Lemma 6.2 establishes H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_{L+2}(Rd), allowing the Riesz transform analysis on the L^2 intersection to be applicable.  The Riesz transforms associated with the adapted gradient are the correct operators for the Hermite Hardy space theory. The boundedness is a direct consequence of the Lusin characterisation, illustrating the structural link between the adapted gradient and the Hardy space.
Proposition 2.5: Every function in H^p_L(Rd) admits an atomic decomposition for d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, and the atom norm is equivalent to the H^p_L quasi-norm. The proof follows from [BDL18, Theorem 2.15], using the atom properties and the bounded property of the atom. The atom norm is defined as the infimum of the l^p norm of atomic coefficients, and equivalence is established. The atomic decomposition requires the restricted range d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, and thus is not available for all p. The atomic characterisation provides a concrete way to represent and manipulate functions in H^p_L(Rd). The atomic structure is preserved under the Lusin characterisation, linking two different perspectives on Hardy space representation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The characterisation requires d ≥ 3, and the paper does not investigate d = 1 or d = 2. The atomic decomposition (Proposition 2.5) requires d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, where δ is determined by heat kernel regularity from JPY16. The proof of Theorem 1.2 reduces to the L^2(Rd) case using the density of L^2_c(Rd), showing that the L^2 characterisation is the critical step. The proof of Theorem 1.1 employs several intermediate spaces: H^p_{L,max}, H^p_A, H^p_{L,at,M}, each serving as a bridge in the chain of equivalences. The multi-scale analysis (Lemmas 5.1-5.4) uses ε, R parameters that are adjusted freely to obtain the final inequality, showing the robustness of the Lusin integral approach.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the complete Lusin characterisation of H^p_L(Rd) for all p ∈(0, 1], establishing that the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup and the Lusin integral with the adapted gradient define equivalent spaces, alongside the boundedness of Riesz transforms. 2. The strongest evidence is the multi-stage proof connecting the maximal function to the Lusin integral through tent-space techniques, atom decompositions, and multi-scale analysis, complemented by the kernel estimates from JPY16 and the heat kernel regularity results. 3. The future path lies in extending these results to other Hermite-type operators, investigating the d=1, 2 cases, exploring connections with other maximal functions and Riesz transform operators, and potentially establishing sharper atomic decomposition bounds.

summary.title: Deep-Learning-based Millimeter-Wave Massive MIMO for Hybrid Precoding
summary.authors: Hongji Huang, Yiwei Song, Jie Yang, Guan Gui, and Fumiyuki Adachi
summary.field_subfield: Wireless Communications / mmWave massive MIMO and hybrid precoding
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical challenges of high computational complexity and suboptimal spatial information exploitation in conventional hybrid precoding schemes for millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. Traditional precoding approaches based on singular value decomposition (SVD) or geometric mean decomposition (GMD) require complicated bit allocation and fail to fully leverage the sparsity and structural characteristics of mmWave channels. To overcome these limitations, the authors propose a deep-learning-enabled mmWave massive MIMO framework where a deep neural network (DNN) is trained as an autoencoder to map input data to optimized precoders, effectively replacing the iterative non-convex optimization. The DNN architecture comprises an input fully connected layer (128 units), two encoding hidden layers (400 and 256 units), a noise layer (200 units) for AWGN/distortion injection, two decoding hidden layers (128 and 64 units), and an output layer with a custom activation function. A geometric mean decomposition-based loss function is minimized using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum, trained in an unsupervised manner over 45,000 iterations. Numerical simulations at 28 GHz with 3 NLoS components demonstrate that the DNN-based approach outperforms SVD-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD-based precoding, fully GMD-based precoding, and new GMD-based precoding schemes across a range of SNR values. The proposed method achieves the lowest bit error ratio (BER) and highest spectrum efficiency, with the advantage widening at higher SNR. Complexity analysis reveals the DNN-based method requires only O(L^2NsN^2_t) operations, significantly reducing the computational burden compared to the O(2^NrNs(N^2_t(K+NsNr))) of SIC-based hybrid precoding. Robustness analyses over batch size (10 to 100) and learning rate (0.001 and others) reveal that lower learning rates and medium batch sizes yield optimal convergence. The MSE-versus-iterations plots show the DNN-based scheme and sparse precoding converge at approximately 11 iterations, while analog precoding requires about 22, further confirming the superior convergence speed of the proposed method.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper addresses the critical challenges of high computational complexity and suboptimal spatial information exploitation in conventional hybrid precoding schemes for millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. Traditional precoding approaches based on singular value decomposition (SVD) or geometric mean decomposition (GMD) require complicated bit allocation and fail to fully leverage the sparsity and structural characteristics of mmWave channels. To overcome these limitations, the authors propose a deep-learning-enabled mmWave massive MIMO framework where a deep neural network (DNN) is trained as an autoencoder to map input data to optimized precoders, effectively replacing the iterative non-convex optimization. The DNN architecture comprises an input fully connected layer (128 units), two encoding hidden layers (400 and 256 units), a noise layer (200 units) for AWGN/distortion injection, two decoding hidden layers (128 and 64 units), and an output layer with a custom activation function. A geometric mean decomposition-based loss function is minimized using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum, trained in an unsupervised manner over 45,000 iterations. Numerical simulations at 28 GHz with 3 NLoS components demonstrate that the DNN-based approach outperforms SVD-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD-based precoding, fully GMD-based precoding, and new GMD-based precoding schemes across a range of SNR values. The proposed method achieves the lowest bit error ratio (BER) and highest spectrum efficiency, with the advantage widening at higher SNR. Complexity analysis reveals the DNN-based method requires only O(L^2NsN^2_t) operations, significantly reducing the computational burden compared to the O(2^NrNs(N^2_t(K+NsNr))) of SIC-based hybrid precoding. Robustness analyses over batch size (10 to 100) and learning rate (0.001 and others) reveal that lower learning rates and medium batch sizes yield optimal convergence. The MSE-versus-iterations plots show the DNN-based scheme and sparse precoding converge at approximately 11 iterations, while analog precoding requires about 22, further confirming the superior convergence speed of the proposed method.

Research Context
Wireless data traffic is projected to increase by over 10,000-fold by 2030, driving 5G development. The millimeter-wave band offers a ten-fold increase in carrier frequency and orders-of-magnitude enhancement in free-space pathloss. Hybrid precoding was introduced to achieve more accurate beamforming with reduced hardware complexity and energy consumption. Existing SVD-based precoding schemes have high computational complexity and require a complicated bit allocation strategy. The geometric mean decomposition-based scheme avoids bit allocation but faces challenges in addressing non-convex constraints on the analog precoder. Conventional mathematical means are too weak to exploit the sparsity statistics of the mmWave massive MIMO channel. Traditional low-complexity schemes are realized at the cost of degrading hybrid precoding performance. Deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for addressing complicated nonlinear problems and high-computation issues in communications.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a deep learning framework can replace conventional non-convex optimization to achieve superior hybrid precoding in mmWave massive MIMO. The paper hypothesizes that a DNN trained as an autoencoder can capture structural information of the hybrid precoding scheme during training. It is predicted that the DNN-based approach will minimize the bit error ratio and enhance spectrum efficiency compared to conventional SVD-based schemes. The authors hypothesize that the DNN can approach each iteration of the optimization algorithm without requiring iterative execution during inference. A secondary hypothesis is that the DNN-based method will substantially reduce computational complexity while maintaining or improving performance. The authors anticipate that the DNN will leverage the sparsity of the mmWave channel through its representation and mapping abilities.

Methodological Details
The system model considers a mmWave massive MIMO configuration with one base station equipped with a uniform linear array of Nt antennas and a user with Nr received antennas. The base station sends Ns independent data streams to the user, and the number of RF chains satisfy Ns ≤ N RF_t ≤ Nt and N RF_t ≤ Nr ≤ Nr. The channel matrix H is modeled using the Saleh-Valenzuela (SV) channel model with P NLoS components. The BS and user are each equipped with N RF_t and N RF_r RF chains, respectively, meeting the required hierarchy. The hybrid precoder comprises a high-dimensional analog precoder and a low-dimensional digital precoder, combined as D = DA * DD. All elements of the analog precoder and combiner must satisfy the constant modulus constraint |{DA}i,j| = 1/√Nt. The DNN framework is implemented using Keras for construction and processing. Numerical simulations are performed at a carrier frequency of 28 GHz with P = 3 NLoS components. The network is trained for 45,000 iterations in the simulation to achieve convergence. The BER performance is evaluated under various learning rates and batch sizes, compared with four conventional precoding methods.

Procedures And Architectures
The DNN architecture consists of an input layer with a fully connected (FC) layer of 128 units for feature capturing. The two subsequent hidden layers for encoding consist of FC layers with 400 and 256 units, respectively. A noise layer comprising 200 units is inserted to simulate AWGN or other signal distortions. The decoding stage employs two hidden layers with 128 and 64 units, respectively. The output layer uses a custom activation function f(s) = min(max(s, 0), Ns) to enforce the transmit power constraint. The rectiﬁed linear unit (ReLU) function is used as the activation function for the input and hidden layers. The DNN is treated as an autoencoder where R1 = f(R_ARD; Ω), mapping the input data to the optimal precoder. The GMD method decomposes the channel matrix into W, Q, R components to linearize the hybrid precoding relation. The loss function is the Frobenius norm of the difference between the DNN-generated precoder and the GMD-based reference precoder. The DNN is trained using an unsupervised learning approach, updating R_A and R_D iteratively. The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm with momentum is employed to update the precoder matrices. The training loop includes a noise layer, environment simulator, and SGD updates with momentum α and learning rate ε. The convergence criterion is an error threshold of τ = 10^-7.

Key Results
The deep-learning-based method outperforms SVD-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD-based precoding, fully GMD-based precoding, and new GMD-based precoding across all SNR values. The performance improvement of the DNN strategy over conventional methods is more apparent at higher SNR, attributed to the excellent representation ability of deep learning. The DNN-based strategy is verified to be superior even to the fully GMD-based digital precoding method, implying that existing non-convex hybrid precoding optimization can be solved with deep learning. With batch size varying from 10 to 100, the BER degrades with increasing batch size, suggesting slower convergence at larger batch sizes. Conversely, too small a batch size leads to unstable convergence, and the optimal batch size must be chosen carefully for optimal performance. Lower learning rates optimize the hybrid precoding performance, as larger learning rates cause higher validation error, although slower convergence occurs. Spectrum efficiency improves as SNR increases in all schemes, with the proposed scheme maintaining the largest margin over competing methods. The MSE converges at approximately 11 iterations for both the deep-learning-based scheme and the sparse precoding method. The analog precoding scheme requires about 22 iterations to reach convergence, confirming faster convergence of the proposed approach. The MSE performance of the proposed deep-learning-based scheme is superior to both the analog precoding and sparse precoding methods at convergence. The computational complexity of the DNN-based method is O(L^2NsN^2_t), which is technically superior to the O(2^NrNs(N^2_t(K+NsNr))) of SIC-based hybrid precoding.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The DNN-based approach is interpreted as an implicit solver that learns the structural statistics of the mmWave channel and the sparsity of the channel matrix. The autoencoder mapping effectively encapsulates the non-convex hybrid precoding problem, converting iterative optimization into a feed-forward inference. The superiority over the fully digital GMD method implies that the hybrid-analog constraint does not prevent DNN from finding near-optimal or optimal solutions. The convergence speed advantage (11 vs 22 iterations) suggests that DNN captures the gradient structure more efficiently than first-order methods. The results support the conclusion that deep learning can fundamentally replace iterative numerical optimization in hybrid precoding problems.

Contradictions And Limitations
The selection of the best learning rate remains an open issue, as the trade-off between convergence speed and asymptotic performance is not resolved. The paper does not report a specific quantitative BER or spectrum efficiency value for the optimal configuration, relying instead on qualitative comparison across figures. The analysis of batch size effects shows a trade-off: larger batch sizes induce slower convergence, while smaller ones cause instability, without a definitive optimal value provided. The study is limited to a single channel condition (28 GHz, P=3) and does not evaluate generalizability across different bands or NLoS counts. The authors note that while lower learning rates enhance performance, slower convergence behavior is a drawback, and the optimal learning rate is not specified.

Claims
A deep-learning-enabled hybrid precoding framework for mmWave massive MIMO achieves superior BER and spectrum efficiency compared to conventional SVD and GMD-based methods. The DNN-based approach outperforms SVD-based, fully digital, fully GMD-based, and new GMD-based precoding methods across the SNR range. The MSE of the DNN-based scheme is superior to both analog and sparse precoding methods at convergence. The DNN-based scheme converges at approximately 11 iterations versus 22 iterations for analog precoding. Larger batch sizes degrade BER performance, indicating a sensitivity to hyperparameter configuration. Larger learning rates cause higher validation error, though lower rates slow down convergence. Deep learning can be deployed as a drop-in replacement for iterative hybrid precoding solvers in practical mmWave systems. The computational reduction could enable real-time hybrid precoding on edge devices with limited processing power.
The proposed DNN framework achieves lower computational complexity than existing hybrid precoding schemes. The complexity is O(L^2NsN^2_t), compared to O(2^NrNs(N^2_t(K+NsNr))) for SIC-based and O(2^N3_r(N^4_rNt+N^2_rL^2+N^2_rN^2_tL)) for spatially sparse methods. The DNN-based approach is described as achieving technical advancement over conventional SVD-based methods. The training phase requires 45,000 iterations with multiple forward and backward passes, incurring significant one-time computational cost not reflected in inference complexity. The paper does not provide a detailed breakdown of the O(L^2NsN^2_t) term or how it scales with real-world parameters. Practical deployment requires offloading training to a powerful offline server while inference runs on resource-constrained devices. The complexity reduction enables more complex DNN architectures with greater precision.
The DNN captures the structural information of the mmWave channel and sparsity statistics to optimize hybrid precoding. The DNN is superior to the fully GMD-based digital precoding method, which does not use the DNN's learned representations. The MSE convergence at 11 iterations indicates that the DNN has learned a gradient direction that is more accurate than first-order methods. The paper does not provide explicit sparsity-related analysis or a direct comparison of how well the DNN captures sparsity versus the GMD approach. The method may generalize well to channels with different sparsity patterns if retrained with appropriate data. A multi-task learning framework could exploit sparsity for both precoding and combining simultaneously.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper evaluates BER sensitivity to batch size, showing a trade-off between convergence speed (large batch) and stability (small batch). Learning rate sensitivity is demonstrated, with lower learning rates yielding better asymptotic performance at the cost of slower convergence. Convergence is verified through MSE-versus-iterations plots at learning rate 0.001, showing monotonic decrease with oscillation in later stages. A noise layer of 200 units is included to inject AWGN/distortion, testing the DNN's robustness to channel impairments. The paper notes that the choice of batch size and learning rate is an open issue requiring careful selection for optimal performance.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents the DNN architecture with input, hidden, noise, and output layers, illustrating the autoencoder mapping. Figure 2 shows BER versus SNR for the proposed DNN-based scheme against SIC-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD-based, fully GMD-based, and new GMD-based precoding. Figure 3 illustrates BER versus SNR for the DNN method with batch sizes 10, 20, 50, and 100. Figure 4 presents BER versus SNR in the DNN method with various learning rates. Figure 5 shows spectrum efficiency versus SNR for the DNN-based, spatially sparse, and fully digital GMD schemes. Figure 6 plots MSE versus iterations for the DNN-based, analog precoding, and sparse precoding methods at learning rate 0.001. Table I compares computational complexity of the DNN-based scheme, SIC-based hybrid precoding, spatially sparse precoding, and a baseline method.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a DNN-based hybrid precoding framework for mmWave massive MIMO that achieves superior BER and spectrum efficiency while reducing computational complexity from exponential to polynomial scaling. 2. The strongest evidence is the DNN's performance surpassing the fully GMD-based digital precoding method, together with convergence in approximately 11 iterations (compared to 22 for analog precoding) and lower MSE at convergence. 3. The future path includes applying deep learning to channel feedback (codebook size and feedback overhead reduction) and adapting to multi-band and multi-user scenarios beyond the single-user setup studied.
