judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BanStereoSet, a 1,194-sentence fill-in-the-blank dataset designed to evaluate stereotypical social biases in multilingual LLMs for the Bangla language. The dataset covers 9 bias categories: race (241), profession (206), gender (178), ageism (134), beauty (130), beauty in profession (126), caste (60), region (63), and religion (56), with a total of 1,194 sentences. Data was localized from StereoSet (Nadeem et al., 2021), GenAssocBias (Kamruzzaman et al., 2024b), and IndiBias (Sahoo et al., 2024), with regionally curated data generated via human-LLM partnership involving 17 Bangladeshi cities. Translations were performed by GPT-4 with few-shot learning, reviewed by four native Bangla-speaking annotators fluent in English, and refined to address five StereotypeSet pitfalls affecting 47, 9, 15, 58, and 35 sentences respectively. Four models (GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, Gemma2-27B) were evaluated across three prompting templates, with results averaged. Key findings show GPT-4o most biased on average (73.78%), Mistral least biased (55.41%), and Gemma second most biased (69.73%). Mistral performs best on 7 of 9 categories, Llama on the remaining 2. Caste bias presents a language-dependent cultural sensitivity: Mistral handles it in Bangla but not in English. On average, GPT-4o and Gemma are more biased in Bangla, while Mistral and Llama are more biased in English. No consistent major difference across languages was found. The dataset addresses a critical gap for Bengali-speaking populations (233.7 million native speakers), promoting more equitable AI in Bangladeshi contexts.

Research Context
The usage of LLMs has increased significantly with people from all over the world employing these models for various tasks. However many recent studies have revealed undesirable biases and stereotypes in these models. Many bias evaluation datasets have been proposed to measure these biases but are predominantly in English. Some research exists in French Hindi Italian and Arabic but research on bias specific to the Bengali remains sparse. Bengali with 233.7 million native speakers worldwide ranks fifth worldwide. Recent studies focusing on Bengali have primarily addressed gender and religious biases through persona-based experiments. Stereotypical biases extend beyond gender and religion to race profession beauty ageism caste and region. To the best of our knowledge there is no dataset that comprehensively covers a broader spectrum of bias categories while focusing on the Bengali cultural context.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a comprehensive dataset covering a broader spectrum of bias categories tailored to the Bengali cultural context exists. The authors propose BanStereoSet a fill-in-the-blank type dataset to measure stereotypical biases in Bangla encompassing nine categories of bias. The nine categories are race profession gender ageism beauty beauty in profession region caste and religion. The hypothesis is that multilingual LLMs will exhibit significant biases when tested on Bangla stereotypes reinforcing the necessity for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets. The study aims to evaluate several language models using this dataset and indicate whether significant biases are present. The dataset serves as a tool for measuring bias in multilingual LLMs and facilitates exploration of stereotypical bias across different social categories.

Methodological Details
The BanStereoSet dataset consists of 1,194 sentences spanning 9 categories of bias. Data for race gender religion and profession categories was derived from the StereoSet dataset (Nadeem et al., 2021). The intrasentence subset of StereoSet was used as it holds the same structure as GenAssocBias. The beauty beauty in profession and ageism categories were derived from Kamruzzaman et al.'s (2024b) GenAssocBias dataset. The caste bias category was adopted from the IndiBias dataset (Sahoo et al., 2024). Data for the regional bias category was freshly curated by the authors. English sentences were translated into Bangla using GPT-4 with few-shot learning to enhance translation accuracy. Four native Bangla-speaking annotators fluent in English reviewed each translation for accuracy and modified incorrect ones. To address the absence of gendered pronouns in Bangla gender-specific phrases ekjon purush and ekjon mohila were added to 76 sentences. English names such as John and Judy were substituted with Bengali names Mehedi and Sumiya in 12 sentences. US city references such as Boston were replaced with Bangladeshi cities such as Dhaka in 6 sentences. Five pitfalls from Blodgett et al. (2021) were addressed affecting 47 9 15 58 and 35 sentences of the final dataset respectively. Corrections were performed manually and required consensus from at least three out of the four annotators. For caste data the sent-more column provided stereotype options and the sent-less column provided anti-stereotype options with manually curated unrelated options. For regional data 17 major cities in Bangladesh were identified and ChatGPT was used to generate 10 stereotypical 10 anti-stereotypical and 10 unrelated attributes per city. Attributes were validated by annotators and sentences were subsequently generated by ChatGPT with blanks designed for regional biases. The final sentence counts per bias type are Race 241 Gender 178 Religion 56 Profession 206 Ageism 134 Beauty 130 Beauty Profession 126 Caste 60 and Region 63. Profession: 206, Ageism: 134, Beauty: 130, Beauty Profession: 126, Caste: 60, Region: 63.

Procedures And Architectures
Four multilingual LLMs were evaluated: GPT-4o Mistral-7B Llama3.1-70B and Gemma2-27B. Three prompting templates were used: a baseline template and two paraphrases. The baseline prompt instructed models to select the appropriate word from options without considering order providing only a single plain Bangla text answer. Results were averaged across all three prompting templates following Gupta et al. (2023). A parallel evaluation was conducted using the English version of the dataset with modified English sentences after removing all pitfalls and adjustments. The English evaluation used zero-shot learning for comparison. Stereotypical engagement rates represent the percentage of responses aligning with stereotypical judgments excluding unrelated engagements. For GenAssocBias unrelated terms were used to examine neutral engagement not influenced by bias. The desired behavior is that stereotypical responses be close to 50 percent for balanced categories. For StereoSet-derived categories the desirable percentage is lower than 50 due to extremely negative attributes.

Key Results
GPT-4o achieved the highest average stereotypical response rate in Bangla at 73.78 percent. Mistral-7B achieved the lowest average stereotypical response rate in Bangla at 55.41 percent. Llama3.1-70B achieved 64.09 percent average in Bangla. Gemma2-27B achieved 69.73 percent average in Bangla. In English the average stereotypical response rates were 81.12 for GPT-4o 72.34 for Mistral 82.74 for Llama and 84.37 for Gemma. Mistral performed best on 7 of the 9 bias categories in Bangla often by considerable margins. Llama performed best in the remaining 2 bias categories. All models showed high levels of profession and region bias in Bangla with average region bias rates of 82.14 67.44 78.72 and 81.48 for the four models. All models showed relatively low levels of religion bias in Bangla with rates of 55.55 59.52 45.09 and 53.70. In English Gemma showed the lowest region bias at 11.53 percent while GPT-4o showed 18.18 percent Llama 14.00 percent and Mistral 21.15 percent. For caste bias in Bangla the rates were 78.78 for GPT-4o 79.31 for Mistral 81.81 for Llama and 71.87 for Gemma. For caste bias in English the rates were 81.12 for GPT-4o 72.34 for Mistral 82.74 for Llama and 84.37 for Gemma. Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla but not in English. GPT-4o exhibits more stereotypical responses on average compared to other models in Bangla. In English Mistral remains the least biased model on average while Gemma is the most biased. Gender bias rates in Bangla were 81.25 58.02 73.91 and 81.25 for GPT-4o Mistral Llama and Gemma respectively. Beauty bias rates in Bangla were 92.38 53.01 69.30 and 73.52. Ageism bias rates in Bangla were 63.80 60.25 52.83 and 56.75.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla but not in English suggesting a degree of cultural sensitivity dependent on the language of communication. The findings demonstrate that LLM capability to handle bias in less common languages is comparable to English but with stark gaps between popular models. Significant biases across multiple categories in Bangla reinforce the necessity for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets for developing equitable language technologies. The language-dependent difference in caste bias handling underscores the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for training equitable AI systems. The dataset addresses unique challenges such as the absence of gendered pronouns and regional reference differences in Bangla requiring specific adaptation strategies.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh as biases can vary markedly between different areas. The focus on binary gender representation (man and woman) restricts the ability to address biases concerning non-binary or gender-nonconforming identities. Challenges in translating stereotypes from English to Bangla may lead to inaccuracies or cultural mismatches despite the annotation process. The relatively small size of certain categories such as region bias (63 sentences) may limit the comprehensiveness of the bias evaluation. The dataset predominantly captures explicit biases which may neglect more subtle or underlying biases. Categories such as sexual orientation socioeconomic status or disability were not included in the dataset. The effectiveness of language model evaluations using this dataset could be compromised by the models limited proficiency in Bangla which might skew the results. The 47 9 15 58 and 35 sentences affected by StereotypeSet pitfalls represent a non-trivial portion of the dataset that required manual correction.

Claims
BanStereoSet addresses a critical gap by providing a comprehensive fill-in-the-blank dataset for measuring 9 categories of stereotypical social bias in the Bangla language. The dataset covers 9 categories including race gender religion profession ageism beauty beauty in profession caste and region. Data was sourced from three established bias datasets and freshly curated for the regional category. The dataset contains 1,194 sentences with specific counts per category. The dataset is limited to 9 categories and does not include sexual orientation socioeconomic status or disability. The dataset predominantly captures explicit biases and may neglect subtle or underlying biases. The small size of certain categories such as region bias with only 63 sentences limits comprehensiveness. The dataset enables benchmarking of bias in Bangla for the 233.7 million native speakers worldwide. It guides the development of more equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts. It expands the scope of bias research beyond English-centric datasets to diverse linguistic contexts.
GPT-4o is the most biased model on average in Bangla while Mistral-7B is the least biased. GPT-4o achieved 73.78 percent average stereotypical response in Bangla. Mistral-7B achieved 55.41 percent average in Bangla. Llama3.1-70B achieved 64.09 percent and Gemma2-27B achieved 69.73 percent. In English Mistral remains least biased but Gemma becomes the most biased. Mistral performs best on 7 of 9 categories in Bangla while Llama performs best on 2. There is a stark gap between popular models in their ability to handle bias in less common languages. Model-specific cultural adaptation varies significantly between English and Bangla contexts.
Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla but not in English, suggesting language-dependent cultural sensitivity. In Bangla Mistral achieved 79.31 percent for caste bias. In English Mistral achieved 72.34 percent for caste bias. The text explicitly states Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla but not in English. The numerical difference is small and may not represent a significant qualitative capability gap. Bias handling capability is dependent on the language of communication. Culturally nuanced datasets are necessary to surface language-specific model behaviors.
All models show high levels of profession and region bias and relatively low levels of religion bias in Bangla. Profession bias rates were 72.53 60.84 71.96 and 75.55 for the four models. Religion bias rates were 55.55 59.52 45.09 and 53.70. Average region bias in Bangla was 82.14 67.44 78.72 and 81.48. In English region bias rates are substantially lower with Gemma at 11.53 percent. Models are more susceptible to certain stereotypical categories in Bangla than in English. Language-specific bias patterns emerge that are not present in English.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Three prompting templates were used with a baseline and two paraphrases. Results were averaged across all three templates following Gupta et al. (2023). An English-language evaluation with the modified dataset was run to compare bias levels across languages. Unrelated engagements were excluded from bias rate calculations to assess neutral engagement. Zero-shot learning was employed for the English comparison. For GenAssocBias unrelated terms were used to examine neutral engagement not influenced by bias.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates a completion task example for race bias with three options and English translation for understanding. Figure 2 presents examples of translations from English to Bangla showing gender pronoun addition name substitution and pitfall corrections. Figure 3 illustrates caste bias data creation from IndiBias showing stereotype anti-stereotype and unrelated options. Figure 4 in Appendix A shows city names and attributes used for region data curation. Table 1 presents bias analysis across models with stereotypical response rates as percentages averaged across three prompting techniques. Table 2 in the main text provides the full prompting templates. Table 3 in Appendix C reports unrelated engagement results.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BanStereoSet a 1,194-sentence Bengali dataset covering 9 bias categories that addresses the gap in Bengali-specific bias evaluation. 2. The strongest evidence is that Mistral-7B performs best on 7 of 9 categories in Bangla while GPT-4o and Gemma are more biased on average. 3. The future path is to develop culturally nuanced datasets for diverse linguistic and cultural realities beyond English to enable equitable AI development.

summary.title: SYSTEMS OF HECKE EIGENVALUES ON SUBSCHEMES OF SHIMURA VARIETIES
summary.authors: Stefan Reppen
summary.field_subfield: Arithmetic Geometry / Automorphic Forms
summary.executive_summary: This paper proves that for any mod p abelian type compact Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology (H0) with coefficients in automorphic line bundles are identical to those appearing in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. The main theorem (Theorem A) extends the pioneering work of Serre and Tate on modular curves, Goldring-Koskivirta on Hodge-type Shimura varieties (zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum), and Terakado-Yu on central leaves, from smooth zero-dimensional subschemes to higher-dimensional and possibly singular, closed Hecke-equivariant subschemes. The author also establishes analogous results for noncompact Shimura varieties, nonclosed subschemes (Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata), and central leaves. The central methodology constructs a smooth, closed subscheme ZK ⊂ YK by intersecting YK with the smallest length stratum it meets nontrivially and successively removing nonsingular points until a smooth scheme is obtained. This ZK admits a nowhere vanishing Hecke-equivariant section (Hasse invariant), which enables a going-down argument via the conormal exact sequence to relate eigenvalues on YK to ZK, followed by a going-up argument to relate them to the full Shimura variety SK. For noncompact varieties, the paper assumes Hodge type and uses toroidal compactifications with suitable positivity conditions on the boundary divisor. Corollary 3.3.3 explicitly confirms that for Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves closed in their respective Ekedahl-Oort strata, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues coincide with those on the Shimura variety. The work also shows that any two G(Apf)-equivariant closed subschemes share the same systems of Hecke eigenvalues (Corollary 3.2.7). The results apply to H0 and do not cover higher cohomology groups. The paper is a pure mathematics article with no experimental data, code, or ethics considerations.

claims.description: The systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in H0(YK, V(η)) for a Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK are identical to those in H0(SK, V(η)) for a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level.
For an Ekedahl-Oort stratum, a length stratum, or a central leaf closed in its containing Ekedahl-Oort stratum, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues coincide with those on SK.
The going-down argument does not require Hasse invariants for smooth zero-dimensional subschemes, but the going-up argument does require them.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper establishes a phenomenological theory for the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in magnets using a group-theoretical approach. The authors demonstrate that AHE in crystalline materials is governed by magnetic point group (MPG) symmetries, and identify 90 type-I and type-III MPGs that host either spontaneous or electric-field-driven AHE. The electric-field-driven AHE arises from linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling, with the nonlinear case yielding conductivities driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields. A key finding is that these electric-field-driven anomalous Hall conductivities are perfectly reversible upon reversing the magnetic order parameter (+L to −L), yielding opposite signs. The theory predicts that the AHE can be probed via electric fields, offering alternative avenues for detecting magnetic orders in spintronics. To verify the theoretical framework, the authors perform first-principles calculations on two representative semiconductors: Cr2O3 (Néel temperature 307 K, ¯3′m′ MPG) and CoF2 (Néel temperature 39 K, 4′/mm′m MPG). In Cr2O3, first-order electric-field responses yield σzy and σxz exceeding 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm, while the third-order σyx is less than 20 S/cm. In CoF2, second-order responses yield σyx exceeding 200 S/cm, while bi-axial σzy and σxz reach approximately 10 S/cm. A quenching behavior is also identified in 10 MPGs under specific electric-field conditions. The work emphasizes nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling as a source of exotic transport phenomena and positions the AHE as a potentially valuable probe of magnetic orders in spintronics. No experimental validation is reported in this theoretical and computational work.

Research Context
The anomalous Hall effect is a fundamental transport phenomenon in which an applied voltage induces a transverse Hall current response. AHE spontaneously occurs in ferromagnets or antiferromagnets with specific magnetic configurations, enabling the probing of magnetic orders. Recent studies have demonstrated electric-field induced AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling, such as the layer Hall effect and electric Hall effect. However, the electric-field induced AHE arising from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling remains largely unexplored in crystalline materials. The AHE is a topology-related transport phenomenon of potential interest in spintronics for data readout in memory devices. External fields capable of inducing magnetization should in principle induce AHE, positioning magnetoelectric coupling as a promising avenue.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling can drive the anomalous Hall effect in crystalline magnets. The authors use a group-theoretical approach to establish the phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE. The hypothesis is that a large variety of magnetic point groups host an AHE driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields. The predicted AHE conductivities are expected to arise from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling and to be reversible by reversing magnetic orders. The theory aims to identify specific MPGs and predict which AHE components emerge under which electric-field configurations. The authors further hypothesize that Cr2O3 and CoF2 will serve as representative candidate materials showcasing the predicted electric-field induced AHE.

Methodological Details
The study employs a symmetry-based group-theoretical analysis of the 122 magnetic point groups classified into three types. Type-I MPGs involve only spatial operations, type-II incorporate time-reversal as an independent operation, and type-III contain time-reversal only in combination with spatial operations. The authors identify 90 type-I and type-III MPGs that exhibit spontaneous or electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivity components. The MAGNDATA database is used to select Cr2O3 and CoF2 as the representative materials for first-principles verification. Both Cr2O3 and CoF2 have no more than 10 ions per primitive cell, making computational costs affordable. Cr2O3 has a Néel temperature of 307 K and belongs to the ¯3′m′ magnetic point group. CoF2 has a Néel temperature of 39 K and its MPG is 4′/mm′m. The AHE conductivity is expressed through the Berry curvature formula involving the Levi-Civita symbol. The Hall vector M is defined as (σzy, σxz, σyx), which behaves like a magnetization vector. The Onsager reciprocity relation requires σαβ(+L) = σβα(−L), leading to σαβ(+L) = −σαβ(−L) due to the antisymmetric nature of conductivity.

Procedures And Architectures
The effective magnetic field Bαeff is expanded in a power series of the electric field components. The λα coefficient in the expansion implies spontaneous Mα magnetization, while subsequent coefficients characterize linear, second-order, and third-order magnetoelectric couplings. Symmetry analysis derives the analytical forms of Bαeff for all 90 type-I and type-III MPGs. Table I summarizes the AHE in all 90 MPGs, color-coded by the driving electric-field configuration (uni-axial, bi-axial, tri-axial, or spontaneous). For the ¯6m2.1 MPG, the effective magnetic fields are explicitly derived as functions of Ex, Ey, and Ez showing specific coupling orders. First-principles calculations compute the anomalous Hall conductivity components as a function of chemical potential relative to the Fermi level. The total electric-field amplitude is set to 4 MV/cm for comparisons in both materials. For Cr2O3, the magnetic order parameter is switched between +L and −L to verify reversibility of the Hall conductivity. For CoF2, the magnetic order parameter is similarly reversed to confirm that reversing magnetic order reverses the AHE conductivities.

Key Results
Ninety type-I and type-III magnetic point groups are shown to host either spontaneous or electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivity. In the ¯6m2.1 MPG, σzy responds to E2xEz or EyEz, σxz responds to ExEz, and σyx responds to E3x. Cr2O3 with +L magnetic order enables σzy driven by Ex, σxz driven by Ey, and σyx driven by Ez or E3y. For Cr2O3, σzy and σxz exceed 100 S/cm at an electric field of 4 MV/cm via first-order response. The maximum σyx in Cr2O3, driven by Ey = 4 MV/cm via third-order response, is less than 20 S/cm. In CoF2, σyx is driven by uni-axial E2x or E2y response, yielding values larger than 200 S/cm at 4 MV/cm. In CoF2, σzy and σxz from bi-axial ExEz and EyEz responses can reach 10 S/cm at a total electric-field amplitude of 4 MV/cm. A quenching behavior occurs in 10 MPGs when the bi-axial or tri-axial electric field is along specific directions. In all tested cases, the conductivities associated with +L and −L are opposite by sign, confirming the reversibility prediction. Figures 2(a)-(d) show Cr2O3 conductivity components, while Figures 2(e)-(h) show CoF2 components against chemical potential.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The anomalous Hall conductivity is a topology-related transport property stemming from the Berry curvature of electronic bands. The Hall vector M behaves like a magnetization vector under symmetry operations, establishing a direct correspondence. The reversibility by magnetic order reversal is a consequence of the Onsager reciprocity relation and the antisymmetric nature of the Hall conductivity. Nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling opens new channels for generating Hall responses in magnets not accessible via linear effects. The AHE provides a practical means for detecting and probing magnetic order parameters in magnets. The work identifies the AHE as an exotic transport phenomenon that can enrich the suite of available probes for magnetic systems.

Contradictions And Limitations
No experimental validation of the predicted electric-field driven AHE in any material is reported. Only two materials (Cr2O3 and CoF2) are examined, while the theory covers 90 MPGs. Type-II MPGs containing time-reversal as an independent operation are excluded from the discussion as they do not host electric-field induced magnetization. Quenching behavior in 10 MPGs imposes practical constraints on the observed AHE under specific electric-field orientations. The paper is purely theoretical and computational; no experimental data or real-device measurements are provided.

Claims
Nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling can drive the anomalous Hall effect in 90 magnetic point groups via uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields. 90 type-I and type-III MPGs exhibit AHE components driven by electric-field configurations. The symmetry analysis for all 122 MPGs provides the analytical effective magnetic field for each case. The color-coded Table I systematically documents all predicted conductivities across 90 groups. 10 MPGs show quenching of AHE under specific electric-field conditions, limiting the effect's observability. Type-II MPGs do not host the predicted electric-field driven AHE. This provides a new set of MPGs where electric-field control of AHE is possible. The AHE can serve as a new probe of magnetic order in spintronic devices.
Cr2O3 and CoF2 are representative semiconductor materials showcasing electric-field induced AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. Cr2O3 yields σzy and σxz > 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm via first-order response. CoF2 yields σyx > 200 S/cm at 4 MV/cm via second-order response. Both materials show reversibility of Hall conductivity upon magnetic order reversal. Third-order σyx in Cr2O3 is limited to < 20 S/cm, much smaller than first-order components. Only two materials are validated, which is a small sample given 90 MPGs. These materials could be tested experimentally as platforms for electric-field controlled AHE. The difference in dominant coupling orders between Cr2O3 and CoF2 highlights the material-specific nature of the effect.
The anomalous Hall conductivity is fully reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter, yielding opposite signs. The Onsager reciprocity and antisymmetric property of σ lead to σ(+L) = −σ(−L). First-principles results for both Cr2O3 and CoF2 confirm opposite-sign conductivities for +L and −L. No experimental confirmation of this reversibility is provided. This property enables the AHE to unambiguously detect the magnetic order parameter. The reversibility is a key experimental signature of the predicted effect.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The quenching behavior in 10 MPGs is documented in Supplementary Table 12, showing sensitivity to electric-field orientation. Chemical potential scanning in Figures 2(a)-(h) explores the dependence of Hall conductivities on Fermi level position. The effective magnetic field expansion is analyzed at different orders to separate linear, second-order, and third-order contributions.

Key Figures Tables
Table I lists the anomalous Hall effect in 90 type-I and type-III MPGs, with color codes for spontaneous and electric-field driven components. Figure 1(a) sketches crystal and magnetic structures of Cr2O3 with +L magnetic order; Figure 1(b) does the same for CoF2 with +L order. Figures 2(a)-(d) depict anomalous Hall conductivity components in Cr2O3 as a function of chemical potential, driven by Ex, Ey, Ey, and Ez. Figures 2(e)-(h) show anomalous Hall conductivity in CoF2, driven by [Ex,Ez], [Ey,Ez], Ex, and Ey.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the establishment of a phenomenological theory showing that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling drives AHE in 90 type-I and type-III magnetic point groups, with conductivities that are reversible by reversing magnetic order. 2. The strongest evidence comes from the symmetry analysis of all 122 MPGs and the first-principles verification on Cr2O3 and CoF2, which yield measurable Hall conductivities (exceeding 100 S/cm and 200 S/cm respectively) that follow the predicted symmetry rules and reversibility. 3. The future path lies in experimental verification of the predicted electric-field driven AHE in the candidate materials and the potential application of AHE as a non-contact, electric-field-tunable probe of magnetic order in spintronic devices.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces DUO (DUplex decOding), a novel channel-division-multiplexing decoding mechanism that equips existing large language models with duplex capabilities—the ability to process user queries and generate responses simultaneously—with minimal additional training. Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm that precludes real-time interactive feedback during response generation. Previous duplex approaches, such as MiniCPM-Duplex which employs a time-division-multiplexing strategy, require substantial computational resources because the designed procedure diverges significantly from the backbone model's original training format. In contrast, DUO establishes parallel input and output channels at the decoding level, using a channel-aware causal mask that prevents tokens in the input channel from attending to those in the output channel, thereby preserving language modeling integrity. Two state tokens, <1> indicating a user query and <2> indicating non-query text, are introduced to signal whether the model should address new input or continue existing generation. The model was trained on MiniCPM-2.4B using 10,000 samples over 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for approximately 25 minutes, compared to the baseline's 5,000,000 samples over 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. Human evaluation with three Bachelor's-degree-holding participants across 40 multi-turn voice-based dialogue sessions demonstrated that MiniCPM-Duo achieves superior responsiveness and human-likeness over MiniCPM-Duplex while maintaining comparable factuality and faithfulness, with a substantial advantage in overall performance. Standard benchmark evaluation on CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, and HellaSwag confirms that MiniCPM-Duo preserves original capabilities while enabling duplex functionality. The authors conclude that DUO offers a versatile, low-overhead path to real-time conversational AI, with potential extension to multimodal settings using encoder-extracted features as input tokens.

Research Context
Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm that precludes real-time interactive feedback during response generation. Human conversations involve simultaneous listening and thinking, contrasting with the passive waiting inherent in traditional turn-based systems. Interruptions in current systems require manual interventions such as a stop function, resulting in communication that lacks fluidity. Recent duplex models like MiniCPM-Duplex employ a time-division-multiplexing strategy splitting and mixing input and output in a time slice format. Other approaches such as LSLM combine channels for autoregressive generation and real-time turn-taking detection using three fusion strategies. These duplex methods typically require substantial computational resources for model retraining because the designed procedure diverges substantially from the backbone model. The data format changes significantly in time-division-multiplexing approaches, requiring heavy retraining to learn the split input-output structure.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether LLMs can be equipped with duplex capabilities—simultaneous autoregressive output generation and input preprocessing—without significant model retraining. The hypothesis is that a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy using parallel input and output channels, combined with minimal state-token training, can enable real-time interactive feedback. The model is predicted to handle non-awakening interactions by filtering out background dialogues and non-query input without interrupting the current output channel. It is further hypothesized that if a user interrupts with a new query during ongoing generation, the model should pause its current output to immediately address the latest query. The expected outcome is that this method will significantly enhance naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions with minimal training costs compared to time-division-multiplexing baselines. The authors anticipate that the original model's capabilities will be preserved because the data format remains largely unchanged, with only state tokens added.

Methodological Details
The foundation model is MiniCPM-2.4B, an LLM from the MiniCPM family, chosen for its efficiency and compatibility. The training dataset consists of 10,000 samples constructed from Duplex-UltraChat, adapted into a turn-based format with state tokens. In contrast, the baseline MiniCPM-Duplex was trained on approximately 5,000,000 samples using the original time-division format. State tokens <1> and <2> are appended: <1> to every user query to signal response required, and <2> for non-query text to signal continuation. Non-query text is generated using ChatGPT with an optimized prompt to ensure relevance to the conversational context. Training hyperparameters include a 1e-5 learning rate with a constant learning rate scheduler, a batch size of 112, and a maximum sequence length of 4,096 tokens. Loss is calculated specifically on the state tokens and the generated output sequence. MiniCPM-Duo is trained for 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for approximately 25 minutes. The baseline MiniCPM-Duplex is trained for 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. The input channel predicted token count α is set to 4 per processing cycle. Human evaluation involves 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions recorded through a voice-based interactive demo. Three human participants, each holding a Bachelor's degree, assess the dialogue histories across five criteria. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech are facilitated by Google’s cloud ASR and TTS APIs. Standard benchmarks include CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, and HellaSwag evaluated on the UltraEval platform.

Procedures And Architectures
DUO processes inputs and outputs cyclically: the output channel generates tokens autoregressively while the input channel pre-fills the KV cache and predicts next tokens. A new input channel is established at time step t1 when a user provides input while the model is generating autoregressively. The channel-aware causal mask ensures tokens generated by input and output channels after t1 do not attend to each other despite sharing prefix tokens. This design preserves language modeling in each channel independently by preventing cross-channel attention. Upon state token <1>, the original output channel is suspended and the input channel transitions to become the new output channel. Upon state token <2>, the model continues responding to the original query and the input channel is disregarded. If neither state token is predicted, the KV cache of predicted tokens is disregarded and the next processing cycle continues. DUO is implemented using Flex-Attention, which facilitates non-standard attention mechanisms via KV cache management. The decoding strategy is based on the Ouroboros repository (https://github.com/thunlp/Ouroboros). DUO does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding; input and output channels share computation within each time slice. The output channel persists in generating tokens rather than terminating immediately when non-query input is received. The case study in Figure 3 illustrates: (left) a query where <1> triggers output generation; (right) an interruption where <2> deletes the new input and the model continues the original output. Figure 1 (left) shows the case where a new input token is received at t1 establishing the second channel; Figure 1 (right) shows the attention mask preventing cross-channel attention; Figure 1 (bottom left) shows channel transition via state tokens. Figure 5 and Figure 6 respectively show training examples of MiniCPM-Duplex and DUO to illustrate data format differences.

Key Results
Human evaluation: MiniCPM-Duo wins on responsiveness and human-likeness, while MiniCPM-Duplex wins on factuality and faithfulness, with ties on overall satisfaction. MiniCPM-Duo demonstrates superior responsiveness: it responds to user queries without dropping the context or stalling. MiniCPM-Duo achieves higher human-likeness scores, with responses resembling human dialogue patterns more closely than the time-division baseline. Factuality and faithfulness levels are comparable between MiniCPM-Duo and MiniCPM-Duplex, indicating minimal degradation of groundedness. MiniCPM-Duo exhibits a substantial advantage in overall performance across the five evaluation criteria. CMMLU: MiniCPM-Duo (50.56), MiniCPM-Duplex (48.53), MiniCPM (51.30); performance drop in Duplex is notable. MMLU: MiniCPM-Duo (53.13), MiniCPM-Duplex (53.76), MiniCPM (53.45); nearly comparable levels. HumanEval: MiniCPM-Duo (51.83), MiniCPM-Duplex (49.39), MiniCPM (50.00); Duo exceeds baseline. HellaSwag: MiniCPM-Duo (59.78), MiniCPM-Duplex (60.79), MiniCPM (61.40); Duo is slightly below. GSM8K: MiniCPM-Duo (42.15), MiniCPM-Duplex (46.10), MiniCPM (42.30); Duplex shows unexpected advantage here. MBPP: MiniCPM-Duo (38.19), MiniCPM-Duplex (38.30), MiniCPM (38.09); nearly identical. ARC-c: MiniCPM-Duo (70.48), MiniCPM-Duplex (69.43), MiniCPM (69.80); Duo slightly ahead. ARC-e: MiniCPM-Duo (84.93), MiniCPM-Duplex (85.19), MiniCPM (84.60); Duplex marginally higher. BBH: MiniCPM-Duo (36.51), MiniCPM-Duplex (35.81), MiniCPM (37.25); Duo outperforms Duplex baseline. The case study in Figure 3 shows a user query where predicting <1> commences autoregressive answer generation, and an interruption where predicting <2> deletes the new query input. MiniCPM-Duo preserves the model's original capabilities to a greater extent than MiniCPM-Duplex, which requires substantial computational resources to learn the time slice format. The duplex capability of inadequately trained MiniCPM-Duplex (on 10K samples) performs relatively poorly on benchmarks.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
DUO shifts the duplex problem from time-division (sequencing) to channel-division (parallelism), allowing the model to retain its standard autoregressive architecture. The use of state tokens as steering mechanisms means the model only needs to learn 'when' to switch channels, not 'how' to format interleaved data. The channel-aware causal mask provides a formal architectural guarantee that input and output sequences remain logically isolated within the transformer, preserving the integrity of each stream. The design enables real-time interactive feedback by decoupling input processing from output generation, allowing the assistant to listen while speaking. DUO is theoretically extensible to multimodal LLMs: input tokens could be features extracted by encoders from various modalities (vision, audio, etc.) while output tokens remain text. The minimal training cost suggests that duplex capability is an architectural property of the decoding strategy rather than a learned linguistic pattern requiring massive data.

Contradictions And Limitations
The experiments primarily focused on language models, limiting the generalizability of findings to other domains such as vision or audio-only duplex. Human evaluation was conducted with only three participants, which may not be sufficient to generalize across diverse user populations and conversational styles. The case study in Figure 3 uses highly specific interactive scenarios; more varied and natural conversational flows remain unexplored. On GSM8K, MiniCPM-Duplex (46.10) outperformed MiniCPM-Duo (42.15), suggesting the time-division approach might have specific advantages in math reasoning that DUO does not replicate. The model was evaluated on 40 multi-turn sessions, a relatively small sample size for robust human-centered dialogue quality assessment. No ablation on the number of state tokens (α=4) or the timeout window for state token prediction is reported, leaving the optimality of these hyperparameters unclear.

Claims
DUO equips LLMs with duplex capabilities requiring minimal training compared to time-division-multiplexing baselines. DUO uses 10K samples, 400 steps, 8 A100s (25 mins) vs. 5,000K samples, 10,000 steps, 40 A100s (36 hours) for MiniCPM-Duplex. The data format remains largely unchanged, with only state tokens added, preserving original model capabilities. MiniCPM-Duo achieves comparable or superior benchmark scores while requiring only 0.2% of the training data of MiniCPM-Duplex. On GSM8K, MiniCPM-Duplex outperforms MiniCPM-Duo by 3.95 absolute points (46.10 vs 42.15). On MMLU, MiniCPM-Duplex scores 53.76 vs. DUO's 53.13, showing the time-division baseline is not universally inferior. This minimal-training approach makes duplex capability accessible to smaller models and resource-constrained environments. The architectural separation of input and output channels provides a principled way to extend duplex to multimodal models.
DUO enables simultaneous autoregressive output generation and input preprocessing without increasing the number of forward passes. DUO processes the input and output channel in each time slice concurrently, sharing the same forward computation. The channel-aware mask ensures that cross-channel attention is disabled, preserving individual stream integrity. Flex-Attention implementation manages KV cache operations that enable this parallel structure efficiently. The paper does not provide a quantitative breakdown of per-token latency or throughput metrics to confirm the zero-overhead claim. DUO offers theoretical zero-overhead duplex compared to standard decoding, which is critical for real-time interactive systems.
State tokens <1> and <2> effectively steer channel transitions for non-awakening and interruption interactions. The case study in Figure 3 demonstrates the model predicting <1> to start generation and <2> to delete interruption input. The output channel persists even when non-query input is received, as shown in the channel transition diagram. The paper does not report on false-positive channel transitions (e.g., when a query is misidentified as non-query or vice versa). The state-token steering mechanism decouples duplex logic from the language model's main weights, allowing for modular upgrades.

Data And Code Availability
The decoding strategy implementation is based on the Ouroboros repository at https://github.com/thunlp/Ouroboros. The interactive demo originally developed for MiniCPM-Duplex was adapted for this work and is available at https://github.com/thunlp/duplex-model. The dataset was constructed by adapting Duplex-UltraChat into a turn-based format with state tokens. The non-query text generation used ChatGPT with an optimized prompt described in Appendix A.1.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A comparison was made by training MiniCPM-Duplex on the same 10K scale dataset as MiniCPM-Duo to isolate training volume from architecture effects. The results showed that inadequately trained MiniCPM-Duplex performed relatively poorly, confirming that the time-division format requires substantial data to learn. Flex-Attention was used to implement the non-standard attention mechanisms via KV cache management. The input channel predicted token count α was set to 4, but no ablation on this parameter is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Illustrates the channel-based parallel decoding with a new input channel established at time step t1, the channel-aware causal mask (right), and channel transition via state tokens (bottom left). Figure 2: A comparison of MiniCPM-Duo vs. MiniCPM-Duplex on responsiveness, human-likeness, factuality, faithfulness, and overall satisfaction, showing Duo winning on the first two and overall. Figure 3: A case study showing (left) a user query where predicting <1> commences autoregressive answer generation, and (right) an interruption where predicting <2> deletes the new query input. Figure 5 and Figure 6: Training examples illustrating the data format for MiniCPM-Duplex (time-division) and DUO (channel-division) respectively. Table 1: Primary results on standard benchmarks (CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, HellaSwag) comparing MiniCPM, MiniCPM-Duplex, and MiniCPM-Duo.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is DUO, a channel-division-multiplexing decoding mechanism that enables simultaneous input preprocessing and output generation in LLMs with minimal training overhead compared to time-division-multiplexing baselines. 2. The strongest evidence is the human evaluation showing MiniCPM-Duo achieves superior responsiveness and human-likeness over MiniCPM-Duplex across 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions with only 10K training samples, compared to 5,000K samples for the baseline. 3. The future path includes extending DUO to multimodal settings where input tokens are features extracted by encoders from various modalities while output tokens remain text, broadening the technology's applications.

summary.title: Spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes
summary.authors: Lina Zhang, Qiyuan Pan, Yun Soo Myung, De-Cheng Zou
summary.field_subfield: General Relativity / Black Hole Physics and Scalar-Tensor Gravity
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes within Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory coupled to a scalar field via two coupling functions: quadratic (1−αϕ²) and exponential (e−αϕ²). Bardeen black holes, which are spherically symmetric and singularity-free, undergo a tachyonic instability at a threshold coupling parameter αₜₕ(g), triggering the formation of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs). The authors identify infinite branches (n = 0, 1, 2, · · ·) of SCBHs corresponding to the number of nodes in the radial scalar field profile. For the n = 0 branch, the instability threshold is exactly the bifurcation point α₀(g). Specifically, for M = 0.5 and g = 0.2, the threshold is α₀ ≈ 12.712, and subsequent bifurcation points are α₁ ≈ 75.114 and α₂ ≈ 190.590. Stability analysis using radial (l = 0) perturbations confirms that the n = 0 branch is stable against perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings, with negative eigenfrequencies indicating decaying modes. Higher branches (n ≠ 0) are predicted to be unstable, consistent with previous results in other scalarization contexts. Numerically obtained SCBH solutions show that the horizon position slightly shifts from the Bardeen value (ln r = −0.0683 versus −0.0671), and the metric function and scalar hair decrease monotonically as ln r increases. The work extends spontaneous scalarization from Kerr and Schwarzschild black holes to regular Bardeen solutions, providing a novel channel for observational implications in alternative gravity theories and offering insights into the role of regular black hole structures in scalarization phenomena.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes within Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory coupled to a scalar field via two coupling functions: quadratic (1−αϕ²) and exponential (e−αϕ²). Bardeen black holes, which are spherically symmetric and singularity-free, undergo a tachyonic instability at a threshold coupling parameter αₜₕ(g), triggering the formation of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs). The authors identify infinite branches (n = 0, 1, 2, · · ·) of SCBHs corresponding to the number of nodes in the radial scalar field profile. For the n = 0 branch, the instability threshold is exactly the bifurcation point α₀(g). Specifically, for M = 0.5 and g = 0.2, the threshold is α₀ ≈ 12.712, and subsequent bifurcation points are α₁ ≈ 75.114 and α₂ ≈ 190.590. Stability analysis using radial (l = 0) perturbations confirms that the n = 0 branch is stable against perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings, with negative eigenfrequencies indicating decaying modes. Higher branches (n ≠ 0) are predicted to be unstable, consistent with previous results in other scalarization contexts. Numerically obtained SCBH solutions show that the horizon position slightly shifts from the Bardeen value (ln r = −0.0683 versus −0.0671), and the metric function and scalar hair decrease monotonically as ln r increases. The work extends spontaneous scalarization from Kerr and Schwarzschild black holes to regular Bardeen solutions, providing a novel channel for observational implications in alternative gravity theories and offering insights into the role of regular black hole structures in scalarization phenomena.

Research Context
Spontaneous scalarization is a dynamic process imparting scalar hair to black holes via tachyonic instability without changing weak-field predictions. The phenomenon is caused by nonminimal coupling between scalar fields and spacetime curvature or matter. Black hole spontaneous scalarization has been extensively studied, including rotation and spin-induced cases. Scalarized black holes are entropically favorable and their n = 0 branches are stable. Dynamics in scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity and other alternative gravity theories have also been explored. The Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory with exponential and quadratic couplings has been previously examined. General relativity singularity theorems suggest singularities are inevitable inside black holes, making alternative theories relevant. Bardeen proposed the first regular, spherically symmetric, singularity-free black hole solution. Nonlinear electromagnetic sources were proposed to explain the matter content of Bardeen black holes. Regular black holes are of great interest for understanding singularities and nonlinear electrodynamics. This work studies spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes by introducing two scalar field couplings.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether Bardeen black holes exhibit spontaneous scalarization when coupled to scalar fields via quadratic or exponential couplings. The hypothesis is that a tachyonic instability develops at a threshold coupling parameter αₜₕ, triggering the formation of scalarized charged black holes. The authors predict infinite branches of SCBHs corresponding to the number of nodes in the scalar field profile. It is conjectured that the n = 0 branch of SCBHs will be stable against radial perturbations, making it potentially observable. The paper aims to numerically determine the n = 0 branch and analyze its stability for both coupling forms. The bifurcation points α₀, α₁, α₂ for different n-branches are predicted to exist and form the threshold for scalarization. The authors hypothesize that the instability becomes harder to realize as magnetic charge g decreases. It is expected that all other branches (n ≠ 0) are unstable against radial perturbations. The stability of the n = 0 branch is expected to be independent of the specific coupling form and the magnetic charge.

Methodological Details
The study considers Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory coupled with a scalar field, described by an action functional with R, ϕ, and a coupling function ˜f(ϕ)L(F). The non-linear function L(F) is given by L(F) = (3/2 sg²) ((2g²F²/2)^(1/2) + ((2g²F²/2)^(1/2))^5/2)^(1/2). The parameter s is defined by s = |g|² / M, where g is the magnetic charge and M is the mass. Varying the action yields three field equations: the modified Einstein equation, a Klein-Gordon equation for the scalar field, and the Maxwell equation. The Bardeen black hole solution is obtained setting ϕ = 0, with metric function f(r) = 1 − 2M r² / (r² + g²)^(3/2). The magnetic field is F_θφ = g sin θ, giving F² = 2g² / r⁴, which violates the strong energy condition at the center. The study uses a typical nonextremal Bardeen black hole with M = 0.5 and g = 0.2, yielding an outer horizon at r₊ = 0.935. The two coupling forms are ˜f(ϕ) = 1−αϕ² (quadratic) and ˜f(ϕ) = e−αϕ² (exponential). Stability is assessed using the l = 0 s-mode of the spherically symmetric scalar perturbation. The tortoise coordinate r* is defined by dr*/dr = 1 / f(r), and the scalar equation is separated via ϕ = u(r)/r e−iωt Y_lm. The scalar potential V(r) for the instability check depends on r, α, g, and l, with the threshold requiring V(r) ≥ 0. Numerical solutions are found by integrating the boundary value problem with ingoing wave conditions at the horizon and outgoing at infinity. Stability is confirmed by solving the linearized scalar equation numerically and verifying that the eigenfrequency Ω is negative. Matching between near-horizon and asymptotic far-region solutions determines the two free parameters ϕ₀ and δ₀. The Arnowitt-Deser-Misner mass M and scalar charge Q_s appear in the far-region asymptotic solution.

Procedures And Architectures
The metric ansatz for the SCBH solutions is ds² = −N(r) e−2δ(r) dt² + dr² / N(r) + r²(dθ² + sin² θ dφ²), with N(r) = 1 − 2m(r)/r. The vector potential solution is A_φ = −g cos θ, reproducing the magnetic field of the Bardeen solution exactly. Substituting the ansatz into the field equations yields three coupled ordinary differential equations for δ(r), m(r), and ϕ(r). The near-horizon approximate solutions are m(r) = r₊² + m₁(r−r₊), δ(r) = δ₀ + δ₁(r−r₊), and ϕ(r) = ϕ₀ + ϕ₁(r−r₊). Coefficients m₁, δ₁, and ϕ₁ are determined by the field equations evaluated at r₊. The far-region asymptotic solutions are m(r) = M − Q_s² / r + · · ·, ϕ(r) = Q_s / r + · · ·, and δ(r) = Q_s² / r² + · · ·. The shooting method is used to match near-horizon and far-region solutions and determine ϕ₀ and δ₀. The n = 0 branch solution is obtained at α = 13.048 for quadratic coupling and α = 13.667 for exponential coupling, with M = 0.5 and g = 0.2. The stability analysis employs the radial (spherically symmetric) perturbation ds² = −N(r) e−2δ(r) [1+ϵH₀(t,r)] dt² + dr² / N(r) [1+ϵH₁(t,r)] + r²(dθ² + sin² θ dφ²). The scalar perturbation is decomposed as δϕ(t,r) = ϕ₁(r) e^Ωt, and the governing Schrödinger-type equation is derived for the l = 0 mode. The tortoise coordinate for the SCBH background is defined as dr*/dr = e^δ(r) / N(r). Stability is determined by imposing outgoing wave conditions at infinity and ingoing at the horizon, and verifying Ω < 0.

Key Results
The instability threshold for Bardeen black holes with g = 0.2 is found to be αₜₕ(0.2) = 12.712, corresponding to the bifurcation point of the n = 0 branch. For g = 0.175, the instability threshold is αₜₕ(0.175) = 17.338; for g = 0.250, it is αₜₕ(0.250) = 7.251. The instability threshold αₜₕ(g) increases as magnetic charge g decreases, making tachyonic instability harder to realize for smaller g. Infinite branches (n = 0, 1, 2 · · ·) of SCBHs appear from infinite scalar modes, with bifurcation points α₀ ≈ 12.712, α₁ ≈ 75.114, and α₂ ≈ 190.590 for g = 0.2. The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is found for any α ≥ αₜₕ(g) with both quadratic and exponential couplings. For quadratic coupling with M = 0.5 and g = 0.2, the n = 0 SCBH solution is obtained at α = 13.048. For exponential coupling with the same parameters, the n = 0 SCBH solution is at α = 13.667. The SCBH horizon at ln r = −0.0683 for α = 13.048 (quadratic) and α = 13.667 (exponential) nearly coincides with the Bardeen horizon at ln r = −0.0671. The metric function N(r) of the SCBH solution approaches the Bardeen function f(r) as ln r increases. The SCBH stability analysis confirms that the n = 0 black hole is stable against the l = 0 scalar mode for all tested magnetic charges. Stability is independent of the magnetic charge g, with negative Ω observed for g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250. The exponential coupling does not affect the stability of scalarized Bardeen black holes, with Ω remaining negative. All other branches (n ≠ 0) are expected to be unstable against radial perturbations, consistent with previous scalarization literature.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The stability of the n = 0 branch makes it the endpoint of the Bardeen black hole, potentially allowing for observational implications. The identification of infinite SCBH branches extends the paradigm of spontaneous scalarization to regular black hole solutions. The fact that the horizon shifts minimally from the Bardeen value suggests that scalar hair does not drastically alter the local horizon geometry. The stability of the n = 0 branch for both quadratic and exponential couplings suggests universality in the scalarization mechanism for Bardeen black holes. The result that smaller magnetic charges suppress scalarization is consistent with the role of magnetic charge in the instability condition.

Contradictions And Limitations
The near-horizon potential V_SCBH for the n = 0 branch contains small negative regions, yet the solutions turn out to be stable. The authors note that a negative potential near the horizon is not always a sufficient indicator of instability. Only the l = 0 (s-mode) perturbation is analyzed; higher angular momentum modes are neglected, which may not capture all unstable channels. The stability of higher branches (n ≠ 0) is based on references [33, 34] rather than direct computation in this work. The paper does not provide numerical values for higher n branches, leaving their stability as a prediction. No random seed, specific numerical solver details, or convergence criteria for the shooting method are reported. The comparison between Bardeen and SCBH horizons is limited to the ln r coordinate, without explicit comparison of physical area or temperature.

Claims
Bardeen black holes with nonminimal scalar coupling undergo spontaneous scalarization at a critical coupling threshold, forming scalarized charged black holes with infinite branches. The threshold is numerically determined at αₜₕ(0.2) = 12.712 with bifurcation points at α₀ ≈ 12.712, α₁ ≈ 75.114, α₂ ≈ 190.590. Infinite branches appear for both quadratic and exponential couplings: α₀ ≈ 12.712, α₁ ≈ 75.114, α₂ ≈ 190.590. The n = 0 branch exists for any α ≥ αₜₕ(g) with both coupling forms. The instability threshold αₜₕ(g) becomes progressively harder to reach as g decreases, limiting the parameter space. The potential V(r) for the perturbed scalar field contains negative regions that would naively indicate instability but do not. This extends the phenomenon of spontaneous scalarization to a novel class of regular black hole solutions. The infinite branch structure implies a rich taxonomy of scalarized black hole states.
The n = 0 branch of scalarized Bardeen black holes is stable against radial (l = 0) perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings. Numerical solutions to the Schrödinger-type equation yield negative eigenfrequencies Ω for all tested g and α. Stability is confirmed for g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250 with the exponential coupling yielding similar stability results to the quadratic case. The stability is consistent across both coupling forms, with the quadratic case showing α = 12.713, 13.048, 14.110 and the exponential case α = 12.714, 14.991. The stability is only verified for the l = 0 mode; higher angular momentum modes are not checked. The potential V_SCBH still contains small near-horizon negative regions which superficially suggest instability. The stability of the n = 0 branch makes it a viable observational target for testing scalarization in the gravitational wave or electromagnetic spectrum. The n = 0 branch is identified as the stable endpoint of the Bardeen black hole solution.
Higher branches (n ≥ 1) of scalarized Bardeen black holes are expected to be unstable against radial perturbations. All other branches (n ≠ 0) are expected to be unstable as suggested by Refs. [33, 34]. The n = 0 branch is the only one shown to be stable, consistent with previous results in other scalarization contexts. No direct numerical stability analysis of n ≥ 1 branches is performed in this paper. The prediction is based on analogy with other systems and not direct computation. Only the n = 0 branch should be physically realizable and observable.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The stability is checked across three different magnetic charges g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250, confirming charge-independence. Both quadratic and exponential coupling forms are independently computed and yield consistent stability and existence results. The n = 0, 1, 2 bifurcation points are computed from the static scalar solution, providing a consistency check on the instability thresholds. The near-horizon and far-region matching is verified by comparing the SCBH horizon position (ln r = −0.0683) with the Bardeen horizon (ln r = −0.0671).

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the α-dependent scalar potential V(r, α) for the Bardeen background, with the negative region indicating the instability zone. Figure 1(b) displays three cross-sections of the potential at α = {10, 12.712, 20}, illustrating how the negative region grows with α. Figure 2 shows the Ω(α) curves for three g values, identifying the threshold αₜₕ(g) where the curves cross the α-axis. Figure 3 plots the radial profiles of the first three static scalar solutions ϕ(z) for M = 0.5 and g = 0.2, with nodes labeling the n = 0, 1, 2 branches. Figure 4(a) and 4(b) display the quadratic and exponential SCBH solutions for n = 0, showing N(r), δ(r), ϕ(r) against the Bardeen f(r) on a ln r scale. Figure 5(a) and 5(b) show the SCBH potentials for quadratic and exponential couplings, respectively, exhibiting small near-horizon negative regions. Figure 6(a) and 6(b) plot negative Ω as a function of α for three g values for both couplings, demonstrating stability (negative Ω) for all cases.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the discovery of spontaneous scalarization in regular Bardeen black holes with infinite branches of SCBHs and a stable n = 0 branch for both quadratic and exponential couplings. 2. The strongest evidence is the numerical confirmation that the n = 0 branch is stable against l = 0 perturbations across three magnetic charges and both coupling forms, with eigenfrequencies remaining negative. 3. The future path involves exploring higher angular momentum perturbations, gravitational wave signatures of the n = 0 branch, and extending the analysis to non-spherical or rotating regular black holes.

summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and experimental framework for three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics. The authors overcome the inherent limitations of two-dimensional valley photonics, which suffer from out-of-plane losses and are confined to planar geometries. They develop a 3D photonic crystal with a complete photonic bandgap characterized by a lattice constant of 20 mm, incorporating face-centered-cubic unit cells with nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor PEC rod couplings (B1=2.4 mm, B2=1.2 mm). By breaking inversion symmetry (D1=6.4 mm, D2=3.6 mm), they create six valley states at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone forming triple pairs of valleys with vectorial valley Chern vectors (VCVs) of ±1/2 along each principal axis. The vectorial valley-contrasting physics, where Bloch modes around each valley possess opposite chirality, is verified via a vectorial chiral source array (four-source phase-winding configuration) and outcoupling field measurements at 13.8 GHz, showing -32.9° and +32.9° directions corresponding to Wy± valleys and 0° for the X point. A chiral valley surface state with linear dispersion is demonstrated at 14.6 GHz on the (001) surface, engineered by a metallic plate and specific parameters (h=6.25 mm, D3=4 mm). The surface states exhibit canalization behavior with flat isofrequency contours, propagating diffractionlessly along the +y direction. Crucially, the authors prove that chiral valley surface states exist on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces, with propagation directions locked to the VCVs, and establish the right-hand-thumb rule relating VCV orientation to surface state circulation. The work positions 3D topological valley photonics as a route to directional radiation, 3D waveguiding, and narrow-beam antenna design, applicable from microwave to terahertz and optical frequencies.
