judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper, Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction by Yu Chen et al., proposes a novel framework that blends the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models, specifically for multivariate time series forecasting. The authors address a key scalability issue: while pure generative models (DDPM, SGM, Flow Matching) capture complex high-dimensional distributions well, their model size scales with both feature dimension and time window length, making them less efficient than RNNs whose model size depends only on feature count. The proposed method extends the theory of stochastic interpolants to a general conditional generation framework with extra control features. In the sequential setting, the model encodes a large context window xt−P : t−1 into a history prompt ht via an RNN. The SI module then performs conditional generation from the current time point xt to the target distribution xt+1, conditioned on ht, following the forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). The framework is trained on a three-tuple (xt+1, xt, xt−P : t−1), learning joint distributions over pairs of consecutive time points conditioned on the past. Importance sampling with a Beta distribution stabilizes training over diffusion time. For inference, the RNN generates the history prompt, and SI transports the context vector xt to the prediction distribution. The authors prove Theorem 1, extending stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions with a continuous-time interpretation that avoids characteristic functions. The method supports multiple-step prediction by recursively applying the step-by-step inference. Empirical evaluation on synthetic two-dimensional datasets (Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) using Wasserstein distance, and on real multivariate time series (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki) using CRPS-sum, NRMSE, and ND, demonstrates that SI outperforms DDPM, SGM, and FM baselines on three out of four real datasets. FM slightly outperforms SI on Traffic, and the authors note that FM cannot capture the data distribution on Wiki. The method also exceeds the recurrent-only Vec-LSTM baseline, suggesting that careful probabilistic modeling is critical for large-dimension time series prediction.

Research Context
Recurrent neural networks and transformer models have become de facto tools for multivariate time series forecasting in finance, biology, medicine, and geophysical applications, capturing both short-term and long-term sequential dependencies. Probabilistic output layers in these models are confined within simple probability families because density parameterization requires differentiability with respect to network parameters. To capture sophisticated distributions and both temporal and cross-feature dependencies, generative modeling using diffusion or flow-based models has been explored. Prior works have applied diffusion models to probabilistic time series imputation and forecasting, learning joint densities of whole time series windows. However, generative model predictors suffer from scalability issues because model size is related to both feature dimension and window size, unlike recurrent models where size is proportional only to the number of features. Starting the generative procedure from an initial distribution proximate to the terminal data distribution can alleviate learning challenges, reduce inference complexity, and enhance sample quality. Time series data is typically continuous and neighboring time points exhibit strong correlations, indicating that the distribution of future time points is close to that of the current time point.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether blending the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models can provide a computationally-friendly framework for large-scale generative time series prediction. The authors hypothesize that a framework mapping between dependent data points, initiated at the current time point, will produce better quality predictions than models mapping from noise. The hypothesis further posits that longer temporal dependency can be encoded by a recurrent neural network, while the embedded history is passed to the generative model as guidance. The proposed method extends the theory of stochastic interpolants to a more general conditional generation framework with extra control features for sequential modeling. The authors predict that the conditional stochastic interpolants module will be computational-friendly while achieving high-quality modeling of the future time point's distribution. Theorem 1 formally extends stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions with a continuous-time interpretation avoiding characteristic functions, providing a theoretical foundation for the approach.

Methodological Details
Synthetic experiments use four two-dimensional datasets with regular patterns: Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll, with details referenced from prior work. The neural networks used for all models are shared to ensure a fair comparison, with all baselines trained under the same hyperparameters including batch size and training epochs. For diffusion-like models, DDPM is implemented with both linear and cosine noise schedulers. All models are assigned to generate data in the same setting by mapping from standard Gaussian to the target distribution. Sample quality on synthetic datasets is measured by Wasserstein distance, Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD), and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). Real-world multivariate time series datasets include Solar, Exchange rate, Traffic, and Wiki, commonly used for probabilistic forecasting tasks. Preprocessing steps follow the conventions in Salinas et al. (2019), with four datasets covering different time series properties. The probabilistic forecasting is evaluated by Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS-sum), normalized root mean square error via the median of samples (NRMSE), and point-metrics normalized deviance (ND). Metric calculations are performed using the gluonts package, with smaller values indicating better performance in all cases. The training dataset consists of three-tuples (xt+1, xt, xt−P : t−1), where the RNN encodes the context window into a history prompt. Importance sampling with a Beta distribution is used to stabilize the integral over diffusion time in the loss functions, addressing the issue that loss values become larger when s is close to two ends. The stochastic interpolant schedule uses α(0)=1, α(1)=0, β(0)=0, β(1)=1, and γ(0)=γ(1)=0, with a cosine-based deterministic and sine-based stochastic component.

Procedures And Architectures
The model diagram (Figure 2) shows that xt ∈ R^D represents a multi-variate time series at time t with D dimensions, and xt−P : t is the context window of length P. A recurrent neural network encodes the large context window xt−P : t−1 into a history prompt ht, which serves as conditional input for the SI module. The SI module learns two neural networks: a velocity function b(s, xs, ht) and a score function s(s, xs, ht), both conditioned on the history prompt. During training, the conditional velocity and score functions are updated by minimizing the mean squared error losses Lb and Ls, averaged over the Beta-distributed diffusion time. The conditional forward SDE used for inference is d˜xs = [b(s, ˜xs, h) + ϵs(s, ˜xs, h)]ds + √2ϵdws, integrating from s=0 to s=1. For multiple-step prediction, the inference is run recursively, where each prediction becomes the context for the next time step. All baseline models (DDPM, SGM, FM, SI) share the same neural network architecture, with field functions corresponding to noise prediction, score, vector field, or velocity/score respectively. The DDPM baseline is modified by replacing the context time point xt with Gaussian noise, while FM is incorporated by replacing the denoising objective with the flow matching objective. Vec-LSTM is included as a pure recurrent neural network baseline whose probabilistic layer is a multivariate Gaussian. Different gamma-functions γ(s) are tested for SI: quad γ(s)=t(1−s), sqrt γ(s)=√2s(1−s), and trig γ(s)=sin(πt)², all paired with linear interpolants.

Key Results
On the Solar dataset, SI achieves a CRPS-sum of 0.359±0.06, matching DDPM (0.359±0.061) and outperforming SGM (0.364±0.029) and FM (0.419±0.027). On the Exchange rate dataset, SI achieves 0.007±0.001, outperforming DDPM (0.009±0.004), FM (0.009±0.001), SGM (0.008±0.002), and Vec-LSTM (64.256±62.596). On the Wiki dataset, SI achieves 0.080±0.007, outperforming DDPM (0.084±0.023), FM (0.09±0.001), SGM (0.108±0.026), and Vec-LSTM (0.391±0.017). On the Traffic dataset, FM achieves 0.038±0.002, outperforming SI (0.083±0.005), SGM (0.071±0.05), and DDPM (0.058±0.014). The only dataset where SI does not outperform all baselines is Traffic, where FM achieves better performance. Vec-LSTM performs poorest on most datasets, notably achieving 64.256±62.596 on Exchange rate and 0.391±0.017 on Wiki. For the 8gaussians synthetic dataset, SI(quad, linear) achieves the lowest Wasserstein distance of 0.52 among all variants. For the Circles dataset, FM achieves the best Wasserstein distance of 0.10, followed by SI(trig, linear) at 0.13. Figure 4 shows forecast paths on the Solar dataset for 6 out of 137 variate dimensions, with median predictions and 50th and 90th confidence intervals from model samples. The authors state that on Wiki data, FM cannot capture the data distribution, which is consistent with the CRPS-sum of 0.09±0.001 versus SI's 0.080±0.007.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
SI is shown to be a suitable generative module for time series prediction, outperforming pure recurrent and pure generative baselines on three out of four datasets. The results imply that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large dimension time series prediction, as both SI and pure generative models exceed the Vec-LSTM baseline. Theorem 1 formally extends stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions with a continuous-time interpretation that avoids characteristic functions, making the analysis more friendly to users. The method guarantees that the generated sample xt+1 follows the marginal distribution ρ1 and the sample pair (xt, xt+1) satisfies the joint density, providing a principled generative framework. The combination of RNN for temporal encoding and SI for conditional generation addresses the scalability bottleneck of pure generative models while retaining their probabilistic quality.

Contradictions And Limitations
Only on Traffic does FM outperform SI (0.038±0.002 vs 0.083±0.005), representing a single-dataset exception to the otherwise consistent dominance of SI. The authors explicitly note that on Wiki data, FM cannot capture the data distribution, indicating a qualitative failure of flow matching for this specific dataset. No ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, or error analyses are reported in the paper, and model hyperparameters are not fully disclosed. The code is not yet publicly available; the authors state they will publish it for the camera-ready version, limiting immediate reproducibility. The evaluation is limited to four datasets, and the paper does not explore different context window lengths or RNN architectures beyond the basic RNN implementation.

Claims
The conditional stochastic interpolants module is a suitable generative module for multivariate time series prediction, achieving high-quality probabilistic forecasts with linear scalability in feature dimension. SI achieves the lowest CRPS-sum on Exchange (0.007±0.001), Solar (0.359±0.06), and Wiki (0.080±0.007), outperforming all baselines except FM on Traffic. SI outperforms the recurrent-only Vec-LSTM on all four real-world datasets. Synthetic dataset results (Figure 3) show SI variants capturing the true distribution structure across different geometries. FM achieves 0.038±0.002 on Traffic, clearly outperforming SI's 0.083±0.005. The authors state FM cannot capture the data distribution on Wiki, suggesting a qualitative limitation of the generative module approach on some datasets. The framework demonstrates that careful probabilistic modeling of the target distribution is critical for accurate multivariate forecasting. SI provides a scalable alternative to pure diffusion/flow-based models for large-scale time series prediction problems.
The combined RNN + SI framework achieves competitive performance in time series forecasting, matching or exceeding DDPM, SGM, FM, and Vec-LSTM on the majority of datasets. SI matches DDPM on Solar (0.359±0.06 vs 0.359±0.061) and beats SGM (0.364±0.029) and FM (0.419±0.027). SI outperforms DDPM (0.009±0.004), FM (0.009±0.001), SGM (0.008±0.002) on Exchange rate. Figure 4 demonstrates the forecast quality on Solar, with 50th and 90th confidence intervals from model samples. FM achieves better CRPS-sum on Traffic (0.038±0.002 vs SI's 0.083±0.005). The authors Ran a search over flow matching hyperparameters without being able to get satisfying results, limiting the comparability of the FM baseline. The method opens a path for combining generative probabilistic modeling with efficient sequence encoding in time series forecasting. The recursive step-by-step prediction extends the framework to multi-step forecasting beyond a single time step.

Data And Code Availability
The authors state that their code will be publicly available for the camera-ready version of the paper. The current version (arXiv:2409.11684v1) does not include a publicly accessible code repository; the placeholder indicates the code is not yet available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors test four different gamma-functions for SI: quad γ(s)=t(1−s), sqrt γ(s)=√2s(1−s), and trig γ(s)=sin(πt)², all paired with linear interpolants. The authors state that most gamma-interpolant function combinations achieve good results modeling the target distribution on synthetic datasets. The use of importance sampling with a Beta distribution is explicitly noted as a technique to stabilize training when the loss becomes large near the ends of diffusion time. The same neural networks and hyperparameters are used across all models on synthetic datasets to ensure a fair comparison of generation quality. The authors run a search over flow matching hyperparameters but were unable to obtain satisfying results, limiting the robustness of the FM baseline.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the schedules α(s), β(s), γ(s) of stochastic interpolants over s ∈ [0, 1], with an example using cosine-sine parametrization. Figure 2 illustrates the model architecture: an RNN encodes context xt−P : t−1 into history prompt ht, and SI performs conditional generation from xt to xt+1. Figure 3 displays generated samples for synthetic datasets (8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) across all model variants (DDPM, FM, SGM, SI variants). Figure 4 shows forecast paths for SI on the Solar dataset, with 50.0% and 90.0% prediction intervals on 6 out of 137 variate dimensions. Figure 5 shows the Time-Grad model for conditional time series prediction, illustrating how RNN, noise, and diffusion components interact. Table 1 reports Wasserstein distances between generated samples and true data for synthetic datasets across all model variants. Table 2 presents CRPS-sum results for the four real-world datasets (Exchange rate, Solar, Traffic, Wiki) across all baselines and SI.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Recurrent Interpolant (SI) framework, which combines RNN temporal encoding with stochastic interpolant-based conditional generation to enable scalable probabilistic time series prediction. 2. The strongest evidence is the CRPS-sum performance on three out of four real-world datasets (Exchange, Solar, Wiki), where SI outperforms DDPM, SGM, FM, and Vec-LSTM, demonstrating empirical superiority. 3. The future path lies in extending the conditional generation framework to multi-step prediction via recursive inference, and generalizing stochastic interpolants to more complex joint distribution settings beyond consecutive time points.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work systematically characterizes the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of a series of highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolyte solutions comprising 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH₃COOK mixed with varying concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, 7 mol kg⁻¹) of CH₃COONa. The most concentrated formulation (7N20K) exhibits a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C, a stability window extending up to 3 V under ideal flooded-cell conditions, and avoids crystallization at room temperature—a critical advantage over fluorinated WISE electrolytes that suffer from high cost and toxicity. These findings are validated by proof-of-concept sodium-ion battery testing: carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (NASICON) reversibly intercalates sodium ions at -0.7 V vs. SHE, achieving a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, average charge efficiency of 96% at low current (and 99.0% at 1 C), and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. EIS analysis reveals a very low charge-transfer activation energy (0.12 eV), indicating excellent kinetic properties at the electrode/electrolyte interface. The study demonstrates that KAc-based WISE electrolytes, by leveraging the solubility of common acetate salts, offer a viable, low-cost, and non-toxic alternative to fluorinated WISE systems for practical energy storage applications.

Research Context
Conventional lithium-ion batteries using non-aqueous organic carbonate electrolytes suffer from safety risks, high cost, and poor low-temperature performance due to low flash points and high viscosities. The non-aqueous LiPF₆ electrolyte is thermally unstable and generates HF in the presence of moisture, corroding battery components. Aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety, low cost, and high ionic conductivity but are limited by a narrow electrochemical stability window of 1.23 V. Diluted aqueous salt solutions kinetically extend this window to 1.5 V, yet these systems cannot compete with organic electrolytes in energy density. The 'Water-in-Salt' (WISE) concept, pioneered by Suo et al. with 21 mol kg⁻¹ LiTFSI in water, achieves a 3 V voltage window by reducing water activity. Despite these gains, fluorinated salts such as LiTFSI, FTFSI, and NaFSI are environmentally concerning, expensive, and exhibit significant toxicity, limiting their practical implementation. The primary bottleneck for new WISE formulations is the lack of suitable, highly soluble, and cost-effective salts to reach super-concentration regimes. CH₃COOK (KAc) has been investigated for K-ion batteries, supercapacitors, and binary electrolytes, offering high solubility and wide availability.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question addresses whether a KAc-based binary aqueous electrolyte system can match or exceed the physicochemical performance of fluorinated WISE systems while using cost-effective, non-toxic acetate salts. The study systematically examines the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH₃COOK mixed with 1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH₃COONa to establish structure-property relationships in the concentrated regime. A secondary implicit hypothesis is that the most concentrated composition (7N20K) will strike the optimal compromise between ionic transport (conductivity) and electrochemical stability, as the ESW is expected to broaden with increasing salt concentration. The paper also tests the practical applicability by investigating Na⁺ intercalation into a carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (NASICON) electrode in the 7N20K electrolyte, with the prediction that the WISE environment will enhance both capacity and efficiency compared to dilute solutions. EIS analysis is employed to quantify the charge-transfer kinetics, with the expected finding that the highly concentrated electrolyte will suppress water decomposition and facilitate ion transfer at low activation energy.

Methodological Details
Four electrolytes were prepared by dissolving 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH₃COOK and varying CH₃COONa concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, 7 mol kg⁻¹) in Milli-Q water (σ = 6.7 µS cm⁻¹) under sonication. A 1 M CH₃COONa solution was prepared as a dilute reference for comparison. The carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (CLTP) was synthesized via a one-pot sol-gel route: 1.78 g NH₄H₂(PO₄)₃ in 40 ml ethanol, 3.51 g Ti(OC₄H₉)₄ as the titanium source, 0.52 g CH₃COOLi·2H₂O as lithium source, and 0.58 g C₆H₁₂O₆ as carbon source. The mixture was stirred for 4 h at 55°C in a sealed container, then heated to 80°C to obtain a gel, dried under vacuum at 100°C, and calcined at 800°C for 6 h under argon flow with a ramp rate of 5°C min⁻¹ and gas flow of 50 ml min⁻¹ in a tubular furnace. Pristine LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (LTP) was synthesized identically without the glucose carbon precursor for comparison. XRD analysis was performed using Rigaku Miniflex 600 with Cu cathode over 10° to 80° with step size 0.02 and scan speed 1 deg min⁻¹. SEM characterization was done using Zeiss Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity was measured with MCR Rheometer 102 (Anthon Paar) using a parallel plate (50 mm) setup at shear rates of 10⁻³⁻³⁰₀ s⁻¹ at 10, 20, 30, and 40°C. Thermal analysis (DSC) was performed with Mettler Toledo DSC 1Star over −120°C to 90°C at 1°C min⁻¹ cooling and heating rates, with samples equilibrated at 30°C for 30 min. Conductivity was measured by EIS using a dip probe cell with two Pt foils in a glass casing (cell factor 1.04 cm⁻¹), from 1 Hz to 200 kHz with 25 mV amplitude, under N₂ flux at 5 to 70°C. Electrode materials were initially characterized in organic electrolytes: slurries (active material:PVDF:carbon black = 8:1:1 in NMP) cast on Al foils for R2032 coin cells in argon-filled glovebox ([O₂]<0.1 ppm, [H₂O]<0.1 ppm). Active material loads were ~2.4, ~2.7, and ~1.7 mg cm⁻² for Li, Na, and K cells, respectively, using 1.0 M LiPF₆ in EC/DMC, 1 M NaClO₄ in PC/FEC, and 0.8 M KPF₆ in EC/DEC. For aqueous measurements, carbon cloth current collectors were dip-coated in active material slurries with an active material load of ~6 mg cm⁻² to avoid corrosion. The Electrochemical Stability Window (ESW) was estimated in flooded three-electrode cells with glassy carbon working, Pt mesh counter, and double-junction SCE reference electrodes. GCPL was conducted at different current rates (0.1C, 0.5C, 1C, 5C, 10C; 1C = 136 mA g⁻¹) with each rate held for 10 cycles. EIS for electrode/electrolyte interface was recorded from 1 kHz to 100 kHz at 50 mV under N₂ in a flooded three-electrode cell inside a Faraday cage, at temperature steps from 20°C to 70°C. The diffusion coefficient calculation used n = 1.7 mobile ions, Faraday constant F = 96485 C mol⁻¹, and mobile ion concentration C = 12930 mol m⁻³.

Procedures And Architectures
Electrolytes were synthesized by dissolving KAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) at 20 mol kg⁻¹ and variable NaAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) in Milli-Q water under sonication. The four electrolytes tested were 1N20K, 2.5N20K, 5N20K, and 7N20K, alongside a 1 M NaAc solution for dilute comparison. The CLTP electrode was synthesized via one-pot sol-gel: NH₄H₂(PO₄)₃ (1.78 g) in ethanol (40 ml), Ti(OC₄H₉)₄ (3.51 g), CH₃COOLi·2H₂O (0.52 g), C₆H₁₂O₆ (0.58 g); stirred 4 h at 55°C, heated to 80°C, dried at 100°C, calcined at 800°C for 6 h in Ar. DSC measurements: Samples equilibrated at 30°C (30 min), cooled from 30°C to −120°C at 1°C min⁻¹, 5 min isotherm at −120°C, then heated to 90°C at 1°C min⁻¹ with STARe® software for data evaluation. Rheology: Parallel plate (50 mm) shear tests at steady-state, shear rates 10⁻³ to 300 s⁻¹ at four temperatures. Conductivity: EIS dip probe cell, frequency 1 Hz to 200 kHz, 25 mV amplitude, samples degassed with N₂ before measurement under N₂ flux. ESW determination: LSV profiles versus SHE on glassy carbon, with decomposition threshold of 0.1 mA cm⁻². GCPL protocol: 10 cycles at 0.1C, increasing every 10 cycles to 0.5C, 1C, 5C, 10C, then decreasing back to 0.1C. EIS interface characterization: Temperature range 20°C to 70°C in climatic chamber, frequency 1 kHz to 100 kHz, sinusoidal voltage 50 mV, Faraday cage shielding. The NASICON structure (R-3c space group, JCPDS: 35-0754) was confirmed by XRD, and phase purity established by absence of secondary peaks. The carbon coating on NASICON was confirmed by SEM and XRD, with no change in peak positions relative to LTP, indicating carbon does not affect crystal structure. The electrolyte solution structure was probed via DSC Tg shifts, rheological VTF/Arrhenius behavior, conductivity VTF/Arrhenius behavior, and Walden plots. The Kohlrausch law of strong electrolytes was applied to evaluate ion dissociation at 25°C: Λₘ = Λ₀ - Ac^{1/2}. EIS spectra for CLTP/7N20K were collected during desodiation, interrupted in the middle of the first plateau, at every 10°C step from 20°C to 70°C.

Key Results
DSC thermograms revealed glass transition temperatures (Tg) below −70°C, cold crystallization exotherms (Tc) below −20°C, and melting endotherms (Tm) around 0°C for all samples, with Tg increasing with salt concentration. Samples 1N20K and 2.5N20K showed no cold crystallization or melting endotherm, remaining frozen in the glassy state under the thermal protocol. Samples 5N20K and 7N20K exhibited single cold crystallization events at −28.06°C and −33.70°C respectively, with melting endotherms starting well below room temperature. Ionic conductivity decreased with increasing salt concentration, but the most concentrated 7N20K electrolyte maintained 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C, comparable to organic counterparts. All conductivity-temperature curves followed Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher (VTF) behavior, with decreasing conductivity associated with Tg shift and increasing viscosity. The activation energy for ionic transport (Ea) increased with concentration, in good agreement with DSC Tg behavior, confirming correlated bulk transport and glass-transition mechanisms. Viscosities followed Arrhenius behavior over the explored temperature range and increased non-linearly with concentration, indicating complex ion interactions at elevated concentrations. The acetate solutions behaved as 'structure-making salts' as no sample showed viscosity decrease with increasing salt concentration, signifying reduced water activity. Walden plots classified all electrolytes as quasi-ideal, with the 7N20K electrolyte following Kohlrausch's law of strong electrolytes at 25°C with Λ₀ = 52.90 Ω·cm²·mol⁻¹. LSV showed cathodic decomposition suppressed (hydrogen evolution reduced) with increasing salt concentration, confirming reduced water activity. Anodic ESW expansion was less significant than cathodic, consistent with previously reported acetate-based electrolyte results. CLTP reversibly inserted Na⁺ at ∼−0.7 V vs. SHE, with preferential sodium over potassium insertion despite 2.85 times lower Na⁺ concentration. In the 7N20K WISE electrolyte, CLTP achieved first-cycle cathodic capacity of 104 mAh g⁻¹ and anodic capacity of 84 mAh g⁻¹ (80% charge efficiency). In the 1 M NaAc diluted solution, capacities decreased to 96 mAh g⁻¹ (cathodic) and 36 mAh g⁻¹ (anodic), yielding only 40% charge efficiency. At 1 C (136 mA g⁻¹), CLTP in 7N20K maintained an average anodic capacity of 68 mAh g⁻¹ with 99.0% average charge efficiency. After 60 cycles at 1 C, the CLTP/7N20K interface retained 90% of initial capacity. EIS on sodiated CLTP revealed a charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV, proving very good kinetic properties at the NASICON/electrolyte interface. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was calculated at ∼10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹, in line with literature; the diffusion activation energy was 0.48 eV, suggesting easy temperature-dependent improvement. Aqueous electrolyte improved alkaline-ion diffusion inside the electrode compared to organic electrolytes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Tg-concentration correlation confirms the transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt character, with ions outnumbering water molecules in the solvation shell. The high-temperature liquidus points (from related systems at 28–50°C) suggest the 7N20K electrolyte will prevent premature cell failure from salt crystallization. The VTF behavior and increased Ea(σ) with concentration attribute conductivity loss to stronger ion-water interactions and higher activation barriers for ion movement. The structure-making behavior (viscosity increase) indicates strongly hydrated cations and acetate anions contribute to molecular ordering, reducing water activity. Quasi-ideal behavior on Walden plots and Kohlrausch law adherence confirm complete salt dissociation even at super-concentrations, validating the electrolyte's ionic nature. The low charge-transfer Ea (0.12 eV) implies rapid interfacial kinetics, enabling efficient ion insertion/extraction at the NASICON/7N20K boundary. The 7N20K electrolyte achieves conductivity and ESW sufficient for Na-ion battery operation while using low-cost, non-toxic acetate salts, establishing a viable path for aqueous-based alkaline storage. The preferential Na⁺ insertion over K⁺ (despite 2.85× lower Na concentration) is attributed to the lower chemical potential and matching NASICON lattice requirements.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ESW estimation via LSV on a quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode with small surface area may overestimate decomposition limits, as the threshold of 0.1 mA cm⁻² involves significant electrolyte. The anodic ESW expansion is notably less significant than the cathodic suppression, limiting the effective high-voltage window available for battery operation. EIS measurements were performed in a flooded cell configuration, which may not fully capture behavior in an operational, non-flooded battery cell. The study reports a single composition (7N20K) for battery testing, and the performance at other concentrations was not independently verified for device applications. The long-term cycling was limited to 60 cycles, insufficient to assess true durability or cycle-life predictions for commercial operation. The diffusion coefficient calculation relies on a fixed volume assumption (C = 12930 mol m⁻³), which may not hold as ions move into and out of the NASICON lattice during cycling. No detailed information on the random seed, specific scan speed for EIS at each step, or individual EIS data points was reported in the main text.

Claims
The 7N20K electrolyte is the optimal composition among the studied binary acetates, providing a superior compromise between ionic conductivity and electrochemical stability window. Conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C remains comparable to organic counterparts even at 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc. ESW extends up to 3 V in ideal flooded conditions, surpassing the 1.5 V limit of diluted aqueous systems. No cold crystallization at room temperature prevents premature cell failure due to salt precipitation. The anodic ESW expansion is less pronounced than the cathodic suppression, constraining the practical voltage window. The LSV measurement procedure may overestimate the ESW due to the quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode. The 7N20K electrolyte is a strong candidate for alkaline-ion battery cathodes using NASICON architectures. The use of KAc and NaAc avoids the environmental and economic burdens of fluorinated WISE electrolytes.
The CLTP/7N20K interface exhibits excellent kinetic and capacity performance for reversibly inserting sodium ions. First-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹ with 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. Average charge efficiency of 99.0% at 1 C (136 mA g⁻¹). Charge-transfer activation energy of only 0.12 eV. Diffusion coefficient of ∼10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹, improving over organic-electrolyte-based diffusion. Only 60 cycles were tested, insufficient for lifetime assessment. No data is provided for potassium-ion insertion into the NASICON electrode in this electrolyte. The CLTP electrode demonstrates practical viability as a sodium anode in WISE electrolytes. The combination of low charge-transfer Ea and favorable diffusion kinetics positions this system well for high-power applications.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information files (shear stress curves, XRPD patterns, SEM images, thermal analysis, and additional electrochemical characterization) are available free of charge via the corresponding author. No specific repository or code availability statement is provided in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A control sample (pristine LiTi₂(PO₄)₃) was synthesized without glucose to isolate the effect of the carbon coating on NASICON. The same electrode was tested in 1 M NaAc diluted electrolyte to isolate the effect of WISE concentration on electrochemical performance. EIS measurements were conducted at every 10°C step from 20°C to 70°C to verify the temperature dependence of charge-transfer kinetics. Rheology was measured at four temperatures (10, 20, 30, 40°C) to establish Arrhenius behavior of viscosity. Conductivity was measured from 5 to 70°C with degassing and N₂ flux to ensure robustness.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents DSC thermograms of the four electrolyte solutions, showing concentration-dependent Tg, Tc, and Tm features (ENDO direction bottom). Figure 2 shows (a) ionic conductivity versus temperature (VTF fit) and (b) conductivity versus concentration for all compositions. Figure 3 displays (a) viscosity versus temperature (Arrhenius fit) and (b) the evolution of viscosity with temperature for all electrolyte samples. Figure 4 shows (a) Walden plots (molar/ionic conductivities vs. fluidity) and (b) Kohlrausch law fit for 7N20K at 25°C. Figure 5 presents LSV profiles versus SHE for all electrolyte samples to determine decomposition potentials. Figure 7 displays (a) GCPL potential profiles for CLTP in 7N20K versus 1 M NaAc, and (b) capacity-vs-cycle for both, with C-rate analysis. Figure 8 shows the EIS spectra (depressed semicircle and Warburg line) at each temperature step for the partially sodiated CLTP. Figure 9 presents the Arrhenius plot of charge-transfer resistance with fitted activation energy and diffusion coefficient calculations. Table 1 lists the electrolyte composition parameters (concentration, molarity). Table 2 reports key transport and thermal parameters: molar conductivity (Λₘ), Ea(σ), activation energy from viscosity (Ea(η)), Tg, T₀, and molar conductivity at infinite dilution (Λ₀). Table 3 summarizes the cathodic and anodic decomposition potentials for all electrolyte samples at 0.1 mA cm⁻² threshold.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the systematic physicochemical characterization of KAc/NaAc binary WISE electrolytes (20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc + 1–7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc), proving that 7N20K achieves 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ conductivity, a 3 V ESW, and no crystallization at room temperature using low-cost, non-toxic salts. 2. The strongest evidence is the proof-of-concept sodium-ion battery testing: CLTP in 7N20K achieved 85 mAh g⁻¹ anodic capacity, 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles, 99.0% charge efficiency at 1 C, and a very low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. 3. The future path involves developing alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries based on KAc-derived WISE electrolytes, utilizing NASICON architectures as anodes, and optimizing electrode/electrolyte interfaces to achieve commercial-level cycling performance and stability.

summary.authors: Yuki Kamijo (The University of Tokyo); Ratmir Derda (University of Alberta)

summary.executive_summary:
This paper presents the development of a high-throughput screening (HTS) implementation of the freeze-float selection platform for measuring ice nucleation events in aqueous droplets, expanding upon a previous proof-of-concept system. The original system used a 1 cm² geometry cuvette containing up to 50 × 1 µL droplets but was limited by the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil, preventing scaling and introducing significant thermal lag (a few degrees' difference among 10 cuvettes in parallel). The new system replaces manual droplet generation with the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system, which generates up to ~3800 uniform 1 µL droplets in a 96-deep-well plate within approximately 15 minutes at 40 droplets per well. Droplet monodispersity is confirmed via image analysis (9.2% polydispersity, corresponding to <±0.09 °C in freezing temperature). Static electricity, which causes droplet coalescence, is mitigated using an Auto-set Ion Pump and wet filter paper during transport. The system's throughput is increased by a factor of 38 (from 50 to 1920 droplets in 48 cryovials). A central methodological improvement is the adoption of the Asymptote VIA Freeze™ Research controlled-rate freezer, providing linear cooling down to -0.5 °C/min. Under constant temperature (-28 °C) in a 96-deep-well plate, cell-to-cell thermal gradient was significant (p = 4.4 × 10⁻⁷); linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) reduced this to p = 0.31 but widened the freezing time range (47.4 and 50.6 min). In the Asymptote freezer (48 × 1 mL cryovials), droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C, while INA-free droplets did not freeze until -12.3 °C. This compared to -7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the commodity freezer. Uniformity in the Asymptote freezer (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) was superior to the 96-deep-well system (p = 0.31, standard deviation 1.6), representing a 36% reduction in dispersion. The authors conclude that the automated dispensing and controlled-rate cooling enable high-throughput, accurate ice nucleation measurements, though droplet stability is compromised when moving between laboratories due to static electricity.

 The system successfully validated by reproducing freeze-float behavior observed in the previous publication, confirming that the new platform maintains the core experimental principle while substantially increasing throughput and temperature uniformity. The detection threshold of INA concentration was investigated, showing improved differentiation in the controlled-rate system at threshold concentrations. The work demonstrates a functional transition from a low-throughput cuvette-based assay to a scalable multi-well/cryovial platform suitable for large-scale screening of ice-nucleating entities.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the development of a high-throughput screening (HTS) implementation of the freeze-float selection platform for measuring ice nucleation events in aqueous droplets, expanding upon a previous proof-of-concept system. The original system used a 1 cm² geometry cuvette containing up to 50 × 1 µL droplets but was limited by the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil, preventing scaling and introducing significant thermal lag (a few degrees' difference among 10 cuvettes in parallel). Droplet monodispersity is confirmed via image analysis (9.2% polydispersity, corresponding to <±0.09 °C in freezing temperature). Static electricity, which causes droplet coalescence, is mitigated using an Auto-set Ion Pump and wet filter paper during transport. The system's throughput is increased by a factor of 38 (from 50 to 1920 droplets in 48 cryovials). A central methodological improvement is the adoption of the Asymptote VIA Freeze™ Research controlled-rate freezer, providing linear cooling down to -0.5 °C/min. Under constant temperature (-28 °C) in a 96-deep-well plate, cell-to-cell thermal gradient was significant (p = 4.4 × 10⁻⁷); linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) reduced this to p = 0.31 but widened the freezing time range (47.4 and 50.6 min). In the Asymptote freezer (48 × 1 mL cryovials), droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C, while INA-free droplets did not freeze until -12.3 °C. This compared to -7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the commodity freezer. Uniformity in the Asymptote freezer (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) was superior to the 96-deep-well system (p = 0.31, standard deviation 1.6), representing a 36% reduction in dispersion. The authors conclude that the automated dispensing and controlled-rate cooling enable high-throughput, accurate ice nucleation measurements, though droplet stability is compromised when moving between laboratories due to static electricity.

 The system successfully validated by reproducing freeze-float behavior observed in the previous publication, confirming that the new platform maintains the core experimental principle while substantially increasing throughput and temperature uniformity. The detection threshold of INA concentration was investigated, showing improved differentiation in the controlled-rate system at threshold concentrations. The work demonstrates a functional transition from a low-throughput cuvette-based assay to a scalable multi-well/cryovial platform suitable for large-scale screening of ice-nucleating entities.

Research Context
The previous proof-of-concept freeze-float system used a 1 cm² geometry cuvette and accommodated up to 50 droplets. The system successfully separated samples with ice-nucleating activity from those without. The low thermal conductivity of silicone oil limited increasing the container footprint without introducing significant thermal lag. Parallel cuvettes exhibited non-uniform results with temperature differences of a few degrees among 10 cuvettes. The system requires a good heat conductor between cuvettes to improve temperature uniformity among multiple samples. Droplet-based assays in 3456-well microtiter plates can carry out more than 100,000 assays per day with volumes less than 5 µL. Crystallization and enzyme production droplet assays reported a million-fold reduction in reagent consumption and 300-fold increase in throughput. Polydispersity is detrimental because freezing temperature is proportional to the logarithm of droplet diameter. A 1 mm diameter and 0.1 mm diameter droplet pair shows a 2.3 °C difference in mean freezing temperature. Statistical confidence requires more than 30 droplets to obtain a reliable freezing temperature. The prior study hypothesized droplet freezing is a random nucleation process accelerated by ice nucleators. Stochastic freezing behavior results in inherent distributions, complicating temperature determination from small sample sizes. Linear cooling rate is important for the droplet freezing assay in the stochastic model of heterogeneous nucleation measurement. Wills et al. reported cooling rates from 0.8 to 10 K/min produced nucleation rates fitting in a single line.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a high-throughput freeze-float system can be implemented to increase throughput, accuracy, and temperature uniformity for ice nucleation measurement. The primary hypothesis is that automating droplet generation and using controlled-rate cooling will overcome the limitations of the manual cuvette-based system. The system is predicted to increase efficiency by reducing manipulation steps through robotic liquid dispensing. Increased accuracy is expected due to a larger sample size (1920 droplets versus 50 droplets). Increased temperature uniformity is predicted by incorporating a controlled-rate freezer with linear cooling. Droplet monodispersity is expected to yield minimal dispersion in freezing temperature measurement. The stochastic freezing model predicts inherent distributions that must be accounted for by sufficient sample numbers. Linear cooling rate is hypothesized to provide a more consistent detection threshold than constant temperature cooling. The system is predicted to reproduce the freezing-floating behavior observed in the previous cuvette-based publication. The improved cell-to-cell thermal uniformity is expected to reduce statistical significance of temperature differences among wells.

Methodological Details
The study is a methods development publication describing a system expansion from the previous publication. Droplets are 1 µL aqueous droplets prepared with silicone oil and HFE-7500 as a cushion. The silicone oil buoyant layer contains 1% silicone surfactant. The HFE-7500 serves as a cushion layer at the bottom of the droplet system. A 96-deep-well plate compatible with the Biomek 3000 was used for automated droplet generation. The Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) was introduced for parallel droplet generation. 30 droplets per well were dispensed at 1 droplet per 2 seconds. 40 uniform droplets were generated in each of the 96 wells, yielding up to ~3800 droplets total. The entire dispensing operation for 96 wells takes approximately 15 minutes. Monodispersity was assessed using 60 droplets with fluorescein dye in a 12-well plate. Images were acquired by a ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad, CA). Droplet diameters were measured by a Matlab automated circle detection program named Droplet_Dispersion.m. Polydispersity was calculated as standard deviation of radii divided by mean radius, yielding 9.2%. The expected dispersion in freezing temperature from polydispersity was ±0.09 °C. Static electricity from the Biomek 3000 was removed using an Auto-set Ion Pump (#19500, Charles Water, MA). Wet filter paper was placed below the plastic plate during droplet transport. Validation droplets contained 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein dye. A commodity freezer was used for the initial validation at constant temperature -28 °C. The Asymptote VIA Freeze™ Research controlled-rate freezer (Cambridge, UK) was used for the HTS implementation. The freezer accommodates up to 48 × 1 mL cryovials in a metal holder. Each cryovial contained 50 µL HFE-7500, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, and 20 droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax. 20 INA-free Milli Q water droplets were marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye per cryovial. Droplets were measured over time during cooling in both generic and controlled-rate freezers. A Python script KStest.ipynb was used for Kolmogorov-Smirnov test comparisons.

Procedures And Architectures
The system architecture was expanded from a 1 cm² cuvette to 48 cryovials, increasing throughput from 50 to 1920 droplets. A metal cooling plate and sample holder achieved homogeneous cooling through the vials. The Asymptote freezer provides constant rate cooling with high precision down to -0.5 °C/min. The freezer was equipped with a custom-made glass lid for automated image recording by a generic digital camera. The Biomek 3000 replaced manual repeat pipetting for droplet generation. Simple modification to the Biomek program allowed changing droplet number and size. The 96-deep-well plate setup was tested first for compatibility with the Biomek 3000. Validation involved 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax in a 96-deep-well system. The KStest.ipynb script compared cumulative distributions of freezing temperatures and calculated p-values. In the 96-deep-well plate at constant temperature -28 °C, the thermal gradient was significant. Linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min decreased thermal gradient but increased freezing time range. In the Asymptote freezer, droplets with INA froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C and INA-free droplets at -12.3 °C. In the commodity freezer, INA droplets froze at -7.5 ± 0.97 °C. The controlled cooling rate provided better differentiation of INA compared to commodity freezer cooling. The detection threshold of INA concentration was investigated to confirm accuracy.

Key Results
The Biomek 3000 successfully prepared 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax in a 96-deep-well system. The Biomek 3000 generated 40 uniform droplets per well in approximately 15 minutes for 96 wells. The droplet polydispersity was 9.2%, which indicates sufficiently uniform droplet volume. Based on polydispersity, the expected dispersion in nucleation temperature was ±0.09 °C. The throughput was increased by a factor of 38 from 50 to 1920 droplets. The p-value for thermal gradient in a 96-deep-well plate at constant temperature -28 °C was 4.4 × 10⁻⁷. Linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min reduced thermal gradient to p = 0.31 but increased freezing time range to 47.4 and 50.6 min. In the Asymptote freezer, droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C. INA-free droplets in the Asymptote freezer did not freeze until -12.3 °C. In the commodity freezer, INA droplets froze at -7.5 ± 0.97 °C. The 96-deep-well system exhibited p = 0.31 with standard deviation 1.6 in freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer exhibited p = 0.83 with standard deviation 0.73 in freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer showed overall 36% lower dispersion compared to the 96-deep-well system. The controlled cooling rate provided better differentiation accuracies for INA at threshold concentrations. Droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories due to static electricity causing coalescence.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results confirm that automating droplet generation and using controlled-rate linear cooling overcomes previous throughput and uniformity limitations. The 9.2% polydispersity confirms that robotic dispensing produces sufficiently monodisperse droplets for quantitative freezing measurements. The improved p-value from 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ to 0.31 (96-well) and 0.83 (Asymptote) demonstrates reduced cell-to-cell thermal gradient. The 36% reduction in dispersion confirms that controlled-rate cooling is superior to constant temperature cooling for uniformity. The stochastic freezing behavior inherent to ice nucleation requires sufficient sample numbers (>30) to extract reliable parameters. The controlled-rate freezer provided better differentiation accuracies for INA at threshold concentrations than commodity freezer cooling. The system is now capable of measuring tens of thousands of ice nucleation events in a single experiment, aligning with droplet assay advantages.

Contradictions And Limitations
While linear cooling reduced thermal gradient (p = 0.31 vs. 4.4 × 10⁻⁷), it significantly increased the range of freezing time (47.4 and 50.6 min). Droplet stability was not sufficient when transferred over distances (e.g., between laboratories) due to static electricity causing coalescence. Due to the coalescence problem, it was not successful to combine the droplets generation system with transport. The paper mentions the previous publication used a commodity freezer, but does not specify the exact model or temperature control specifications beyond constant temperature -28 °C. The statistical confidence formula n ≈ (2k·CI/s)² implies a dependence on s²; however, the exact value of s (standard deviation) used for the calculation is not reported. The paper does not report on the effect of droplet-to-droplet interactions within the cryovial at 20 droplets per vial. Sensitivity to INA concentration below threshold is mentioned but the exact threshold value is not reported in this publication. The exact random seed or specific Biomek 3000 parameters beyond dispensing rate and volume are not detailed.

Claims
The automated freeze-float system achieves high throughput (factor of 38) and superior temperature uniformity compared to the previous cuvette-based approach. The system expanded from 50 to 1920 droplets in 48 cryovials, a 38-fold throughput increase. The Asymptote freezer showed p = 0.83 and standard deviation 0.73 in freezing temperature, vs p = 0.31 and std dev 1.6 in the 96-well plate. Overall dispersion in the Asymptote freezer was 36% lower than in the 96-deep-well system. The Biomek 3000 generated 40 uniform droplets per well in approximately 15 minutes. Linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min increased the freezing time range (47.4 and 50.6 min) despite reducing the thermal gradient. Droplet stability was insufficient for inter-laboratory transport due to static electricity causing coalescence. The system can be implemented for large-scale screening of ice-nucleating entities with reliable freezing temperatures. The controlled-rate freezer overcomes thermal gradient limitations that hindered scaling in the commodity freezer.
Robotic droplet generation produces sufficiently monodisperse droplets for quantitative freezing temperature measurement. Polydispersity was measured at 9.2%, confirming droplets have sufficiently uniform volume. The expected temperature dispersion from polydispersity was ±0.09 °C. Droplets from the Biomek system showed freezing and floating behavior in good agreement with the previous cuvette-based publication. The 9.2% polydispersity still corresponds to a ±0.09 °C uncertainty, which may be limiting for precision applications. Robotic dispensing is a viable replacement for manual repeat pipetting in droplet-based nucleation assays. The use of a cushion layer and ion pump is necessary to maintain droplet integrity.

Data And Code Availability
Source code for droplet dispersion measurement (Droplet_Dispersion.m) is cited as Source Code S1. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test script (KStest.ipynb) is cited as Source Code S3. No explicit code repository or data availability statement is provided in the publication.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The thermal gradient was compared at constant temperature -28 °C versus linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) in the 96-deep-well plate. The commodity freezer vs. Asymptote freezer comparison served as an ablation-like comparison of temperature uniformity. Uniformity was assessed at two positions: well-to-well in a single plate and across 48 cryovials in the freezer. The statistical significance was quantified using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test p-values for different cooling modes and freezer types.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows the 96-deep-well plate compatible with the Biomek 3000. Figure 1C shows fluorescent image of droplets for monodispersity assessment. Figure 1D-E show the polydispersity analysis results. Figure 2 shows the freeze-float validation experiment with Snomax droplets in the commodity freezer. Figure 3 shows freezing temperature distributions in the 96-deep-well plate at constant temperature. Figure 4 shows droplet freezing temperatures in the Asymptote freezer. Figure 5 shows well-to-well freezing temperature distribution in the Asymptote freezer. Figure 6 shows the overall 36% lower dispersion comparison between systems. The paper mentions Figure 6 specifically for the dispersion comparison.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of a high-throughput freeze-float platform that scales ice nucleation measurement from 50 to 1920 droplets using a Biomek 3000 robotic dispenser and an Asymptote controlled-rate freezer, achieving a 38-fold throughput increase. 2. The strongest evidence is the 36% reduction in freezing temperature dispersion and the improved p-value (0.83 vs. 0.31) in the Asymptote freezer compared to the 96-deep-well plate, confirming that controlled-rate linear cooling overcomes the thermal gradient limitation. 3. The future path involves addressing the droplet stability and static electricity issue for inter-laboratory transport, improving monodispersity below 9.2%, and characterizing the INA concentration detection threshold in the high-throughput system.

summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.field_subfield: Synthetic organic chemistry; organophotoredox catalysis; continuous flow synthesis
summary.executive_summary: This work reports a continuous flow protocol for the radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition dimerization of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, using organophotoredox catalysis. The method combines a commercially available off-the-shelf continuous flow platform with a homogeneous small-molecule, sustainable, pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst, delivering cyclobutane functional materials and natural products without the cryogenic temperatures, deoxygenated solvents, and extended reaction times required by traditional batch conditions. A batch versus continuous flow study on vinyl carbazole (VCZ) demonstrates that continuous flow at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min) with 2 mol% catalyst and 450 nm irradiation provides t-DCzCB (1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane) in 98% isolated yield, whereas the batch conditions required 3 mol% catalyst, deoxygenated acetone, and cryogenic temperatures with lower yield. Further optimization revealed that reducing flow rate to 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 100 min) drops the yield to 53% and generates carbazole byproduct, indicating that reaction kinetics favor shorter residence times. The 10 mmol scale synthesis of t-DCzCB achieved 79% isolated yield with only 0.1 mol% catalyst, nearing the 0.025% catalyst loadings reported for ruthenium- and iridium-photoredox systems. A broad substrate scope was explored, including various bromo-substituted vinyl carbazoles, mono- and disubstituted carbazoles, and electron-rich styrenes. Notable flow-improved substrates include 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (48% to 64%), 4-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole, and 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (65%). In contrast, 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole failed to dimerize, and 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole showed comparable batch and flow yields. The method was extended to styrene dimerization: 4-methoxystyrene provided the dimer in 44%, styrene with diethylaniline gave pellucidin A in 22%, and E-aserone gave magnosalin in 40% (10 mmol scale), all under flow conditions without cryogenic cooling. The protocol is framed as a general, robust, and scalable route to valuable carbazole host materials and styrene-based lignan dimeric natural products, demonstrating distinct advantages over conventional batch photoredox chemistry in scalability and operational simplicity.

claims.description: Continuous flow provides superior yields and reduced reaction times for radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition dimerization compared to traditional batch organophotoredox conditions.
The protocol delivers cyclobutane functional materials possessing functionality for exploitation as novel photophysical host materials.
The continuous flow protocol provides a scalable synthesis of the styrene-based lignan dimeric natural product magnosalin.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports a continuous flow protocol for the radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition dimerization of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, using organophotoredox catalysis. The method combines a commercially available off-the-shelf continuous flow platform with a homogeneous small-molecule, sustainable, pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst, delivering cyclobutane functional materials and natural products without the cryogenic temperatures, deoxygenated solvents, and extended reaction times required by traditional batch conditions. A batch versus continuous flow study on vinyl carbazole (VCZ) demonstrates that continuous flow at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min) with 2 mol% catalyst and 450 nm irradiation provides t-DCzCB (1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane) in 98% isolated yield, whereas the batch conditions required 3 mol% catalyst, deoxygenated acetone, and cryogenic temperatures with lower yield. Further optimization revealed that reducing flow rate to 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 100 min) drops the yield to 53% and generates carbazole byproduct, indicating that reaction kinetics favor shorter residence times. The 10 mmol scale synthesis of t-DCzCB achieved 79% isolated yield with only 0.1 mol% catalyst, nearing the 0.025% catalyst loadings reported for ruthenium- and iridium-photoredox systems. A broad substrate scope was explored, including various bromo-substituted vinyl carbazoles, mono- and disubstituted carbazoles, and electron-rich styrenes. Notable flow-improved substrates include 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (48% to 64%), 4-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole, and 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (65%). In contrast, 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole failed to dimerize, and 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole showed comparable batch and flow yields. The method was extended to styrene dimerization: 4-methoxystyrene provided the dimer in 44%, styrene with diethylaniline gave pellucidin A in 22%, and E-aserone gave magnosalin in 40% (10 mmol scale), all under flow conditions without cryogenic cooling. The protocol is framed as a general, robust, and scalable route to valuable carbazole host materials and styrene-based lignan dimeric natural products, demonstrating distinct advantages over conventional batch photoredox chemistry in scalability and operational simplicity.

Research Context
The dimerization of electron-rich alkene building blocks such as enamines and styrenes provides a convenient synthetic route to valuable cyclobutane functional materials and natural products. Vinyl carbazole (VCZ), a monomer for conductive polymers, serves as a precursor to 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane, used as a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs. Naturally occurring styrenes such as E-aserone can be viewed as precursors of dimeric cyclobutyl natural products such as the anti-inflammatory lignan magnosalin. Synthesis of these cyclobutanes is accomplished via a radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition where the key intermediate is a radical cation. The radical cation intermediate can be generated through chemical oxidation or photochemical methods of an electron-rich alkene. Photochemical dimerization of VCZ was first reported by Ellinger and Ledwith in 1965 using organophotosensitizers, and more recently a TiO₂ photodimerization was achieved by Mizuno. With the emergence of visible light photoredox catalysis, Yoon demonstrated the effectiveness of Ru- and Ir-complexes in synthesizing symmetrical and unsymmetrical cyclobutanes. Nicewicz reported the dimerization of several classes of electron-rich alkenes using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst. The use of organophotoredox catalysts over metal-based catalysts offers advantages in environmental, sustainability, and cost factors. However, reaction times for organophotoredox-catalyzed dimerizations were excessive, cryogenic conditions were required, and catalyst loadings of 3 mol% were higher than the 0.025% achievable with Ru/Ir systems. Continuous flow technology offers advantages in photoredox transformations, transferring batch reactions to flow can lead to more efficient irradiation and higher conversions. A heterogeneous photoredox fixed-bed flow process using metal-free polymeric carbon nitrides was reported for a scalable route to magnosalin through E-aserone dimerization.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether merging a small-molecule, sustainable organophotoredox catalyst with continuous flow technology can deliver cyclobutane functional materials and natural products more efficiently than traditional batch conditions. The hypothesis is that a batch versus continuous flow study will demonstrate that continuous flow provides a convenient synthetic route to t-DCzCB with reduced reaction times and catalyst loadings compared to conventional batch chemistry. A secondary hypothesis is that the protocol can be extended to a novel class of functional materials (functionalized t-DCzCBs) and improved synthetic routes to styrene-based lignan dimeric natural products. The authors anticipate that the continuous flow approach will provide a convenient, environmentally beneficial methodology showcasing advantages over the existing conventional batch chemistry approach. A sub-hypothesis is that the flow rate and catalyst loading can be optimized to balance reaction kinetics, yield, and product purity, particularly for more challenging or sensitive substrates. The authors further hypothesize that the bromine-substituted cyclobutane products could serve as viable synthetic building blocks amenable to subsequent synthetic manipulation, thereby expanding the utility of the methodology.

Methodological Details
The study began with a comparison of continuous flow versus batch reaction conditions on commercially available vinyl carbazole (VCZ). The batch synthesis of t-DCzCB used organophotoredox catalyst 10 at 3 mol% under the conditions of Nicewiez, in deoxygenated acetone, at cryogenic temperatures, with extended reaction times. The continuous flow platform was a commercial, off-the-shelf system selected for its excellent usability and improved availability. Optimization of the continuous flow synthesis of 1 was determined through HPLC analysis using p-terphenyl as an internal standard, requiring calibration of substrates 2 and 1. The flow reactions were performed at a concentration of 0.4 M in acetone using the flow rate, catalyst loading, and wavelength stated for each entry. The batch versus flow comparison for brominated substrates required a reduced concentration of 0.2 M in acetone due to solubility limitations of the vinyl carbazole intermediates. The 10 mmol scale experiment for t-DCzCB used 0.1 mol% of catalyst 10 at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹. Styrene dimerization substrates were added with an electron relay (anthracene or diethylaniline) to suppress undesired polymerization, following the strategy of Nicewicz and co-workers. The electron relay (0.25 eq. of anthracene) was added to the starting solution of the styrene before introduction into the continuous flow apparatus. For styrene building blocks, the substrates were E-aserone, 4-methoxystyrene, and styrene, tested at a 10 mmol scale. Vinylation of brominated carbazoles was achieved using the method of Obora and co-workers, providing each vinyl carbazole in moderate to good yields, with the exception of 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole.

Procedures And Architectures
The organophotoredox catalyst 10 is a pyrillium catalyst, used as a homogeneous small-molecule, sustainable photocatalyst for the radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition. The batch reaction conditions (entry 9a) used 3 mol% catalyst 10 in deoxygenated acetone at cryogenic temperatures with extended reaction times to achieve optimal conversion. Optimal continuous flow conditions for VCZ to t-DCzCB were realized at a flow rate of 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min), with 2 mol% catalyst loading at 450 nm irradiation. Two additional wavelengths, 405 nm and 420 nm, were tested at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ and provided comparable yields to 450 nm. For the 10 mmol scale synthesis, 0.1 mol% catalyst 10 was used at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹, yielding t-DCzCB 1 in 79% isolated yield. Brominated vinyl carbazoles (12a–17a) were dimerized under both batch and continuous flow conditions, with the flow rate adjusted to 0.2 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 50 min) for the 0.2 M experiments. Substrates were further functionalized: 2-chloro-(18a), 2-methoxy-(19a), bis-vinylated 2-hydroxycarbazole (20a), and Suzuki-derived arylated vinyl carbazoles (21a–24a). The styrene scope used anthracene as an electron relay (0.25 eq.) added to the styrene solution prior to flow entry. Post-dimerization, the 13b product underwent palladium-mediated Suzuki cross-coupling with 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid using Kumar and Tao conditions. A palladium-mediated borylation using bis(pinacolato)diboron was used as a second post-dimerization transformation. The UV absorbance profile of catalyst 10 guided the selection of the two probing wavelengths at 405 nm and 420 nm.

Key Results
In the batch conditions, the organophotoredox dimerization of VCZ using 3 mol% catalyst 10 provided t-DCzCB 1 in 82% isolated yield under cryogenic conditions. At the optimal continuous flow conditions (0.5 mL.min⁻¹, τ = 20 min, 2 mol% catalyst, 450 nm), the yield of t-DCzCB 1 was 98% isolated. Increasing catalyst loading to 4.5 mol% (entry 2) reduced the yield to 90%. Reducing catalyst loading to 1 mol% (entry 3) resulted in a marginal yield reduction to 93%. Reducing the flow rate from 2 to 1 mL.min⁻¹ dropped the yield to 79% (at 2 mol% catalyst) and 82% (at 1 mol% catalyst), respectively. At a very low flow rate of 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 100 min), the yield of 1 dropped to 53% and carbazole was formed as a significant byproduct. At 10 mmol scale with only 0.1 mol% catalyst at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹, t-DCzCB 1 was obtained in 79% isolated yield. For 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (12a), the batch dimerization gave 12b in 48% isolated yield over 5 days, while continuous flow at 0.2 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 50 min) gave 12b in 64% isolated yield in a considerably shorter time. Batch dimerization of 4-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave 13b in 31% isolated yield, whereas continuous flow at 0.2 mL.min⁻¹ gave 13b in 71% isolated yield in a considerably shorter time. For 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (16a), continuous flow conditions provided 16b in 65% isolated yield, with completion under 1h. For 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (17a), batch conditions slightly outperformed continuous flow, giving 17b. 2-chloro-9-vinylcarbazole (18a) gave 18b in 61% yield; 2-methoxy-9-vinylcarbazole (19a) gave 19b in 45% yield. The bis-vinylated 2-hydroxycarbazole (20a) dimerized to the cyclobutyl bis-enolether 21b in 25% isolated yield. The 2-fluoroarylated vinyl carbazole (22a) gave cyclobutane 22b in 65% isolated yield, while the 2-poor-solubility 21a gave 22% yield. 3,6-di-tert-butylcarbazole vinylation gave 23a in quantitative yields, and dimerization gave 23b in 57% yield. The 3,6-bisarylated 9-vinyl carbazole (24a) dimerized to 24b in 50% yield. Post-dimerization, 13b was coupled with 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid to give 25 in 75% yield; borylation of 13b gave 26 in 36% yield. In the styrene scope, 4-methoxystyrene gave dimer 28 in 44% isolated yield with anthracene as electron relay. Styrene with diethylaniline as electron relay provided pellucidin A in 22% isolated yield. E-aserone dimerized to magnosalin 4 in 40% isolated yield on a 10 mmol scale with anthracene as electron relay.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observation that reducing flow rate (increased residence time) decreases yield and promotes carbazole formation suggests that the dimerization may be partially reversible and that carbazole arises from 1 O₂ oxidation of the alkene radical cation to N-formylcarbazole, followed by hydrolysis. The significant yield improvement in flow versus batch for brominated substrates (48% to 64%; 31% to 71%) indicates that the continuous flow regime better manages reaction kinetics and perhaps residence time, suppressing over-reaction or degradation. The success at 0.1 mol% catalyst loading for t-DCzCB demonstrates that organophotoredox catalysis in flow can approach the efficiencies of metal-photoredox systems (0.025% loadings), validating the sustainability claims. The formation of a new family of functionalized t-DCzCBs through direct vinylation of pre-functionalized carbazoles, rather than electrophilic aromatic substitution, expands the accessibility of functional carbazole host materials. The extension to styrene-based lignan dimer synthesis confirms that the radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition is a general mechanism applicable beyond carbazoles, validated by the biomimetic relevance to magnosalin synthesis. The post-dimerization synthetic transformations (Suzuki coupling, borylation) establish the brominated cyclobutanes as genuine synthetic intermediates, not just final products.

Contradictions And Limitations
The 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) substrate failed to dimerize in both batch and flow conditions, with no 1H NMR evidence for 15b, indicating a structural limitation for the methodology. For 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (17a), batch conditions slightly outperformed continuous flow, contradicting the general trend of flow improvement and suggesting a substrate-specific kinetic regime. Solubility of the brominated vinyl carbazole intermediates at 0.4 M proved challenging, necessitating reduction to 0.2 M in acetone, which in turn required readjusting the flow rate. The 21a substrate (poorly soluble) gave only 22% yield for cyclobutane 21b, a significantly lower result compared to its 4-fluoro analogue at 65%, highlighting substrate-specific performance. The bis-vinylated enolether dimer 21b was obtained in only 25% yield, a modest result that may limit practical utility despite the presence of enol ether handles. The styrene scope yields (44%, 22%, 40%) are generally lower than the VCZ yields, suggesting that styrene dimerization faces greater kinetic or stability challenges. summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan; Ken Yamazaki; Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba; Dhananjayan Vasu; Trevor A Hamlin; Darren J Dixon
summary.field_subfield: Organic chemistry / Asymmetric catalysis and total synthesis
summary.executive_summary: The authors report the 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a structurally complex pentacyclic marine natural product isolated from Xestospongia sea sponges. The central breakthrough is a new catalytic and highly enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral ketone to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin, which simultaneously constructs a chiral bicyclic core, establishes three stereogenic centers (including a quaternary carbon), and achieves near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity. The pathway for the key desymmetrization was developed by expanding upon a previously reported intramolecular Michael addition to α,β-unsaturated esters using bifunctional primary amine thiourea organocatalysts. A series of chiral amine catalysts was screened; Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f proved uniquely effective, providing the desired bicyclic adduct in 70% yield with 99% ee as a single diastereomer. The relative and absolute stereochemistry was confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. DFT computations rationalized the enantioselectivity: the transition state TS1 is 3.0 kcal/mol lower in energy than the next-lowest TS, yielding a computed 99% ee in excellent agreement with experimental results. The reaction is highly exergonic (ΔGrxn = −19.4 kcal/mol) and proceeds via a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism stabilized by hydrogen bonding interactions between the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. In the total synthesis, the desymmetrization reaction was applied to a multigram-scale substrate (17E, >5 g), yielding the bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield with >99% ee and single diastereomer. Subsequent steps included an oxidative lactamization (Iwabuchi conditions), two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and two complementary ring-closing metatheses (Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation with p-benzoquinone) to close the macrocyclic rings, completed by a final double amide reduction with LiAlH4 to give synthetic madangamine E. The key RCM step required strategic reconfiguration: the initial RCM route failed due to distant spatial arrangement of terminal alkenes, necessitating an earlier elimination and two-step RCM sequence through a Z-configured skipped diene. All analytical data were consistent with previously reported values for madangamine E, and the method is scalable (17 g intermediate) and reproducible.

The relative and absolute stereochemistry was confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. The reaction is highly exergonic (ΔGrxn = −19.4 kcal/mol) and proceeds via a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism stabilized by hydrogen bonding interactions between the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. In the total synthesis, the desymmetrization reaction was applied to a multigram-scale substrate (17E, >5 g), yielding the bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield with >99% ee and single diastereomer.
