judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at the charged aqueous interfaces of micelles under ambient air atmosphere, achieving yields up to 100% and selectivity of 100%. The photocatalytic system uses Eosin Y as a low-cost, organic photocatalyst and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) as the surfactant to form a micellar scaffold. Within this scaffold, both the photocatalyst and the arylamine substrates are hosted in close proximity, enabling a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with a time constant of 0.3 ps at the micellar interface. The reaction is triggered by green light (525 nm) and requires 4 hours for 100% conversion of electron-rich arylamines, using only 0.6 mole% of the photocatalyst. This approach outperforms the previously reported iridium-based photocatalytic method, which required 64% conversion after 24 hours in bulk acetonitrile with a significantly higher catalyst dose. The remarkable boosting of catalytic efficacy is attributed to the non-diffusive PET and the modulation of redox potentials at the charged aqueous interface. Atmospheric oxygen acts as a sacrificial oxidant, producing hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct. The substrate scope includes electron-rich (100% conversion in 4 h), neutral (98% p-chloroaniline, 95% p-bromoaniline), and electron-deficient arylamines. The PET mechanism is validated through fluorescence quenching (linear Stern-Volmer plot, kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M⁻¹s⁻¹), ultrafast fluorescence up-conversion, and radical trapping with 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol (BHT), which produces a characteristic adduct peak at 342.2399 g/mol with negligible azo product formation (~5.0%). The micellar association of EY with CTAB is confirmed by a 9 nm bathochromic shift in absorption at 516 nm, a 2.4-fold fluorescence enhancement at or near the critical micellar concentration (0.75-1.0 mM), and an enhanced lifetime of 2.74 ns compared to 1.17 ns in water. The study represents the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds via metal-free photocatalysis, offering a green alternative to traditional diazotization and metal-catalyzed azo synthesis routes.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are an important class of organic molecules with potential in optical storage and molecular switches. Traditional synthesis of azoaromatics involves diazotization with stoichiometric nitrile salts producing unstable diazonium intermediates. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed synthesis of azo compounds has been reported but suffers from slow kinetics and poor selectivity. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes requires an inert atmosphere and produces azoxyaromatics or nitrosobenzene as byproducts. Photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics using Ir-based photocatalysts suffers from slow kinetics and moderate yields. All earlier reports utilized organic solvents due to the low solubility of amine substrates in aqueous medium. Charged aqueous interfaces can dramatically modulate chemical and photochemical reactions that are otherwise inefficient in bulk medium. CAIs of micelles provide a unique microenvironment to solubilize both hydrophilic and hydrophobic probes at distinct locations.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics can be achieved at charged aqueous interfaces under ambient conditions. The authors hypothesize that the micellar interface will host both the photocatalyst and substrates in close proximity, enabling a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer. It is predicted that the micellar environment will modulate redox potentials and facilitate product selectivity due to the unique electric fields at the interface. The hypothesis is that Eosin Y, a common low-cost organic photocatalyst, can replace expensive iridium-based catalysts. The study aims to demonstrate 100% conversion under ambient atmosphere with minimal photocatalyst loading compared to prior reports. The authors predict that the reaction will be feasible only in the presence of a base for proton abstraction. Atmospheric oxygen is hypothesized to act as a sacrificial oxidant for photocatalyst regeneration via hydrogen peroxide formation. The broad substrate scope is predicted to encompass electron-rich and electron-deficient arylamines.

Methodological Details
The photocatalytic system uses Eosin Y as the organic photocatalyst in an aqueous medium. The surfactant CTAB forms spherical micelles at an optimized concentration of 40 mM. Micellar association of EY with CTAB was confirmed by a bathochromic shift of 9 nm in the absorption peak at 516 nm. Fluorescence quenching of EY was observed in the presence of CTAB and TX-100 at premicellar concentrations. Enhanced fluorescence of 2.4-fold was observed only in the presence of CTAB at or near the critical micellar concentration of 0.75-1.0 mM. The fluorescence lifetime of EY@CTAB increased from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon micellization. Stability experiments showed EY@CTAB is stable with K3PO4 while EY@TX-100 suffers disassembly. SDS showed no interaction with EY, signifying a higher binding affinity of EY towards CTAB. The optimized reaction uses 0.6 mole% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB in water. The reaction is triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. Substrates include electron-rich amines (p-anisidine, aniline), neutral amines (p-chloroaniline, p-bromoaniline), and others. Products were characterized by GC-MS and NMR measurements. Micellar morphology was confirmed by HR-TEM measurements. The formation of H2O2 was detected using H2O2 sensing strips. Base options tested included K3PO4, KOH, and DABCO. The reaction was also feasible under blue light, requiring 6 h for 100% conversion.

Procedures And Architectures
Photophysical behavior of EY was first characterized in the presence of CTAB, SDS, and TX-100. Micellar association was probed by monitoring absorption shifts and fluorescence quenching at premicellar and micellar concentrations. Stability of EY@CTAB composites in the presence of K3PO4 was assessed by fluorescence lifetime measurements. For the photocatalytic reaction, 40 mM CTAB, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 0.6 mole% EY were combined in water. The reaction was irradiated with green light (525 nm) for 4 hours under ambient atmosphere. Fluorescence quenching experiments were performed by adding increasing concentrations of p-anisidine to EY@CTAB and monitoring intensity at 545 nm. A Stern-Volmer plot was constructed with the quenching rate constant extracted. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements determined the PET time constant. Radical trap experiments involved irradiating the reaction mixture with green light for 5 min, adding 1 equivalent of BHT, and irradiating for an additional 4 h. H2O2 sensing strips were used before and after light irradiation to detect oxygen reduction. The conversion of arylamines was monitored by GC-MS measurements. Substrate scope was expanded to electron-rich and electron-deficient amines, with characterization by GC-MS and NMR.

Key Results
100% conversion of electron-rich arylamines was observed within 4 h of reaction under standard conditions. This represents an 8.3-fold lower EY dose compared to the previous iridium-based report. The previously reported conversion was only 64% after 24 h in bulk acetonitrile. 100% conversion was also observed with aniline as substrate under standard conditions. P-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline showed conversion yields of 98% and 95%, respectively. A linear Stern-Volmer plot gave a quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M⁻¹s⁻¹. Fluorescence up-conversion revealed a PET time constant of 0.3 ps in the presence of p-anisidine. BHT-trapped radical experiments showed a characteristic HR-MS peak at 342.2399 g/mol. With BHT present, conversion to the azo product was negligible, approximately 5.0% after 4 h. CTAB formed spherical micelles at 40 mM as confirmed by HR-TEM. A blue light (6 h) also achieved 100% conversion under standard conditions. The reaction was feasible only in the presence of a base, with K3PO4 and KOH superior to DABCO. The EY@CTAB absorption peak showed a bathochromic shift of 9 and 16 nm with CTAB and TX-100, respectively. Enhanced fluorescence of 2.4-fold was observed only near the CTAB CMC. Fluorescence lifetime increased from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. p-Nitroaniline showed no fluorescence quenching, indicating lack of electron transfer. The presence of K3PO4 had no noticeable effect on the SV plots. The color change of the H2O2 strip confirmed atmospheric O2 reduction. The fluorescence quenching was found to be a non-diffusive bimolecular process.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The non-diffusive PET mechanism with a 0.3 ps time constant is the key driver for the accelerated kinetics. The micelle scaffold brings the photocatalyst and substrates into close proximity at the interface. Modulation of redox potentials at the CAI facilitates the oxidative coupling step. The Stern layer of the micelle provides a less polar hydrocarbon/aqueous environment that solubilizes arylamines. PET precedes the proton abstraction step by the base, as the SV plot is unaffected by K3PO4. The cationic CTAB interacts electrostatically with the negatively charged EY at pH 7. The micelle provides a unique microenvironment that brings PC and substrates together for bimolecular reactions. This aqueous-phase approach eliminates the need for organic solvents and inert atmosphere. The study establishes the charged aqueous interface as a platform for enhancing photocatalytic efficiency.

Contradictions And Limitations
CTAB-induced aggregation at premicellar concentrations could interfere with the photocatalytic process. SDS showed no interaction with EY, limiting surfactant applicability to ionic surfactants. Conversion yields were slightly less with the organic base DABCO compared to inorganic bases. P-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline did not reach 100% conversion. The quantum yield of the photocatalytic reaction was not reported. Turnover number and turnover frequency for the Eosin Y photocatalyst were not determined. Statistical replicates and error bars are not provided for the conversion data. No random seed or experimental reproducibility data are mentioned for the computational-like metrics. The text does not mention the concentration of p-anisidine used in the quenching experiments. The specific conditions for the blue light experiment were not fully detailed. p-Nitroaniline showed no quenching, which validates the PET mechanism but limits the scope to electron-donating amines.

Claims
Metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics is feasible at charged aqueous interfaces under ambient air with 100% yields. 100% conversion was achieved for electron-rich arylamines in 4 hours using 0.6 mole% EY. The reaction operates under ambient air atmosphere without an inert atmosphere. The micellar scaffold is confirmed by bathochromic shift of 9 nm and HR-TEM imaging of spherical micelles. The PET time constant of 0.3 ps supports the non-diffusive electron transfer mechanism. P-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline only reached 98% and 95% conversion, respectively. The conversion is slightly less with DABCO than with K3PO4. SDS showed no interaction with EY, limiting the applicability to CTAB. p-Nitroaniline showed no electron transfer, narrowing the substrate scope to electron-rich amines. The methodology eliminates the need for organic solvents and metal catalysts in azo synthesis. This opens newer opportunities in the synthesis of azoaromatics for optical and industrial applications. The charged aqueous interface can be a general platform for enhancing photocatalytic bimolecular reactions.
The mechanism proceeds via a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer with a 0.3 ps time constant at the micellar interface. Fluorescence up-conversion gave a PET time constant of 0.3 ps. The SV plot was linear with a rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M⁻¹s⁻¹, indicating non-diffusive bimolecular quenching. BHT trapping yielded a characteristic radical adduct at 342.2399 g/mol with only ~5.0% azo formation. The fluorescence lifetime increased from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns, authenticating excited state quenching. The paper states PET occurs in a few picoseconds, but 0.3 ps is exceptionally fast and might be near the detector resolution limit. The BHT experiment shows ~5.0% azo formation even with the trap, suggesting a minor parallel pathway. The p-nitroaniline control confirms the PET mechanism but doesn't prove it applies to all substrates. Non-diffusive PET at the interface bypasses diffusion limitations inherent in bulk media. The proximity of PC and substrate within the micelle scaffold is critical for the bimolecular reaction. The temporal separation of PET and proton abstraction explains the observed kinetics.
The micellar charged aqueous interface enables an 8.3-fold lower catalyst loading and 4-fold faster kinetics compared to previous reports. The EY dose was 0.6 mole% compared to the 8.3-fold higher dose in the prior report. The current method achieves 100% conversion in 4 h, while the prior was 64% in 24 h. The prior method required an Ir-based photocatalyst and bulk acetonitrile. The present method is water-based and ambient-atmosphere, while the prior required organic solvents. The comparison is with a single prior report; other photocatalytic methods might not be surpassed. The 64% conversion figure is from a specific study (ref 24), and different conditions may yield different comparisons. The micellar approach significantly improves the economic and environmental viability of azo synthesis. This demonstration could influence design of other interfacial photocatalytic systems.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Stability of EY@CTAB was confirmed in the presence of K3PO4 by fluorescence lifetime measurements, while EY@TX-100 disassembled. SDS showed no interaction with EY, serving as a negative control for surfactant type. p-Nitroaniline showed no fluorescence quenching, confirming the requirement of an electron-rich amine. The presence of K3PO4 had no effect on SV plots, confirming PET precedes base-mediated proton abstraction. Conversion was tested with inorganic bases (K3PO4, KOH) and organic base (DABCO), with slight yield differences. Blue light irradiation (6 h) achieved the same 100% conversion as green light (4 h). Radical trapping with BHT reduced azo formation to ~5.0%, confirming the radical intermediate. CTAB-induced aggregation at premicellar concentrations was noted as a potential interference. The CTAB concentration was optimized to 40 mM based on HR-TEM measurements of spherical micelles. No quantum yield, TON, or TOF data were reported as robustness checks.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the absorption spectrum of EY in water at 516 nm, exhibiting 9 nm shift with CTAB and 16 nm with TX-100 micelles. Figure 1b shows fluorescence quenching of EY in the presence of premicellar CTAB and TX-100. Figure 1c shows EY undergoes CTAB-induced aggregation at premicellar concentration and dissociates at or near the CMC. Figure 1d shows fluorescence lifetime of EY from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization, confirmed by Table S2. Figure S2 and S3 show EY@TX-100 disassembly in the presence of K3PO4. Table 1 tabulates optimized reaction conditions: 525 nm green light, 4 h, 0.6 mole% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, 40 mM CTAB, with 100% conversion for electron-rich amines. Figure S4 shows HR-TEM images of CTAB spherical micelles at 40 mM. Figure S5 shows blue light experiment requiring 6 h for 100% conversion. Figure S6 shows H2O2 sensing strips detecting H2O2 formation before and after irradiation. Scheme 2a shows the substrate scope with electron-rich, neutral, and electron-deficient amines. Figure 2b shows the SV plot for p-anisidine quenching of EY@CTAB at 545 nm, with linear fit and kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M⁻¹s⁻¹. Figure 2c shows the PET mechanism with a base-mediated proton abstraction step. Figure 2d shows fluorescence up-conversion with a PET time constant of 0.3 ps. Scheme 3a shows the radical trap experiment with BHT. Figure S13 shows fluorescence intensity of EY@CTAB decreasing with p-anisidine. Figure S14 shows K3PO4 does not affect SV plots. Figure S15 shows the BHT adduct peak at 342.2399 g/mol. Table S1 provides phisical data for EY in micelles. Table S2 contains fluorescence lifetime data. Table S3 tabulates quenching parameters for other arylamines. Table S4 provides PET mechanism details and base effects.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at charged aqueous interfaces under ambient conditions with 100% yield. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of a 0.3 ps PET time constant from fluorescence up-conversion, a linear SV plot with kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M⁻¹s⁻¹, and BHT radical trapping producing an adduct at 342.2399 g/mol. 3. The future path involves generalizing the micellar charged aqueous interface approach to other photocatalytic bimolecular reactions and exploring further substrate scope beyond arylamines.

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara (Osaka Metropolitan University); Takashi Kobayashi (Chuo University); Tetsuji Dohi (Chuo University); Takeshi Yoshimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Norifumi Fujimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Daisuke Kiriya (Osaka Metropolitan University)
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science / Two-Dimensional Materials / Optoelectronics
summary.executive_summary: This research presents a universal postpreparation method for enhancing the photoluminescence (PL) intensity of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) by removing the substrate-induced electronic effects through spontaneous crystal fluctuation, achieved by coating with paraffin, a simple hydrocarbon. Unlike prior strategies—such as p-type doping with F4TCNQ or superacid treatment with TFSI—which are effective only for sulfur-based TMDCs (MoS 2 and WS 2), this paraffin-coating strategy is applicable to both sulfur-and selenium-based compounds (MoS 2, WS 2, MoSe 2, and WSe 2). The experimental system comprises monolayer TMDCs on Si/SiO 2 or quartz substrates, coated with paraffin (melting point 42–45 °C) applied via spin coating at 80 °C while under a heat blower to prevent premature solidification. The paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient applies strain to the TMDCs during the coating process, inducing gradual spontaneous fluctuation and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. Quantitative PL measurements show enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 50-, and 9-fold for MoS 2, WS 2, MoSe 2, and WSe 2, respectively, relative to as-exfoliated flakes. Raman spectroscopy on 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 confirms the mechanism: the Eʹ peak shifts negatively by approximately -0.72 cm -1, indicating strain, and the Aʹ peak shifts positively by 1.03 cm -1, indicating decreased carrier concentration from reduced substrate electron doping. Optical microscopy and PL mapping reveal spatially non-uniform enhancement and localized wrinkling, with PL intensity approximately 2.3 times greater in the center than at the rim of a constrained monolayer. When unconstrained by surrounding bulk flakes on three sides, the monolayer spontaneously deforms and bundles into a shrunk structure. The deformation is observed to occur gradually and spontaneously over several hours at room temperature. The paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent, making the method suitable for flexible optoelectronic device packaging. The authors conclude that this strategy is applicable to other 2D layered materials due to the underlying physics of strain-induced desorption and the versatile material properties of paraffin. Furthermore, the method is described as useful for straining thin 2D materials and applicable for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices in two-dimensional semiconductor materials, extending the design of TMDC applications to flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.

The experimental system comprises monolayer TMDCs on Si/SiO 2 or quartz substrates, coated with paraffin (melting point 42–45 °C) applied via spin coating at 80 °C while under a heat blower to prevent premature solidification. The paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient applies strain to the TMDCs during the coating process, inducing gradual spontaneous fluctuation and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. Quantitative PL measurements show enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 50-, and 9-fold for MoS 2, WS 2, MoSe 2, and WSe 2, respectively, relative to as-exfoliated flakes. Raman spectroscopy on 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 confirms the mechanism: the Eʹ peak shifts negatively by approximately -0.72 cm -1, indicating strain, and the Aʹ peak shifts positively by 1.03 cm -1, indicating decreased carrier concentration from reduced substrate electron doping. Optical microscopy and PL mapping reveal spatially non-uniform enhancement and localized wrinkling, with PL intensity approximately 2.3 times greater in the center than at the rim of a constrained monolayer. When unconstrained by surrounding bulk flakes on three sides, the monolayer spontaneously deforms and bundles into a shrunk structure. The deformation is observed to occur gradually and spontaneously over several hours at room temperature. The paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent, making the method suitable for flexible optoelectronic device packaging. The authors conclude that this strategy is applicable to other 2D layered materials due to the underlying physics of strain-induced desorption and the versatile material properties of paraffin. Furthermore, the method is described as useful for straining thin 2D materials and applicable for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices in two-dimensional semiconductor materials, extending the design of TMDC applications to flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.

Research Context
Monolayer TMDCs exhibit a thin crystal structure with a layer thickness of only three atoms and excellent mechanical robustness. They possess a direct band gap at the K and Kʹ points in the Brillouin zone, making them suitable for optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells. A primary drawback is poor optical property, such as poor PL intensity, caused by over-carrier concentrations, strains, and crystalline lattice defects. For n-type sulfur-based compounds MoS 2 and WS 2, p-type doping with 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-7,7,8,8-tetracyanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) successfully enhances PL intensity. Treatment with the superacid bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI) can produce PL enhancement of hundreds of times for sulfur-based compounds. However, these sulfur-specific methods are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe 2 and WSe 2. For selenium-based compounds, oleic acid treatments on MoSe 2 and hydrohalic acid treatments show some PL enhancement. Defect repairing has succeeded in MoSe 2 but has not been reported for application in WSe 2 to the best of the authors' knowledge. For WSe 2 specifically, substrate removal by floating or inserting ions has been reported, but no universal strategy exists for all TMDCs. No universal strategy has been found for improving the optical behavior of a large variety of 2D semiconductor materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a universal strategy can remove substrate effects and enhance PL in both sulfur-and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs. The hypothesis is that coating with paraffin exploits its large thermal coefficient to induce spontaneous fluctuation and removal of the substrate effect. The authors predict that the removal of the substrate effect is the key factor in enhancing PL intensity in the monolayers. They hypothesize that PL intensity will improve remarkably in both sulfur-and selenium-based compounds after paraffin coating. The authors also predict that the paraffin's insulative, flexible, and transparent properties will enable device packaging applications. A corollary hypothesis is that in extreme cases, the fluctuation will form the shape of a bundle when the monolayer is not surrounded by bulk flakes. The authors posit that the underlining science of strain by the large thermal expansion coefficient is applicable to other 2D layered materials. The expected PL enhancement factors were hypothesized to be in the double-to-triple digits across all tested TMDC compounds. The hypothesis further extends to the ability of paraffin to strain thin 2D materials generally.

Methodological Details
The study tested monolayer TMDCs of four compounds: MoS 2, WS 2, MoSe 2, and WSe 2. The paraffin used had a melting point of 42–45 °C. For coating, the paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance. The paraffin was dropped onto a sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower (hair dryer) was applied during spin coating to keep the paraffin in a melted state. Raman spectroscopy was performed on 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 before and after paraffin coating. The as-exfoliated flakes served as the baseline for all PL and Raman measurements. PL spectra were measured on both Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates to confirm substrate independence. The optical microscopy images captured the as-exfoliated, immediately post-coated, and time-dependent deformed states. PL mapping images were used to confirm uniform versus nonuniform enhancement across the monolayer. Raman spectroscopy monitored the Eʹ and Aʹ peak positions. The Eʹ peak represents in-plane vibrations sensitive to strain, while the Aʹ peak represents out-of-plane vibrations sensitive to carrier concentration. Statistical information of Raman shifts was tabulated in Table 2. Time-resolved measurements were taken after 2 hours and after a further 1 hour at room temperature. A constrained monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides was examined for spatially dependent PL. The prepared paraffin film was observed to be transparent under optical microscope. A thick paraffin film achieved by simple casting, not spin coating, was shown to be non-transparent with a glassy appearance. The different band gaps and emission wavelengths of the as-exfoliated TMDCs were quantified.

Procedures And Architectures
The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance before the coating process. The melted paraffin was dropped onto a sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower was applied because the paraffin would immediately solidify when cast on the sample without heat. For PL measurements, the paraffin-coated sample was measured through the paraffin film on both Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates. Optical microscopy confirmed that paraffin covers the entire monolayer for WS 2. PL mapping confirmed monolayer PL enhancement in the whole plane, with a partial specific area showing greater enhancement. The time-series microscopy tracked the monolayer MoS 2 at three time points: as-exfoliated, immediately after coating, after 2 hours, and after a further hour. PL spectra were collected for the deformed sample identified by white circles in each microscopy figure. Raman spectra of 30 MoS 2 samples were collected before and after paraffin coating. The Eʹ peak was monitored for negative shift (strain) and the Aʹ peak for positive shift (carrier concentration). PL mapping was performed on a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides to study spatially dependent properties. The constrained PL mapping quantified PL intensity ratio between center and rim. The constrained PL peak position was measured at slightly lower energy in the center. A secondary experiment on a folding edge involving bilayer MoS 2 confirmed the strain/bundle mechanism. All measurements were performed at room temperature for time-resolved observations.

Key Results
The paraffin coating produced PL enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold for MoS 2, WS 2, WSe 2, and MoSe 2, respectively, from as-exfoliated flakes. A specific WS 2 sample showed PL enhancement of about 36 times through paraffin coating. The normalized WS 2 PL spectrum showed a decrease in the shoulder at the low-energy side, suggesting decreased trion-derived PL signal. PL mapping confirmed that the monolayer shows PL enhancement in the whole plane, with the center approximately 2.3 times greater than the rim. The Raman Eʹ peak shifted in the negative direction after paraffin coating by about -0.72 cm -1 on average. The Raman Aʹ peak shifted in the positive direction by 1.03 cm -1 after paraffin coating. The PL peak position around the center shifts slightly 5-10 meV lower in energy than the rim. The constrained monolayer shows the PL peak position distribution of electronic states in the plane. The Eʹ peak in Raman spectra of the folded bilayer MoS 2 shifts to lower energy, confirming strain from paraffin coating. The monolayer MoS 2 deformed spontaneously with time while surrounding bulk flakes maintained their morphology. The deformed MoS 2 shows PL peak upshift and remarkable PL enhancement. The paraffin coating process removes the substrate effect from the TMDCs, as shown by the penetration of paraffin underneath the monolayer. PL mapping images show nonuniform high PL intensity around the center, dependent on the state of fluctuation. The enhancement factor for MoS 2 is over 200 times, attributable to its low initial PL signal in the as-exfoliated state. The PL enhancement was observed not only on the Si/SiO 2 substrate but also on the quartz substrate, confirming substrate-independence.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin applies strain that drives the spontaneous fluctuation and gradual desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. The mechanical stress inside the plane induces the fluctuation, then a partial area desorbs and forms a wrinkle inside the plane. The penetration of paraffin between the monolayer and the substrate reduces the substrate effect, specifically electron doping from the substrate. The strain-induced funnel effect in wrinkles decreases the local band gap and traps excitons, further enhancing PL intensity. The decrease in Aʹ peak position indicates a reduction in carrier concentration, reducing trion-mediated quenching. The deformation into bundles in extreme cases occurs when the monolayer is not surrounded by bulk flakes, confirming stress-driven morphological change. The paraffin's insulative, flexible, and transparent properties extend TMDC applications to packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The underlying science of strain by the large thermal expansion coefficient is applicable to other 2D layered materials beyond TMDCs. This engineering method of hydrocarbon-coating is useful for straining thin 2D materials in general. The method is suitable for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices in two-dimensional semiconductor materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
PL enhancement is spatially nonuniform across the monolayer plane, with the center showing ~2.3 times greater intensity than the rim. The enhancement factor varies significantly by TMDC type, from 215-fold for MoS 2 to only 9-fold for WSe 2. The Raman statistics are based on only 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 before and after coating. The mechanism of PL enhancement is suggested to be partial strain and deformation, rather than proven deterministically. The paraffin coating requires heating to 80 °C, which may not be compatible with all substrate types or device environments. The paper does not report the specific random seed, train/test split, or demographic information (not applicable here). A thick paraffin film achieved by casting, not spin coating, resulted in a glassy appearance that was not transparent. The deformation and bundle formation are described as occurring in extreme cases, not as a universal observation. No specific sensitivity analysis or error bar reporting is provided for the Raman shift values.

Claims
Paraffin coating provides a universal postpreparation strategy for PL intensity enhancement in both sulfur-and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs. PL enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold were achieved for all four TMDCs relative to as-exfoliated flakes. The paraffin coating was shown to be effective on both Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates. Raman spectroscopy confirmed strain (Eʹ shift) and carrier reduction (Aʹ shift) across 30 samples. The mechanism was demonstrated in all tested TMDCs, with no compound failing to show enhancement. The WSe 2 enhancement factor (9-fold) is substantially lower than for MoS 2 (215-fold). PL enhancement is nonuniform across the monolayer plane, dependent on the state of fluctuation. The deformation into bundles occurs only in extreme cases. The method is applicable to other 2D layered materials due to the underlying physics of paraffin-induced strain. Paraffin's material properties enable flexible, transparent, and biocompatible optoelectronic device packaging.
The key mechanism of PL enhancement is the removal of the substrate effect via strain-induced desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. The Eʹ peak shifted negatively, indicating in-plane strain, while the Aʹ peak shifted positively, indicating reduced carrier concentration. The PL peak upshifted during the deformation process, consistent with reduced trion-derived PL. Raman spectra showed strain in the folded bilayer MoS 2 region. Optical microscopy showed spontaneous deformation over time with the surrounding bulk maintaining morphology. The authors state the mechanism is suggested to be partial strain and deformation, rather than proven. The contribution of the funnel effect in wrinkled areas to total PL enhancement is not quantitatively isolated. This mechanism is applicable to all TMDCs and other 2D materials, providing a fundamental design rule for substrate effect removal.
Paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient drives the spontaneous fluctuation and morphological change of the TMDCs. The paraffin melting point is 42–45 °C, and it was coated at 80 °C. The authors cite the large thermal coefficient as the source of strain during the coating process. The Eʹ Raman shift of -0.72 cm -1 quantifies the strain experienced by the monolayer. The exact thermal expansion coefficient value is not reported. The time-course of deformation (over several hours) suggests a thermal relaxation process that may involve more than just the coating-time strain. The approach can be generalized to any 2D material that responds to thermal strain.
Paraffin is suitable for optoelectronic device packaging due to its insulative, flexible, and transparent properties. The paraffin film was confirmed to be transparent under optical microscope. The authors explicitly state paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent. The method is applicable for flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The thick paraffin film achieved by casting was non-transparent with a glassy appearance. No specific device fabrication or packaging demonstration is provided. This extends the design of TMDC applications beyond bare flakes to integrated flexible devices.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The method was tested on both Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates, confirming substrate independence of the PL enhancement. The Raman statistics were derived from 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2, providing a statistical basis for the Eʹ and Aʹ shifts. A thickness control was performed: spin-coated paraffin yielded a transparent film, while simple casting yielded a thick, non-transparent glassy film. Time-dependent observations (0, 2, 3 hours) tracked the gradual deformation of the monolayer. The constrained monolayer (surrounded on three sides) served as a control for the bundling mechanism. PL enhancement was confirmed across all four TMDCs (MoS 2, WS 2, MoSe 2, WSe 2).

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the experimental setup: (a) paraffin melting on hot plate; (b) PL spectra for WS 2 showing ~36-fold enhancement; (c) and (d) optical microscopy and PL mapping of the WS 2 monolayer. Figure 2 presents (a) the band gaps and emission wavelengths of as-exfoliated TMDCs, and (b) the factors of enhancement for each original monolayer. Figures 3a–d show time-series optical microscopy images of monolayer MoS 2 (as-exfoliated, immediately post-coated, after 2 hours, after a further hour). Figure 3e shows the PL spectra for the deformed MoS 2 sample with PL peak upshift and remarkable enhancement. Figure 3f illustrates the paraffin penetrating underneath the monolayer, removing the substrate effect. Figure 4 shows the statistical Raman shift distributions of Eʹ and Aʹ peak positions for 30 MoS 2 samples. Figure 5 shows (a) a constrained monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides, (b) PL peak position distribution, and (c,d) the plausible enhancement mechanism with strain and wrinkle formation. Table 2 reports the quantitative Raman shift values: Eʹ at -0.72 cm -1 and Aʹ at 1.03 cm -1 on average. Figure S1 shows PL enhancement on a quartz substrate, confirming substrate independence. Figures S2, S3 show enhancement factors for MoSe 2 and other samples. Figure S5 shows the deformation of monolayer TMDCs involving a folding edge and bilayer formation.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a universal postpreparation paraffin-coating method that achieves remarkable PL enhancement (up to 215-fold) in both sulfur-and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs by removing the substrate effect via strain-induced desorption. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative Raman confirmation of in-plane strain (Eʹ shift of ~-0.72 cm -1) and reduced carrier concentration (Aʹ shift of +1.03 cm -1) across 30 samples, combined with the observed time-dependent spontaneous deformation. 3. The future path lies in exploiting the strain engineering principle for other 2D layered materials and integrating the paraffin-coated TMDCs into flexible, transparent optoelectronic devices like light-emitting displays and solar cells.

summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H 2 O 2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod
summary.field_subfield: Heterogeneous Catalysis / Methane Partial Oxidation
summary.executive_summary: This study reports a catalytic breakthrough in the partial oxidation of methane (POM) by achieving continuous flow conversion to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure using H₂O₂ over a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica. The core innovation lies in combining a bimetallic Au-Fe system with a hydrophobically modified silica support (HS) to enable methane activation under benign conditions—specifically, at atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures—surpassing previous reports that required high pressure and temperature. The AuFeHS catalyst, synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method, was characterized by ICP-OES confirming Fe loading of 0.46 wt% and Au of 0.23 wt%, and by multiple spectroscopic techniques (XPS, XANES, EXAFS, in-situ IR, HRTEM, XRD, contact angle analysis) revealing an atomic dispersion of Fe with low valent Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ species stabilized by Au, alongside 1.3-3.0 nm Au nanoparticles and a specific surface area of 392 m²/g. In batch POM at 10 bar CH₄/10 bar H₂O₂ at 0 °C, AuFeHS achieved 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol with 95% selectivity within 30 min. With CO co-feeding at 20 bar (15:5 CH₄/CO) at 50 °C, the selectivity switched to acetic acid (3403 µmol/gcat, 1 h). In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure for 7 h, AuFeHS produced 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol at 4 h, corresponding to 422 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ (0.42 mol kg⁻¹ h⁻¹), significantly outperforming the previously best reported H₂O₂-based POM (1.81 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ with O₂; 0.081 mol kg⁻¹ h⁻¹ with H₂O₂ at 20 bar). Co-feeding CO in continuous flow produced 648 µmol/gcat acetic acid within 4 h. The study confirmed that the hydrophobic environment is essential to prevent moisture-induced active site blocking and to facilitate methanol desorption, while the synergetic Au-Fe interaction generates and stabilizes the Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ active site that simultaneously activates CH₄ and H₂O₂. Isotopic labeling (CD₄) and N₂ feed control experiments ruled out background reactions from the support, and the results demonstrated that the atmospheric-pressure continuous process outperforms high-pressure batch conditions for both methanol and acetic acid production.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a catalytic breakthrough in the partial oxidation of methane (POM) by achieving continuous flow conversion to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure using H₂O₂ over a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica. The core innovation lies in combining a bimetallic Au-Fe system with a hydrophobically modified silica support (HS) to enable methane activation under benign conditions—specifically, at atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures—surpassing previous reports that required high pressure and temperature. The AuFeHS catalyst, synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method, was characterized by ICP-OES confirming Fe loading of 0.46 wt% and Au of 0.23 wt%, and by multiple spectroscopic techniques (XPS, XANES, EXAFS, in-situ IR, HRTEM, XRD, contact angle analysis) revealing an atomic dispersion of Fe with low valent Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ species stabilized by Au, alongside 1.3-3.0 nm Au nanoparticles and a specific surface area of 392 m²/g. In batch POM at 10 bar CH₄/10 bar H₂O₂ at 0 °C, AuFeHS achieved 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol with 95% selectivity within 30 min. With CO co-feeding at 20 bar (15:5 CH₄/CO) at 50 °C, the selectivity switched to acetic acid (3403 µmol/gcat, 1 h). In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure for 7 h, AuFeHS produced 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol at 4 h, corresponding to 422 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ (0.42 mol kg⁻¹ h⁻¹), significantly outperforming the previously best reported H₂O₂-based POM (1.81 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ with O₂; 0.081 mol kg⁻¹ h⁻¹ with H₂O₂ at 20 bar). Co-feeding CO in continuous flow produced 648 µmol/gcat acetic acid within 4 h. The study confirmed that the hydrophobic environment is essential to prevent moisture-induced active site blocking and to facilitate methanol desorption, while the synergetic Au-Fe interaction generates and stabilizes the Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ active site that simultaneously activates CH₄ and H₂O₂. Isotopic labeling (CD₄) and N₂ feed control experiments ruled out background reactions from the support, and the results demonstrated that the atmospheric-pressure continuous process outperforms high-pressure batch conditions for both methanol and acetic acid production.

Research Context
Methane is a major constituent of natural gas, waste landfills, and manure feedstocks, contributing to global warming. Methane has a high calorific value but requires compression to 10-100 atm for commercial storage and transportation. Activation of non-polar methane with a regular tetrahedral CH₄ structure requires harsh reaction conditions. Partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol or other platform molecules is considered a holy grail problem in catalysis. Thermodynamics suggests that an activated C-H bond is so reactive it readily undergoes complete oxidation to CO₂. Most prior reports suffer from low product yield, high temperature, and high-pressure reaction conditions. Direct POM to methanol in continuous flow reactors is limited, with most reports using molecular oxygen as oxidant. H₂O₂ is considered a green oxidant with future commercialization potential due to cheaper production technologies.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a catalyst can activate methane at atmospheric pressure and selectively produce methanol and acetic acid using H₂O₂. The authors hypothesize that an Au-Fe bimetallic catalyst supported over hydrophobic silica can achieve selective POM under mild conditions. The hypothesis extends to the prediction that co-feeding CO can switch the selectivity from methanol to acetic acid. The authors further hypothesize that the hydrophobic support will improve selectivity by preventing over-oxidation and site blocking. The predicted outcome is that the atmospheric-pressure continuous process will surpass high-pressure batch processes in yield. The authors anticipate that low valent Fe species, stabilized by Au, serve as the critical active sites for CH₄ activation.

Methodological Details
A modified deposition precipitation (DP) method was used to disperse atomic clusters of Fe onto hydrophobic silica support. The hydrophobic silica support was prepared using NaOH-assisted deposition, confirmed by Si-O-Na framework detection. ICP-OES confirmed an optimum Fe concentration of 0.46 wt% and Au concentration of 0.23 wt% for the AuFeHS catalyst. The hydrophobicity of the silica was confirmed by contact angle analysis with an observed angle of 118°. A specific surface area of 392 m²/g was observed for the AuFeHS catalyst using the present synthesis method. XPS revealed Fe 2p at 710.6 eV (Fe³⁺) and 709.5 eV (low valent Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺), and Au 4f at 83.9 eV (Au⁰) and 85 eV (Auδ⁺). XANES at Fe K-edge showed no Fe-Fe interaction, revealing the single atomic nature of Fe species. Linear combination fitting showed the AuFeHS catalyst has a 72% Fe³O₄ and 28% FeO contribution. In-situ IR with CO adsorption showed signals at 2105 cm⁻¹ (Au⁰-CO) and 2175 cm⁻¹ (Auδ⁺-CO). Batch experiments were conducted at 10 bar CH₄ and 10 bar H₂O₂ at 0 °C for methanol production. CO co-feeding experiments used 20 bar total pressure (15 bar CH₄ : 5 bar CO) at 50 °C in batch. Continuous flow experiments used a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure for up to 7 h. Isotopic labeling with CD₄ and N₂ feed experiments were used as control and verification. Product quantification was performed by gas chromatography (GC) using standard calibrations.

Procedures And Architectures
The hydrophobic silica support was functionalized with NaOH, and the Si-O-Na framework was confirmed by ²⁹Si NMR, ²³Na NMR, and XPS. Fe was deposited onto HS, followed by Au deposition, with loadings screened to find optimum bimetallic composition. ICP-OES was used to determine exact Fe and Au metal contents in the finished catalysts. XRD confirmed the absence of characteristic Fe and Au reflections, indicating fine metal dispersion over the support. HRTEM showed no contrast difference characteristic of Fe particles, suggesting atomic dispersion. Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm were observed, with particle size distribution in the range of 1.4-2.8 nm. Elemental mapping confirmed Au nanoparticles are finely dispersed over FeHS with strongly interfaced boundary. XANES and EXAFS measurements at Fe K-edge and Au L3-edge characterized oxidation states and local environment. In-situ IR with CO adsorption was used to probe isolated metal atoms on the surface. Pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR at 1400-1500 cm⁻¹ confirmed Lewis acid sites bonded to pyridine at 1449 cm⁻¹. Batch POM was conducted in a reactor with optimized conditions: 0 °C, 10 bar CH₄, 10 bar H₂O₂ for methanol; 50 °C, 20 bar for acetic acid. Continuous flow POM was carried out in a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure for up to 7 h, with 80 °C as optimized temperature. CD₄ labeling experiment confirmed the methyl group in methanol originated from CD₄, not support ligands. N₂ feed experiment showed no products, confirming the reaction requires CH₄ as reactant.

Key Results
In batch POM at 10 bar CH₄ and 10 bar H₂O₂ at 0 °C, AuFeHS gave 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol with 95% selectivity within 30 min. The Fe-HS catalyst gave 285 mmol/gFe of methanol with 82% selectivity under identical batch conditions. The Au-HS catalyst gave only 47.6 mmol/gAu of methanol, demonstrating synergistic effects of both metals. Oxo dicopper on carbon nitride produced 129.7 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ of oxygenates with only 4% methanol selectivity. SBA-15 supported AuFe gave only 111 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol, confirming the role of hydrophobic support. With CO co-feeding in batch at 50 °C, 20 bar, acetic acid became the main product with 3403 µmol/gcat yield within 1 h. Methanol was the only other liquid oxygenate with 166 µmol/gcat yield upon CO co-feeding. CO₂ selectivity was 10% with CO co-feeding at 50 °C, versus 5-6% with methane only. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, AuFeHS produced 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol over 4 h. The continuous flow methanol yield was 422 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ (0.42 mol kg⁻¹ h⁻¹) at 4 h under optimized conditions. FeHS produced 24.2 mmol/gFe of methanol in continuous flow. AuHS produced 12 mmol/gAu of methanol within 4 h in continuous flow. With CO co-feeding in continuous flow, 648 µmol/gcat of acetic acid formed within 4 h. The CD₄ labeling peak at 3.3 ppm confirmed the methyl group in methanol originated from CD₄. The N₂ feed experiment yielded no products, confirming methane-dependent activation. The continuous flow methanol yield of 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) at atmospheric pressure exceeds the previous H₂O₂-based POM report of 0.081 mol kg⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 20 bar. The atmospheric pressure continuous flow yield surpasses the high-pressure batch process for both methanol and acetic acid.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The hydrophobic environment prevents active site blocking by moisture and Au particle growth in aqueous conditions. Hydrophobicity also facilitates easy desorption of methanol, preventing over-oxidation to CO₂. The low valent Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ site is identified as the key active site for methane activation. This site provides the OH moiety from H₂O₂ activation to the activated methane for CH₃OH formation. Au nanoparticles, as excellent CO oxidation catalysts, provide low-energy activation sites for CO adsorption. The activated C-H σ-complex is converted to CH₃ radical on the Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ sites, followed by methanol formation and CO insertion. The synergetic Au-Fe interaction is confirmed by STEM line analysis and XANES/XPS data. Au particles stabilize the Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ species through electronic interaction, a phenomenon not observed in AuHS. The bimetallic modulation approach offers a pathway to tune active Fe species for converting lower alkanes to oxygenates. The role of Na and Lewis acid sites in the overall POM reaction is suggested but not explored in this study.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a ChemRxiv preprint and has not been peer-reviewed. Au particles formed even at small loadings (1.3-3.0 nm), which might affect site isolation. XRD showed no characteristic Fe or Au reflections, consistent with low metal loading but not definitive for atomic dispersion. FeHS showed poor catalysis because the low valent Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ species was absent, indicating that just Fe is insufficient. The role of Na and Lewis acid sites in the POM reaction is explicitly stated as beyond the scope of the study. Only two liquid oxygenates (methanol, acetic acid) were quantified; other potential products were not detailed. Stability of the catalyst over extended continuous flow beyond 7 h was not reported. The precise random seed and train/test splits are not applicable as this is a catalysis study, not a computational or ML paper.

Claims
AuFeHS achieves continuous flow partial oxidation of methane to methanol at atmospheric pressure with a yield of 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) and excellent selectivity. The continuous flow yield of 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) at atmospheric pressure surpasses the high-pressure batch yield of 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au). The 422 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ continuous flow yield is orders of magnitude higher than the 1.81 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ H₂O₂-based POM report. Steady methanol production was observed for up to 7 h at atmospheric pressure in a fixed-bed reactor. Au particles formed as 1.3-3.0 nm nanoparticles, not individual atoms, which may complicate site-isolation claims. This demonstrates that methane can be converted to value-added oxygenates at benign conditions without high pressure. The work opens the doors for commercialization of M2O technologies.
Co-feeding CO with methane switches the selectivity from methanol to acetic acid in both batch and continuous flow processes. In batch at 20 bar, acetic acid became the main product with 3403 µmol/gcat yield within 1 h. In continuous flow, 648 µmol/gcat of acetic acid was formed within 4 h with CO co-feeding. The mechanism involves CO insertion into the CH₃ radical formed on Fe³⁻ᵟ⁺ sites. Methanol was still produced as a side product (166 µmol/gcat in batch, ~224 mmol/g in continuous flow when CO-fed). This dual-functionality allows production of both methanol and acetic acid from the same catalyst platform.
The hydrophobic silica support is essential for high-yield POM by preventing site blocking and facilitating product desorption. AuFe supported on SBA-15 gave only 111 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol compared to 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) on HS. Fe-SBA-15 and Au-SBA-15 yielded only 0.30 and 0.15 mmol/gcat, respectively. Contact angle of 118° confirms hydrophobicity, and XRD/TEM show fine metal dispersion. The exact mechanism of how hydrophobicity interacts with the catalytic cycle is not fully elucidated. Support functionalization is a critical design parameter for low-pressure methane oxidation catalysts.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Fe loading was screened and found to be optimum at 0.5 wt%, with Au loading varied to find the best bimetallic composition. A support comparison was conducted between hydrophobic silica (HS) and hydrophilic SBA-15 for both monometallic and bimetallic catalysts. Control experiments showed no product without methane flow, oxidant, or catalyst. Isotopic labeling with CD₄ confirmed the methyl group in methanol originated from methane, ruling out background reactions from support organic groups. N₂ feed experiment confirmed that products only form when CH₄ is the reactant.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents HRTEM, TEM, EDS mapping, and particle size distribution for the AuFeHS catalyst, showing atomic Fe dispersion and 1.3-3.0 nm Au nanoparticles. Figure 2 displays XPS (Fe 2p, Au 4f), XANES (Fe K-edge, Au L3-edge), EXAFS (Fe K-edge, Au L3-edge), and in-situ IR spectra characterizing the catalyst's electronic and atomic structure. Figure 3 presents batch POM results for all tested catalysts under optimized conditions, including methanol and acetic acid production with CO co-feeding. Figure 4 shows continuous flow POM data for all catalysts over 7 h, demonstrating steady methanol and acetic acid production at atmospheric pressure. Figure 5 presents ²⁹Si and ²³Na NMR spectra characterizing the disordered hydrophobic silica structure and Si-O-Na framework. Figure 6 presents the pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR spectrum of the AuFeHS catalyst, identifying Lewis acid sites at 1449 cm⁻¹ and physisorbed water features. Table S1 provides specific surface area data; Table S2 provides best-fit EXAFS parameters; Table S4 and S5 contain detailed activity data and optimization parameters. Table S6 compares the present results with best literature values for H₂O₂-based POM to methanol.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration of continuous flow partial oxidation of methane to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure with a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst on hydrophobic silica. 2. The strongest evidence is the continuous flow methanol yield of 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) at atmospheric pressure, which is >240 times higher than the best H₂O₂-based POM report (0.081 mol kg⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 20 bar) and demonstrates the feasibility of benign-condition methane conversion. 3. The future path lies in tuning bimetallic modulation to control active Fe species, exploring the role of Na and Lewis acid sites, and commercializing M2O technologies for producing value-added chemicals from methane.

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.field_subfield: Computational Materials Science / Solid-State Ion Conductors
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a novel computational workflow for identifying and energetically ordering all crystallographically predicted structures of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent candidate solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries. The central problem is that c-LLZO has a Hermann-Mauguin space group of Ia3d with Li atoms partially occupying 24d and 96h sites, and experimental/theoretical works have been unable to uncover its ground state configuration. The authors develop a three-step pipeline: (1) elimination of overlapping Li structures using a nearest-neighbor distance cutoff of 1.7 Å; (2) symmetry reduction of the remaining configuration space using local sensitive hashing (LSH); and (3) machine-learning-based energetic ordering of unique structures using multiple linear regression (MLR) trained on DFT energies. The method constrains the configuration space from approximately 7.4 × 10^34 combinations to around 2 × 10^6 symmetry-unique structures, of which only ~1% are symmetry-unique. A total of 1235 single-point DFT calculations were performed using the ONETEP code with PBE GGA exchange functional and 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff. The resulting MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 with DFT energies, with all structures falling within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy configuration. The analysis reveals that 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures adopt an 8:48 24d:96h ratio, with four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the global minimum. Geometry relaxations on a small subset (20 structures) confirmed that the lowest-energy structure arises from a 96h→24d site transition, reducing the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The authors also provide a freely accessible database of all generated structures to improve reproducibility in c-LLZO research. The method is broadly applicable to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a novel computational workflow for identifying and energetically ordering all crystallographically predicted structures of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent candidate solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries. The central problem is that c-LLZO has a Hermann-Mauguin space group of Ia3d with Li atoms partially occupying 24d and 96h sites, and experimental/theoretical works have been unable to uncover its ground state configuration. The authors develop a three-step pipeline: (1) elimination of overlapping Li structures using a nearest-neighbor distance cutoff of 1.7 Å; (2) symmetry reduction of the remaining configuration space using local sensitive hashing (LSH); and (3) machine-learning-based energetic ordering of unique structures using multiple linear regression (MLR) trained on DFT energies. The method constrains the configuration space from approximately 7.4 × 10^34 combinations to around 2 × 10^6 symmetry-unique structures, of which only ~1% are symmetry-unique. A total of 1235 single-point DFT calculations were performed using the ONETEP code with PBE GGA exchange functional and 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff. The resulting MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 with DFT energies, with all structures falling within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy configuration. The analysis reveals that 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures adopt an 8:48 24d:96h ratio, with four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the global minimum. Geometry relaxations on a small subset (20 structures) confirmed that the lowest-energy structure arises from a 96h→24d site transition, reducing the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The authors also provide a freely accessible database of all generated structures to improve reproducibility in c-LLZO research. The method is broadly applicable to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Research Context
Solid electrolytes like c-LLZO are important for high-energy-density Li-ion batteries due to higher energy density, improved safety, and reduced production costs compared to liquid electrolytes. Dendrite formation through the electrolyte causing batteries to short-circuit has been reported even for the most stable solid electrolytes. c-LLZO has the best interfacial stability of all popular fast ion conducting solid electrolytes against metallic Li. Despite intensive study, there is no consensus on c-LLZO's Li occupancy, and previous computational studies use arbitrary experimental values as starting points. Without knowing if the structures used are close to the ground state, more complicated thermodynamic and observable properties calculated from these structures may not be well described. The combinatorial space of populating 120 sites with 56 Li atoms yields approximately 7.4 × 10^34 structures, rendering brute-force methods unviable.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a combinatorial approach can identify the true ground state of c-LLZO by producing all possible 24d:96h Li occupancy structures and ordering them energetically. The study aims to determine if a significant energy difference exists between different structure choices and whether the 24d:96h ratio is indicative of a structure's energy. The authors hypothesize that the majority of previously reported structures may not be feasible or stable given the geometric constraints of the crystal structure. The method is designed to uncover the lowest-energy configurations, with the expectation that the most energetically favourable structures will cluster at a specific occupancy ratio. The study further hypothesizes that a simple geometrical constraint (Li-Li distance cutoff) is sufficient to dramatically reduce the configuration space while retaining the true ground-state structures. The authors also expect that a machine-learning model trained on a small subset of DFT energies will generalize to the entire configuration space due to the assumption that energy differences are dominated by Li placement.

Methodological Details
The study targets c-LLZO with Hermann-Mauguin space group Ia3d, where Li atoms partially occupy 24d (tetrahedral) and 96h (tetrahedral/octahedral interface) sites. The total number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is 120C56 ≈ 7.4 × 10^34, making brute-force enumeration impossible. A Li-Li distance cutoff of 1.7 Å is imposed to eliminate overlapping structures, chosen because it is less than twice the ionic radius of Li and smaller than the 2.56 Å minimum in t-LLZO. This constraint imposes two geometric consequences: a maximum of 48 out of 96h sites can be occupied (pairs within 0.68 Å), and each 24d occupation eliminates 4 96h sites within 1.67 Å. All possible 24d permutations for each occupancy are generated first, then 96h sites are populated such that no nearest neighbours are simultaneously occupied. The framework is based on the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. (19) for c-LLZO. The initial generation produces approximately 2.3 × 10^8 structures, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates, for one unit cell. Symmetry reduction is achieved by constructing an upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice for each structure, flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity. Local sensitive hashing (LSH) is used to perform fast approximate similarity searches, reducing pairwise comparison scaling from O(N^2) to O(N) for over 100 million structures. Symmetry reduction leaves approximately 2 × 10^6 unique structures, reducing the count by a factor of approximately 100. Energetic ordering uses a multiple linear regression (MLR) model trained on DFT energies with a 1:3 train/test split. A total of 1235 single-point DFT calculations were performed: 200 lowest energy structures (COMPASSIII forcefield) and ~1000 random structures across the configuration space. All DFT calculations used the ONETEP code with PBE GGA exchange correlation functional, a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV, and CASTEP on-the-fly generated pseudopotentials. The structures are represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions, a reformulation of the connectivity matrix. The DFT energies were paired with this numerical representation and fit using the MLR model. A separate validation was performed for both 13:43 and 12:44 occupancy ratios using the ASE symmetry equivalence check. The Li-dimer optimal distance was determined by 30 single-point calculations in a large unit cell to prevent self-interaction, with the minimum energy at approximately 2.7 Å. Geometry relaxations were performed on a small dataset of 20 structures using BFGS for 96h→96h, 96h→48g, and 96h→24d transitions.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow begins with a geometry-driven pre-filter: all structures with Li-Li distances below 1.7 Å are eliminated based on nearest-neighbour counts. Following Li-Li filtering, the configuration space is narrowed: each 96h site exists as a pair within 0.68 Å of each other, and at most one can contain a Li atom. Each 24d occupation further eliminates 4 96h sites as they fall within 1.67 Å of the 24d site. Structures are generated in the order: all 24d permutations for a given occupancy, followed by population of 96h sites respecting the nearest-neighbour constraint. The connectivity matrix for each structure contains distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom, which is flattened and sorted for uniformity. LSH pairwise comparison identifies symmetry equivalents, reducing the dataset to ~2 × 10^6 unique conformations. The MLR model is trained on 1235 DFT energies: 200 structures from the COMPASSIII forcefield ranking plus ~1000 random structures for coverage. The ONETEP code's linear scaling with the number of atoms (vs cubic scaling in conventional DFT) enables efficient calculation of these structures. The MLR features are a frequency occurrence list of Li-Li interactions, exploiting the assumption that majority energy changes arise from Li placement. The MLR was cross-validated: a correlation of 0.9996 was found on the test set, indicating robust energy prediction. The model was also tested on the COMPASSIII forcefield alone, which achieved a correlation of 0.991 for the 13:43 ratio but failed on broader ranges. Geometry relaxation used BFGS with three atom-migration steps: 96h→96h, 96h→48g, and 96h→24d, listed by frequency occurrence. A single 96h→24d transition was recorded, lowering the energy by 0.58 eV and changing the occupancy ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. A negative correlation was found in Figure S7a between mean Li atom displacement and final structure energy, suggesting greater structural mobility correlates with lower energy. A weaker negative correlation between distance to crystallographic site and energy (Figure S7b) indicates movement from original sites is preferable but movement to another site is not essential for lower energy. The Li-dimer energy was fitted with a 3rd order polynomial close to the optimal distance, yielding the 2.7 Å minimum and a large penalty approaching 1.7 Å.

Key Results
The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 with DFT energies on the test set, demonstrating that Li-Li interaction statistics alone can predict energies to high precision. All structures fall within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy configuration found by the workflow. 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures adopt a 24d:96h ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. Four structures, all 8:48, lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest-energy structure found. The average energy of all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground-state structures. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation where possible. The four lowest-energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates, the same 24d configuration, and only slight variations in the 96h configuration. Geometry optimisation of the final four structures narrows the energy gap further, confirming their near-degeneracy. A single 96h→24d site transition, recorded only once among 20 structures, reduced the energy by 0.58 eV and changed the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The COMPASSIII forcefield achieved a correlation of 0.991 for the 13:43 ratio alone but failed to generalize across wider structure ranges (Figure S3). Only approximately 1% of the structures are symmetry-unique, a factor of 100 reduction from the symmetry-preprocessed dataset. The most symmetric space group appears for the 8:48 ratio, followed by 12:44 and 10:46, with few odd 24d occupancies having symmetry higher than identity. Including space group symmetry in the MLR model made a negligible difference to overall results.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The energetic preference against 24d occupation (higher energy with increasing 24d occupancy) suggests that the 24d site is locally unstable for Li in this geometry. The clustering of 19/20 lowest structures at 8:48 ratio strongly implicates the 24d:96h ratio as a key determinant of stability, with the 8:48 stoichiometry being the ground-state basin. The near-degeneracy of the four lowest structures (within 0.026 eV) suggests multiple structurally distinct (at the 96h level) configurations may share the global minimum. The finding that movement from crystallographic sites correlates negatively with energy indicates that structural relaxation is essential for reaching the ground state. The workflow demonstrates that a purely geometric constraint (Li-Li exclusion) is sufficient to eliminate a vast majority of physically implausible structures. The method highlights that a large proportion of previously reported experimental and theoretical structures may be unfeasible, potentially explaining discrepancies in the literature. The workflow provides all generated structures in a freely accessible database, aiming to improve accuracy and reproducibility in future c-LLZO research.

Contradictions And Limitations
The energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions, which may be significant at room temperature. The workflow assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, but this is only tested on a small dataset of 20 structures. A large-scale energy prediction of geometry-optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. The LSH symmetry checking is limited to monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions and cannot handle structures with rearranged framework atoms. The COMPASSIII forcefield, while effective for ordering, shows a more pronounced separation of energies by occupancy ratio than ONETEP, indicating the forcefield may bias the relative ordering. The 96h→24d transition occurred only once among 20 geometry optimisations, limiting the robustness of this finding. No random seed for the ~1000-structure subset generation is reported, making the exact random sample unverifiable. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and has not undergone peer review.

Claims
The proposed workflow can identify the ground-state Li occupancy of c-LLZO by generating and energetically ordering all crystallographically possible structures. 1235 DFT calculations with MLR trained at 0.9996 correlation predict the lowest-energy structures. 19/20 lowest structures at 8:48 occupancy confirm a consistent ground-state basin. Four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT) indicate the ground state is a near-degenerate set. The 96h→24d transition occurred only once, and geometry relaxations on only 20 structures limit the certainty of the final ordering. No entropic contributions are included in the energetic ordering. The ground-state occupancy of c-LLZO may be revised from previous experimental estimates. The 8:48 ratio becomes the new reference for all future computational LLZO studies.
A Li-Li distance cutoff of 1.7 Å is a sufficient and physically motivated criterion for eliminating unfeasible structures from the configuration space. The cutoff is less than twice the Li ionic radius and smaller than t-LLZO minimum (2.56 Å). It is also significantly less than Li-Li distances in metallic Li. The paper notes that any distance between 1.67 Å and 2.3 Å would be suitable, indicating the choice is somewhat arbitrary within a window. A large proportion of previously reported structures are now identified as not reflective of a real system.
Machine-learning energetic ordering via Li-Li interaction statistics can replace full DFT calculation of the configuration space for partially occupied crystals. MLR correlation of 0.9996 proves energy can be predicted to within 5.8 eV of the ground state. COMPASSIII achieved 0.991 correlation on the 13:43 ratio, showing forcefields can also partially order. COMPASSIII showed too large an energy separation by ratio, considered too large to surmount in this paper. The model assumes that majority energy changes are due to Li placement only, neglecting framework effects. The workflow can be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Data And Code Availability
All generated structures are provided in a freely accessible database. The ONETEP code, CASTEP pseudopotential generation, and other computational details are described in the SI sections. LSH symmetry-checking scripts are provided in the Supporting Information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Symmetry checking was validated against the ASE symmetry equivalence check for both 13:43 and 12:44 ratios, yielding identical counts. The MLR model was tested with and without space group symmetry as a feature; inclusion of symmetry made negligible difference. Geometry relaxation was tested on a small dataset of 20 structures to assess its effect on ordering. A correlation of 0.991 was achieved by COMPASSIII forcefield alone for the 13:43 ratio, validating the approach but revealing ratio-specific biases.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: The crystallography of c-LLZO, the Hermann-Mauguin space group Ia3d, Li occupancy on 24d and 96h sites, Li-Li interaction diagrams, and the 1.7 Å cutoff. Figure 2b: Energy ranking of the 20 lowest-energy structures, showing 19 at 8:48 and the 19th at 9:47. Figure 3: The workflow showing the four final structures from given occupancies, with their 24d:96h ratios and identity numbers. Table 1: The number of unique structures for each 24d:96h ratio after symmetry reduction. Figure S3: Comparison of 1235 relative DFT energies versus COMPASSIII energies, showing more pronounced ratio-dependent separation in the forcefield. Figure S4: Li-dimer energy versus inter-atomic distance, showing minimum at ~2.7 Å and a polynomial fit close to the optimum. Figure S5: MLR energies plotted against space group order for each 24d:96h ratio, showing slight correlation between lower energy and higher symmetry. Figure S7a: Negative correlation between mean Li atom displacement and final structure energy. Figure S7b: Weaker negative correlation between distance to a crystallographic site and energy.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a complete combinatorial workflow—spanning geometric filtering, symmetry reduction via LSH, and MLR energetic ordering—that identifies the ground-state Li occupancy of c-LLZO for the first time and provides a freely accessible database of all viable structures. 2. The strongest evidence is the clustering of 19 out of 20 lowest-energy structures at the 8:48 24d:96h ratio, with four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT) of the minimum, and a 0.9996 MLR correlation that places all structures within 5.8 eV of the ground state. 3. The future path lies in extending the methodology to other ion conductors with partially occupied sites, performing large-scale geometry relaxation on the full dataset, and incorporating entropic contributions for room-temperature applicability.

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology); Takahiro Muraoka (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Biomaterials / Supramolecular chemistry
summary.executive_summary: This feature article presents a comprehensive overview of bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic dynamic bio-interfaces that govern cellular activities. The authors highlight three key platforms: self-assembling peptide hydrogels for artificial extracellular matrix (ECM) mimicry, redox-responsive peptide fibres for controlled cargo release, and phospholipid nanosheets stabilized by peptide-conjugated surfactants for extended blood circulation, alongside a photoresponsive molecular machine for endocytosis-like viral encapsulation. In the first platform, structural modulation of RADA-based peptide nanofibres (RADA16, A8G, A16G) enables stiffness-tuning of hydrogels; curved A16G fibres yield lower-stiffness, thixotropic gels suitable for injection, and A16G-N-cadherin hydrogels significantly enhance neuroblast migration in injured neonatal neocortex in vivo. In the second platform, the jigsaw-shaped peptide JigSAP (Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2) exhibits robust nanofibre formation (3.2 nm width, 1.1x10^4 Pa rigidity) and exceptional protein incorporation (93 mol% for EGFP-JigSAP vs. 3 mol% for untagged) with sustained release (39 mol% at 168 h), enabling sustained VEGF delivery for angiogenesis in stroke models. The third platform uses Cu2+-crosslinked DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets that maintain disc morphology upon dilution to 0.2 wt%, enabling homogeneous blood circulation compared to aggregated vesicles observed by IV-CLSM. Finally, the diazocine-cored molecular machine AzoMEx induces outside-in fission of GUVDOPC liposomes ([DOPC] = 180 µM, [AzoMEx] = 20 µM), encapsulating M13 phage virus (22.6×10^11 virions/mL) with retained infectivity distributed to six organs after tail vein injection of 100 µL. The article concludes that these bottom-up supramolecular approaches offer unprecedented strategies for regenerative medicine and drug delivery, positioning the field as an emerging frontier for biomedical applications.

Cu2+-stabilized DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets maintain disc morphology upon dilution to 0.2 wt% and enable homogeneous blood circulation in mice.
AzoMEx induces outside-in endocytosis-like fission of GUVDOPC liposomes, encapsulating M13 phage virus with retained infectivity distributed to multiple organs.

Bio-interfaces govern cellular functions through biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies such as ECM, phospholipid bilayers, and membrane proteins. Stimuli-responsive transformation and membrane deformation regulate substance transportation via exocytosis and endocytosis. Rapid progress in supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology has made it possible to construct and functionalize dynamic bio-interfaces. Peptide fibres formed via β-sheet-type hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interaction from alternating hydrophilic and hydrophobic residues.
