JigSAP incorporates the AXXXA motif which undergoes α-helix-to-β-strand transition, generating a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface. Chol-MBP incorporates a PHGGGPHGG peptide sequence that binds two Cu2+ ions via imidazole coordination. Chol-MBP self-assembles at the DPPC membrane edge to inhibit nanosheet dissociation. JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII variants differ by a single methionine-to-methionine substitution for redox sensitivity. Oxidation with 30% H2O2 aq triggers gel-to-sol transition by producing methionine sulfoxide. AzoMEx contains a diazocine core that undergoes photoisomerization opening-closing motion. judge_context:
Executive Summary
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) built on the RDKit software (version 2022.9.5) for calculating molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations of molecules. Developed using the tkinter package, it provides easy access to RDKit's descriptor calculation tools for chemoinformatics users without programming skills. The application supports: 1) calculation of molecular descriptors already implemented in RDKit (RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA, and exact molecular weight); 2) generation of grid representations of 3D molecular structures using electrostatic potential (EP) or voxel encoding, with parameters such as grid center, side size, cube size, cutoff distance (for EP), or sigma (for voxel) user-defined via the GUI; 3) 3D structure generation from SMILES using MMFF94 optimization (5000 iterations) with options to remove metals, keep the largest fragment, and neutralize structures; 4) a command-line interface (CLI) for EP and voxel grid calculations. Descriptors are saved in CSV format, including molecule name and ID. The source code is released under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol. The paper also notes a reproducibility issue: for some molecules and specific descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), different values were obtained with the same RDKit version across different runs or operating systems, with the 3D structure of COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br cited as an example.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors are at the core of the QSPR/QSAR methodology, used by a range of scientists from different areas with varying levels of computer skills. Chemoinformatics is gradually permeating the curricula of chemistry, biology, and material science degrees, and software for teaching is thus required. Several computer programs are currently available to calculate molecular descriptors on different platforms, including open-source options like the Chemistry Development Kit (CDK) with PaDEL, BlueDesc, Tetko, and ChemDes. Proprietary software options include MOE, VolSurf+, CORINA Symphony, ChemAxon Calculator Plugins, and alvaDesc. The open-source RDKit software has implemented a wide range of chemoinformatics tools including molecular descriptors and is much used in machine learning projects, while Mordred provides another Python package for descriptor calculation. The Python programming language enables the easy development of GUIs based on tkinter, the standard Python interface to the Tcl/Tk GUI toolkit. Shi and Borchardt previously combined RDKit and tkinter to write JRgui, a GUI for Joback and Reid group contribution molecular descriptors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The application is presented as a Note developed as a minimalist interface to routine chemoinformatics tasks and the calculation of well-established descriptors. The central goal is to provide easy access to RDKit tools for chemoinformatics users with no programming skills, while remaining adaptable to other descriptors or procedures. Beyond standard RDKit descriptors, GUIDEMOL implements direct representations of 3D molecular structures, which have recently gained attention for processing by complex artificial intelligence algorithms with larger data sets. Electrostatic potentials generated by point charges localized at atom centers have long been used to establish relationships with molecular properties in 3D-QSAR or to assess molecular similarity. Direct 3D representations can be used for data sets of pre-aligned structures or processed by convolutional neural networks. GUIDEMOL enables the calculation of 3D grids representing molecules based on electrostatic potential or voxel encoding, with parameters specified by the user through the graphical interface. The hypothesis is that a simple, programmable GUI can bridge the gap between raw RDKit descriptor functionality and practical use by scientists with varying computer skills.

Methodological Details
GUIDEMOL is a Python computer program based on the RDKit software to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors with a GUI using the tkinter package. The 3D molecular models are obtained with the RDKit function MMFFOptimizeMolecule using the arguments mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000. Options available prior to model generation include removing metals based on the MetalDisconnector class, keeping the largest fragment using LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True), or neutralizing structures using Uncharger. Hydrogen atoms are added using Chem.AddHs() with the option addCoords=True for 3D coordinate calculation without changing other atom coordinates. The interface enables selection of seven 3D descriptors from the RDKit rdMolDescriptors module: RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA, plus exact molecular weight. The grid of electrostatic potential is generated using Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges calculated with RDKit (AllChem.ComputeGasteigerCharges() or GetMMFFPartialCharge()). The EP at each cube c is obtained as EP c = ∑ q_i r_ic, where q_i is the partial charge at atom i, r_ic is the distance to the cube center, and N atoms are excluded by distance criteria. The coordinates of the grid center, side size in Angstrom, and cube size are defined by the user. Voxelisation uses a user-defined 3D grid based on one of four atomic properties: atomic number, partial atomic charge (Gasteiger or MMFF), molecular refractivity, or logP using the Wildman-Crippen approach. The final voxel value at each cube c is calculated as VoxG c = ∑ p_i × exp(-r_ic^2 / σ^2), where p_i is the property of atom i and σ is a user-defined decay parameter. Molecular descriptors are saved in a csv output file including the molecule name and position ID. The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license.

Procedures And Architectures
The GUI interface uses tkinter widgets controlled by its grid geometry manager including buttons to trigger calculations, checkbuttons for YES/NO options, radiobuttons for mutually exclusive choices, entries for numeric inputs, labels for text display, and a scrollbar. The generation of 3D structures and descriptor calculation start with native look-and-feel dialog windows for file/directory selection implemented with the tkinter.filedialog module. A log file is created in the same directory to register successful processing and failures for each molecule. The descriptors are calculated from the 3D structure supplied by the user, with an option for adding missing hydrogen atoms using AddHs() with addCoords=True. The EP grid uses a cutoff distance parameter, while the voxel grid uses a sigma value and grid size in each direction. A CLI is provided for the calculation of EP and voxel grids using the command: guidemol_version.py -i I -o O -g {pot,vox} -p {Gasteiger,MMFF,MR,LogP,AtomicNumber} -cx CX -cy CY -cz CZ -r R -w W -sx SX -sy SY -sz SZ. Example CLI usage: guidemol.py -i input.sdf -g pot -p Gasteiger -cx 0 -cy 0 -cz 0 -r 0.5 -w 3 -sx 5 -sy 5 -sz 5 -o outfile.csv calculates an EP grid with Gasteiger charges centered at (0,0,0) with 5 Å side length, 0.5 Å resolution, 3 Å cutoff, saved to outfile.csv. The RDKit version used throughout is 2022.9.5.

Key Results
The GUIDEMOL application was successfully developed as a GUI for RDKit descriptor calculation and 3D grid representation generation. The 3D structure of the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br was identified as an example molecule for which different values were obtained with the same RDKit version. For some molecules and specific descriptors including GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM, different values were obtained with RDKit version 2022.9.5 in different runs or different operating systems. The application was tested and validated for the seven 3D descriptors and EP/voxel grid generation through the GUI and CLI. The CLI provides a direct alternative to the GUI for EP and voxel grid calculations, requiring only command-line specification of all parameters. The source code is released under a BSD license, enabling both commercial and non-commercial use and easy extension.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The minimalist design aims to lower the barrier for scientists and students to access well-established RDKit descriptors without programming knowledge. The inclusion of 3D grid representations (EP and voxel) positions GUIDEMOL as useful for workflows involving deep learning and convolutional neural networks for molecular data. The EP grid formula EP c = ∑ q_i r_ic leverages point-charge electrostatic potentials for 3D-QSAR and similarity assessment, linking classical structure-property relationships with modern grid representations. The voxel grid formula VoxG c = ∑ p_i exp(-r_ic^2 / σ^2) with the sigma decay parameter is amenable to voxel-based deep learning architectures. The application can be adapted to calculate other descriptors or trigger other procedures, serving as a template for additional chemoinformatics GUI development.

Contradictions And Limitations
A reproducibility issue was identified: for some molecules and some GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors, different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or in different operating systems. The application is a Note and does not include quantitative benchmarking or performance comparison against existing tools like PaDEL, BlueDesc, or ChemDes. The software is described as a minimalist interface, implying limited depth of functionality beyond the implemented descriptors and grid types. Possible bugs or limitations may exist, which the author notes can be easily detected and fixed due to the open-source BSD license. The RDKit version used (2022.9.5) may not represent the current stable release, limiting reproducibility for users on newer versions. No quantitative metrics (e.g., CPU time, memory usage, or descriptor consistency checks) are reported in the Note.

Claims
GUIDEMOL provides easy access to RDKit molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations for users without programming skills via a tkinter GUI. The application is built on tkinter for GUI access and requires no programming skills from the user. The GUI includes buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, and a scrollbar for complete parameter control. The application is adaptable to other descriptors or chemoinformatics procedures. The reproducibility issue for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors suggests inconsistent output under identical RDKit version conditions. The minimalist design may limit applicability to users needing more advanced RDKit features. The software can serve as a template for additional RDKit-based GUIs. The open-source BSD license facilitates community-driven extension and bug fixing.
3D grid representations (EP and voxel) in GUIDEMOL can be used for processing molecules by complex artificial intelligence and deep learning neural networks. The paper explicitly mentions that 3D representations have gained attention for AI with larger datasets. Voxel representations have been used to train deep learning neural networks. The EP grid and voxel grid are parametrized for user specification of grid center, side, cube size, cutoff, and sigma. No quantitative examples of AI/deep learning applications using GUIDEMOL outputs are provided in the Note. The output formats are amenable to convolutional neural networks. Users can combine pre-aligned structure data with grid representations for 3D-QSAR workflows.
The source code is publicly available and freely extendable for commercial and non-commercial use. The code is available at the GitHub repository under the BSD license. The three-clause BSD license allows both commercial and non-commercial use. No formal versioning or release cycle is described beyond the static GitHub link. The software can be integrated into larger chemoinformatics workflows. Extension to other RDKit modules is feasible for future development.

Data And Code Availability
The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license. The license allows both commercial and non-commercial use.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A reproducibility issue was observed: for some molecules and some GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors, different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or in different operating systems. The specific example cited was the 3D structure generated for COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the GUIDEMOL interface built with tkinter widgets controlled by the grid geometry manager.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a minimalist Python GUI (GUIDEMOL) built on tkinter and RDKit that provides easy access to molecular descriptor calculation and 3D grid representation generation for users with no programming skills. 2. The strongest evidence of practical utility is the demonstration of descriptor calculation, 3D structure optimization (MMFF94, 5000 iterations), EP and voxel grid generation with user-tunable parameters, and the availability of a CLI alongside the GUI. 3. The future path lies in extending the application to other descriptors, triggering additional chemoinformatics procedures, and leveraging the BSD-licensed open-source code as a template for additional RDKit-based GUIs.

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang, Tianzuo Li, Jiyeon Lee, Dahye Lim, Lianjie Xu, Yajie Liu, Jongcheol Seo, Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.field_subfield: Protein Engineering / Synthetic Biology
summary.type_of_paper: Research article reporting the first design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the first design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane, cat-DHFR, based on the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme from Escherichia coli. The authors rewrote the genetic connectivity between secondary structural motifs of linear DHFR to introduce artificial entanglement, creating two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically into a compact, integrated structure. The design identified a cleavage site at residues 88 and 89 yielding two highly intertwined segments (Gaussian linking number +0.726), which were converted to catenane topology with a GLN of +1.120 upon cyclization. The synthetic strategy employed two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs acting on the entangled linear segments as a self-templating scaffold, coupled with circular permutation (residues 23 and 24) and a TEV protease recognition site for topologic proof. Gene cassettes were expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) at 16°C for 20 hours, with proteins purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography. SDS-PAGE revealed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for the linear control (l-DHFR) and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR, consistent with a more compact interlocked topology. Far-UV CD confirmed that cat-DHFR remains folded but with reduced ellipticity intensity, suggesting minor secondary structure loosening. Enzymatic activity assays at 25°C monitoring absorbance at 340 nm showed cat-DHFR retained approximately 5 U/mg compared to approximately 14 U/mg for l-DHFR, representing a significant portion of activity compared to rethreaded controls that showed no activity. Kinetic analysis by Hanes-Woolf plot revealed cat-DHFR with Km approximately 5-fold higher and kcat approximately 38% of l-DHFR, with catalytic efficiency reduced by an order of magnitude. ITC determined disassociation constants approximately 173-fold higher for DHF and approximately 14-fold for NADPH, indicating compromised substrate and cofactor affinity. Notably, cat-DHFR exhibited enhanced thermal and chemical resilience, retaining 87% activity in 5% DMSO versus 74% for l-DHFR, attributed to conformational restriction. Topology was confirmed through TEV cleavage, IMS-MS, and CID analysis. The work demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with preserved function and elevated stability, opening an entirely new horizon in protein science.

claims.description: The first single-domain protein catenane has been designed and synthesized using a linear fold as the entangled template.
Cat-DHFR retains significant catalytic activity despite extensive topological rewiring.
Mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal and chemical resilience of the folded protein.
The synthetic method using split-intein pairs on an entangled template is robust and generally applicable.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the first design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane, cat-DHFR, based on the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme from Escherichia coli. The authors rewrote the genetic connectivity between secondary structural motifs of linear DHFR to introduce artificial entanglement, creating two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically into a compact, integrated structure. The design identified a cleavage site at residues 88 and 89 yielding two highly intertwined segments (Gaussian linking number +0.726), which were converted to catenane topology with a GLN of +1.120 upon cyclization. The synthetic strategy employed two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs acting on the entangled linear segments as a self-templating scaffold, coupled with circular permutation (residues 23 and 24) and a TEV protease recognition site for topologic proof. Gene cassettes were expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) at 16°C for 20 hours, with proteins purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography. SDS-PAGE revealed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for the linear control (l-DHFR) and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR, consistent with a more compact interlocked topology. Far-UV CD confirmed that cat-DHFR remains folded but with reduced ellipticity intensity, suggesting minor secondary structure loosening. Enzymatic activity assays at 25°C monitoring absorbance at 340 nm showed cat-DHFR retained approximately 5 U/mg compared to approximately 14 U/mg for l-DHFR, representing a significant portion of activity compared to rethreaded controls that showed no activity. Kinetic analysis by Hanes-Woolf plot revealed cat-DHFR with Km approximately 5-fold higher and kcat approximately 38% of l-DHFR, with catalytic efficiency reduced by an order of magnitude. ITC determined disassociation constants approximately 173-fold higher for DHF and approximately 14-fold for NADPH, indicating compromised substrate and cofactor affinity. Notably, cat-DHFR exhibited enhanced thermal and chemical resilience, retaining 87% activity in 5% DMSO versus 74% for l-DHFR, attributed to conformational restriction. Topology was confirmed through TEV cleavage, IMS-MS, and CID analysis. The work demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with preserved function and elevated stability, opening an entirely new horizon in protein science.

Research Context
Nature uses protein domains as independent modules that can be slotted into the genome during evolution, yet their linear polypeptide backbone confers limited topological diversity. Artificial topological proteins including star, cyclic, lasso, and protein catenanes have been designed through assembly-reaction synergy, but these constructions typically contain multiple domains. Multi-domain topological proteins complicate the study of how chemical topology alone affects structure-property relationships. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein should exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology and provide an unusual scaffold for further engineering and evolution. Single-domain topological proteins remain challenging to prepare even for the simplest catenane or Hopf link. Circular permutation and loop rethreading in DHFR have shown that rewired domains can fold into similar structures with preserved function, but the sequence remains linear. Previously reported rethreaded DHFR shows no reducing activity at all, and circular permutation alone can cause decreases in catalytic activity. No prior work has moved beyond the linear backbone as defined by the template polymerization mechanism of cellular ribosomal machinery.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a single-domain protein catenane can be designed and synthesized from a linear fold without collapsing the overall protein fold. The authors hypothesized that rewiring the connectivity between secondary structural motifs of the wild-type DHFR could introduce sufficient artificial entanglement to form two interlocked rings. The computational hypothesis was that a specific cleavage position between residues 88 and 89 would yield the largest Gaussian linking number (+0.726), identifying the potential entangling core. The synthesis hypothesis was that two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs could drive streamlined catenane formation in cells without additional in vitro reactions. The functional hypothesis predicted that the catenated DHFR would retain significant catalytic activity compared to rethreaded controls, and the stability would be enhanced by conformational restriction. A predicted outcome was that circular permutation would be necessary to place cyclization motifs on opposite sides, minimizing steric hindrance between bulky split-intein pairs. The authors envisioned that the need for an exogenous entangling motif as a template for catenane synthesis could be eliminated by exploiting spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures. The ultimate predicted outcome was that linear proteins could be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability.

Methodological Details
The study used DHFR from Escherichia coli as the model enzyme, with the wild-type sequence comprising 159 residues. In silico design of cat-DHFR was performed by virtually cleaving the wild-type DHFR backbone at all unstructured loops. The extent of intertwinement between the two resulting sub-chains was quantitatively evaluated by Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrices. The wild-type DHFR structure (PDB: 4KJJ) was used as the reference for GLN matrix calculation. Design criteria prioritized cleavage at residues 88 and 89, yielding two highly intertwined segments with GLN of +0.726. The catenane topology yielded a GLN of +1.120 upon cyclization of the two fragments. Ring 1 was composed of residues 1-88 and Ring 2 of residues 89-159. A streamlined biosynthesis used two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs for ring closure. Circular permutation was applied to ring I to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. The gene cassette included two DHFR segments as the entangling template, two mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs for ring closure, and a TEV protease recognition sequence in the first ring. A linear control (l-DHFR) was designed with identical amino acid composition bearing extra residues at the N-and C-terminus. Genes were synthesized and subcloned into pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors respectively. Plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Protein expression was carried out at 16 o C for 20 h to ensure proper folding. After cell lysis, proteins were purified under native conditions using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Eluted products were further purified by size exclusion chromatography. Characterization included SDS-PAGE, LC-MS for accurate molecular weights, far-UV and near-UV CD spectra, IMS-MS, and collision-induced dissociation. Catalytic activity was assayed by monitoring absorbance at 340 nm at 25 o C in the presence of NADPH. Kinetic parameters Km and kcat were determined by fitting Michaelis curves and Hanes-Woolf plots. Binding affinities were measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) for NADPH, DHF, and THF. Tolerance to organic solvents was tested by adding DMSO to a final concentration of 5%. Proteolytic topology proof used a TEV protease recognition site pre-programmed in the first ring. For the linker effect study, L2 of ring II was tested with different sequences and lengths.

Procedures And Architectures
In silico design involved generating all possible connectivity combinations by splitting M out of N loops, then filtering for those with appropriate spatial relationships. The entangling core was identified by the Gaussian linking number matrix of the wild-type (PDB: 4KJJ), determining the cleavage site at residues 88 and 89. Retrosynthetic analysis guided the selection of ring closure sites and linker lengths to ensure reconstitution and cyclization while keeping the correct spatial relationship. Ring I was circularly permutated to place the cyclization motifs on the opposite side of DHFR, minimizing steric hindrance between the bulky split-intein pairs. New loop designs were given lengths of at least 16residues to bridge split structural motifs. The gene cassette incorporated two DHFR segments as the entangling template, two mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs for ring closure, and a TEV protease recognition site in ring I. Genes were synthesized, subcloned into pMCSG19 and pET21a, and expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) at 16 o C for 20 h. Proteins were purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography under native conditions. SDS-PAGE demonstrated a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. SEC showed cat-DHFR eluting as a broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume, consistent with a compact and dynamic interlocked structure. Far-UV CD revealed reduced intensities of the positive peak at ~200 nm and negative peak between 210 nm and 230 nm, suggesting secondary structure loosening. Near-UV CD showed positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to l-DHFR, confirming a folded structure. Activity assays monitored absorbance at 340 nm at 25 o C with NADPH and DHF substrate. Kinetic data were analyzed via Michaelis curves and Hanes-Woolf plots to determine Km and kcat. ITC was used to measure disassociation constants (KD) for NADPH, DHF, and THF with both l-DHFR and cat-DHFR. DMSO tolerance was tested at 5% concentration by adding DMSO to the final reaction mixture. Topology proof involved enzymatic cleavage at the TEV protease site in ring I, confirmed by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS. IMS-MS and CID were applied to generate collision cross-section (CCS) values and secondary product ions for topological characterization. A control experiment tested ring closure on the same side of DHFR with similar amino acid composition and linker length. Linker effect was tested by varying the length and sequence of L2 in ring II.

Key Results
SDS-PAGE of purified products showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR, with faint lower-MW bands likely representing individual component rings. The apparently faster mobility of cat-DHFR in SDS-PAGE is attributed to its more compact interlocked topology versus the fully unfolded linear chains. SEC revealed cat-DHFR elutes as a broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume than l-DHFR, consistent with a dynamic structure from coupled movement of two interlocked rings. LC-MS spectra confirmed the identities of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR by accurate molecular weights as expected. Far-UV CD showed cat-DHFR remains folded but with substantially reduced ellipticity intensities, indicating secondary structure loosening similar to circularly permutated DHFR. Near-UV CD of cat-DHFR exhibited positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to l-DHFR, confirming a folded structure albeit slightly deviated from the linear one. The entangling design yielded two fragments with GLN of +0.726, which converted to catenane topology with GLN of +1.120 upon cyclization. The previously reported rethreaded DHFR shows no reducing activity at all, while the reconstituted physical complex of two DHFR fragments retained only 15% of the enzymatic activity. cat-DHFR retained approximately 5 U/mg of catalytic activity compared to approximately 14 U/mg for l-DHFR. Kinetic analysis showed cat-DHFR has a Km approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR at a saturation concentration of NADPH. The kcat of cat-DHFR is approximately 38% that of l-DHFR, and catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) is reduced by an order of magnitude. ITC determined KD values for DHF are approximately 173-fold larger for cat-DHFR than l-DHFR. ITC determined KD values for NADPH are approximately 14-fold larger for cat-DHFR than l-DHFR. The KD between cat-DHFR and THF is increased by approximately 3.6-fold relative to l-DHFR. The reduced enzymatic activity is mainly attributed to compromised affinity toward substrate and cofactor rather than impaired turnover. In the control experiment using same-side ring closure, much less catenane was formed with approximately 33% single-ring side products. Among ring closure sites, the site between residues 23 and 24 was found to be the most efficient. With the shortest linker, the yield of catenane is only about one-fifth that of the longest, approximately 12 mg/L of culture. The method is generally robust before the linker becomes too short, with catenated products still obtainable even at reduced yield. TEV protease cleavage converted cat-DHFR to a linear fragment and a cyclic fragment, confirmed by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS. cat-DHFR preserved 87% activity in 5% DMSO compared to 74% for l-DHFR, indicating enhanced thermal and chemical resilience. IMS-MS and CID revealed distinguishable differences in CCS values and secondary product ions between l-DHFR and cat-DHFR.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The mechanical interlocking of two polypeptide rings confers conformational restriction that enhances thermal and chemical resilience of the folded protein. The reduced catalytic activity is not due to fold collapse but to compromised binding affinity of the interlocked catenane toward DHF and NADPH. The preservation of significant enzymatic activity (approximately 35% of l-DHFR) despite extensive topological rewiring and split-intein cyclization is a major finding. The dynamic structure of cat-DHFR suggested by broader SEC elution reflects the coupled movement of the two mechanically interlocked rings. The secondary structure loosening observed in CD spectra, similar to circular permutation effects, suggests that while the overall fold is intact, local topology change induces minor structural distortion. The result implies that the spatial entangled relationships among secondary structures can serve as a self-templating scaffold for catenane synthesis. The authors envision that directed evolution could further restore or surpass the catalytic activity of cat-DHFR to match or exceed that of l-DHFR. This work demonstrates that the chemical topology of a protein domain can be altered without collapsing the fold, bringing in profound changes in properties. The finding represents an entirely new horizon in protein science, opening access to single-domain topological proteins with identical chemical composition to linear wild-types.

Contradictions And Limitations
No crystal structure of cat-DHFR could be obtained due to unsatisfactory purity, disordered linkers, or reduced binding affinity with substrates. The reduced catalytic activity (5 U/mg versus 14 U/mg) remains a limitation, although still significantly higher than rethreaded DHFR which shows no activity. The circular permutation required to place cyclization motifs on opposite sides was necessary because same-side ring closure yielded only ~33% catenane with significant single-ring by-products. A broader SEC peak at a slightly larger retention volume suggests a more dynamic structure, which may limit downstream applications or crystallization. The CD spectra indicate a loosening of secondary structure intensities, suggesting that the topological change is not entirely benign to the fold. The linker effect study revealed that the shortest linker yields only about one-fifth the catenane product, limiting design flexibility for minimal sequence addition. Only a single design (residues 1-88 and 89-159) was reported, with no systematic exploration of alternative cleavage sites or loop lengths. The study does not report absolute structural data beyond GLN matrices and CD, leaving the three-dimensional conformation of the interlocked rings uncharacterized by atomic-resolution methods. The far-UV CD intensities of cat-DHFR are substantially reduced compared to l-DHFR, a change the authors describe as consistent with circular permutation, but the full extent of this loosening is not quantified.

Claims
The first single-domain protein catenane has been designed and synthesized using a linear fold as the entangled template. Cat-DHFR was achieved by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs of DHFR to introduce artificial entanglement. Two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings fold synergistically into a compact and integrated structure. The GLN of +1.120 confirms the catenane topology upon cyclization of the two fragments. TEV cleavage confirmed production of one linear fragment and one cyclic fragment. The design was based on a single cleavage site (88/89), and no crystal structure could be obtained to confirm the exact topology. Same-side ring closure yielded ~33% single-ring by-products, suggesting the method requires specific geometric optimization. Linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition and preserved function. This opens an entirely new horizon in protein science for topological design.
Cat-DHFR retains significant catalytic activity despite extensive topological rewiring. cat-DHFR retains approximately 5 U/mg activity versus approximately 14 U/mg for l-DHFR. The previously reported rethreaded DHFR shows no reducing activity at all, making 5 U/mg substantial. Reconstituted physical complexes of two DHFR fragments (split 88/89) retain only 15% of full-length DHFR activity. cat-DHFR has a Km 5-fold higher and kcat approximately 38% of l-DHFR, with catalytic efficiency reduced by an order of magnitude. ITC revealed KD values 173-fold higher for DHF and 14-fold higher for NADPH, indicating compromised affinity. The reduced activity is due to compromised affinity rather than fold collapse, suggesting directed evolution could restore full activity. The preservation of activity confirms that the hydrophobic core and active site remain functional despite topological change.
Mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal and chemical resilience of the folded protein. cat-DHFR retained 87% activity in 5% DMSO versus 74% for l-DHFR. The authors attribute this to conformational restriction imposed by the catenane topology. Both results (activity and DMSO tolerance) suggest mechanical interlocking enhances resilience. No explicit thermal denaturation assays were reported; the claim is based on DMSO tolerance. The exact delta in melting temperature or denaturation kinetics is not quantified. Topological design offers a mechanism to enhance protein stability without altering the amino acid composition. This represents a new strategy for engineering thermostable and chemically resistant enzymes.
The synthetic method using split-intein pairs on an entangled template is robust and generally applicable. The yield with the shortest linker is only about one-fifth that of the longest, but catenated products are still obtained. The method is generally robust before the linker becomes too short. Two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-inteins enabled streamlined biosynthesis in cells without in vitro reactions. Site 23/24 was found to be the most efficient, and other sites were not tested as thoroughly. Steric hindrance from bulky split-intein pairs required circular permutation on the opposite side, indicating geometric constraints. The approach can be extended to other single-domain proteins that tolerate rethreading. Further optimization of linker design and ring closure sites could improve yield and robustness.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A control experiment using same-side ring closure yielded ~33% single-ring side products, confirming that circular permutation to opposite sides is necessary. Among different ring closure sites, the site between residues 23 and 24 was found to be the most efficient. The linker effect was tested by varying the sequence and length of L2 in ring II, with shorter linkers decreasing catenane yield to approximately 1/5 of the longest. The yield with the shortest linker is approximately 12 mg/L of culture, demonstrating the method remains functional under sub-optimal geometry. The design was validated by GLN analysis at two stages: first as the GLN +0.726 split and second as the +1.120 catenane, confirming topology change.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the retrosynthetic analysis and design schematic for cat-DHFR, including the 1-88 and 89-159 fragment division, circular permutation, and TEV protease placement. Figure 1b depicts the gene cassette architecture with the two DHFR segments, mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, and the TEV recognition sequence. Figure 1c shows the linear control l-DHFR with extra amino acids at the N-and C-terminus. Figure 1d displays the Gaussian linking number matrix used to identify the splitting position. Figure 2a shows SDS-PAGE of purified products with a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. Figure 2b presents the SEC overlay showing cat-DHFR eluting as a broader peak at a larger retention volume than l-DHFR. Figure 2c shows LC-MS spectra confirming accurate molecular weights of both cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure 2d displays far-UV CD spectra showing reduced intensities of the positive peak at ~200 nm and negative peak between 210 nm and 230 nm for cat-DHFR. Figure 2e shows SDS-PAGE and LC-MS after TEV cleavage, confirming a linear fragment and a cyclic fragment. Figure 4c shows kinetic curves of DHFR activity monitored at 340 nm at 25 o C, comparing cat-DHFR (~5 U/mg) with l-DHFR (~14 U/mg). Figure S1 shows GLN matrices of split DHFR (S1a) and cat-DHFR (S1b). Figure S2 shows the near-UV CD spectrum of cat-DHFR with positive ellipticity at ~290 nm. Figure S3 shows the same-side ring closure control (S3a) and the efficiency of different ring closure sites (S3b-d). Figure S4 shows the linker effect study with varying L2 sequences and lengths. Figure S7 shows the Michaelis curves and Hanes-Woolf plots for Km and kcat determination. Table 1 reports the kinetic parameters (Km, kcat, kcat/Km) and ITC binding constants (KD) for cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure S11 shows the DMSO tolerance assay results, with cat-DHFR at 87% versus l-DHFR at 74%.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane (cat-DHFR) from a linear fold without exogenous entangling templates, achieved by rewiring secondary structural connectivity and using mutually orthogonal split-inteins. 2. The strongest evidence is that cat-DHFR retains approximately 35% of catalytic activity (~5 U/mg versus ~14 U/mg), is confirmed as a catenane by TEV cleavage and IMS-MS, and shows enhanced thermal resilience (87% versus 74% in 5% DMSO), while a rethreaded control shows no activity. 3. The future path involves further optimization of ring closure geometry and linker design, directed evolution to restore full catalytic activity, and exploration of other single-domain proteins capable of folding with rewired topology.

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng, Vineet Padia, Joseph H Maalouf, Aditya M Limaye, Alexander H Liu, Michael A Yusov, Ian W Hunter, Karthish Manthiram
summary.field_subfield: Electrochemistry / Electrocatalysis
summary.executive_summary: This work introduces a robotic platform designed to automate electrochemical reaction rate data collection for cohesive kinetic analysis, a strategy traditionally underutilized in electrocatalysis due to its heavy data requirement. The robotic system sequentially tests up to ten electrochemical cells, each with potentially different electrode, electrolyte, gas-phase reactant composition, and applied voltage. The platform was applied to the carbon dioxide reduction reaction to carbon monoxide at three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc), at low loadings of 5.98 × 10⁻¹¹ to 8.04 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol/cm². Cohesive kinetic analysis revealed that bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences for all three catalysts are non-linear and potential-dependent, with the FePc catalyst exhibiting the most complex behavior where CO2 order decreases at less reductive potentials and potential-dependent curves intersect. For CoPc and CoTPP, bicarbonate inhibition is attenuated at more reductive potentials, consistent with a model of bicarbonate poisoning with positive electrosorption valency combined with potential-dependent mixed control between bicarbonate-dependent and bicarbonate-independent pathways. For FePc, bicarbonate inhibition is amplified at more reductive potentials, explained by a model where the most abundant reactive intermediate is a species prior to the unoccupied catalytic site. CO2 dependence for CoPc is nearly first-order, for CoTPP is slightly below one with potential-dependent attenuation, and for FePc the apparent order is most attenuated at less reductive potentials with a net-negative voltage effect at low CO2 pressures. These findings, along with the identification of electrolyte poisoning and coverage effects as critical mechanistic determinants, suggest that complex non-idealities are prevalent across the class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts and are undetectable by standard linearization techniques. The system is validated against literature CoPc data, showing newly measured rates up to ten times lower and CO Faradaic efficiencies below 30%, yet preserving established kinetic trends and exhibiting clear hallmarks of non-ideal mechanisms. The work demonstrates that the convergence of automation with cohesive kinetic analysis provides a powerful framework for dissecting complex electrocatalytic reaction mechanisms.

claims.description: A robotic platform can automate flexible and sequential reaction rate data collection for cohesive kinetic analysis of electrocatalytic reactions, enabling testing of multiple conditions per electrode in a single experimental effort.

Non-ideal reaction mechanisms, specifically bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control, are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts and are undetectable by standard linearization techniques.

Cohesive kinetic analysis revealed that bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences for all three catalysts are non-linear and potential-dependent, with the FePc catalyst exhibiting the most complex behavior where CO2 order decreases at less reductive potentials and potential-dependent curves intersect. For CoPc and CoTPP, bicarbonate inhibition is attenuated at more reductive potentials, consistent with a model of bicarbonate poisoning with positive electrosorption valency combined with potential-dependent mixed control between bicarbonate-dependent and bicarbonate-independent pathways. For FePc, bicarbonate inhibition is amplified at more reductive potentials, explained by a model where the most abundant reactive intermediate is a species prior to the unoccupied catalytic site. CO2 dependence for CoPc is nearly first-order, for CoTPP is slightly below one with potential-dependent attenuation, and for FePc the apparent order is most attenuated at less reductive potentials with a net-negative voltage effect at low CO2 pressures. These findings, along with the identification of electrolyte poisoning and coverage effects as critical mechanistic determinants, suggest that complex non-idealities are prevalent across the class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts and are undetectable by standard linearization techniques. The system is validated against literature CoPc data, showing newly measured rates up to ten times lower and CO Faradaic efficiencies below 30%, yet preserving established kinetic trends and exhibiting clear hallmarks of non-ideal mechanisms. The work demonstrates that the convergence of automation with cohesive kinetic analysis provides a powerful framework for dissecting complex electrocatalytic reaction mechanisms.

Research Context
Traditional electrocatalysis relies on linearized rate equations via Tafel and reactant order analyses. Linearization requires simplifying assumptions about factorable dependences and constant coverage. Coverage effects, mixed rate control, and side reactions complicate linear interpretation. The 59 mV/dec scaling for elementary charge transfer steps rapidly changes intermediate coverage. Solvent and electrolyte displacement effects further complicate reaction rate data. Cohesive kinetic analysis uses large volumes of data over wide reaction conditions. The analysis is more common in heterogeneous thermocatalysis than electrocatalysis. Meta-analysis showed Tafel slopes do not follow standard 120, 60, or 40 mV/dec values. Cohesive kinetic analysis at CoPc revealed mixed control and competitive electrolyte adsorption. One barrier to cohesive kinetic analysis is the heavy data requirement of manual collection. Existing electrocatalysis automation targets high-throughput screening rather than kinetic analysis. Miniaturized scanning droplet cells cannot quantify kinetics for non-100% Faradaic efficiency reactions. A sequential electrochemical testing workflow with online product quantification is ideal for automated kinetic analysis.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a robotic platform automate electrochemical reaction rate data collection for cohesive kinetic analysis in CO2RR? What are the underlying mechanisms for CO2RR to CO at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles under a wide range of conditions? The central hypothesis is that non-ideal reaction mechanisms are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts. Bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences are predicted to be non-linear and potential-dependent. Electrolyte poisoning, mixed control, and coverage effects are identified as the primary explanatory phenomena. Non-ideal kinetic signatures across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc should confirm the prevalence of complex mechanisms. The mechanistic analysis aims to explain unambiguous existence of mechanistic complexity rather than propose a single specific mechanism.

Methodological Details
Three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts were tested: CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. CoPc was drop-casted onto calcined Toray060 carbon paper at 5.98 × 10⁻¹¹ mol/cm². CoTPP was loaded at 5.11 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol/cm² with carbon black to avoid aggregation. FePc was loaded at 8.04 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol/cm² also with carbon black. Electrolytes were prepared from 0.5 mol/L Na₂CO₃ and 1 mol/L NaClO₄ stock solutions. Stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO2 before use. The robotic system sequentially tests up to ten electrochemical cells per batch. A leak-free Ag/AgCl reference electrode was calibrated daily against saturated calomel. A 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire served as the counter electrode. Carbon paper disk working electrodes with 10 mm diameter were used. A gas chromatograph provided online detection of CO and H2. Data files were automatically uploaded to an SQL database. A Python script processed run conditions and output partial currents to Excel.

The robot design consists of a single cell body housing reference and counter electrodes. Ten cell pan pairs each house a carbon paper working electrode. The cell body moves horizontally to sequentially access each cell pan. The cell body moves vertically to open and close onto any given cell pan. Electrolyte is pumped through the "electrolyte in" port for each electrolysis. Two electrolyte configurations were available: individual vials or a common reservoir. Cell body cleaning is performed at a wash station with milliQ water. The cell body was rinsed after each full set of ten electrolyses. The user queues up to ten electrolyses in an Excel file. Each run uses the same electrolyte composition within a batch of ten.

For CoPc and CoTPP, apparent bicarbonate inhibition is most negative at less reductive potentials. For CoPc and CoTPP, the bicarbonate dependence becomes positive at more reductive potentials. For FePc, greater bicarbonate inhibition occurs at more reductive potentials. CoPc CO2 order dependence appears as simple first-order within error at both potentials. For CoTPP, the apparent CO2 order is slightly below one and decreases at more reductive potentials. For FePc, the apparent CO2 order is most attenuated at less reductive potentials. The CO2 order dependence curves for the two FePc potentials intersect. CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism, consistent with previous proposals. The FePc mechanism likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as MARI. Across all runs, only c.a. 60% of Faradaic efficiency was attributable to CO and H2. The newly measured CoPc CO production rates were up to ten times lower than literature. Faradaic efficiencies toward CO were typically under 30% in the newly measured data. Previously reported kinetic trends in CO production were preserved and well-correlated with new data. Hallmarks of non-ideal reaction mechanisms, including curvature and potential-dependent bicarbonate order changes, were clearly evident. FE toward HER was typically around 30 to 60%. Aggregated rates and selectivities for all three catalysts are in the Supplemental Information.

Bicarbonate poisoning is modeled with a positive electrosorption valency. Negative charge on bicarbonate is more repelled as electrode becomes more negatively charged. A quantitative model for CoPc bicarbonate kinetics was previously reported. For FePc, bicarbonate inhibition is stronger at more reductive potentials in contrast to local equilibrium. Alternatively, apparent bicarbonate inhibition can be explained by mixed control between two catalytic pathways. This bicarbonate-dependent surface intermediate can be an on-cycle poisoning species. Opposing kinetic observations in the literature may be reconciled by differences in operating conditions.

The one-compartment cell design allows crosstalk between working and counter electrodes. Incomplete Faradaic efficiency closure indicates oxygen crossover from the counter electrode. Data files and run information were automatically uploaded to a database. The cell washing sequence still requires manual cleaning of cell pans. The common reservoir configuration limits independent electrolyte changes between experiments in a batch. summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada, M Ondráček, M Lamanec, A Gallardo, A Jiménez-Martín, B De La Torre, P Hobza, P Jelínek
summary.field_subfield: Chemical Physics / Surface Science / Molecular Electronics
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first direct experimental observation of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon compounds—resolved at the single-molecule level using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The π-hole concept, previously developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations, predicts a positive quadrupole moment in molecules where peripheral hydrogen atoms are replaced by more electronegative substituents such as fluorine or chlorine. For the specific molecule 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (C14F8Cl2), the electronegative halogen substituents reverse the electron population of the delocalized π-bond system, creating a positively charged central cavity, in contrast to anthracene (C14H10) which retains its electron-rich, negatively charged π-system. The authors grew a heterogeneous molecular self-assembly of FCl-An and An on an atomically clean Au(111) surface by simultaneous sublimation in ultrahigh vacuum at room temperature for 15 seconds. Noncontact atomic force microscopy with a functionalized CO tip, combined with DFT-calculated electronic structure, resolved the rhombic unit cell containing one An and two FCl-An molecules, whose arrangement is governed by attractive electrostatic interactions between fluorine, chlorine (σ-hole), and hydrogen atoms. KPFM, recording the local contact potential difference (LCPD) at atomic resolution by fitting a parabolic expression to frequency-versus-bias spectroscopy, revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the LCPD signal at the FCl-An carbon skeleton that was absent in An. Simulated KPFM images from DFT-derived electrostatic potentials and the Probe Particle model confirmed the experimental findings. Furthermore, specific-site force-distance spectroscopy showed that FCl-An adsorbs 30 pm higher above the Au(111) surface than An (360 pm vs. 330 pm), consistent with DFT-predicted adsorption heights (360 pm and 325 pm). SAPT0 energy decomposition confirmed that while dispersion dominates adsorption, the induction energy—stabilization from electrostatic interaction between permanent charge multipoles and the induced charge—is larger for An than FCl-An, fully consistent with reduced induced electron density in the π-hole-bearing molecule. These results confirm that the π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppresses charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface, weakens induced electrostatic interactions, and increases adsorption height, extending the applicability of scanning probe microscopy to submolecular charge distribution studies that fundamentally affect molecular physical and chemical properties.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first direct experimental observation of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon compounds—resolved at the single-molecule level using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The π-hole concept, previously developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations, predicts a positive quadrupole moment in molecules where peripheral hydrogen atoms are replaced by more electronegative substituents such as fluorine or chlorine. For the specific molecule 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (C14F8Cl2), the electronegative halogen substituents reverse the electron population of the delocalized π-bond system, creating a positively charged central cavity, in contrast to anthracene (C14H10) which retains its electron-rich, negatively charged π-system. The authors grew a heterogeneous molecular self-assembly of FCl-An and An on an atomically clean Au(111) surface by simultaneous sublimation in ultrahigh vacuum at room temperature for 15 seconds. Noncontact atomic force microscopy with a functionalized CO tip, combined with DFT-calculated electronic structure, resolved the rhombic unit cell containing one An and two FCl-An molecules, whose arrangement is governed by attractive electrostatic interactions between fluorine, chlorine (σ-hole), and hydrogen atoms. KPFM, recording the local contact potential difference (LCPD) at atomic resolution by fitting a parabolic expression to frequency-versus-bias spectroscopy, revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the LCPD signal at the FCl-An carbon skeleton that was absent in An. Simulated KPFM images from DFT-derived electrostatic potentials and the Probe Particle model confirmed the experimental findings. Furthermore, specific-site force-distance spectroscopy showed that FCl-An adsorbs 30 pm higher above the Au(111) surface than An (360 pm vs. 330 pm), consistent with DFT-predicted adsorption heights (360 pm and 325 pm). SAPT0 energy decomposition confirmed that while dispersion dominates adsorption, the induction energy—stabilization from electrostatic interaction between permanent charge multipoles and the induced charge—is larger for An than FCl-An, fully consistent with reduced induced electron density in the π-hole-bearing molecule. These results confirm that the π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppresses charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface, weakens induced electrostatic interactions, and increases adsorption height, extending the applicability of scanning probe microscopy to submolecular charge distribution studies that fundamentally affect molecular physical and chemical properties.

Research Context
Submolecular charge distribution significantly affects the physical-chemical properties of molecules and their mutual interaction. The presence of a π-electron-deficient cavity in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon compounds, the so-called π-holes, was predicted theoretically. However, the direct experimental observation of the π-hole has been lacking so far. Until now, the concept of π-hole has been developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations. Scanning probe microscopy emerges as the most appropriate tool for the direct visualization of π-holes in molecular systems. The Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) method, which enabled resolution of the sigma-hole, is positioned as an ideal imaging tool for the real-space observation of the π-hole system.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the π-hole can be directly resolved and imaged on a single molecule. The study hypothesizes that KPFM can confirm the theoretical prediction of the π-hole's existence by mapping the local contact potential difference. A secondary hypothesis is that the π-hole significantly affects the electrostatic interactions, thereby influencing the adsorption of molecules on solid-state surfaces. The expected outcome is that FCl-An (bearing a π-hole) will show a distinct LCPD pattern absent in the control molecule anthracene (An). It is predicted that the π-hole will increase the adsorption height of FCl-An relative to An due to weakened electrostatic interaction.

Methodological Details
Experiments were conducted at a temperature of 4.2 K using a commercial STM/nc-AFM microscope from Createc GmbH. Pt/Ir tips, sharpened by focused ion beam (FIB), were cleaned and shaped by gentle indentation of approximately 1 nm into the bare metallic substrate. nc-AFM used a qPlus sensor with a resonant frequency ≈ 30 kHz, stiffness ≈ 1800 N/m, and oscillation amplitude of 200 pm. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by repeated cycles of Ar+ sputtering at 1 keV followed by annealing at ~800 K. 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An) were sublimated from two Knudsen cells simultaneously in UHV at room temperature for 15 s on the Au(111) surface. LCPD maps were obtained by fitting a parabolic expression to Δf(V, x, y) data collected at all points of a 64 x 80 pixels rectangular grid of size 3 nm x 5 nm. Each data point was acquired in approximately 3 seconds, with each parabola containing 600 points, over a bias range of (-150, 400) mV. The acquisition height was chosen to be in the attractive regime to maximize the electrostatic contribution for both molecules. DFT calculations employed the PBE functional with the FHI-AIMS code, a lightweight setup with PBE functional, no k-grid, and a 4-atomic-layer Au(111) slab. The surface supercell for isolated molecules was 6×6 unit cells; for the supramolecular structure, a √39×√39 surface cell deformed by 1.20% and 1.06% was used. Van der Waals correction was applied using the Tkatchenko-Scheffler method with Hirshfeld partitioning, excluding direct Au-Au interaction. Molecular orbitals and electrostatic potential maps of free-standing molecules were calculated at the MP2/cc-pVTZ level for optimized geometries. Both molecules were optimized on the gold layer using PBE0 functional with Grimme's D3 dispersion correction and def2-TZVPP basis set in ORCA. SAPT0 energy decomposition was performed on a cluster model using PSI4 in the cc-pVDZ (cc-pwCVDZ-PP for Au) basis set. Specific-site force-distance Δf-z spectroscopy was acquired above the central benzene unit of both An and FCl-An molecules.

Procedures And Architectures
The molecular self-assembly was grown by simultaneous sublimation of An and FCl-An at room temperature in ultrahigh vacuum on the Au(111) surface. STM images at 4.8 K revealed large-scale ordered molecular islands with both species alternating in a periodic fashion. nc-AFM with a functionalized CO tip in constant height mode resolved the detailed arrangement, distinguishing the two molecular species. The supramolecular assembly comprises a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules in the unit cell. The arrangement is dictated by attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between negatively charged fluorine, σ-hole on chlorine, and positively charged hydrogen atoms. KPFM was employed to record the spatial variation of the local contact potential difference (LCPD) across the surface. A parabolic expression of the form Δf(V) = a × (V - LCPD)² + Δf* was fitted to each data point. The LCPD value, corresponding to the bias at the parabola maximum, and the Δf* maximum frequency shift were extracted for mapping. Tip-sample distance was carefully controlled; at far distances, intramolecular features are absent, while at short distances, tip relaxations cause deviations. A tip-sample height close to the Δf minima was chosen to ensure absence of tip relaxation and maximize contrast. Simulated KPFM images were generated using the Probe Particle (PP) model adapted to a CO-terminated tip, with a lateral spring constant of 0.25 N/m for the CO molecule. DFT-calculated electron densities of the sample surface were used in the PP model to evaluate Pauli repulsion. DFT-calculated maps of electrostatic potential and electrical polarizability generated the simulated KPFM maps, assuming a dz²-like charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å² for the CO tip termination.

Key Results
The KPFM images of FCl-An (C14F8Cl2) revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern of the LCPD signal presented in the central part of the molecule. This submolecular variation of the LCPD signal was absent in the images of anthracene (C14H10), confirming the presence of a π-hole in FCl-An. Simulated KPFM images match very well with the experimental evidence, reproducing the submolecular LCPD signal variation and the bow-tie pattern. The simulated LCPD matches the distribution of the electrostatic potential calculated for a free-standing FCl-An molecule, confirming the heterogeneous charge distribution of the π-hole. The π-hole heterogeneity is associated with the different electronegativity of fluorine and chlorine modulating the charge transfer from the π-system locally. The supramolecular assembly was unambiguously resolved as a rhombic unit cell with one An and two FCl-An molecules, confirmed by perfect agreement between experimental and theoretical nc-AFM images. Δf-z spectroscopy over bare Au(111) determined relative molecular adsorption heights of 330 pm for An and 360 pm for FCl-An. The difference between the minima of two Δf-z curves for An and FCl-An was 30 pm, directly related to the difference in adsorption height. DFT total energy calculations predicted adsorption heights of 325 pm for An and 360 pm for FCl-An on Au(111), matching the experimental values reasonably well. Both molecules are physisorbed with negligible hybridization of molecular orbitals, and the interaction is dominated by dispersion interaction. Induced electron density at the molecule/metal interface is more significant for An than for FCl-An, confirming reduced charge induction in the π-hole-bearing molecule. In the SAPT0 energy decomposition, the induction energy describing stabilization from permanent charge multipoles and induced charge is larger for An than for FCl-An. The induction energy is larger for An than FCl-An, fully agreeing with the relative magnitude of induced electron densities from the DFT slab calculation. The attractive interaction dominates the dispersion energy compared to the electrostatic and induction terms in all three molecules. The mere deposition of An on the surface does not result in the formation of self-organized molecular structures, confirming the assembly depends on FCl-An.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule, which inhibits the induction of charge density at the molecule/metal interface. This inhibition results in weakened induced electrostatic interactions and consequently in larger adsorption height of the molecule. The experimental bow-tie pattern in the LCPD map directly reflects the submolecular charge distribution of the π-hole, confirming its existence at the single-molecule level. The agreement between experimental KPFM, simulations, and electrostatic potential calculations validates KPFM as an ideal imaging tool for submolecular charge structures. This study expands the understanding of π-hole systems and opens possibilities for studying the influence of submolecular charge distribution on chemical properties and mutual interaction. The results establish a fundamental link between submolecular electronic structure and macroscopic properties like adsorption height and intermolecular assembly.

Contradictions And Limitations
The AFM images do not provide any direct experimental evidence of the π-hole; FCl-An molecules are systematically imaged brighter than An due to a topographic effect. The obtained KPFM contrast is highly dependent on tip-sample distance; at far distances, the images do not exhibit intramolecular features, while at short distances, tip relaxations generate measurement artifacts. KPFM measurements show a noticeable deviation in the LCPD signal from its parabolic shape at short tip-sample distances due to tip relaxations, unlike nc-AFM where tip relaxations improve resolution. The Δf* images (Δf(V) maximum at compensated LCPD) show no submolecular resolution for either An or FCl-An, limiting their diagnostic value for π-hole identification. SAPT0 was performed on a cluster model, which gives very similar results to the slab model, but the cluster model simplifies the surface environment. The SAPT0 analysis uses a cluster model with 38 gold atoms, which may not fully capture the metallic environment compared to the full slab model. The lightweight DFT setup (PBE functional, no k-grid) was chosen for large supercells, raising questions about the precision of the electronic structure in the presence of the metal surface.

Claims
Kelvin probe force microscopy directly resolves the π-hole in a single FCl-An molecule, confirming the theoretical prediction of its existence. The experimental KPFM images reveal a characteristic bow-tie pattern of LCPD variation at the FCl-An carbon skeleton. The submolecular LCPD variation is completely absent in anthracene, the control molecule without a π-hole. Simulated KPFM images reproduced the experimental bow-tie pattern and submolecular LCPD variation very well. The internal variation of the LCPD signal matches the electrostatic potential calculated for a free-standing FCl-An molecule. AFM images do not show direct evidence of the π-hole due to a topographic contrast effect. The Δf* images, which would capture the compensated LCPD, do not exhibit submolecular resolution. KPFM is validated as a suitable tool for real-space imaging of submolecular charge distributions in individual molecules. The π-hole concept extends from theoretical prediction to experimental fact at the single-molecule level.
The π-hole increases the ionization potential and suppresses induced charge density at the molecule-metal interface, leading to weakened electrostatic adsorption. SAPT0 induction energy is larger for An than FCl-An, consistent with reduced induced electron density in the π-hole molecule. DFT calculations show more significant induced electron density at the An-Au(111) interface compared to FCl-An/Au(111). The π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppressing charge density induction. Both molecules are physisorbed with negligible orbital hybridization, confirming the interaction is electrostatically dominated. The SAPT0 calculations were performed on a cluster model, which may differ from the full slab environment. The SAPT0 and DFT adsorption energies give very similar results, suggesting the qualitative trend is robust. Submolecular charge distribution directly modulates macroscopic adsorption properties of molecules on surfaces. The electrostatic quadrupole moment of π-hole molecules can be tuned via substituent electronegativity.
The FCl-An molecule adsorbs 30 pm higher above the Au(111) surface than anthracene, a result consistent with DFT predictions of the π-hole's electrostatic effect. Specific-site Δf-z spectroscopy gave relative heights of 360 pm (FCl-An) and 330 pm (An). The 30 pm difference between Δf-z minima corresponds directly to the adsorption height difference. DFT calculated adsorption heights of 325 pm (An) and 360 pm (FCl-An) match the experimental values reasonably well. The rhombic assembly with one An and two FCl-An is stabilized by attractive electrostatic interactions between peripheral halogens and σ-holes. The SAPT0 cluster model uses only 38 gold atoms, which may simplify the surface interaction. The exact mechanism of electrostatic stabilization in the heterodimer remains complex, with both dispersion and electrostatics contributing. Molecular design via electronegative substituents can be used to tune adsorption height and orientation on metallic surfaces. Intermolecular electrostatic interactions, mediated by the π-hole, govern the self-assembly pattern.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The KPFM contrast was shown to depend strongly on tip-sample distance, with intramolecular features appearing only at short distances. Tip relaxations, which improve resolution in nc-AFM, generate measurement artifacts and noticeable deviation from parabolic LCPD in KPFM. Δf* images show no submolecular resolution for either molecule, serving as a control confirming that submolecular contrast arises from the electrostatic LCPD signal. The SAPT0 analysis on a cluster model gave very similar results to the slab model, validating the cluster approximation. DFT and SAPT0 calculations give very similar results of adsorption energies, reinforcing the reliability of both methods. For free-standing molecules, hybrid PBE0 calculations with the tight basis showed no substantial changes in geometry or charge distribution compared to PBE.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates that larger carbon electronegativity generates a negative quadrupole in PAHs, while electronegative substituents reverse it to a positive quadrupole. Figure 2a shows STM images of the ordered molecular assembly grown on Au(111) with alternating An and FCl-An molecules. Figure 2b displays high-resolution nc-AFM images clearly distinguishing the two molecular species. Figure 2c shows the rhombic unit cell structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules. Figure 2d shows the attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions dictating the arrangement. Figure 3a shows the electrostatic potential map of a free-standing FCl-An molecule with the heterogeneous π-hole. Figure 3c shows the simulated KPFM image reproducing the bow-tie LCPD pattern at the FCl-An carbon skeleton. Figure 3d shows the KPFM image with the spatial variation of LCPD at atomic resolution. Figure 4a displays Δf-z spectroscopy over the central benzene unit, showing a 30 pm difference between An and FCl-An minima. Figure 4b and 4c show the calculated induced electron density between the molecules and the Au(111) surface, greater for An than FCl-An. Figure 6 shows a series of constant-height AFM images revealing submolecular contrast emerging on FCl-An. Table S2 presents adsorption energies and interaction energy decomposition for all three molecules. Table S3 presents the SAPT0 energy decomposition for An, FCl-An, and the surface model.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first direct real-space experimental observation of a π-hole at the single-molecule level by KPFM, confirming the theoretically predicted π-electron-deficient cavity in FCl-An. 2. summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime, Galina Lebedev, Jackline Abo-Nassar, Sally Marzouk, Moshe Inbar, Murad Ghanim, Radi Aly
summary.field_subfield: Entomology / Plant Protection - Phytoecdysteroids as insect growth regulators
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the biological activity of crude leaf and stem extracts of Ajuga iva, a plant containing phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone) and clerodane diterpenes, against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis. The authors hypothesized that the phytoecdysteroids, which are steroid analogs of insect molting hormones, would impair larval development and survival. The study employed three concentrations of crude extract (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl) on first-instar larvae and tested developmental impacts on third-instar larvae through 11-day feeding periods, including sequence-of-treatment assays and comparison with a purified phytoecdysteroid fraction. First-instar larvae showed dose-dependent mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl, respectively, against a 5% control. Third-instar larvae fed on the highest concentration showed significantly reduced larval weight gain (F3.104 = 13.007, p < 0.001) and decreased relative growth rate (RGR) by 0.05 g/g day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g day on day 8. Survival was significantly reduced after 11 days (X² = 6.221, p = 0.038), with no larvae surviving beyond 8 days at 250 µg/µl. A fractionated mixture of the three phytoecdysteroids at 250 µg/µl replicated the crude extract effects (F2.20,18 = 6.172, p = 0.001), while a commercial standard mixture at 100 ppm had no significant effect. Gut histology revealed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filaments in treated larvae. Pupation was completely blocked: no larvae completed development to adult moths; pupae exhibited short limbs, small heads, and decreased weight, with only stomach and chest pupated. The authors conclude that A. iva phytoecdysteroids interfere with developmental stages during metamorphosis, likely by disrupting hormonal balance and causing gut histolysis with apoptotic features. The study supports the use of A. iva as a potential IPM component for S. littoralis management with reduced risks to human health and the environment.
