judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the biological activity of crude leaf and stem extracts of Ajuga iva, a plant containing phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone) and clerodane diterpenes, against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis. The authors hypothesized that the phytoecdysteroids, which are steroid analogs of insect molting hormones, would impair larval development and survival. The study employed three concentrations of crude extract (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl) on first-instar larvae and tested developmental impacts on third-instar larvae through 11-day feeding periods, including sequence-of-treatment assays and comparison with a purified phytoecdysteroid fraction. First-instar larvae showed dose-dependent mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl, respectively, against a 5% control. Third-instar larvae fed on the highest concentration showed significantly reduced larval weight gain (F3.104 = 13.007, p < 0.001) and decreased relative growth rate (RGR) by 0.05 g/g day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g day on day 8. Survival was significantly reduced after 11 days (X² = 6.221, p = 0.038), with no larvae surviving beyond 8 days at 250 µg/µl. A fractionated mixture of the three phytoecdysteroids at 250 µg/µl replicated the crude extract effects (F2.20,18 = 6.172, p = 0.001), while a commercial standard mixture at 100 ppm had no significant effect. Gut histology revealed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filaments in treated larvae. Pupation was completely blocked: no larvae completed development to adult moths; pupae exhibited short limbs, small heads, and decreased weight, with only stomach and chest pupated. The authors conclude that A. iva phytoecdysteroids interfere with developmental stages during metamorphosis, likely by disrupting hormonal balance and causing gut histolysis with apoptotic features. The study supports the use of A. iva as a potential IPM component for S. littoralis management with reduced risks to human health and the environment.

Research Context
The African cotton leafworm S. littoralis is a major pest affecting cotton, maize, rice, alfalfa, potato, tomato, ornamentals, and orchard trees. Insect control primarily relies on insecticides that pose risks to human health and the environment. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroid analogs of insect molting hormones found in 5-6% of plant species. They mimic insect 20-hydroxyecdysteroid, bind ecdysone receptors, and elicit abnormal larval development, feeding deterrence, and death. Ecdysteroids are not toxic to mammals due to structural differences and lack of binding to vertebrate steroid receptors. Discovery of the same phytoecdysteroids in several plant species suggests they may be effective against insect herbivores as antifeedants and endocrine disruptors. Low concentrations of phytoecdysteroids (2-25 ppm) deter some insects, while others are resistant to 400-1000 ppm. Kubo reported that an Ajuga remota extract containing 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone inhibited ecdysis in Bombyx mori, causing death. Greenhouse whitefly exhibited 100% mortality when fed on Ajuga reptans plants. A. iva extract containing 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone showed high activity against Oligonychus perseae, with 5 μg/ml pure extracted ecdysterone reducing fecundity, fertility, and survival. The authors previously identified high contents of three phytoecdysteroids and two clerodanes in A. iva growing in Israel. Ajuga also contains bioactive clerodane diterpenes and iridoid glycosides, with clerodanes exhibiting potential as natural pesticides. Koul showed that dihydroclerodin and clerodin hemiacetal from Caryopteris divaricata exhibit 100% antifeedant activity at 50 ppm and were deadly to Spodoptera litura.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors hypothesized that the crude extract of A. iva leaves containing the three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone), which specifically interfere by controlling molting and are responsible for metamorphosis and antifeedant activities, might be a promising pest-control agent. The central research question was whether A. iva crude leaf extract affects S. littoralis larvae. The second question was whether phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude leaf extract and commercial standards have different effects on the larvae. The third question was whether phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut. The study aimed to evaluate the efficiency of A. iva extracts (containing phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes) at reducing damage caused by S. littoralis larvae. The predicted outcome was dose-dependent reduction in larval growth, survival, and pupation, with specific morphological changes in the gut. The hypothesis was that effects on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance effected by internal levels of ecdysone. Another predicted mode of action suggested that abnormal gut development could lead to reduced weight and mortality. The authors also posited that reduced growth reflects a different mode of action of phytoecdysteroids beyond the known molting disruption.

Methodological Details
Young and mature leaves and stems of fresh A. iva were collected after blooming (July-November), oven-dried at 55 • C for 3-4 days, and homogenized to a fine powder. First and third instar S. littoralis larvae were obtained from Murad Ghanim's laboratory at the Agricultural Research Organization and reared on castor bean leaves. For crude extract preparation, 24 g of pooled leaf and stem powder were soaked in 240 ml of 100% MeOH, homogenized at 2500 rpm for 1 h, centrifuged at 112 g for 10 min, filtered, vacuum-concentrated, and dried in a chemical vaporizer for 5 days. LC-TOF-MS was performed using an Agilent 1290 Infinity Series liquid chromatograph coupled with Agilent DAD and Agilent 6224 Accurate Mass TOF mass spectrometer. TLC used silica gel GF-254 plates (0.25 mm; 20 × 20 cm) to separate components. Three concentrations of crude leaf extract were prepared: 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl. For first-instar bioassays, 10 larvae per replicate were placed on 1 treated castor bean leaf in a petri dish. Leaves were smeared with aqueous A. iva crude extract (24 g dissolved in 240 ml MeOH, 1:10) and Tween 20 (1.5 mg), then dried in a chemical hood for 2 h. Larvae were allowed to feed for 3 days in a climate-controlled room at 25 • C. Control leaves were smeared with double-distilled water and Tween 20. Concentrations were prepared by dissolving 1.2 g dried extract in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20 (0.5 mg/ml) for 250 µg/µl, with serial dilution for 100 and 50 µg/µl. Data for the first-instar experiment represented the results of 11 replicates (10 larvae/replicate). Differences in mortality were analyzed by t-test. For third-instar assays, 1 or 10 larvae were fed on 1 treated castor bean leaf for 4 or 8 days in a climate-controlled room at 25 • C. Four treatments tested: (1) 250 µg/µl crude extract for 4 days then 4 days on freshly treated leaf; (2) same but with 250 µg/µl fractionated mixture of three phytoecdysteroids; (3) crude extract for 4 days then control for 4 days; (4) control for 4 days then crude extract for 4 days. In parallel, control leaves were smeared with ddH2O and Tween 20 for 8 days. Relative growth rate was calculated as (ln W2 - ln W1) / (t2 - t1). RGR data (n = 20 replicates) were compared using mixed-model ANOVA (repeated measures ANOVA until day 4, two-way ANOVA after). Survival rates were analyzed using a Friedman test because larval survival data did not follow a normal distribution. Larval weight gain data (n = 10 replicates) were compared using repeated measures ANOVA. Pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days. Statistical significance was reported at p < 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed with IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows. For gut morphology, larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude extract for 8 days were tested after 7 days of treatment. Guts were dissected in 1X PBS, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min, washed in 0.1% Triton X-100 for 30 min, washed three times in PBST, incubated in 0.1% phalloidin in PBST for 30 min, washed three times, and mounted in 0.1% DAPI in hybridization buffer. Visualized under a Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope.

Procedures And Architectures
The phytoecdysteroid extraction followed a published procedure: 100 g leaf and stem powder soaked in 300 ml methanol, homogenized, filtered, vacuum-concentrated, and treated with H2O to yield 30% aqueous methanol. This 30% aqueous methanol solution was extracted as previously described by Aly et al. (2011). For identification, crude leaf extract (1 µl) was injected into the Agilent 1290 LC system coupled with DAD and accurate mass TOF detector. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on silica gel GF-254 plates separated compounds into well-defined spots. Flash chromatography on silica gel yielded three isolated compounds: 20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone. Retention factor (Rf) values of isolated phytoecdysteroids were compared to commercial ecdysteroid standards to confirm identity. For the fractionated mixture, a mixture of three commercial standards (ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) was prepared at a maximum concentration of 100 ppm each. This commercial mixture was applied to castor bean leaves at 100 ppm of the three standards for 8 days. For the commercial control, S. littoralis larvae were fed on castor bean leaves treated with 100 ppm of the mixture for 8 days. The study noted the commercial standards were very expensive and not feasible as a control treatment at treatment concentrations. The authors explicitly stated they did not fractionate clerodanes due to the difficulty of calibrating the fractionation protocol and high cost of commercial clerodane standards. Larvae were fed in a climate-controlled room at 25 • C throughout all bioassays. Control leaves for the sequence-of-treatment experiment were smeared with ddH2O and Tween 20 for 8 days. For the 3rd instar sequence experiment, freshly treated leaves were provided after 4 days of feeding to avoid feeding on decayed leaves. The sequence of treatments tested four permutations of control and crude extract/fractionated mixture application order. In the gut morphology experiment, larvae exposed to 250 µg/µl crude extract were analyzed after 8 days of treatment, with guts dissected in PBS and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde.

Key Results
First-instar S. littoralis larvae showed dose-dependent mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% after feeding on 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl A. iva crude leaf extract, compared to 5% in the water control. Third-instar larvae fed on 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract showed significantly reduced larval weight gain (F3.104 = 20.334, 17.246, and 13.007, respectively; p < 0.001). All crude extract concentrations significantly decreased (p < 0.001) larval RGR compared to control larvae. At the highest concentration (250 µg/µl), RGR decreased by 0.05 g/g day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g day on day 8 (F3.16,18 = 12.641, p < 0.001). All concentrations of A. iva crude leaf extract significantly reduced third-instar larval survival after 11 days (X² = 6.221, p = 0.038). None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days at the highest concentration (250 µg/µl) and 10 days at the other concentrations, whereas all control larvae survived. In the control-then-extract sequence, RGR was affected after day 5 (F3.16,18 = 7.310, p < 0.001) and continued to decrease with no surviving larvae (X² = 9.282, p = 0.021). In the extract-then-control sequence, RGR significantly decreased on days 2-4 (F3.16,18 = 4.595, 3.608, and 8.113; p = 0.034, 0.02, and 0.001) for 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl respectively. The fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture at 250 µg/µl significantly reduced RGR (F2.20,18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) and few larvae survived (X² = 11.305, p = 0.04). Overall, larvae fed on either 250 µg/µl crude extract or 250 µg/µl phytoecdysteroid mixture lost weight, stopped growing, and ultimately died. Larvae fed on the commercial standard mixture (100 ppm of ecdysterone, makisterone A, cyasterone) for 8 days showed no significant effect. Gut histology revealed smaller nuclei with abnormal shape (moved to cell edges, thinner than normal) in larvae treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract for 8 days. In guts from larvae treated with crude extract or the phytoecdysteroid fraction, actin filaments were smaller and their amount reduced. Larvae fed 250 µg/µl of crude extract or its phytoecdysteroid fraction for 8 days were unable to complete development and pupate after 15 days. Incomplete pupae exhibited short limbs, small heads, decreased weight, and only stomach and chest pupated, classified as nonpupation. None of the treated larvae completed development to adult moths. Gut cells showed histolysis with clear signs of apoptosis, massive deterioration of the epithelium, destruction of microvilli, and formation of vacuoles. In smaller larvae, mortality occurred during molting between instars; in larger larvae, most mortality was at the prepupal stage. The damage to the gut continued until the insects died.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results confirm that A. iva crude leaf extract and its fractionated phytoecdysteroids significantly reduce development and survival of S. littoralis larvae throughout all stages, including pupation. Phytoecdysteroids may affect insects by interfering with developmental stages, especially during metamorphosis, by disrupting endogenous endocrine levels. The reduced growth rate suggests that larvae are adversely affected by ingestion of the crude leaf extract and the three-phytoecdysteroid mixture, reflecting a possible mode of action beyond the known molting disruption. Abnormal gut development, evidenced by histolysis and destruction of microvilli, could lead to reduced larval weight gain and subsequent mortality. Disruptions in gut morphology and disappearance of actin microfilament structures could be a consequence of phytoecdysteroid titers in the extract. Actin microfilaments are associated with viral infection responses and secondary metabolite responses, suggesting a cellular signaling disruption. The effect on pupation is consistent with disruptions in hormonal balance affecting internal ecdysone levels, preventing larvae from reaching the threshold weight for pupation. The authors conclude that A. iva phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes may be useful for managing economically important insect pests like S. littoralis while reducing risks to human health and the environment. The dose-dependent response in this study agrees with other reports of ecdysteroid effects on lepidopteran pests.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors did not fractionate clerodanes from the A. iva crude extract due to difficulty in calibrating the fractionation protocol and high cost of commercial clerodane standards. Only a few commercial standards were used because they are very expensive and not feasible as control treatments at the same concentrations as the applied treatment. The commercial standard mixture (100 ppm) was at a maximum concentration very low (100 ppm) compared to the treatment concentrations (250,000 ppm), limiting comparison. The authors acknowledge that S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg in a previous study, contrasting with their finding that the A. iva extract did deter feeding. The larval survival data did not follow a normal distribution, necessitating the use of the Friedman test instead of parametric methods. The gut morphology experiment was limited to 250 µg/µl crude extract for 8 days and did not test the effect of the commercial standard mixture on the gut. The study did not include a direct toxicity test of the A. iva extract on non-target organisms to assess environmental safety. The paper was a preprint at the time of writing (bioRxiv, March 2020), and the authors noted it was not certified by peer review.

Claims
The crude leaf extract of A. iva, containing the three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone), significantly reduces survival, growth, and pupation of S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner. First-instar mortality reached 85% at 250 µg/µl compared to 5% in control. Third-instar survival was significantly reduced after 11 days (X² = 6.221, p = 0.038). The fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture at 250 µg/µl produced a similar phenotype to the crude extract (F2.20,18 = 6.172, p = 0.001). No larvae completed development to adult moths; pupae exhibited short limbs, small heads, and decreased weight. Larval RGR decreased by 0.20 g/g day on day 8 at the highest concentration. The commercial standard mixture at 100 ppm showed no significant effect on larvae. Previous studies (Jones and Firn 1978) reported S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg. Phytoecdysteroids may be viable IPM components for cotton pests. The dose-dependent effect supports the use of crude extracts rather than pure standards in practical applications.
The A. iva phytoecdysteroids interfere with larval development by causing gut histolysis with apoptotic features and disrupting hormonal balance, leading to failed pupation. Gut histology showed histolysis, massive deterioration of the epithelium, destruction of microvilli, and formation of vacuoles. Incomplete pupae exhibited short limbs, small heads, decreased weight, and only stomach and chest pupated. The effects on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance affected by internal levels of ecdysone. Disruptions in gut morphology and disappearance of actin microfilament structures could be a consequence of phytoecdysteroid titers. The study did not directly measure ecdysone titers, so the hormonal balance mechanism remains inferred from histological and behavioral observations. The commercial mixture was not tested on the gut, so its effect on histology is unknown. Gut integrity may be a critical target for phytocontrol agents against Lepidoptera. The mechanism may involve secondary metabolite response pathways affecting actin filaments.
The crude extract of A. iva provides a potent and viable plant-based alternative for pest control with reduced risks to human health and the environment compared to conventional insecticides. The ecdysteroids are not toxic to mammals due to structural differences and lack of binding to vertebrate steroid receptors. Phytoecdysteroids mimic insect molting hormones and elicit the same responses in arthropods but not in mammals. Multiple plant sources contain these compounds, supporting their role as natural biocontrol agents. The study used a plant-derived extract that specifically targets Lepidopteran molting, providing selectivity. The study did not include non-target species testing (e.g., on honeybees or other beneficial insects). Commercial standards at the same concentration as the treatment were not feasible, complicating direct comparison with conventional pesticides. Green control using phytoecdysteroids may be integrated into IPM programs. Further research is needed to evaluate the persistence and ecological safety of A. iva extracts in field settings.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sequence-of-treatment assays tested both control-then-extract and extract-then-control permutations, showing RGR reduction regardless of order, confirming the effect is not merely delayed feeding. Three concentrations (50, 100, 250 µg/µl) established a clear dose-dependent response across all endpoints (mortality, LWG, RGR). Comparison between crude extract and the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction demonstrated that the fraction alone recapitulated the crude effect at 250 µg/µl. The commercial standard mixture at 100 ppm served as a low-dose comparison, showing no significant effect and highlighting the potency of the A. iva extract. Larval age was tested (first and third instar), showing effects at both developmental stages. Gut morphology was assessed at 8 days post-treatment, with damage continuing until death. Pupation was monitored for an additional 15 days to capture the full developmental sequence. Multiple statistical methods (t-test, mixed-model ANOVA, Friedman test, repeated measures ANOVA) were used appropriately for different data types.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: TLC chromatograms comparing A. iva crude leaf extract with commercial ecdysteroids to confirm identity of isolated compounds. Figure 2a: Larval mortality of first-instar S. littoralis after feeding on three concentrations of crude leaf extract compared to water control. Figure 2b: Larval weight gain (LWG) of third-instar S. littoralis fed on three crude extract concentrations versus control. Figure 3a: Relative growth rate (RGR) over time for third-instar larvae on crude extract treatments, showing a clear decline. Figure 3b: Third-instar larval survival after 11 days on three crude extract concentrations versus control. Figure 4a-d: RGR and survival results for the four sequence-of-treatment groups, showing effects regardless of application order. Figure 5a: Larval growth and survival on castor bean leaves treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract or the phytoecdysteroid mixture. Figure 5b: Survival data for larvae exposed to the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction. Figure 6: Confocal microscopy images showing DAPI (nuclei) and phalloidin (actin) staining of larval guts from control and treated larvae, illustrating smaller nuclei and reduced actin. Figure 7: Pupation results showing no adult moths and incomplete, aberrant pupae after 15 days of treatment with crude extract or phytoecdysteroid fraction. Figure 7b, c: Close-up images of incomplete pupae with short limbs, small heads, and decreased weight.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that A. iva crude leaf extract containing phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone) dose-dependently inhibits S. littoralis larval development, survival, and pupation, with the fractionated phytoecdysteroids recapitulating the effect of the crude extract. 2. The strongest evidence is the complete failure of any treated larvae to pupate or emerge as adults, coupled with clear dose-dependent mortality (up to 85% in first instars), significant RGR decline (0.20 g/g day reduction), and histological confirmation of gut histolysis with apoptotic features. 3. The future path involves field-scale testing of A. iva extracts in IPM programs, toxicological safety assessment on non-target species, and exploration of the synergetic role of clerodanes, which were not fractionated in this study.

summary.title: Sorry, we're open: Golden Open Access and inequality in the natural sciences
summary.authors: Russell J Gray
summary.field_subfield: Bibliometrics / Open Access / Natural Sciences
summary.executive_summary: This study by Russell J Gray investigates the nexus between publication costs (Article Processing Charges, APCs), scholarly metrics (Impact Factor, Eigen Factor, citability), and publisher country within the context of Golden Open Access (GOA) journals in the natural sciences. Analyzing metadata from 237 open-access natural science journals extracted from the Directory of Open Access Journals, the author demonstrates a consistent linear trend: as APC increases, so do IF, EF, and total citation counts. Furthermore, journal publishers from developed countries exhibit systematically higher APCs, IFs, EFs, and citability than their counterparts in developing countries, revealing structural inequality in global science communication. The paper argues that the GOA model, by linking prestige and cost to visibility and citation, disadvantages researchers without robust institutional funding, particularly those from developing nations, independent researchers without institutional affiliation, and groups whose work may be sidelined due to cost constraints. The author grounds these claims in a personal anecdote about publication barriers for conservation research on the critically endangered Sumatran elephant and situates the findings within the broader debate on predatory publishing, research reliability, and the equity of the global scientific infrastructure. The study does not find that higher APCs correlate with increased research reliability; instead, it highlights how the commercialization of prestige through APCs may prioritize publisher profit over scientific integrity while simultaneously reinforcing institutional and geographic disparities in research exposure. The findings have direct implications for ecology and conservation research in tropical biodiversity hotspots, where external authorship from developed countries can nullify APC assistance eligibility. Ultimately, the paper calls for addressing these systemic inequalities to create a more inclusive environment for important research to be recognized on a global scale, regardless of country or institutional affiliation.

The GOA model prioritizes publisher profit over scientific integrity, creating an environment prone to predatory behavior and editorial complacency.

Executive Summary
This study by Russell J Gray investigates the nexus between publication costs (Article Processing Charges, APCs), scholarly metrics (Impact Factor, Eigen Factor, citability), and publisher country within the context of Golden Open Access (GOA) journals in the natural sciences. Analyzing metadata from 237 open-access natural science journals extracted from the Directory of Open Access Journals, the author demonstrates a consistent linear trend: as APC increases, so do IF, EF, and total citation counts. Furthermore, journal publishers from developed countries exhibit systematically higher APCs, IFs, EFs, and citability than their counterparts in developing countries, revealing structural inequality in global science communication. The paper argues that the GOA model, by linking prestige and cost to visibility and citation, disadvantages researchers without robust institutional funding, particularly those from developing nations, independent researchers without institutional affiliation, and groups whose work may be sidelined due to cost constraints. The author grounds these claims in a personal anecdote about publication barriers for conservation research on the critically endangered Sumatran elephant and situates the findings within the broader debate on predatory publishing, research reliability, and the equity of the global scientific infrastructure. The study does not find that higher APCs correlate with increased research reliability; instead, it highlights how the commercialization of prestige through APCs may prioritize publisher profit over scientific integrity while simultaneously reinforcing institutional and geographic disparities in research exposure. The findings have direct implications for ecology and conservation research in tropical biodiversity hotspots, where external authorship from developed countries can nullify APC assistance eligibility. Ultimately, the paper calls for addressing these systemic inequalities to create a more inclusive environment for important research to be recognized on a global scale, regardless of country or institutional affiliation.

Research Context
The proliferation of Sci-Hub and ResearchGate has largely nullified the previous paywall system for journal capitalization. Many high-impact journals have consequently transitioned to mandatory Golden Open Access to maintain profitability. The cost associated with open-access publishing, and the perceived reliability tied to that cost, makes the system problematic. Researchers from developing countries still pay full prices to publish in developed western Mega-Journals to gain exposure. Alternatively, researchers may be forced to publish in lower-impact journals or predatory outlets with low-quality peer review. High-impact journals generate exposure through increased citations and a reputation of credibility that accelerates careers.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study examines how Article Processing Charges correlate with Impact Factor, Eigen Factor, and total citability in open-access natural science journals. A secondary question examines whether there are disparities in these metrics based on the country of the journal publisher. The author hypothesizes that higher publishing costs (APC) are positively associated with higher impact, relative importance, and citation volume. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that publishers from developed countries would systematically report higher values across all metrics.

Methodological Details
Data was acquired from the Directory of Open Access Journals, capturing journal name, APC, country of publisher, and currency records. The initial dataset contained 14,275 records. R statistical software was used for all analyses, with packages including scholar, quantmod, dplyr, reshape2, ggplot2, and ggpubr. The scholar package generated impact factors from journal name strings. The quantmod package converted all currencies to USD for standardization. The dplyr and reshape2 packages were used for data cleaning and selection. A subset of 1,047 journals with biological science topics was queried using keywords such as ecology and forest. Journals with an Impact Factor greater than 40 were excluded to remove medical and engineering journals. The final analyses were performed on a vetted dataset of 237 open-access, natural science journals. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to analyze associations between APC, IF, Eigen Factor, and citability. Functions from the ggpubr package facilitated the statistical computations.

Procedures And Architectures
APC was examined in relation to citability, Impact Factor, and Eigen Factor. The country of each journal publisher was examined against APC, citability, IF, and Eigen Factor to identify disparities. Currencies were standardized to USD using the quantmod package. Keyword data was created from the original DOAJ dataset to identify biological science topics. Excluded journals were cross-checked with keywords to ensure none related to natural sciences. The analysis focused on linear trends and correlations rather than multivariate regression. The study is a single-author observational data analysis using existing metadata.

Key Results
A linear trend was found between Impact Factor, Eigen Factor, and citability in relation to APC. Publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability. The mean APC of the analyzed open-access journals was $1,344.27 USD. The mean Impact Factor across the 237 journals was 2.855. The mean Eigen Factor was 0.017. The mean total citation count (citability) was 5,925.92. APC was significantly positively correlated with Impact Factor, with Pearson's r of 0.391 at p < .001. There was a highly significant positive correlation between APC and Eigen Factor, with Pearson's r of 0.303 at p < .001. A highly significant positive correlation existed between APC and citability, with Pearson's r of 0.323 at p < .001.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results suggest that higher publishing costs are structurally linked to greater prestige and visibility in the natural sciences. Developed countries dominate the high-APC, high-impact segment of the GOA landscape. The findings imply that research from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure, while journals from those countries generate less profit and credibility. The paper argues that GOA may create an environment where publisher profit is prioritized over scientific integrity. The false ideology that journal prestige equals research reliability is identified as a critical concern. The results have direct implications for tropical biodiversity hotspots, where APC funding constraints may hide important conservation research. The author advocates for a more inclusive global research environment that does not reward publication cost with exposure.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is limited to natural sciences and excludes medical, oncology, and engineering journals. The analysis relies on metadata from a single source (DOAJ) and does not include direct journal content or editorial processes. The single-author, observational design limits the ability to establish causality rather than just association. The study does not report the random seed, train/test split, or specific journal-level diagnostics, as it is not a machine learning approach. The author notes that APC assistance eligibility has complex caveats that can invalidate funding, as illustrated in the Sumatran elephant example. The study lacks a comparison with non-GOA or hybrid journal models. The paper does not report confidence intervals or standard errors for the correlation coefficients. The sample is constrained to open-access journals, excluding the broader scholarly publishing landscape.

Claims
Higher APC correlates with higher prestige metrics (IF, EF, citability) in natural science GOA journals, creating a cost-prestige linkage. APC was significantly positively correlated with Impact Factor (r=0.391, p < .001). APC was highly significantly positively correlated with Eigen Factor (r=0.303, p < .001). APC was highly significantly positively correlated with citability (r=0.323, p < .001). A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC. Brembs (2018) states that expensive APC in prestigious journals are not linked to the reliability of research published in them. The author themselves calls the linkage a 'false ideology' that prestige and costliness equal reliable science. The cost-prestige linkage creates a gatekeeping mechanism that disadvantages unfunded researchers. Researchers without institutional affiliation have options narrowed significantly to low-impact journals.
Publishers in developed countries systematically outperform those in developing countries across all key metrics (APC, IF, EF, citability). Journal publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability. The mean APC of $1,344.27 reflects the high-cost tier dominated by developed-country publishers. The author's personal experience shows that even when the study subject (Sumatran elephant) is from a developing country, the author from the US (developed country) without institutional affiliation cannot access funding. Research from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure, while journals from those countries generate less profit. This compounds geographic inequality in scientific communication and resource distribution.
The GOA model prioritizes publisher profit over scientific integrity, creating an environment prone to predatory behavior and editorial complacency. The paradox of GOA journals is that the system itself is inherently flawed, giving rise to predatory journals and editorial complacency. GOA journals may create an environment where publisher profit is prioritized over scientific integrity of published research. No quantitative evidence of actual predatory practices or compromised peer review is presented within the journal-level analysis. The system promotes a false ideology that journal prestige and costliness are equivalent to reliable science. The commercialization of prestige through APCs may entrench inequality in the global scientific community.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
To clean the data and account for large disparities between natural sciences and medical science, journals with an IF > 40 were excluded from the analysis. Excluded journals were checked by keywords to ensure none were related to natural sciences; excluded journals were related to oncology, medical, and engineering. Currencies were standardized to USD using the quantmod package to ensure comparability across all 14,275 initial records.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 is referenced in the results as displaying the linear trend between APC, IF, EF, and citability, and the country-based disparities.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that publication cost (APC) is systematically linked to prestige metrics (IF, EF, citability) in natural science GOA journals, with developed countries dominating the high-APC, high-impact segment. 2. The strongest evidence is the set of three significant Pearson correlations (r=0.391, 0.303, 0.323, all p<.001) and the finding that publishers in developed countries have higher values across all four metrics. 3. The future path lies in addressing the systemic inequality of APC funding mechanisms, particularly for tropical biodiversity hotspots, to ensure important research is not hidden by cost barriers.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study develops and validates a highly sensitive multiplex PCR-based detection method for SARS-CoV-2, addressing the limitations of standard RT-PCR which typically detects only 4–8 viral copies at 95% probability and fails to identify 47–59% of true positive cases. The authors designed a panel of 343 primer pairs (172 + 171) covering the full SARS-CoV-2 genome with average amplicon length of 99bp and gaps of 76±10bp, yielding a theoretical detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Validation using spiked plasmids showed detection from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies, with an experimentally observed 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies, exceeding the initial 6% single-strand amplification efficiency estimate. The method was applied to 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/μL, achieving 95–99% full-genome coverage at 100× depth with an average sequencing depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon on the Illumina MiSeq. Mutations were identified across all 13 genomes, with the D614G mutation found in 11 specimens and several loci showing clustering, consistent with transmission events. Furthermore, a metagenomic multiplex PCR approach using random hexamer-adapters achieved 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery at approximately 0.6 million reads per library, with 16% of recovered bases within N and S genes and 0.08% of human chromosomal regions amplified. The authors caution against interpreting intra-host mutations at low viral copy numbers and sequencing depths, noting that no UMI was used in the multiplex PCR and false positives can arise from PCR and sequencing noise.

Research Context
RT-PCR is the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis due to high sensitivity, detecting 4–8 copies in laboratory conditions. Despite its status, only 47–59% of true positive cases were identified by some RT-PCR methods, leaving 75% of negative results false negatives. Low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, and mutations spanning primer binding sites are cited as reasons for sub-optimal RT-PCR detection. Heat inactivation of clinical samples causes loss of viral particles, further hindering downstream diagnosis. Existing RT-PCR methodologies are limited by relatively short amplicon lengths (78–158bp) targeting only specific viral gene regions. The SARS-CoV-2 genome of 29,903bp exceeds the single-target capacity of standard RT-PCR, limiting sensitivity. There is a demonstrated need for robust, specific, and highly quantitative methods distinguishable from other respiratory pathogens and bacterial causes of pneumonia. Full-length viral genome sequencing via next-generation sequencing is essential for SARS-CoV-2 surveillance and evolution monitoring.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether multiplex PCR targeting multiple genomic regions simultaneously can substantially improve SARS-CoV-2 detection sensitivity over standard RT-PCR. The theoretical hypothesis is that targeting hundreds of amplicons simultaneously increases the detection probability and accommodates degraded viral RNA fragments. A mathematical model was constructed to estimate the limit of detection for RT-PCR and multiplex PCR to predict performance. The authors predicted that a single pool of 172 primer pairs would yield a detection limit of 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Using both overlapping pools of 172 and 171 primer pairs, the authors predicted a detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The second research question concerns whether a metagenomic multiplex PCR approach could recover the full SARS-CoV-2 genome with moderate sequencing depth. The metagenomic hypothesis predicts that random hexamer-adapters could detect SARS-CoV-2 and novel pathogens at approximately 1 million reads per library. A complementary hypothesis suggests that the multiplex PCR approach could tolerate genomic variations, making it suitable for detecting new viral strains.

Methodological Details
The authors designed a panel comprising 343 pairs of SARS-CoV-2-specific multiplex PCR primers, split into two overlapping pools of 172 and 171 pairs respectively. The average amplicon length is 99bp, and the amplicons span the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome with an average gap of 76±10bp between adjacent amplicons. RT-PCR modeling assumed a 100bp amplicon length, a 30kb genome size, and 99% amplification efficiency, yielding a 4.8 copy LOD at 95% probability. Multiplex PCR amplification efficiency was initially estimated at 6% for single-stranded cDNA, based on a 26% efficiency for human chromosome amplification with UMIs. An amplification success rate of 80% for targeted regions was assumed, based on prior reporting that 79% of variants are recovered from 600 amplicons in a single cell. Two plasmids containing full SARS-CoV-2 S and N gene sequences were used for validation, spiked into human total RNA cDNA. Plasmid copy numbers were precisely determined by droplet-based digital PCR using a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. Plasmid dilutions ranged from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy, and were amplified in multiplex PCR reactions. Thirteen nasopharyngeal swab specimens previously diagnosed by RT-PCR as SARS-CoV-2 positive provided the full-genome interrogation dataset. Viral loads ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/μL across the 13 specimens. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform, with libraries prepared from purified DNA. The metagenomic method utilized random hexamer-adapters to amplify targets, followed by background removal using Paragon Genomics' reagent. For RNA samples, reverse transcription reagents from Paragon Genomics converted RNA to cDNA with reduced ribosomal RNA. The metagenomic validation library contained 4,500 copies of N and S gene-containing plasmids spiked into 10 ng of human gDNA, representing approximately 3,300 haploid genomes.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow involved multiplex PCR followed by a secondary PCR in which sample indexes and NGS sequencing primers were added. PCR products were first analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize target amplicons by their defined size distribution. NGS sequencing was performed using CleanPlex library preparation, with CleanPlex libraries typically sequenced at about 1,000 paired-end reads. Two independently developed algorithms were used to identify mutations, with only those detected by both methods reported. Mutations with an allele frequency (%AF) > 60% were considered empirically true, while mutations with %AF ≤ 60% were assessed for intra-host heterogeneity. A 20% %AF cutoff was selected to eliminate noise from PCR amplification and sequencing, based on synthetic SARS-CoV-2 RNA controls. No UMI (Unique Molecular Identifier) was used in the multiplex PCR amplification, meaning intra-host mutations could be contaminated with PCR/sequencing noise. Sub-sampling of 5 genomes to 150,000 and 100,000 total reads per library (437 and 291 reads per amplicon) tested sequencing depth requirements. The metagenomic method required no additional host depletion reagents to remove human gDNA or rRNA. After initial metagenomic sequencing, the method was further optimized to achieve 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery.

Key Results
The mathematical model showed that RT-PCR, with 99% efficiency and 100bp amplicons, detects only 4.8 copies at 95% probability. The predicted probability of RT-PCR detecting a single copy of SARS-CoV-2 is only 26%. The first pool of 172 multiplex PCR primer pairs achieved a detection limit of 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Combining both overlapping pools (343 total primer pairs) yielded a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Plasmid validation showed library peaks with expected sizes from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies. Peak quantification demonstrated a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies, with saturation starting at 1,700. The RT-PCR single-target S gene detection rapidly dropped when using 2.85 copies. Experimentally, the probability to detect 1.1 copies was 56%, significantly higher than the theoretical 12% predicted with 6% efficiency. Recovered reads were within a 20-fold relative depth, uniformly distributed across the GC range. Approximately 96% of amplicons were recovered with 14 plasmid copies, 77% with 2.8 copies, and 37% with 0.6 copies. At 8 copies of virus, about 95% of the genome was covered at 100X. For 22 to 675,885 copies, 98–99% of genomes were covered at 100X with an average depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon. With 150,000 total reads, 93% of the genome was covered at 100X; with 100,000 reads, 86% coverage; with 50,000 reads, 58% coverage. 16% of the recovered bases (13% of recovered reads) were within the viral N and S genes in the metagenomic library. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered, while only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified. The human exonic regions were preferentially amplified over other regions. After optimization, 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered in the metagenomic approach. All 13 strains contained at least one mutation reported to be associated with SARS-CoV-2 virulence. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of the 13 specimens. 0% of sequencing reads from any of the 13 samples aligned to MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Multiplex PCR, by targeting hundreds of regions, is theoretically more sensitive than RT-PCR and can detect nucleotide fragments from degraded viral RNA. The mathematical models confirm that LOD is independent of viral genome size for genomes from 4 to 100kb, indicating the method is applicable across different virus families. The experimentally observed 56% detection probability at 1.1 copies suggests multiplex PCR efficiency for single-stranded cDNA is higher than the initially assumed 6%. The clustering of mutations around 7 loci in the 13 genomes likely reflects transmission within close communities or transmission events. The high specificity (0% cross-alignment to other coronaviruses) supports the potential expansion of the panel to include other respiratory viruses like influenza. The metagenomic method achieves >96% SARS-CoV-2 coverage at ~0.6M reads, surpassing the 50% threshold recommended for genome drafting. The preferential amplification of human exonic regions by random hexamers suggests base composition influences amplification bias. The 10-fold range in recovered base depth is a known characteristic of the multiplex PCR technology and increasing sequencing depth alone may not further improve coverage.

Contradictions And Limitations
RT-PCR fails to identify 47–59% of true positive cases, and 75% of negative RT-PCR results are false negatives. The mathematical model predicts a 12% chance to detect 1.1 copies at 6% efficiency, while the experimental observation of 56% suggests the model underestimates true efficiency. One genome with 5,000 estimated viral copies achieved only 96% coverage at 100X, lower than the 98–99% expected for other samples. The authors attribute this lower coverage to poor sample quality resulting from processing or handling of viral RNA or library. Because no UMI was used in multiplex PCR, intra-host mutations with %AF < 20% may be contaminated by PCR and sequencing noise. Low viral copy numbers and low sequencing depth can exacerbate the occurrence of noise, potentially introducing false intra-host mutations. The metagenomic method requires very high sequencing depth for broad detection and is therefore economically prohibitive as a diagnostic assay. Simple fluorometric or spectrophotometric measurement of dsDNA is insufficient to differentiate viral amplicons from primer-dimers in negative samples, necessitating high-resolution electrophoresis. The detection of intra-host mutations from low-input samples and low-depth sequencing requires cautious interpretation due to the potential for noise.

Claims
Multiplex PCR is more sensitive than RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection, achieving a theoretical detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The mathematical model predicts a 0.29 copy LOD with 343 primer pairs compared to 4.8 copies for RT-PCR at 95% probability. Plasmid validation detected library peaks down to 2.8 copies, whereas single-target RT-PCR dropped at 2.85 copies. Experimentally, the detection probability at 1.1 copies was 56%, confirming the method works at very low viral loads. 95% genome coverage at 100X was achieved even with only 8 copies of virus. The actual multiplex PCR efficiency could be lower than the assumed 6%, and amplicons might not be equally amplified on single-strand cDNA. One clinical sample with 5,000 copies showed only 96% coverage at 100X, not the expected 98–99%. This method could identify SARS-CoV-2 positive cases that are missed by standard RT-PCR, potentially reducing false negatives. The electrophoretic peaks with defined size distributions allow direct identification of positives by electrophoresis, facilitating rapid clinical use.
A metagenomic multiplex PCR method can recover 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome at approximately 0.6 million reads per library, without host depletion. The optimized metagenomic method achieved 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery at ~0.6M reads per library. 16% of recovered bases were within N and S genes, while only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified. Base coverage was significantly higher for viral targets than for human targets. The coverage exceeds the 50% threshold recommended for genome drafting. The method is noted as economically prohibitive as a diagnostic assay due to sequencing depth requirements. The authors state that increasing sequencing depth alone might not improve targeted region coverage due to the 10-fold depth range characteristic of the multiplex PCR technology. The method could be applied to identify novel or emerging SARS-CoV-2 isolates and other pathogens at moderate sequencing depth. The high specificity against human coronaviruses supports expansion to other respiratory viruses.
The SARS-CoV-2 panel is highly specific, with 0% of reads aligning to known human coronaviruses in all 13 clinical samples. Zero percent of sequencing reads from each of the 13 samples aligned to the genomes of MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1. This is in contrast to what was reported for a similar SARS-CoV-2 panel. The paper references a similar SARS-CoV-2 panel (reference 42) that did not achieve 0% cross-alignment, indicating differences in specificity between panels. This high specificity argues strongly that the panel could be expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza virus.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sub-sampling analysis demonstrated that 150,000 total reads (437/amplicon) yield 93% coverage at 100X, while 100,000 reads (291/amplicon) yield 86% coverage, and 50,000 reads yield at least 58% coverage. The 10-fold range in recovered base depth was noted as a routine characteristic of the multiplex PCR technology, observed in Supplemental Figure 4 and Supplemental Table 5. The %AF cutoff of 20% was selected based on the mutation profile from sequencing synthetic SARS-CoV-2 RNA controls from Twist Bioscience. The 75% false-negative rate for RT-PCR was cited as a motivation for developing the more sensitive multiplex PCR method.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A presents the mathematical model showing RT-PCR detects 4.8 copies at 95% probability with 99% efficiency. Figure 1B shows the design of the 172-amplicon panel, with average amplicon length of 99bp and 76±10bp gaps. Figure 1C presents the mathematical model predicting the multiplex PCR detection limit of 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Figure 1D illustrates the workflow from multiplex PCR to secondary PCR, library preparation, and NGS sequencing. Figure 2A shows plasmid library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 copies, validating the multiplex PCR detection range. Figure 2B quantifies peak heights demonstrating a dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies, with saturation at 1,700. Figure 2C shows the experimentally observed 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies, compared to the 12% theoretical prediction. Figure 2D displays sequencing data showing read depth within a 20-fold relative range and uniform GC distribution. Figure 2E quantifies the percentage of amplicons recovered (96%, 77%, 37%) at 14, 2.8, and 0.6 plasmid copies respectively. Figure 3A shows genome coverage versus viral copy number across 13 specimens, with 95–99% coverage at 100X. Figure 3B illustrates the effect of sequencing depth sub-sampling on coverage (93%, 86%, 58% at 100X). Figure 3C shows uniformity of amplicons amplified and recovered in sequencing. Figure 3D shows the log10 distance of the number of each amplicon to the mean number in the library. Figure 3E displays the spatial clustering of mutations around 7 loci across the 13 specimens. Figure 4A shows that 16% of recovered bases are within viral N and S genes in the metagenomic library. Figure 4B shows 80% SARS-CoV-2 and 78% mitochondrial target coverage. Figure 4C shows base coverage is significantly higher for viral targets than for human targets. Figure 4D shows human exonic regions are preferentially amplified by random hexamers. Figure 4E shows long gaps and lack of coverage in large human repetitive regions. Figure 4F shows SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial gaps are significantly shorter than human gaps. Figure 4G shows the optimized 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery. Supplemental Table 2 lists the viral loads of the 13 specimens (8 to 675,885 RNA copies/μL). Supplemental Table 3 details the mutation profiles and intra-host heterogeneity across the three specimen groups. Supplemental Table 4 provides base and read counts for viral versus human targets in the metagenomic library. Supplemental Table 5 reports the 10-fold coverage difference across amplicons, routinely observed with the multiplex PCR technology. Supplemental Figure 1 shows the predicted probability of RT-PCR detecting one copy of SARS-CoV-2 (26%). Supplemental Figure 2 shows the 26% multiplex PCR efficiency estimate using UMI-labeled primers. Supplemental Figure 3 shows the RT-PCR single-target S gene detection drop-off at 2.85 copies.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a multiplex PCR panel of 343 primer pairs that achieves a theoretical detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability, more than 15-fold sensitive than standard RT-PCR (4.8 copies). 2. summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.field_subfield: Molecular biology / Ribosome translation fidelity
summary.executive_summary:
This paper investigates the translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome (Ribo-T) in Escherichia coli, in which the 30S and 50S subunits are covalently linked by a hybrid rRNA linker. The Ribo-T ribosome was previously described as functional and capable of sustaining cell growth, but with a significantly slower doubling time (107 minutes versus 35 minutes for wild-type) and a protein synthesis rate of 50% compared to wild-type ribosomes. The authors examined three specific recoding events as proxies for translational fidelity: -1 frameshifting, +1 frameshifting, and stop codon readthrough, along with internal translation initiation.

Key results demonstrate that Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to SD sequences during -1 frameshifting, with efficiencies for IS911 (14% vs. 13% WT, p=0.54), IS3 (33% vs. 33%, p=0.77), and dnaX (45% vs. 43%, p=0.77) virtually identical to wild-type. In contrast, Ribo-T ribosomes are highly impaired for +1 frameshifting at the prfB site, reducing efficiency from 33% (WT) to 2% (p=8.9e-9). At translation initiation, Ribo-T ribosomes use SD sequences four-fold less efficiently than wild-type (p=4.7e-4) in a dual reporter system. For stop codon readthrough at the mtmB1 site, Ribo-T ribosomes terminate less efficiently across all three stop codons: 0.07% vs. 0.013% for UAG (p=4.7e-7), 0.26% vs. 0.11% for UGA (p=5e-3), and 0.04% vs. 0.01% for UAA (p=2.5e-4).

The authors conclude that covalent subunit tethering modifies the geometry of helix 44, altering SD-ASD interaction during elongation and limiting A-site conformational dynamics during termination, thereby compromising translational accuracy in specific contexts while maintaining near-wild-type fidelity in others.

Ribo-T ribosomes are impaired for +1 frameshifting and stop codon termination, with termination readthrough rates approximately 5- to 10-fold higher than wild-type.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome (Ribo-T) in Escherichia coli, in which the 30S and 50S subunits are covalently linked by a hybrid rRNA linker. The Ribo-T ribosome was previously described as functional and capable of sustaining cell growth, but with a significantly slower doubling time (107 minutes versus 35 minutes for wild-type) and a protein synthesis rate of 50% compared to wild-type ribosomes. The authors examined three specific recoding events as proxies for translational fidelity: -1 frameshifting, +1 frameshifting, and stop codon readthrough, along with internal translation initiation.

Key results demonstrate that Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to SD sequences during -1 frameshifting, with efficiencies for IS911 (14% vs. 13% WT, p=0.54), IS3 (33% vs. 33%, p=0.77), and dnaX (45% vs. 43%, p=0.77) virtually identical to wild-type. In contrast, Ribo-T ribosomes are highly impaired for +1 frameshifting at the prfB site, reducing efficiency from 33% (WT) to 2% (p=8.9e-9). At translation initiation, Ribo-T ribosomes use SD sequences four-fold less efficiently than wild-type (p=4.7e-4) in a dual reporter system. For stop codon readthrough at the mtmB1 site, Ribo-T ribosomes terminate less efficiently across all three stop codons: 0.07% vs. 0.013% for UAG (p=4.7e-7), 0.26% vs. 0.11% for UGA (p=5e-3), and 0.04% vs. 0.01% for UAA (p=2.5e-4).

The authors conclude that covalent subunit tethering modifies the geometry of helix 44, altering SD-ASD interaction during elongation and limiting A-site conformational dynamics during termination, thereby compromising translational accuracy in specific contexts while maintaining near-wild-type fidelity in others.

Research Context
Ribosomes consist of two unequal subunits, the large and small ribosomal subunits, which associate with each other in a labile manner via bridges. This organization is thought to be essential for biogenesis, successful protein synthesis and cell viability. A ribosome with tethered subunits, in which the two subunits were covalently linked in a single entity, was recently engineered in Escherichia coli. The resulting ribosome, Ribo-T, with its inseparable subunits, was shown to be functional and able to sustain the cell growth. Although doubling times were slower (107 min for Ribo-T, 35 min for wild-type ribosomes), the ribosome was shown to be functional. The rate protein synthesis with Ribo-T catalysis was 50% that with wild-type ribosomes. The slow growth of Ribo-T cells was probably due to Ribo-T biogenesis being slower than the biogenesis of wild-type ribosomes, rather than impaired Ribo-T activity. Translational error rates remain low throughout all steps in the process, but recoding events can occur during elongation (frameshifting) or at the termination step (stop codon readthrough). These recoding events constitute powerful tools for investigations of the translation accuracy of Ribo-T ribosomes, as the sequences concerned alter ribosome proofreading activity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Do these Ribo-T ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes? Do they terminate translation accurately at stop codons? Do they translate messenger RNA accurately, including internal translation initiation? The authors specifically investigate the behavior of Ribo-T ribosomes with recoding signals instructing the ribosome to change translational reading frame (frameshifting). They also investigate whether the ribosome reads stop codons as sense codons (stop codon readthrough). Additionally, they investigate the preferential mode of translation used by Ribo-T ribosomes to express adjacent open reading frames on the same mRNA, given that the two subunits were inseparable. The implicit hypothesis is that covalent attachment of the two subunits modifies the properties of the ribosome, altering its ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly. The authors predict that Ribo-T ribosomes will show impairments in specific recoding contexts where SD-ASD interaction or A-site dynamics are critical.

Methodological Details
Experiments were performed with the E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain, using the poRibo-T2 vector carrying Ribo-T ribosomal DNA for Ribo-T ribosome expression. The ASD sequence of the Ribo-T 16S rRNA was altered from the wildtype sequence (5'-UCACCUCCUUA-3') to an orthogonal sequence (5'-UCAUUGUGGUA-). The authors used the bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system, which carries the lacZ-luc fusion gene encoding b-galactosidase and luciferase enzymes under the T7 promoter. The streptomycin resistance gene and the CloDF13-derived CDF replicon are also present in the pCL99 plasmid. Target sequences were inserted by oligocloning into the MscI restriction site of pCL99, placing them at the junction between the lacZ and luc genes. The cloned double-stranded oligonucleotides were obtained by hybridizing two complementary oligonucleotides in ligation buffer after heating for 5 min at 100°C and incubation at room temperature. All constructs were verified by sequencing, and in-frame controls were constructed for each target sequence. For -1 frameshifting, three programmed sites were selected: IS911, IS3, and the E. coli dnaX gene. For +1 frameshifting, the site from the E. coli prfB gene was selected. For stop codon readthrough, the mtmB1 gene encoding monomethylamine methyltransferase from the archaea Methanosarcina barkeri was used. For internal translation initiation, the 46-nucleotide intergenic E. coli lacZ-lacY sequence carrying the SD sequence promoting initiation at the lacY start codon was used. The translational efficiency was calculated as the ratio of luciferase activity to β-galactosidase activity for the target, divided by the same ratio for the corresponding in-frame construct. The median value was calculated for at least six independent experiments. Significance of differences was determined using Student's t-tests. For WT ribosome assessments, constructs with a wild-type SD sequence AGGAGG upstream from lacZ were used. For Ribo-T ribosome assessments, constructs with a mutated SD sequence CACCAC upstream from lacZ, in the presence of the Ribo-T vector, were used. The mutated SD sequence was complementary to the 3' end of the 16S ribosomal RNA of the Ribo-T ribosomes. In strains containing the Ribo-T vector, both wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes are present, but only Ribo-T ribosomes can initiate lacZ translation because of the mutated SD sequence. Crosstalk was checked: in the presence of wild-type ribosomes only, constructs with a mutated SD sequence generated too little b-galactosidase activity for measurement. Similarly, expression of the luc gene with the mutated SD sequence resulted in activity one tenth those observed with Ribo-T ribosomes.

Procedures And Architectures
Frameshifting is triggered by a slippery sequence favoring tRNA slippage and one or more stimulatory elements inducing a ribosomal pause. For -1 frameshifting at IS911 and dnaX, the stimulatory element is a stem-loop downstream; for IS3, it is a pseudoknot. WT frameshifting efficiencies were 13% for IS911, 8% for IS3, and 60% for dnaX, as previously reported. For +1 frameshifting at prfB, the efficiency depends on a poor termination context (UGA C) and a stimulatory SD sequence upstream. WT +1 frameshifting efficiency was 33%, confirmed by previous results. For the reverse experiment, the dnaX SD was replaced with an SD recognized by Ribo-T (dnaXRibo-T). For the SD-recognition assay, the SD sequence upstream from the luc gene was either deleted, kept as wild-type, or replaced with the Ribo-T SD sequence. To test for 70S re-initiation, the Ribo-T SD was placed in front of the lacZ start codon, and the lacZ-lacY intergenic sequence had three successive stop codons. A stable stem loop structure was inserted immediately downstream from lacZ to act as a roadblock for potential scanning ribosomes. The Ribo-T vector (poRibo-T2) expresses the Ribo-T ribosomal DNA, making both wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes co-present in the cell. The covalent link is formed via short RNA linkers between the small and large subunit rRNA sequences.

Key Results
For -1 frameshifting at IS911 with wild-type ribosomes, the efficiency was 13%, and with Ribo-T ribosomes it was 14%, with a p-value of 0.54, indicating no significant difference. For IS3, frameshifting efficiency was 33% with either type of ribosome (p-value of 0.77). For dnaX, frameshifting efficiency was 43% with wild-type ribosomes and 45% with Ribo-T ribosomes (p-value of 0.77). In the reverse experiment, replacing dnaX WT SD with Ribo-T SD reduced WT frameshifting to 11% (vs. 43%; p-value of 1.7x10^-3), but Ribo-T frameshifting remained unchanged (45% vs. 44%; p-value of 0.85). These results confirm that Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift independently of the SD sequence. For +1 frameshifting at prfB, wild-type ribosomes gave 33% efficiency, while Ribo-T ribosomes gave only 2% (p-value of 8.9x10^-9 versus wild-type). Replacing the WT SD with Ribo-T SD at the prfB site did not restore Ribo-T frameshifting to 1.8% (p-value of 0.56 versus 2%), but reduced WT frameshifting to 0.6% (p-value of 1.6x10^-5 versus 33%). In the SD recognition assay without Ribo-T, almost no luciferase activity was observed when the SD sequence upstream of the luc gene was removed. With the WT SD sequence, high levels of luciferase activity were obtained, demonstrating correct SD dependence of the reporter system. With the Ribo-T SD sequence, no statistically significant difference (p-value 0.04 versus no SD) was observed in luciferase activity, indicating WT ribosomes cannot use this alternative SD. In the presence of Ribo-T ribosomes, luciferase induction was increased by a factor of four (p-value 4.7x10^-4), indicating Ribo-T can use the alternative SD, albeit inefficiently. With the Ribo-T SD placed in front of the lacZ start codon, luciferase expression was four times stronger than with no SD (p-value 9.8x10^-6). The higher activity ratio for Ribo-T ribosomes translating both lacZ and luc resulted from lower b-galactosidase activity when Ribo-T translated lacZ. A stable stem loop downstream of lacZ had no effect on luc translation initiation (p-value 0.22), strongly suggesting internal loading of Ribo-T ribosomes. For stop codon readthrough at the mtmB1 site, Ribo-T ribosomes terminated less efficiently than wild-type across all three stop codons: 0.07% vs. 0.013% for UAG (p-value of 4.7x10^-7), 0.26% vs. 0.11% for UGA (p-value of 5x10^-3), and 0.04% vs. 0.01% for UAA (p-value of 2.5x10^-4). These data reveal an impairment of tethered ribosomes for +1 frameshifting and termination, but show they are otherwise as effective as wild-type.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Ribo-T ribosomes do not use SD sequences for either frameshifting or translation initiation, suggesting a general trend toward SD-insensitivity in tethered ribosomes. The covalent link via helix 44 (H44) is hypothesized to modify the orientation of the ASD sequence at the top of H44, preventing normal SD-ASD interaction during both initiation and elongation. The tethering may reduce the conformational dynamics of the ribosome during termination, making the A-site less able to bind termination factors. Key conformational motions during termination include subunit rotation, swiveling of the small subunit body and head domains, L1 protein movement, and tRNA movement, all of which may be constrained by tethering. These results are consistent with prior ribosome profiling in Ribo-T cells showing increased ribosome density at start codons and close to 3' ends of genes. The tethering has mild effects on initiation and termination/recycling steps, as evidenced by the slight impairment in stop codon recognition. The greater-than-expected flexibility of ribosomes is highlighted by the ability of Ribo-T to function and sustain cell growth despite subunit tethering.

Contradictions And Limitations
A functional ribosome with covalently linked subunits was successfully created independently by two groups, which calls into question the hypothesis that subunit mutual mobility is essential for translocation. The slow-growth phenotype of Ribo-T cells (107 min doubling) was attributed to slower rRNA processing rather than translational defects by the prior work, but this study's translational impairments may contribute. No natural stop codon readthrough sequence has ever been identified in E. coli, so the mtmB1 archaeal sequence was used as a surrogate. Cross-talk was described as 'too low to affect the results' and 'almost no luciferase activity,' which are qualitative assessments without quantitative confirmation. The mechanism by which Ribo-T ribosomes initiate translation in the absence of SD remains unclear, and a high-resolution structure of Ribo-T is needed for resolution. Whether tethered ribosomes would be efficient in eukaryotes, which have a different translation initiation mechanism not involving SD-ASD interaction, is speculative. The pCL99 system with co-present WT and Ribo-T ribosomes means the Ribo-T SD mutation exclusively selects Ribo-T, but this single SD change may not capture all compensatory mechanisms.

Claims
Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to the SD sequence during -1 frameshifting and maintain wild-type frameshifting efficiencies across three programmed sites (IS911, IS3, dnaX). Frameshifting efficiency for IS911 was 14% with Ribo-T vs. 13% with WT (p=0.54). Frameshifting efficiency for IS3 was 33% with both types (p=0.77). Frameshifting efficiency for dnaX was 45% with Ribo-T vs. 43% with WT (p=0.77). In the reverse experiment, Ribo-T frameshifting was unchanged (45% vs. 44%, p=0.85) when WT SD was replaced with Ribo-T SD. Ribo-T ribosomes show a stark contrast to WT for +1 frameshifting, with only 2% vs. 33% efficiency. This suggests that SD-ASD interaction has differential roles in -1 versus +1 frameshifting that are uniquely compromised by tethering. Ribo-T ribosomes do not rely on SD-ASD base pairing for -1 frameshifting, challenging the generality of SD-mediated recoding. The -1 frameshifting mechanism in Ribo-T may be dominated by slippery sequence and RNA structure features rather than SD-dependent pausing.
Ribo-T ribosomes are impaired for +1 frameshifting and stop codon termination, with termination readthrough rates approximately 5- to 10-fold higher than wild-type. +1 frameshifting efficiency at prfB was 2% for Ribo-T vs. 33% for WT (p=8.9e-9). UAG stop codon readthrough was 0.07% for Ribo-T vs. 0.013% for WT (p=4.7e-7). UGA stop codon readthrough was 0.26% for Ribo-T vs. 0.11% for WT (p=5e-3). UAA stop codon readthrough was 0.04% for Ribo-T vs. 0.01% for WT (p=2.5e-4). The absolute readthrough rates remain low (0.01-0.07%), and the relative impairment (approx. 5-10 fold) may not be physiologically critical given the slow-growth phenotype already attributed to rRNA processing. The +1 frameshifting mechanism, which requires SD-mediated release of E-site tRNA to destabilize the ribosome, is fundamentally broken in Ribo-T. Reduced A-site dynamic capacity in tethered ribosomes limits the ability to bind termination factors, increasing readthrough.
Ribo-T ribosomes use SD sequences four-fold less efficiently than wild-type during translation initiation, yet can still drive protein synthesis at 50% wild-type levels. Luciferase activity with Ribo-T SD was four-fold lower than with WT SD (p=4.7e-4) in the presence of Ribo-T ribosomes. Ribo-T ribosomes translated lacZ-luc with a protein synthesis rate 50% that of wild-type ribosomes. The stem loop roadblock showed no effect on luc initiation (p=0.22), confirming internal loading rather than scanning or re-initiation. The p-value of 0.04 (versus no SD) is near the conventional significance threshold, and the qualitative 'almost no luciferase' statement requires more quantitative backing. The SD sequence is neither necessary nor sufficient for initiation in Ribo-T, consistent with the existence of mRNAs devoid of SD. The slower doubling time of Ribo-T cells (107 min vs. 35 min) likely reflects the aggregate effect of reduced initiation efficiency across multiple genes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Cross-talk was checked by running the Ribo-T SD construct with WT ribosomes only and confirming b-galactosidase activity was 'too little' for measurement. Expression of luc with the Ribo-T SD in the absence of Ribo-T ribosomes yielded activity one tenth those observed with Ribo-T ribosomes, confirming specificity. The reverse frameshifting experiment (WT ribosomes + Ribo-T SD) confirmed Ribo-T insensitivity to the SD sequence while demonstrating that WT ribosomes are SD-dependent. A stable stem loop roadblock downstream of lacZ confirmed that internal loading, not scanning, was the initiation mode. Each translational efficiency was calculated from at least six independent experiments, providing median values and statistical robustness. Three independent frameshifting sites and three stop codons were tested, providing cross-context validation of the Ribo-T phenotype. The authors noted that the cross-talk was 'too low to affect the results,' a qualitative but necessary negative control.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the three programmed -1 frameshifting sites (IS911, IS3, dnaX) and their corresponding slippage and stimulatory elements. Figure 2A displays the -1 frameshifting efficiencies for IS911, IS3, and dnaX with WT and Ribo-T ribosomes, showing near-identical values. Figure 2B shows the reverse experiment results: WT with Ribo-T SD reduces to 11% frameshifting, while Ribo-T remains at 45%, confirming SD-independence. Figure 3A presents the +1 frameshifting site at prfB with its UGA stop codon context and stimulatory SD. Figure 3B shows Ribo-T +1 frameshifting at 2% versus WT at 33%, with the p-value of 8.9x10^-9. Figure 3C shows the SD-rescue experiment: WT with Ribo-T SD drops to 0.6%, while Ribo-T with Ribo-T SD remains at 1.8%. Figure 4A-D present the SD recognition assays: (A) no SD vs. WT SD, (B) Ribo-T SD with WT vs. Ribo-T, (C) Ribo-T SD at lacZ, (D) stem loop roadblock. Figure 5 shows stop codon readthrough at mtmB1 with three stop codons (UAG, UGA, UAA), demonstrating Ribo-T terminates less efficiently across all. Table 1 lists all target sequences tested, including their respective SD, frameshifting, and stop codon sequences.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the systematic characterization of Ribo-T ribosome translational accuracy, revealing that subunit tethering renders the ribosome SD-insensitive for -1 frameshifting, impaired for +1 frameshifting and stop codon termination, and inefficient at SD-dependent initiation, despite maintaining near-WT -1 frameshifting fidelity. 2. The strongest evidence is the near-identical -1 frameshifting efficiencies between WT and Ribo-T at all three programmed sites (13% vs. 14%; 33% vs. 33%; 43% vs. 45%) combined with the 4-fold reduced SD recognition and 2% vs. 33% +1 frameshifting impairment, establishing a consistent phenotype of altered SD-ASD interactions. 3. The future path involves obtaining a high-resolution structure of Ribo-T to resolve the proposed geometry modification of helix 44, and testing whether tethered ribosomes would retain any function in eukaryotic translation, where SD-ASD interaction is not the primary initiation mechanism.

summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak, Laura Serra-Saurina, Raquel Rabionet Janssen, Laura Domènech, Mattia Bosio, Francesc Muyas, Xavier Estivill, Georgia Escaramís, Stephan Ossowski
summary.field_subfield: Bioinformatics / Statistical Genetics
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces BATI (Bayesian Association Test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation), a novel Bayesian rare variant association test framework that integrates categorical and numeric variant-specific characteristics as covariates within a hierarchical Bayesian model. The central methodological innovation is the application of INLA to estimate full-model posterior distributions for rare variant association in case-control studies, circumventing the computational limitations of MCMC for genome-wide scans while retaining the flexibility of a full Bayesian framework. BATI is implemented within the rvGWAS framework, which unifies quality control, interactive filtering, and six rare variant association tests: Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR, and BATI. The study uses realistic 'semi-synthetic' whole-exome sequencing cohorts—combining real WES samples from 1000GP and the Iberian cohort with real breast cancer risk variants introduced from ClinVar—to benchmark the six methods. The primary finding is that BATI substantially outperforms established methods when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function (LoF) variants, achieving power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail to identify risk genes at variance explained below 0.5%. At a 0.01% type I error rate and 0.5% variance explained, BATI identifies all risk genes at the 0.1% TIER with >80% power, while Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently miss BRCA2, BARD1, and CHEK2 due to high benign background variant counts. The framework is applied to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, identifying eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The paper also introduces ∆DIC for model selection, providing a quantitative criterion for choosing between null and alternative models in Bayesian RVAS. Overall, BATI demonstrates that integrating biological variant characteristics with fast and accurate INLA model estimation provides a flexible and powerful alternative to standard RVAS tests, capable of coping with complex population structure and other confounders.
