The central methodological innovation is the application of INLA to estimate full-model posterior distributions for rare variant association in case-control studies, circumventing the computational limitations of MCMC for genome-wide scans while retaining the flexibility of a full Bayesian framework. BATI is implemented within the rvGWAS framework, which unifies quality control, interactive filtering, and six rare variant association tests: Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR, and BATI. The study uses realistic 'semi-synthetic' whole-exome sequencing cohorts—combining real WES samples from 1000GP and the Iberian cohort with real breast cancer risk variants introduced from ClinVar—to benchmark the six methods. The primary finding is that BATI substantially outperforms established methods when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function (LoF) variants, achieving power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail to identify risk genes at variance explained below 0.5%. At a 0.01% type I error rate and 0.5% variance explained, BATI identifies all risk genes at the 0.1% TIER with >80% power, while Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently miss BRCA2, BARD1, and CHEK2 due to high benign background variant counts. The framework is applied to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, identifying eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The paper also introduces ∆DIC for model selection, providing a quantitative criterion for choosing between null and alternative models in Bayesian RVAS. Overall, BATI demonstrates that integrating biological variant characteristics with fast and accurate INLA model estimation provides a flexible and powerful alternative to standard RVAS tests, capable of coping with complex population structure and other confounders.

Research Context
Next-generation sequencing technologies now allow the study of genetic variants with complex diseases at a genome-wide scale. Unlike GWAS, which uses variants with minor allele frequency greater than 1%, WES and WGS enable analysis of rare genetic variants across the entire exome or genome. Previous evidence indicates that rare variants play an important role in the etiology of complex diseases and are more likely to affect protein structure, stability, or function than common variants. Rare variant association studies (RVAS) were developed to identify novel disease loci based on the burden of damaging variants within genomic units. However, RVAS lack power when cohorts are small or medium-sized because few individuals carry rare alternative alleles. Score-based methods pool minor alleles per unit into a measure of burden for association with phenotypic traits. When variants exhibit heterogeneous effects, variance-component methods such as SKAT and C-alpha are more powerful than burden tests. Recent developments include SKAT-O as a linear combination between burden and variance-component tests, and HBMR incorporating variant detection errors. Sun et al. proposed MiST within a hierarchical mixed-effects framework that considers variant biological characteristics, but the full model is too computationally intensive for genome-wide scans. The limitation of MCMC for large-scale Bayesian inference motivated the use of INLA, a non-sampling-based numerical approximation procedure.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a full-model Bayesian rare variant association test using INLA can integrate variant characteristics while remaining computationally feasible for genome-wide scans. The hypothesis is that BATI will outperform existing RVAS methods when prior information on the functional effect of variants is included, particularly in scenarios with low variance explained and high variant heterogeneity. The paper predicts that BATI will be more accurate than MCMC given the same computational resources, as demonstrated by Rue and Martino. A secondary hypothesis is that BATI will successfully cope with complex population structure and other confounders in realistic datasets. The authors also aim to develop and validate a model selection criterion based on ∆DIC to choose between null and alternative models. The expected outcome is that BATI will achieve high power (>75%) even when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance, while competing tests fail to identify risk genes. In a real-world application, the framework is expected to identify candidate predisposition genes in a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia cohort.

Methodological Details
The study employs a Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation, implemented via the R-INLA project at version 17.06.20. The framework, rvGWAS, unifies quality control, interactive filtering, and data stratification detection with six rare variant association tests. The six tests included are Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR (Bayesian), and BATI (the proposed method). To create realistic benchmarks, the authors developed a semi-synthetic simulator that combines thousands of real WES datasets with known risk variants for a disease. Two large datasets served as the basis for simulation: 1000GP and the Iberian cohort. For the breast cancer cohort, risk variants were queried from ClinVar, filtered by exonic or splicing annotation, and restricted to MAF no higher than 0.01 in EVS, 1000GP, or ExAC. For the Iberian cohort, one third of samples were assigned as cases and two thirds as controls; in 1000GP, half were cases and half were controls. Ten random cohort splits were performed to obtain comparable significance thresholds for all methods. P-value thresholds were calculated for Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O, MiST, HBMR, and BATI, translating to 5%, 0.1%, and 0.01% type I error rates. The median threshold across 10 splits was used to label a gene as significant for subsequent power analyses. The benchmark study used 100 simulations of risk variants for each gene separately across both cohorts. For the practical application, a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study cohort was analyzed using rvGWAS.

Procedures And Architectures
The BATI model assumes the phenotype Y belongs to an exponential family, where the latent effect is modeled as a GLMM. Variant-specific effects are treated as the random part of the model, with patient and variant characteristics forming the fixed part. BATI integrates a large number of categorical and numeric genetic variant characteristics as covariates, leveraging INLA's ability to estimate complex random-effects structures. Model selection between null and alternative hypotheses is based on the Deviance Information Criteria (DIC). The ∆DIC criterion, defined as DIC(H0) - DIC(H1), is used to reject the null hypothesis. To determine the appropriate ∆DIC threshold, the authors randomly assign individuals to cases or controls and generate an empirical distribution of the statistic under the null model. The median of ∆DIC thresholds from S=10 shuffled datasets was used for model selection in the benchmark study. The INLA algorithm uses a Laplace approximation to produce numerical posteriors of the latent Gaussian model, avoiding MCMC sampling. The rvGWAS framework supports association analysis at the gene level or for other biological units such as promoters. Quality control and interactive filtering functionalities are integrated into the workflow, along with detection of technical or population-based data stratification.

Key Results
At 0.01% TIER and 0.5% variance explained, BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes, with a median power of 55% across all risk genes. In contrast, all methods except BATI show power close to 0 under the same low VE and strict TIER conditions. At 0.1% TIER and 0.5% VE, BATI calls all risk genes with greater than 80% power. BATI calls most risk genes at the 0.01% TIER even at 0.5% VE, while Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently fail to call BRCA2 (both missense and LoF versions). HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 at the 0.1% TIER even at 0.5% VE. The power plots at 0.5% VE for Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O look very similar, indicating these methods share the same strengths and weaknesses across genes. BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size of the Iberian cohort (1,167 vs. 1,810 individuals). In the Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia application, rvGWAS identified eight candidate predisposition genes. Among the identified genes, EHMT2 and COPS7A were specifically highlighted as candidate risk genes. All methods except MiST identify all risk genes at 0.01% TIER in the 2% variance explained setting. MiST showed favorable results on purely artificial benchmark sets but performed poorly on the realistic WES cohorts, failing to identify any risk gene at low VE.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The superior performance of BATI suggests that incorporating biological variant characteristics as covariates in a full Bayesian framework provides meaningful information about the genetic architecture. The gain in power for BATI is strongest when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function variants, indicating that functional annotation is a critical covariate. BATI performs at least as well as other methods when testing genes containing mostly missense variants, demonstrating flexibility across variant architectures. The success of INLA over MCMC for these models confirms that non-sampling approximation is both feasible and accurate for full-model inference in RVAS. The framework demonstrates that realistic semi-synthetic cohorts, combining real noise with real variants, reveal substantial method differences that artificial simulations hide. The findings imply that combining Burden and SKAT-type methods with completely different approaches like BATI may be beneficial to compensate for specific method weaknesses. The rvGWAS framework establishes a reproducible, interactive pipeline that democratizes access to multiple RVAS tests for genomics researchers.

Contradictions And Limitations
MiST was noted to perform well on purely artificial benchmark sets but poorly on realistic WES cohorts, raising questions about the generalizability of prior RVAS benchmark results. The paper does not report a specific random seed or exact train/test split, which may limit reproducibility of the 100 simulations per gene. The 0.5% variance explained scenarios were simulated using semi-synthetic variants, so the biological realism of the variance estimates is not fully verified. The number of risk genes (8) in the breast cancer cohort is relatively small, limiting the breadth of the generalizability conclusion. The paper does not include a specific sample size for the Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, only the number of identified genes. The ∆DIC model selection criterion has been validated via simulations but not through independent external replication. The exact definition of 'meaningful biological context' varies across applications, and the study doesn't test all possible combinations of covariates.

Claims
BATI substantially outperforms established RVAS methods when risk genes contain functional variants, particularly when variance explained is low. At 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, BATI calls all genes at 0.1% TIER with >80% power while Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O fail on BRCA2. BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail to identify risk genes at VE < 0.5%. The performance gap between BATI and other methods is more profound than previously appreciated at low VE. In the 2% VE setting, all methods except MiST identify all risk genes at 0.01% TIER, meaning the advantage disappears at higher variance explained. For genes with mostly missense variants, BATI performs at least as good as other methods, not significantly better. The results suggest that for real-world WES cohorts with low-effect-size risk, BATI should be a first-line RVAS test. The framework can be extended to other disease types and genetic architectures beyond breast cancer.
The semi-synthetic simulation approach reveals substantial method performance differences that were hidden by previous purely artificial simulations. Previous simulations produced completely artificial cohorts with unrealistic noise levels and overly optimistic performances. Semi-synthetic cohorts combined real WES background noise with real ClinVar variants, producing realistic functional impact profiles. MiST performed poorly on realistic WES cohorts despite favorable results on artificial benchmark sets. The simulator still uses semi-synthetic variants introduced from ClinVar, so the true biological variance structure is not fully natural. Future RVAS benchmarking should adopt semi-synthetic approaches to avoid over-optimistic performance estimates.
The rvGWAS framework provides a unified, user-friendly pipeline for RVAS that integrates data QC, filtering, and multiple statistical tests. rvGWAS combines QC, interactive filtering, detection of data stratification, and six RVAS tests. The framework supports genes or any other biological unit such as promoters. A Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study was successfully analyzed, identifying eight candidate predisposition genes. The specific implementation details and availability of the interactive filtering are not fully described in the paper. The framework reduces the barrier for genomic researchers to perform RVAS analysis at genome-wide scale.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors performed 100 simulations per gene, 1000GP cohort (Fig 3, Table 2), and a second Iberian cohort (Supplementary S9 Fig), providing robustness across two different WES backgrounds. The 10 random cohort splits were used to generate and validate the ∆DIC thresholds, demonstrating stability of the model selection procedure. The results were confirmed in the Iberian cohort, showing mostly similar performance despite the smaller cohort size (1,167 vs. 1,810). Ablation: The study compared BATI with five other tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR), providing a comprehensive comparison of different RVAS architectures. The authors showed BATI achieves comparable or better performance than SKAT-O and others for missense variants, while significantly outperforming them for LoF variants. Sensitivity analysis: The power was assessed at three TIER thresholds (5%, 0.1%, 0.01%) and multiple variance explained settings (2%, 1%, 0.5%).

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 presents gene-wise power plots for the 1000GP cohort, showing three TIER thresholds (red, green, blue) and BATI calling all risk genes at 0.01% TIER even at 0.5% VE. Table 2 provides the quantitative median power values for all six RVAS tests across 8 risk genes at different TIER thresholds and VE levels. Supplementary S6 Fig shows the estimated significance thresholds across 10 randomized case-control splits, demonstrating stability. Supplementary S8 Fig shows the Iberian cohort benchmark results, confirming power patterns similar to the 1000GP cohort. Supplementary S4 Table presents the ∆DIC thresholds for each method across the 10 random splits. The paper notes that at 0.01% TIER, only 2 genes out of ~20,000 are expected to be significant by chance, contextualizing the threshold.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BATI, a full-model Bayesian rare variant association test using INLA that integrates variant characteristics as covariates, outperforming established methods in low-variance-explained scenarios. 2. The strongest evidence is that at 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, BATI achieves power >80% for all risk genes while Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O fail on BRCA2, BARD1, and CHEK2. 3. The future path involves extending the rvGWAS framework to more disease types, refining the ∆DIC model selection procedure, and potentially incorporating more complex variant-function covariates.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes the creation of the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK), a crowdsourced platform containing 182 curated Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs), of which 98 are unique small molecules. The work was motivated by the urgent need for antiviral treatments against Nipah virus, a pathogen with over 75% case fatality rate and high mortality (50-100%) that has been a public health concern since outbreaks in Malaysia (1998), Bangladesh, and India (Kerala, 2018). The authors systematically curated NVIs from PubMed and Google searches, initially identifying 838 relevant papers. A four-tier scoring system (scores 10, 5, 4, 0) was used to select papers for manual curation, resulting in the NVIK dataset. The platform was built using LAMP server technology with PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS. For compound characterization, 1875 descriptors were computed per inhibitor using PaDel software, and chemical similarity was assessed using NNeib (v5.12.0) and Jarp (v6.0.2) with a dissimilarity threshold of 0.15. Visualization employed customized CIRCOS and Cytoscape for compound network diagrams. The 98 unique small molecules clustered into 90 groups (84 singletons/93.3% and 14 non-singletons/15.5%), demonstrating high chemical diversity. The EC50/IC50 values ranged from 0.47 nM to 7,562,710 nM. A two-pronged combined evidence strategy was applied for prioritization: (i) assay robustness evaluation (prioritizing 11 NVIs based on experimental evidence) and (ii) drug-likeness assessment using DruLito (8 filters: Lipinski, MDDR-like, Veber, Ghose, BBB, CMC-50, and weighted/unweighted QED) and PAINS filters. Only two of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except CMC. The highest-prioritized compounds (NVIC0025, NVIC0032, NVIC0048) showed overlap with FDA-approved compounds (2346 total) and Enamine antiviral library (4644 total). The work was motivated by WHO's 2018 R&D Blueprint designating Nipah as a priority disease. The NVIK platform is publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah and accepts community submissions.

Research Context
Nipah virus is an infectious negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus causing severe disease with case fatality rates exceeding 75%. The virus is a public health concern with outbreaks in Malaysia (1998), Bangladesh, and India (Kerala, 2018) showing mortality of 50-100%. WHO's 2018 R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases identifies Nipah as requiring urgent accelerated research and development. Broad-spectrum antiviral ribavirin shows contradictory results with mortality reduction significantly below 50%, and no single drug is under clinical trial. Various groups have identified Nipah inhibitors using syncytia formation or titre reduction assays, including three sulfonamide compounds from large library screens. Despite reports of Nipah inhibitors, no systematic evaluation of the reported compounds has been performed. Existing antiviral inhibitor databases like IRD, ViPR, and Enamine contain very limited or no information focused on Nipah virus. The compounds with focus on Nipah inhibitors are scattered datasets or curated versions with limited evaluation as drug discovery starting points.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to systematically evaluate, characterize, and prioritize Nipah virus inhibitors for drug discovery. The authors hypothesized that a combined evidence strategy—prioritizing by both assay robustness and drug-likeness—would identify high-quality drug candidates among the reported inhibitors. The two-pronged strategy comprises: (i) prioritization based on the robustness of assays used to identify compounds, and (ii) estimation of drug-likeness parameters. The drug-likeness analysis includes diversity analysis, similarity to FDA-approved compounds, PAINS and DruLito filtering, and comparison to ZINC lead-like libraries. The platform is designed to allow both prioritization of existing inhibitors and submission of new molecules by the community.

Methodological Details
The data source comprised PubMed and Google, with a keyword search for 'Nipah' that initially identified 838 relevant papers. A four-tier scoring system assigned values: 10 for confirmed inhibitor information in abstracts, 5 for potential information, 4 for peptide inhibitors, and 0 for no relevant information. Papers with scores of 10, 5, and 4 were manually curated to create the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK) sheet. To ensure data quality, a separate team of curators re-performed the curation independently; errors were marked in red and verified in green. The NVIK platform is built on open-source LAMP server technology with PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS. Search tools include a text-based 'Simple Search', a logical operator-based 'Query Builder', and a 'Structure Search' supporting SMILES, SDF, and MOL formats. A compound drawing interface using JSME browser is available for structural queries. For compound analysis, 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. Chemical similarity is assessed using NNeib (version 5.12.0) for near neighbors and Jarp (version 6.0.2) for clustering, based on the dissimilarity threshold (1-Tanimoto coefficient) of 0.15. Visualization employs customized CIRCOS for physicochemical property distribution and Cytoscape for compound network diagrams. In the DruLito filter, compounds are screened against eight filters: Lipinski's rule, MDDR-like rule, Veber rule, Ghose filter, BBB rule, CMC-50 like rule, and weighted/unweighted QED. The PAINS filter is used to study the toxicity profile of the compounds.

Procedures And Architectures
The paper curation was performed manually and the data is stored in NVIK-Open resource Sheet, which serves as the crowdsourcing platform. Each entry is tagged with its contributor's email ID to track curation provenance. For the DruLito analysis, compounds are screened against eight physicochemical rules including Lipinski, Veber, and Ghose filters. Comparison to FDA-approved compounds (2346 entries) and Enamine antiviral library (4644 entries) is conducted on six parameters: molecular weight, H-bond donors, H-bond acceptors, rotatable bonds, XlogP, and topological polar surface area. In the CIRCOS visualization, 98 inhibitors are defined with a band of width 1000 representing the baseline for cyclic and aliphatic compounds. The EC50/IC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7,562,710 nM for 182 entries, and 0.47 nM to 7,562,710 nM for 125 small molecule entries. The dataset includes 182 entries, with 125 small molecules, and the remaining 57 are either peptides or lack complete information. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 of the 98 unique small-molecule inhibitors.

Key Results
The NVIK contains 182 entries, 98 of which are unique small-molecule inhibitors; 70 have EC50/IC50 values and all 98 have available structures. The reported EC50/IC50 values range from a minimum of 0.47 nM to a maximum of 7,562,710 nM for the small molecule inhibitors. Clustering of the 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters, of which 84 clusters (93.3%) were singletons and 14 clusters (15.5%) were non-singletons, indicating high chemical diversity. In DruLito filtering, only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except the CMC filter, highlighting the stringent criteria for drug-likeness. The independent assay-robustness prioritization identified 11 NVIs for further study. Among the prioritized compounds, NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and were accepted in FDA drug analysis. NVIC0048 displayed the highest degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges. NVIC0032 exhibited better bioactivity among the three and considerable overlap with the physicochemical properties of FDA-approved drugs. There are 34 NVIs similar to 76 FDA-approved drugs. One example is 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine (NVIC0097), which shows structural similarity against four FDA molecules: Adenosine, Vidarabine, Fludarabine, and Ademetionine.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high diversity (93.3% singletons) suggests that Nipah virus inhibitors occupy a broad chemical space with many unique scaffolds. Near neighbor identification revealed that compounds with different molecular weight ranges (e.g., GS-441524 at 531.202 g/mol and GS-441524 (NUC) at 291.267 g/mol) are related, suggesting common structural features responsible for NiV activity. This approach is useful for identifying potential pharmacophore features important for antiviral properties. The prioritization based on assay robustness addresses a critical gap: not all reported inhibitors are derived from high-quality experimental assays. The combined evidence strategy positions the dataset not just as a collection of compounds, but as a vetted tool for prioritized drug discovery.

Contradictions And Limitations
The abstract states 'a few compounds passed DruLito & PAINS filters', but the DruLito section reports only 'two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than CMC', indicating inconsistencies in the reported subset sizes. The total number of entries in DruLito analysis is reported as 91, while the total unique small molecules is 98 and those with EC50/IC50 are 70, leaving the exact inclusion criterion for the 91 ambiguous. The paper does not report statistical comparisons between the prioritized and non-prioritized sets beyond descriptive physicochemical overlap. The curation and quality check were performed manually, which is susceptible to human error despite the two-team verification process. The paper does not disclose the exact criteria for the 'robustness' of assays beyond a qualitative prioritization, leaving the specific assay-quality threshold undefined. No validation of the prioritization against a gold-standard set of confirmed active compounds is reported.

Claims
The NVIK platform provides a systematically curated and prioritized knowledgebase of Nipah virus inhibitors that addresses the lack of a centralized, evaluated resource. The platform contains 182 curated NVIs, 98 unique small molecules, with EC50/IC50 values for 70 and structures for all 98. The 98 NVIs were validated by a two-team manual curation and quality check process. The platform includes a combined evidence strategy prioritizing compounds by both assay robustness and drug-likeness. The paper does not report any functional validation that the prioritized compounds actually inhibit Nipah virus in a biological assay. The DruLito filtering results show only two compounds out of 91 passed most filters, suggesting the overall quality of the curated set may be low. The platform serves as a jumping-off point for rational drug design, reducing the search space from thousands of random compounds to a dozen vetted candidates. The provision for community submissions enables the database to evolve in real-time with new inhibitor reports.
The prioritized NVIs (NVIC0048, NVIC0032, NVIC0025) possess drug-like physicochemical properties overlapping with those of FDA-approved compounds. NVIC0048 displayed a high degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges of FDA-approved drugs. NVIC0032 has better activity among the three and considerable overlap with FDA-approved physicochemical properties. The EC50/IC50 of prioritized compounds falls within the nanomolar to micromolar range, consistent with druglike antivirals. Only two compounds passed all DruLito filters except CMC, indicating that most reported NVIs fail drug-likeness criteria. The paper does not provide pharmacokinetic data (ADME, metabolism, etc.) for any of the prioritized compounds. The overlap with FDA compounds suggests these candidates may be amenable to traditional drug development pipelines. DrugBank toxicity data for similar FDA compounds is provided to aid in selection of compounds with safer profiles.

Data And Code Availability
The data were made publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah since the inception of the project in May 2018. The platform allows submission and assessment of new molecules reported as NVIs. Compound structure data is readily available for further studies. The NVIK is developed using open-source LAMP technology, making the server architecture accessible.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A separate team of curators re-performed the curation independently to verify the initial curation; errors were flagged in red and cleared in green after verification. The prioritization was conducted as an independent evaluation based on assay robustness, separate from the drug-likeness filtering. Each entry is tagged with the contributor's email ID, providing provenance for individual curated records. The DruLito analysis uses eight independent filters, providing multiple checkpoints for drug-likeness assessment. The Jarp clustering uses a dissimilarity threshold of 0.15, which was chosen for structural diversity assessment. The paper does not report any random seed values, train/test splits, or demographic information as this is a computational/data paper.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 defines the predefined data structure used by all curators to organize the NVIK sheet. Figure 1 shows the 16 unique fields in the NVIK database and the browsing interface. Figure 2 depicts the distribution of important physicochemical properties of NVIs and includes the near-neighbor graph and compound network diagram. Figure 3 compares the physicochemical property distribution of NVIs with 2346 FDA approved compounds and 4644 Enamine antiviral library compounds. Figure 4 shows the DruLito filter results, indicating only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except CMC. Table 2 lists the six DruLito filters and the results for the three shortlisted compounds (NVIC0025, NVIC0032, NVIC0048). The paper refers to compound network diagrams made using Cytoscape and CIRCOS for visualization.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the NVIK platform, a crowdsourced, two-tier curated knowledgebase of 182 Nipah virus inhibitors with 98 unique small molecules, combining assay-robustness prioritization with multi-filter drug-likeness screening. 2. The strongest evidence is the combined prioritization: 11 compounds were selected based on assay robustness, and of those, NVIC0048 showed the highest overlap with FDA-approved physicochemical ranges, while NVIC0032 had the best bioactivity. 3. The future path involves community-driven continual curation and analysis, submission of new inhibitors by the scientific community, and potential application of the identified compounds to other antiviral targets.

summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang; Leping Zhang; Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.field_subfield: Hematology / Cancer Genomics / 3D Genome Architecture
summary.executive_summary: This study presents an integrated 3D genome and transcriptome analysis of 18 newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients and 4 healthy T cell controls, characterizing how 3D chromatin architecture drives gene expression and defines clinical subtypes in T-ALL. Combining BL-Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq, the authors demonstrated that 3D genome organization at the compartment, topologically associated domain (TAD), and loop levels, along with gene expression profiles, can hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. Notably, approximately 29% (996/3392) of the differentially expressed genes were associated with 3D genome alterations, with nearly 45% of upregulated genes linked to structural changes. The authors identified 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions, generating 44 new translocation-mediated loops. Key findings include the identification of HOXA cluster enhancer hijacking, where translocations on chromosome 14 and chromosome 7 mediate new loops linking active enhancers of BCL11B and CDK6 to the 5' TAD of the HOXA cluster, driving ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression. This phenotype is associated with the immature ETP phenotype and poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALL, with HOXA13+ status serving as an independent survival predictor. Conversely, T-ALLs with TAL1/2 positivity (mutually exclusive with HOXA positivity) are associated with better survival. The study revealed that the 11 HOXA genes are partitioned into two TADs, and different fusion events preferentially alter the 3D interactome, controlling specific HOXA gene expression patterns. The findings demonstrate that 3D genome alterations, in addition to oncogenic mutations, play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and may provide new diagnostic and therapeutic targets, specifically anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors for HOXA11-A13+ T-ALL.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents an integrated 3D genome and transcriptome analysis of 18 newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients and 4 healthy T cell controls, characterizing how 3D chromatin architecture drives gene expression and defines clinical subtypes in T-ALL. Combining BL-Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq, the authors demonstrated that 3D genome organization at the compartment, topologically associated domain (TAD), and loop levels, along with gene expression profiles, can hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. Notably, approximately 29% (996/3392) of the differentially expressed genes were associated with 3D genome alterations, with nearly 45% of upregulated genes linked to structural changes. The authors identified 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions, generating 44 new translocation-mediated loops. Key findings include the identification of HOXA cluster enhancer hijacking, where translocations on chromosome 14 and chromosome 7 mediate new loops linking active enhancers of BCL11B and CDK6 to the 5' TAD of the HOXA cluster, driving ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression. This phenotype is associated with the immature ETP phenotype and poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALL, with HOXA13+ status serving as an independent survival predictor. Conversely, T-ALLs with TAL1/2 positivity (mutually exclusive with HOXA positivity) are associated with better survival. The study revealed that the 11 HOXA genes are partitioned into two TADs, and different fusion events preferentially alter the 3D interactome, controlling specific HOXA gene expression patterns. The findings demonstrate that 3D genome alterations, in addition to oncogenic mutations, play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and may provide new diagnostic and therapeutic targets, specifically anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors for HOXA11-A13+ T-ALL.

Research Context
3D genome alterations have been demonstrated to play important roles in tumorigenesis, including the development of hematological malignancies. However, how such alterations may provide key insights into T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients is largely unknown. The genome alterations could link to the etiology of T-ALL development.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether integrated 3D genome alterations and gene expression profiles can classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. A second hypothesis is that chromosomal organizations of T-ALL may represent different frozen stages of T cell development. A third hypothesis is that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking or fusion events drive ectopic transcription factor activation, leading to specific pathogenic gene expression profiles. A final hypothesis is that ectopic HOXA cluster gene expression is associated with poor prognosis and could serve as a therapeutic target.

Methodological Details
Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee of the Institute of Hematology at Peking University. Leukemia blast cells were prepared by density-gradient centrifugation of bone marrow samples. Cells were further purified to CD19 -CD14 -CD235 -CD45 + CD7 + populations using FACS analysis with anti-human antibodies. Peripheral blood samples were obtained from four healthy donors under the approval of the ethics committee of Peking University. T cells were purified using the EasySep Direct Human T Cell Isolation Kit. RNA-seq libraries were prepared with the TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2 (Illumina). Paired-end RNA-seq reads of the 18 patients and 4 healthy controls were generated with an average depth of 15 million read pairs. Reads were aligned to the hg19 genome with TopHat (v2.1.0) using default settings. Differentially expressed genes were identified with DESeq2 using FDR <0.01 and fold change >2. Hi-C was performed on one million cells per sample according to the BL-Hi-C protocol. The average depth of patient Hi-C samples was 486 million read pairs with a read length of 150 bp. ChIP-seq reads were mapped to hg19 with Bowtie2 (v2.3.5) and ATAC-seq reads were mapped with Bowtie2 using -X 2000. Aligned reads were filtered for a minimum MAPQ of 20 and duplicates were removed using SAMtools. Signal tracks and peaks were generated using the -SPMR option in MACS2. FIMO was used to detect the 20 bp CTCF motif from the Homer motif database in Loucy and Jurkat CTCF peaks.

Procedures And Architectures
Raw BL-Hi-C reads were processed by the in-house HiCpipe framework integrating ChIA-PET2 for bridge linker trimming, HiC-Pro for alignment and filtering, and Juicer for contact matrix generation. Knight-Ruiz (KR) normalized matrices were used for compartment and TAD analyses. The compartment was calculated using the eigenvector command of Juicer under 100 kb resolution. For every 100 kb bin, A or B compartments were defined by the over 70% sample majority rule. TAD boundaries were calculated by the Insulation score method on pooled 40 kb Hi-C matrices using parameters: -is 1000000 -ids 200000 -im mean -nt 0.1. Differential TAD boundaries were defined with a t-test FDR <0.01 and a difference between cases and controls higher than the 50% quantile of the overall difference. Loops were called by HiCCUPS, and differential loop detection was adapted from Douglas et al. with loops split into two distance ranges (> or < 150 kb) to minimize bias. Differential loops were called within each range with FDR <0.1 and then combined. hic_breakfinder was adapted to detect translocations in 18 T-ALL patient samples. After filtering translocations detected in normal controls, breakpoints were manually assessed to single base-pair resolution using the BL-Hi-C bridge linker. Chimeric reads were defined as single ends mapping to two different chromatins without the BL-Hi-C bridge linker. For each translocation, exact locations supported by more than 3 chimeric reads were identified as actual breakpoints. Translocation-mediated loops were manually recorded on interchromosome Hi-C maps using Juicebox. The HOXA cluster genes were partitioned between two TADs, with 6 enhancer regions (E1 to E12) identified in each TAD. Gene ontology analysis used the GREAT tool with the nearest gene within 100 kb for biological process enrichment. KEGG pathway enrichment was performed using DAVID with genes whose promoters (5 kb around TSS) overlapped loop anchors. Hi-C maps were normalized by cis interaction pairs and V4C plots were generated under 10 kb resolution. Hi-C heatmaps and Visual 4C plots of the reassembled chromatin were generated by MATLAB code.

Key Results
Approximately 29% (996/3392) of the DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. Among the DEGs, the genes associated with B-to-A compartment switches, increased domain scores (D-score), and enhanced loops were mostly upregulated. Genes associated with A-to-B compartment switches, decreased D-scores, and reduced loops were mostly downregulated. Upregulated DEGs were functionally enriched in pathways such as hematopoietic cell lineage, transcriptional misregulation in cancer, and cell cycle. Downregulated DEGs were enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and T cell receptor signaling. CDK6, a potential target for T-ALL treatment, exhibited a strong intra-TAD interaction and was upregulated in all T-ALL samples. Several upregulated oncogenic driver genes and T-ALL-associated transcription factors such as MYB, MYCN, BCL11A, SOX4, and WT1 also had increased D-scores. Transcription factors SOX4, WT1, and TFDP2 had structural alterations at all three levels (compartment, TAD, loop). When RcisTarget was used to predict key transcription factors, SOX4, WT1, and TFDP2 were top candidates potentially regulating approximately 28% of the upregulated genes. 3D genome alterations were estimated to associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL, with 56% directly related to structural alterations. PCA revealed that most ETP ALL samples were arrested at the immature stage (LMPP to Thy1) while non-ETP samples were arrested at the Thy2 to Thy4 stages. ETP and non-ETP ALLs were better separated at the loop level with 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops in ETP. A strong positive correlation (Pearson's correlation coefficient 0.685) was found between gene expression changes and combined loop strength/D-score changes. Approximately 20% of upregulated genes in ETP and 16% in non-ETP ALL harbored chromatin structure changes. Key transcription factors and oncogenes associated with chromatin changes included CEBPA, MYCN, and LYL1 for ETP; LEF1, TCF12, and PAX9 for non-ETP. 46 translocations were identified in 14/18 T-ALL samples, of which 34 were novel and 26 were interchromosomal. Among 78 unique breakpoints, 47% were located in noncoding regions and 66% were located in the stable A compartment. 44 new translocation-mediated loops were formed, and nearly 78% of those with CTCF motifs were linked to pairs of convergently orientated CTCF motifs. Loop-based hierarchical clustering showed complete match with T-ALL subtypes (HOXA, TLX, TAL). The cis mechanism involved translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking in ETP, TLX, and TAL subtypes with BCL11B-TLX3, TRB-TAL2, and 3 novel HOXA translocations. The trans mechanism involved translocation-mediated gene fusions: PSIP1-NUP98, SET-NUP214, and MLL (KMT2A-MLLT1, PICALM-MLLT10, DDX3X-MLLT10) gene fusion events. The 11 HOXA genes were partitioned between two TADs, with CTCF binding site C11/13 as the 3' boundary of the 5' TAD in all samples. C7/9 was used as the 5' boundary by most HOXA - (6/8) and all 5'HOXA + samples; C10/11 was used by most 3'HOXA + samples (4/5). Significantly enhanced interactions were found between E2-E6 and genes in the 3'HOXA subgroup; between E8, 9, 11, 12 and genes in the 5'HOXA subgroups. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity, alone or in combination, but not other HOXA genes, was associated with poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALLs. HOXA13+ status could serve as an independent predictor for the overall survival of pediatric and young adult T-ALLs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
3D genome alterations can hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes along the T cell differentiation trajectory, suggesting chromosomal organizations represent frozen stages of development. Translocations activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors via cis (enhancer hijacking) or trans (gene fusions) mechanisms, rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome. The HOXA cluster is heterogeneous; different fusion events preferentially alter the 3D interactome within the cluster and control specific subsets of HOXA gene expression. Translocations and inversion at the 5' TAD of the HOXA cluster lead to dysregulated 5'HOXA expression through new loop formation-mediated enhancer hijacking. HOXA11-A13 expression is associated with the immature DN and ETP phenotypes and a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit T-ALL patients with ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, which is currently incurable by standard treatments.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study includes only 18 T-ALL patient samples and 4 healthy controls, a small cohort size that may limit generalizability. Only 14 out of 18 samples exhibited translocations, and the number of HOXA-T samples was very small (three cases). The 5/7 HOXA + samples with detectable translocation-mediated fusion events represent a limited subset. ChIP-seq analysis was performed only on the HOXA + Loucy cell line and non-ETP Jurkat cell line, not on patient samples. HOXA9, previously used as a biomarker, was not associated with poor survival, contradicting previous clinical usage. The prognostic cohort was analyzed separately in a companion paper, and the multivariate analysis was not fully detailed in the main text. The study does not report specific random seeds, train/test splits, or detailed patient demographics beyond age groups.

Claims
3D genome alterations in T-ALL are associated with gene expression changes and drive clinical differentiation. Approximately 29% of DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. PCA and hierarchical clustering showed transcriptome changes were highly consistent with 3D genome structural changes. 3D genome organization could hierarchically classify different subtypes of T-ALL according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. The majority of DEGs (over 70%) were not associated with structural changes, suggesting other mechanisms predominate. Only 56% of the ~45% of upregulated genes could be directly related to structural alterations. 3D genome architecture may provide a diagnostic readout for T-ALL classification. Genome-wide 3D organization analysis could identify new prognostic biomarkers beyond conventional sequencing.
Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking drives ectopic HOXA cluster gene expression and poor prognosis in ETP T-ALL. Translocations on chromosome 14 and chromosome 7 mediate new loops between active enhancers and the 5' TAD of the HOXA cluster. HOXA11-A13 positivity was associated with poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALLs. HOXA13+ status served as an independent predictor for overall survival. Other HOXA genes (HOXA1-A10) were not associated with poor survival, indicating specificity to HOXA11-A13. TAL1/2 positivity was mutually exclusive from HOXA positivity and associated with better survival, showing divergent clinical implications. The mechanism identifies a specific molecular driver for the incurable ETP subtype of T-ALL. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may represent a targeted therapeutic for patients with ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression.
ETP and non-ETP ALLs represent different frozen stages of T cell development marked by distinct 3D chromatin organizations. ETP ALL samples were arrested at the immature stage (LMPP to Thy1) while non-ETP were arrested at Thy2 to Thy4. ETP and non-ETP samples were better separated at the loop level with 1820 enhanced loops in ETP versus 831 reduced loops. Loop anchors in ETP were enriched for immune response-activating signal transduction, myeloid cell differentiation, and B cell activation. Sample 093 fell between ETP and non-ETP, having significant TCR rearrangement, suggesting transitional states. The separation was less distinct at the compartment and TAD levels than at the loop level. The 3D genome provides a mechanistic explanation for ETP-specific transcription factor expression. T-ALL may be modeled as a continuum of T cell developmental arrest rather than discrete clinical categories.

Data And Code Availability
Raw RNA-seq data for Loucy and Jurkat cell lines were downloaded from the GEO database. Hi-C raw data were processed by the in-house HiCpipe framework, and V4C plots were generated by MATLAB code. Hi-C heatmaps and V4C plots were generated with MATLAB code; the paper does not explicitly mention public code deposition.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Differential loops were split into two distance ranges (> or < 150 kb) to minimize potential bias from loop detection tools. A TAD was defined only when its boundaries were detected in at least two conditions among normal T cells, ETPs, and non-ETPs. Hi-C maps were normalized by cis interaction pairs for visualization to reduce bias from sequence-specific contact patterns. For translocation-mediated loop calling, manual assessment with Juicebox was performed because loops were difficult to identify with standard tools. ChIP-seq of the HOXA + Loucy cell line was used to correlate increased interactions with H3K27ac gains.

Ethical Considerations
Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee of the Institute of Hematology at Peking University. Peripheral blood samples were obtained from four healthy donors under the approval of the ethics committee of Peking University. The study does not report explicit informed consent language beyond ethical committee approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the PCA of RNA-seq and Hi-C data, demonstrating hierarchical classification of T-ALL subtypes by 3D genome and transcriptome. Figure 1c and 1d display the distribution of DEGs across compartment, D-score, and loop changes, with red for upregulated and blue for downregulated. Figure 1e shows functional enrichment of genes associated with each structural change level. Figure 1f shows the CDK6 locus intra-TAD interaction and expression in T-ALL samples. Figure 2a shows PCA of ETP versus non-ETP ALL samples; Figure 2b shows loop differences; Figure 2c shows the correlation between gene expression and loop strength/D-score. Figure 2d shows Gene Ontology enrichment for ETP and non-ETP loop-associated genes. Figure 2e shows Hi-C maps demonstrating TCR rearrangement differences. Figure 2f shows RAG1 and PTCRA expression in T-ALL samples. Figure 2g and 2h show subtype-specific loops and expression at the MEF2C and PAX9 loci. Figure 3a shows Hi-C maps with 46 translocations highlighted; 3b shows translocation-mediated loops anchoring at CTCF sites; 3d shows loop-based hierarchical clustering matching subtypes. Figure 3e shows translocation-mediated loops linking enhancers to the HOXA cluster. Figure 4a shows unsupervised hierarchical clustering of HOXA gene expression separating T-ALL into HOXA-negative and HOXA-positive groups. Figure 4b shows Hi-C maps and CTCF motif orientations for the 11 HOXA genes partitioned between two TADs with differentially positioned boundaries. Figure 4c shows the 6 enhancer regions per TAD and their interaction with the HOXA cluster. Figure 4d shows ChIP-seq H3K27ac peaks and interaction dynamics for different HOXA fusion events. Figure 5a and 5b show breakpoint mapping and new loop formation at the HOXA cluster with gene expression data for three HOXA-T cases. Figure 5c shows the inter-TAD inversion in case 108 leading to ectopic HOXA11-A13. Figure 6a shows overall and event-free survival of T-ALL patients stratified by HOXA, TAL, and TLX status. Figure 6b shows phenotypic and clinical characteristics stratified by subtype. Figure 6d shows the multivariate analysis of HOXA13 status as an independent predictor of overall survival.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that 3D genome alterations (compartment, TAD, and loop changes) combined with transcriptome profiling can hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes and provide a mechanistic explanation for ectopic transcription factor activation via translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of 34 novel translocations and 44 translocation-mediated loops that physically link BCL11B/CDK6 enhancers to the HOXA cluster 5' TAD, driving HOXA11-A13 ectopic expression in DN/ETP phenotypes with poor survival. 3. The future path points toward anti-JAK-STAT targeted therapies for HOXA11-A13+ T-ALL and the use of 3D genome profiling as a diagnostic and prognostic tool for leukemia classification.

summary.title: ProNetView-ccRCC: A web-based portal to interactively explore clear cell renal cell carcinoma proteogenomics networks
summary.authors: Selim Kalayci; Francesca Petralia; Pei Wang; Zeynep H Gümüş
summary.field_subfield: Bioinformatics / Cancer Proteogenomics and Network Visualization
summary.executive_summary:
ProNetView-ccRCC is an interactive web-based portal designed for the visual exploration of the clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) phosphopeptide co-expression network, derived from the National Cancer Institute's Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) phosphoproteomics data. The network comprises 3,614 genes and 30 functional pathway-enriched modules, constructed from phosphoproteomics data of 103 ccRCC tumor samples using a random-forest based network construction algorithm. The core problem addressed is that while co-expression networks capture complex higher-order regulatory relationships between proteins and posttranscriptional modifications, their large dimensions and complicated topologies make them challenging to visually communicate, interpret, and navigate. Existing network visualization tools primarily produce static 2D images suitable only for print publication and lack the interactive capabilities required for user-initiated exploration of network metadata in tandem with biological pathways and clinical outcomes.

The portal addresses this gap by providing a 3D network exploration interface built on the Three.js framework with WebGL rendering and 3D layout algorithms from iCAVE. It enables users to rotate, zoom, and query the network interactively. Key features include: (1) 3D visualization of the full phosphopeptide co-expression network and each of the 30 module networks; (2) gene and module querying with automatic highlighting; (3) association queries between phosphoprotein abundance and clinical variables such as tumor grade, stage, age, and gender with user-defined FDR cut-offs; (4) pathway enrichment tables with interactive filtering; and (5) direct links to the ProTrack multi-omics data portal for deeper data exploration. The tool is a freely available, open-access resource (http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/) requiring no specialized plugins or browser extensions. The portal aims to democratize access to CPTAC co-expression network analysis, enabling researchers from diverse computational skill levels to conduct their own analyses, generate hypotheses, and communicate results. The authors do not report user-testing, formal validation with external cohorts, or comparative evaluation against alternative visualization approaches, and the primary validation is descriptive of the tool's functionality rather than its scientific utility.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
ProNetView-ccRCC is an interactive web-based portal designed for the visual exploration of the clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) phosphopeptide co-expression network, derived from the National Cancer Institute's Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) phosphoproteomics data. The network comprises 3,614 genes and 30 functional pathway-enriched modules, constructed from phosphoproteomics data of 103 ccRCC tumor samples using a random-forest based network construction algorithm. The core problem addressed is that while co-expression networks capture complex higher-order regulatory relationships between proteins and posttranscriptional modifications, their large dimensions and complicated topologies make them challenging to visually communicate, interpret, and navigate. Existing network visualization tools primarily produce static 2D images suitable only for print publication and lack the interactive capabilities required for user-initiated exploration of network metadata in tandem with biological pathways and clinical outcomes.

The portal addresses this gap by providing a 3D network exploration interface built on the Three.js framework with WebGL rendering and 3D layout algorithms from iCAVE. It enables users to rotate, zoom, and query the network interactively. Key features include: (1) 3D visualization of the full phosphopeptide co-expression network and each of the 30 module networks; (2) gene and module querying with automatic highlighting; (3) association queries between phosphoprotein abundance and clinical variables such as tumor grade, stage, age, and gender with user-defined FDR cut-offs; (4) pathway enrichment tables with interactive filtering; and (5) direct links to the ProTrack multi-omics data portal for deeper data exploration. The tool is a freely available, open-access resource (http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/) requiring no specialized plugins or browser extensions. The portal aims to democratize access to CPTAC co-expression network analysis, enabling researchers from diverse computational skill levels to conduct their own analyses, generate hypotheses, and communicate results. The authors do not report user-testing, formal validation with external cohorts, or comparative evaluation against alternative visualization approaches, and the primary validation is descriptive of the tool's functionality rather than its scientific utility.

Research Context
Recent advances in molecular profiling technologies have enabled large-scale integrative proteomic and genomic studies of cancers. The NCI Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) has performed comprehensive proteogenomic characterizations of tumor samples from breast, colon, ovarian, and kidney cancer patients. Integrative analyses based on rich proteogenomic profiles have greatly advanced understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying these cancers. Co-expression networks derived from proteomics and phosphoproteomics data have revealed regulatory relationships between proteins and posttranscriptional modifications. These networks bring new insights on complicated pathway interactions and dysfunctions that drive tumor initiation and progression. While co-expression networks contain rich information for identifying active pathways and oncogenic drivers, they are challenging to visually communicate due to their large dimensions and complicated topologies. These networks are best visually explored together with associated information between gene/protein activities and biological pathway annotations as well as clinical outcomes. Current network data visual exploration tools are mainly used for visually communicating networks as static 2D images in print publications. While these provide advanced capabilities for visual customizations, they are not well suited for user-initiated interactive network explorations. As incorporating and exploring the meta-data associated with CPTAC co-expression networks will make them readily available to the cancer research community, a centralized platform is necessary.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central challenge is how to effectively visualize and navigate network models that capture higher-order structures in proteogenomic profiles. There is a pressing need for a new open community resource tool for intuitive visual exploration, interpretation and communication of gene/protein regulatory networks by the cancer research community. The specific problem is that current tools are not well suited for user-initiated interactive network explorations incorporating associated meta-data. The authors hypothesize that a web-based interactive portal, ProNetView-ccRCC, will provide an intuitive and customized exploration environment for phosphopeptide co-expression network and other analysis results. The portal is predicted to enable quick and easy interactions with the ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network as well as 30 functional network modules and their associated meta-data. Users are expected to be able to conveniently query for association between abundance of each phosphopeptide and clinical variables such as tumor grade. The portal is designed to enable quick, user-intuitive visual interactions with a network comprising 3,614 genes. Users can easily query for proteins of interest, neighbors they are connected to, mapping peptides or pathways, at user-defined filters on clinical variables. The tool aims to facilitate hypothesis generation for future studies by helping users understand the phosphopeptide network in the context of markers of user interest.

Methodological Details
ProNetView-ccRCC enables visual explorations of two network types: the phosphopeptide co-expression network of ccRCC tumors and 30 different network modules derived based on the topology of the overall network. The network characterizes the co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC. The network was derived using a random-forest based network construction algorithm based on phospho-peptide level data of 103 ccRCC samples. Two genes are connected in the network if at least two phosphopeptides mapping to the two genes are associated to each other. Network modules were identified by using the Glay clustering algorithm based on the overall network topology. 30 modules containing at least 20 genes were identified and each was presented as a different module network. For each module network, pathway enrichment analysis was performed via Fisher Exact test and overrepresented pathways were incorporated as associated meta-data. The network displays association among genes based on phosphopeptide level data. The portal provides the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network and links it to functional network modules. Six modules within the network were significantly associated with biological pathways, as highlighted within the network using different coloring of nodes. The network exploration panel enables rotation and zoom in/out of the 3D view. Node sizes are proportional to the number of connections to let users easily identify the genes that are more central. Hovering over a node displays the gene name of the phosphopeptide, and clicking on the node displays the associated gene-level meta-data in a separate panel. A direct link to the ProTrack tool provides a web-based interface to explore ccRCC multi-omics data through interactive heatmaps.

Procedures And Architectures
For intuitive exploration of dense and complex networks, ProNetView-ccRCC enables interactive explorations in 3D. This capability was implemented by building on the Three.js framework, which provides an interface for WebGL. Network layouts were calculated using 3D layout algorithms within iCAVE, a desktop-based tool previously developed for stereoscopic and immersive exploration of networks. Multiple client-side Javascript libraries were utilized to handle various user interaction events in real time. Specifically, D3.js, dataTables.js, and JQuery were used for interactive components. For the styling of web interface elements, Bootstrap v3.3.7 was primarily utilized, integrated with custom styling. Since ProNetView-ccRCC utilizes only standard libraries, it does not require the use of any additional plug-ins and runs on all modern web browsers. The landing page provides the global co-expression network and links it to functional network modules. Users can interactively explore the topology by rotating and zooming the view in 3D. Six modules within the network were significantly associated with biological pathways, highlighted using different node coloring. Module 26, the Angiogenesis enriched module, is displayed with nodes whose sizes are proportional to connection count. A query for the oncogene ERG highlights the node in red and identifies it as a member of the Angiogenesis enriched module network. The query further returns a list of genes whose phosphopeptides were directly connected to ERG, along with tumor grade association. Users can click on the Heatmap link to be directed to the ProTrack tool for interactive multi-omics data exploration. A pathway enrichment table displays pathways sorted by their p-values, with interactive clicking to show associated genes.

Key Results
The overall phosphopeptide co-expression network in ccRCC comprises 3,614 genes and 30 functional pathway-enriched modules. The network was constructed from co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC. 30 modules containing at least 20 genes were identified using the Glay clustering algorithm. The oncogene ERG was identified as a gene associated to VEGF response in the CPTAC ccRCC paper. Searching for ERG in ProNetView-ccRCC highlights the node in red and identifies it as a member of the Angiogenesis enriched module network. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes within the same module and maps to 5 different peptides. The association of ERG's corresponding phosphoprotein with tumor grade is reported as p-value 0.003 and FDR 0.118. Users can construct a simple query for genes with a specified phenotype and FDR cut-off, for example FDR=20%. Module 18 is shown with an interactive table listing enriched pathways sorted by their p-values. The Cell cycle pathway shows associated genes including BRCA1, CDC20, and CDK1. Six modules within the network were significantly associated with biological pathways, highlighted using different node coloring. The portal runs on all modern web browsers without the need for installing any specific plugins or libraries.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
ProNetView-ccRCC provides a free, open-access and custom environment for the interactive exploration of CPTAC ccRCC networks and their associated meta-data. The tool is anticipated to facilitate researchers from a wide-spectrum of computational skill levels to conduct their own analyses on the rich CPTAC ccRCC network data. Users can share and communicate their results, enabling collective hypothesis generation and verification in the ccRCC research community. The 3D visualization with proportional node sizing allows users to easily identify the most central genes in each module. By enabling simultaneous exploration of the network topology, pathway enrichments, and clinical associations, the tool supports integrative analysis at the system level.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report any formal validation, user-testing, or comparative evaluation against other visualization approaches. The primary validation is descriptive of the tool's functionality rather than its scientific utility or accuracy. The paper is a tool/portal description and does not present new biological findings or experimental results beyond what is available in the underlying CPTAC data. The 3D layout algorithms are borrowed from a previously developed desktop tool (iCAVE), and their performance in a web environment is not explicitly evaluated. The tool's performance, rendering quality, and usability are not formally benchmarked across different web browsers or hardware configurations. The paper does not discuss whether the random-forest network construction produces reproducible results or how sensitivity to hyperparameters was assessed. The scope is limited to the CPTAC ccRCC dataset, and generalizability to other cancer types or networks is not addressed.

Claims
ProNetView-ccRCC enables interactive 3D exploration of the ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network and 30 module networks with associated clinical and pathway meta-data. The portal provides the global co-expression network and links it to 30 functional network modules. The 3D network exploration interface enables rotation and zooming in/out of the view. Node sizes are proportional to the number of connections, allowing identification of central genes. Clicking a node displays gene-level meta-data in a separate panel. The paper is descriptive of functionality and does not report user testing or formal validation. No comparative evaluation against other visualization tools is provided. Researchers with varying computational skill levels can access and analyze the CPTAC ccRCC network data without specialized expertise. The tool can facilitate hypothesis generation by contextualizing network topology with clinical variables and pathway annotations.
The portal supports querying of phosphoprotein abundance against clinical variables such as tumor grade with user-defined FDR cut-offs. ERG shows association with tumor grade as p-value 0.003 and FDR 0.118. Users can construct queries with specific phenotype and FDR cutoff, e.g., FDR=20%. Satisfying genes are listed in a text box and highlighted in red in the network panel. The FDR values and p-values are derived from the underlying CPTAC data analysis, not re-computed by the portal. Clinically relevant nodes can be identified and prioritized for further functional validation.

Data And Code Availability
The portal is a freely available, open-access resource at http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/. The portal does not explicitly mention a code repository (e.g., GitHub) for the software or a supplementary materials repository for the underlying data.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network in the portal. Figure 1B shows the 30 functional network modules with six modules highlighted in different colors based on biological pathway association. Figure 1C illustrates a search for the oncogene ERG, highlighting the node in red and showing its connection to the Angiogenesis module. Figure 2A displays a snapshot of the Angiogenesis enriched module network (module 26) with proportional node sizing. Figure 2B shows a node selected in the module network with a separate panel displaying gene-level meta-data and a link to the ProTrack tool. Figure 2C shows a query interface for genes with a specified phenotype and FDR cut-off. Figure 2D shows the results of the query with satisfying genes highlighted in red in the network panel. Figure 3A displays the interactive table of enriched pathways sorted by p-values for module 18. Figure 3B shows a pathway selected in the table with the list of associated genes returned in a text box and highlighted in the network.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the ProNetView-ccRCC portal, an interactive 3D web-based tool for visual exploration of the CPTAC ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network with 3,614 genes and 30 functional modules, including clinical and pathway meta-data. 2. The strongest evidence of the tool's functionality is the demonstration of querying the oncogene ERG, showing it connected to 11 genes with p-value 0.003 and FDR 0.118 for tumor grade, and the pathway-enriched tables with interactive gene listing for module 18 pathways. 3. The future path involves enabling researchers from a wide-spectrum of computational skill levels to conduct their own analyses on the CPTAC ccRCC network data and share their results, potentially facilitating hypothesis generation for future studies.

summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee; Anabel Eckerling; Boaz Israeli; Gali Yanovich; Ella Rosenne; Suzana Fichman-Horn; Ido Ben Zvi; Liat Sorski; Ronit Satchi-Fainaro; Tamar Geiger; Erica K Sloan; Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu

summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the phenomenon of spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastases following primary tumor excision—a rare clinical observation with unknown mechanisms. Using a mouse model of MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer with high-sensitivity luciferase reporting, the authors demonstrate that PT excision induces a dramatic, 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal within 24 hours (p<0.0001). The regression is specific to early-stage micro-metastases (~10⁶ photons/s) and is significantly less prominent in larger metastases (~10⁷ photons/sec; p<0.000), suggesting that larger foci may become self-sufficient. Sham surgery (PT untouched) did not induce regression (p<0.05), excluding surgical trauma as a mechanism. In vitro assays showed tumor-cell conditioned medium (CM) enhanced viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and induced HUVEC tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo, osmotic minipump supplementation of CM reduced metastatic regression by 10-fold compared to serum-free medium (p<0.005), indicating that PT-secreted factors actively promote early metastatic growth. Cytokine array and LC-MS proteomics identified four key factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF, whose in vivo neutralization completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Retrospective analysis of a public TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort revealed that high protein levels of these four factors correlated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio of 2.05, p<0.05). The study concludes that the perioperative period offers a window of opportunity to control minimal residual disease by blocking PT-secreted pro-metastatic factors. If generalized, these findings suggest novel perioperative and surveillance strategies for early metastasis detection and intervention.
