judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the phenomenon of spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastases following primary tumor excision—a rare clinical observation with unknown mechanisms. Using a mouse model of MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer with high-sensitivity luciferase reporting, the authors demonstrate that PT excision induces a dramatic, 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal within 24 hours (p<0.0001). The regression is specific to early-stage micro-metastases (~10⁶ photons/s) and is significantly less prominent in larger metastases (~10⁷ photons/sec; p<0.000), suggesting that larger foci may become self-sufficient. Sham surgery (PT untouched) did not induce regression (p<0.05), excluding surgical trauma as a mechanism. In vitro assays showed tumor-cell conditioned medium (CM) enhanced viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and induced HUVEC tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo, osmotic minipump supplementation of CM reduced metastatic regression by 10-fold compared to serum-free medium (p<0.005), indicating that PT-secreted factors actively promote early metastatic growth. Cytokine array and LC-MS proteomics identified four key factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF, whose in vivo neutralization completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Retrospective analysis of a public TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort revealed that high protein levels of these four factors correlated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio of 2.05, p<0.05). The study concludes that the perioperative period offers a window of opportunity to control minimal residual disease by blocking PT-secreted pro-metastatic factors. If generalized, these findings suggest novel perioperative and surveillance strategies for early metastasis detection and intervention.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, yet it has been suggested to accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease through processes triggered by the surgical procedure itself. Alternatively, elimination of inhibitory signaling from the primary tumor may remove suppressive constraints on metastases. Conversely, several case studies report spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis, clearly documented in breast and lung cancers. Several underlying mechanisms have been suggested, including surgical trauma and elimination of stimulating factors secreted by the primary tumor or induced by its presence. Unfortunately, postulated mechanisms have not been empirically tested as no animal model of spontaneous regression currently exists. The need to study interactions between the primary tumor and metastases is stressed by the realization that a primary tumor is a systemic disease with continuous crosstalk between the tumor, its microenvironment, and distant organs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether primary tumor excision can induce spontaneous regression of micro-metastases and what molecular mechanisms drive this phenomenon. The authors hypothesized that the primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases, and its elimination by surgery results in metastatic regression. They further hypothesized that in vivo supplementation of the tumor secretome would diminish this regression, confirming that PT-secreted factors promote early metastatic growth. They predicted that specific secreted factors, identified by cytokine array and proteomics, drive metastatic growth, and that in vivo neutralization of these factors would arrest metastasis. A secondary hypothesis proposed that high protein levels of identified factors would correlate with poor survival in human lung adenocarcinoma patients. They also predicted that the phenomenon would be stage-specific, with larger metastatic foci being less susceptible to regression.

Methodological Details
The model utilized a highly metastatic variant of the triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma cell line MDA-MB-231 HM. Cells were transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector for high-sensitivity bioluminescent monitoring. Cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% glutamax, 4.5 g/L D-glucose, and 110 mg/L sodium pyruvate, maintained at 37 °C and 5% CO₂ and mycoplasma-free. Eight-week-old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were housed under SPF conditions on a 12 h dark/light cycle. Mice received 2×10⁵ cells in 20 μl PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad under 2% isoflurane anesthesia to form a primary tumor. Primary tumors were measured by caliper, with volume calculated as (length × width)² × 0.5. Metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging using an IVIS spectrum apparatus after i.p. injection of 150 mg/kg D-luciferin sodium salt. Primary tumors were excised when metastatic foci reached a total flux of 10⁶ photons/s, approximately 3-4 weeks post injection, with average size of 80 mm³. Complete PT removal was verified by bioluminescence imaging and metastases were monitored over 50 days. Sham surgery involved an identical incision with the primary tumor left untouched, with the skin immediately sutured. Tumor cell-conditioned medium (CM) was produced by incubating ~80% confluent MDA-MB-231 HM cells with serum-free medium for 24 h at 37°C, 5% CO₂. CM was collected from ~30 million cells, filtered through a 0.45 μm strainer, concentrated by 3 kDa Amicon filters to a final volume of 100 μl/mouse, and stored at -20°C. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with CM or serum-free medium (SM) and implanted i.p. immediately following tumor excision. The amount of secretome released daily by the minipumps was estimated at ~1/8 of the amount produced in vivo by the 80 mm³ primary tumor containing ~50×10⁶ secretome-producing cells. Adhesion studies involved seeding cells in SM or CM and imaging for 8 hours in 20 min intervals using the IncuCyte system to determine the number of adhered cells. Apoptosis studies involved incubating cells in CM or SM for 24 hrs, then washing and staining for AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD, with analysis by flow cytometry. Tube formation used 50 μl basement membrane extracellular matrix (Cultrex BME) layered on 24-well plates, with HUVEC reconstituted in CM or SM, imaged at 20 min intervals for 24 h using the IncuCyte system. Human cytokine analysis compared 102 soluble human proteins in CM samples and plasma from mice bearing PT, mice one day post excision, and control mice; each plasma sample was pooled from 3 mice. LC-MS utilized nano-ultra high performance liquid chromatography (Easy-nLC1000) coupled to a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer with 50 cm long EASY-Spray PepMap columns and a 140 min linear gradient of water/acetonitrile. MS used the top10 method with higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) for all high-resolution MS scans. Proteins were digested with LysC/Trypsin mix and sequencing-grade modified Trypsin overnight at room temperature, then desalted on C18 StageTips. MS/MS spectra were referenced to the Uniprot human proteome via the Andromeda search engine, with a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.01 at both peptide and protein levels. Enrichment analysis used Gene Ontology annotations with a Fisher exact test and FDR threshold of 0.02. Neutralizing antibodies against IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF were injected at 1 μg each/mouse once daily for two days; IgG1 served as isotype control. Histology involved imaging lungs ex vivo, fixing lobes in 4% paraformaldehyde, paraffin embedding, and 6 μm sections stained for Hematoxylin and Eosin, confirmed by a pathologist. Patient outcome was analyzed using the public TCGA provisional dataset (cBioPortal) for a lung adenocarcinoma cohort, with Kaplan Meier Analysis and hazard ratio calculation in R software. Statistical analysis included repeated-measures or factorial ANOVA (p=0.05), Fisher PLSD for post hoc comparisons, and paired or unpaired student's t-test with F-test for equality of variance; all tests were two sided.

Procedures And Architectures
Primary tumor resection was performed under anesthesia with 2% isoflurane using a small skin incision without injuring the peritoneal cavity to excise the tumor. Following complete removal of the PT (verified by bioluminescence), the skin was immediately sutured; for sham surgery, an identical incision was made but the PT was left untouched. In vivo secretome supplementation used Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) implanted i.p. immediately following tumor excision, with animals randomly assigned to CM or SM conditions. The estimate that the minipump secretome per day (~1/8 in vivo) was based on ~50x10⁶ secretome-producing cells in an 80 mm³ primary tumor. The cytokine array used 102 soluble human proteins compared across four conditions (CM, PT-bearing plasma, post-excision plasma, control plasma) with each plasma sample pooled from 3 mice. LC-MS/MS employed a 50 cm long EASY-Spray PepMap column with a 140 min linear gradient of water/acetonitrile, coupled to the Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer. MS analysis used the top10 method, where every high-resolution MS scan was followed by fragmentation of the 10 most abundant peaks by higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD). Bioinformatics utilized MaxQuant, Perseus software, String database, Cytoscape software, and Gene Ontology for enrichment, with FDR 0.01 for MS analysis and 0.02 for GO. Antibody neutralization was performed by injecting a cocktail of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies 24 h prior to tumor excision at an early metastatic stage. Early metastatic stage was defined as chest bioluminescence < 10⁶ p/s, and neutralization was 1 μg each/mouse once daily for two days.

Key Results
Within 24 h following PT excision, metastatic bioluminescent signal decreased up to 100-fold (p<0.0001), but not immediately following excision. Metastases regressed into latent foci, confirmed by no in vivo bioluminescent signal increase for 50 days post-excision and H&E-verified microscopic malignant foci on day 1 and day 50. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases (10⁷ photons/sec) compared to small metastases (10⁶ photons/sec), p<0.000. Sham surgery (PT untouched) resulted in continued metastatic increase, while PT excision led to significant regression, p<0.05. CM enhanced viability (p<0.001) and adhesion (p<0.01) of cancer cells in vitro, and induced tube formation of HUVEC (p<0.0001). Mice treated with tumor-cell CM showed 10-fold less regression than mice that received serum-free medium, p<0.005, confirming that secreted factors support metastatic survival. 28 cytokines were identified as highly expressed in cancer cell CM; four factors (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) were selected as known pro-metastatic mediators. LC-MS identified 2,600 proteins in CM, of which 359 were annotated as extracellular factors by GO analysis, including all four prior-identified factors. Pathway enrichment identified proteins engaged in apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. Antibody neutralization of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely blocked metastatic progression, p<0.0001. No difference in regression was evident on post-excision day-1 between antibody and control groups, as excision completely removed all secreted factors in both groups. Larger metastases showed lower or no regression, suggesting established metastatic foci may be self-sufficient. In a public TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort, high protein levels of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF were associated with significantly lower survival, hazard ratio of 2.05, p<0.05.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The PT secretome plays a crucial supportive role in survival and progression of distant metastatic foci, and removal of PT and its factors induces metastatic regression. IL-8, MIF, SerpinE1, and PDGFaa are identified as key secreted proteins that maintain and promote metastases through shared and distinct pro-survival and pro-angiogenic pathways. The primary tumor is a systemic disease with continuous crosstalk between the tumor, its microenvironment, and distant organs, playing a significant role in disease etiology and progression. The perioperative period could be exploited to control minimal residual disease by blocking PT support for micro-metastases and targeting prometastatic factors before and after surgery. Radiation or cryotreatment of the PT may cease factor secretion, potentially explaining reported regression cases in those treatment modalities. The use of high-sensitivity luciferase enabled detection of regression into latent foci that would be overlooked under lower sensitivity.

Contradictions And Limitations
Regression was only significant in early metastatic stages; larger metastases (10⁷ photons/sec) were less or not regressive, suggesting potential self-sufficiency of established foci. Only four key secreted factors were tested in vivo; other secreted factors identified by LC-MS likely also contribute to metastatic progression. The study used a single tumor type (MDA-MB-231 HM) in BALB/c nu/nu mice; generalizability to other tumor types or syngeneic lines remains unknown. The in vivo secretome replacement via minipumps was only ~1/8 of in vivo production, so the rescue effect was partial. The prevalence of post-operative regression of micro-metastases in cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations. No patient-level data on regression prevalence was obtained; the TCGA analysis was a retrospective cohort association, not prospective validation.

Claims
Primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases, and the PT secretome supports metastatic survival through specific secreted factors. Metastatic signal decreased up to 100-fold within 24 h of excision (p<0.0001). Regression was absent in sham surgery (p<0.05). CM supplementation reduced regression by 10-fold (p<0.005). Antibody blockade of four factors completely arrested metastasis (p<0.0001). Larger metastases (10⁷ photons/sec) showed significantly less regression than small metastases (p<0.000). No regression difference was observed on day-1 post-excision between antibody and control groups. The perioperative period represents a therapeutic window for controlling minimal residual disease. Targeting specific PT-secreted factors could arrest metastatic progression and tilt the balance toward eradication.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF are key PT-secreted factors promoting micro-metastatic survival and angiogenesis. Four factors were identified via cytokine array and confirmed by LC-MS and ELISA. Pathway enrichment showed these factors involved apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. High levels of these four factors correlated with poor survival in lung adenocarcinoma (HR=2.05, p<0.05). Only four of many potentially relevant factors were tested; other secreted factors were not ruled out. Combinatorial targeting of these four factors may be more effective than individual neutralization. Tailored antibody combinations could be designed based on pre-surgical tissue biopsy.
The perioperative period offers a window of opportunity to control minimal residual disease through blockade of PT-secreted pro-metastatic factors. Blocking PT factors arrested metastatic progression in the presence of the PT. The perioperative period was explicitly identified as a high-impact opportunity window. Surgery itself has been suggested to accelerate metastatic progression (inhibitory signaling elimination). The prevalence of regression in patients is currently unknown. Perioperative analysis of serum samples could identify patient-specific mediating factors. Tailored combination of neutralizing antibodies could be deployed before and after surgery.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sham surgery served as a control to exclude surgical trauma as a mechanism of regression. CM vs SM in vivo supplementation demonstrated that PT-secreted factors (rather than surgery alone) drive metastatic growth. The cytokine array was combined with unbiased LC-MS to narrow down candidates, with CM, non-tumor, PT-bearing, and post-excision plasma compared. Factors also present in non-tumor bearing plasma or post-excision plasma were excluded from the final four-factor panel. Antibody neutralization was performed in the presence of the PT at an early metastatic stage, and a 24-h pretreatment was used. Neutralizing antibody injection (1 μg/day for two days) versus IgG control tested the necessity of the four factors.

Ethical Considerations
All procedures were approved by Monash University or Tel-Aviv University Animal Ethics Committees. Mice were housed under SPF conditions, and surgical procedures were performed under anesthesia. Animals were euthanized 10 min following luciferin injection at the endpoint.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B show bioluminescence curves demonstrating 100-fold regression within 24 h of PT excision (p<0.0001). Figure 1C shows 50 days of no in vivo signal increase post-excision, and Figure 1D shows H&E-confirmed foci on day 1 and day 50. Figure 1E shows regression was significantly less prominent in large metastases (10⁷ photons/sec) versus small (10⁶ photons/sec). Figure 1F shows continued metastatic increase in sham surgery versus regression after PT excision (p<0.05). Figure 2A-C show CM enhanced viability, adhesion, and tube formation of HUVEC. Figure 2D shows 10-fold less regression with CM supplementation (p<0.005). Figure 3A shows protein-protein interaction networks and pathway enrichment for the 359 extracellular proteins. Figure 3B shows antibody blockade of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely blocked metastasis (p<0.0001). Figure 3C shows no regression difference on post-excision day-1 between antibody and control. Figure 3D shows Kaplan Meier survival curves for the TCGA cohort with HR=2.05 (p<0.05). Table S1 lists cytokines excluded based on presence in non-tumor or post-excision plasma.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first animal model demonstrating that PT excision induces spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases, mediated by elimination of PT-secreted factors. 2. The strongest evidence is the 100-fold metastatic signal decrease (p<0.0001) within 24 h of PT excision, the 10-fold rescue with CM supplementation (p<0.005), complete blockade by four-factor antibody neutralization (p<0.0001), and HR=2.05 survival association in patients. 3. The future path involves exploiting the perioperative period to control minimal residual disease by identifying and blocking patient-specific pro-metastatic factors, and validating the phenomenon in other tumor types and human cohorts.

summary.title: Activation of Macrophages by CpG DNA and LPS: an FTIR Spectroscopic Study
summary.authors: Emrulla Spahiu (Middle East Technical University); Senol Dogan (Leipzig University); Jörg Schnauß (Leipzig University); Mayda Gursel (Middle East Technical University); Feride Severcan (Middle East Technical University)
summary.field_subfield: Biophysics / Spectral Imaging - ATR-FTIR spectroscopy of innate immune cell activation
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates for the first time the use of Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor the activation dynamics of murine macrophage (RAW 264.7) cells upon stimulation with two potent innate immune activators: CpG DNA (1 µM K3 ODN) and lipopolysaccharide (0.5 µg/mL LPS). The approach captures a comprehensive biochemical fingerprint of the cell, simultaneously detecting changes in nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids without the complex sample preparation required by traditional omics techniques. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified two principal components capturing the vast majority of spectral variance, with PC-1 accounting for 83% of the variability and PC-2 for 1%, pinpointing the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region as the source of the highest variation among treatment groups. For CpG DNA stimulation, a significant increase in RNA content (915 cm⁻¹) was detected from 10 minutes to 2 hours post-treatment (p < 0.001***), followed by a shift to DNA synthesis starting at 6 hours, consistent with established biological kinetics. Protein content (amide I band at 1639 cm⁻¹) rose from 10 minutes to 2 hours (p < 0.001***) and then declined, an effect attributed to the short-lived, synchronized immune activation and subsequent protein secretion and degradation pathways. LPS stimulation similarly elevated total protein but showed a more rapid attenuation. Lipid metabolism was activated in both groups: triglycerides and cholesterol (ester C=O stretching near 1741 cm⁻¹) increased from the first minutes, and fatty acids (COO⁻ stretching at 1400 cm⁻¹) showed a significant increase, indicating de novo lipogenesis. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ enabled definition of macrophage activation at the very first minutes post-treatment, filling a temporal gap in the understanding of activation kinetics. This work establishes FTIR spectroscopy as a rapid, non-invasive bulk analysis tool capable of monitoring global molecular changes during innate immune responses in a single measurement.

Executive Summary
This study demonstrates for the first time the use of Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor the activation dynamics of murine macrophage (RAW 264.7) cells upon stimulation with two potent innate immune activators: CpG DNA (1 µM K3 ODN) and lipopolysaccharide (0.5 µg/mL LPS). The approach captures a comprehensive biochemical fingerprint of the cell, simultaneously detecting changes in nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids without the complex sample preparation required by traditional omics techniques. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified two principal components capturing the vast majority of spectral variance, with PC-1 accounting for 83% of the variability and PC-2 for 1%, pinpointing the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region as the source of the highest variation among treatment groups. For CpG DNA stimulation, a significant increase in RNA content (915 cm⁻¹) was detected from 10 minutes to 2 hours post-treatment (p < 0.001***), followed by a shift to DNA synthesis starting at 6 hours, consistent with established biological kinetics. Protein content (amide I band at 1639 cm⁻¹) rose from 10 minutes to 2 hours (p < 0.001***) and then declined, an effect attributed to the short-lived, synchronized immune activation and subsequent protein secretion and degradation pathways. LPS stimulation similarly elevated total protein but showed a more rapid attenuation. Lipid metabolism was activated in both groups: triglycerides and cholesterol (ester C=O stretching near 1741 cm⁻¹) increased from the first minutes, and fatty acids (COO⁻ stretching at 1400 cm⁻¹) showed a significant increase, indicating de novo lipogenesis. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ enabled definition of macrophage activation at the very first minutes post-treatment, filling a temporal gap in the understanding of activation kinetics. This work establishes FTIR spectroscopy as a rapid, non-invasive bulk analysis tool capable of monitoring global molecular changes during innate immune responses in a single measurement.

Research Context
FTIR spectroscopy is a powerful biomedical tool allowing non-destructive, rapid, and high-throughput analysis of biological systems in both qualitative and quantitative manners. From a single spectrum, all delicate alterations in both the conformation and concentration of vital macromolecules, such as nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids, can be revealed. The infrared spectrum serves as a fingerprint for all metabolites of the cell system, where the area under the curve provides quantitative concentration data while specific absorption frequencies reveal the nature of the chemical bond. The absorbance of IR light by water molecules, however, is a limitation of infrared spectroscopy since it superimposes other signals of the aqueous cell systems, a disadvantage overcome by the Fourier transform procedure. The ATR unit offers a handy spectrometer use since the sample is directly put onto the crystal with no sample preparation step required, and very little amount of sample is enough for a good quality spectrum. ATR-FTIR spectroscopy has multiple applications in hematology, including analysis of live cell activation, screening of numerous diseases, response of cells to chemical stress, identification of disease states in early stages, and cellular differentiation. Macrophage cells constitute the front line of the immune system, possessing high structural and functional plasticity that allows them to continually inspect the body and respond to challenges. An intriguing challenge is bacterial DNA containing unmethylated CpG oligodeoxynucleotides, which triggers macrophage proliferation, production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, Th1 induction, and B cell proliferation. Synthetic CpG oligodeoxynucleotides serve as potential immune adjuvants with therapeutic uses, but how CpG ODN-mediated immune activation impacts relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, proteins, and other metabolites has not been studied. LPS, as a main constituent of the gram-negative bacterial cell wall occupying approximately 75% of their external surface, stimulates monocytes and macrophages through the TLR4 pathway. The recognition of LPS through TLR4 shares high homology with TLR-9 signaling by CpG DNA, both requiring MyD88 as the adaptor protein and activating NF-kB as well as AP-1 transcription factors. While trending omics techniques yield precise quantitative data on specific molecules, they require complex sample preparation steps that can result in alterations of chemical ratios and post-translational modifications in lipidomics and proteomics. The simple, rapid, and non-invasive experimental setup using bulk FTIR analysis proves to give a broad view of the relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, proteins, and other metabolites that are not readily accessible by other techniques.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to global molecular changes in macrophages detectable by FTIR spectroscopy, filling a gap in the temporal understanding of activation. The study hypothesizes that both CpG DNA and LPS will induce detectable alterations in the relative concentrations of nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids in murine RAW 264.7 macrophages at various time points following stimulation. The prediction is that CpG DNA will induce RNA synthesis detectable at very early time points (915 cm⁻¹), followed by DNA synthesis at later stages, while LPS will inhibit DNA synthesis and elicit cell cycle arrest. Protein content is predicted to increase upon stimulation due to cytokine production but then decline as activation is short-lived and protein secretion and degradation pathways are engaged. Lipid metabolism is hypothesized to be activated, with both triglycerides and cholesterol increasing through de novo lipogenesis, a pathway previously linked to TLR agonists. The study further predicts that the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ will enable definition of the macrophage activation state as early as the first minutes post-treatment, filling the gap in the activation kinetics timeline. The study also posits that the ATR-FTIR approach, by yielding statistically significant data sets from multiple cells probed simultaneously, provides a broader molecular view than targeted omics techniques.

Methodological Details
Murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 2 mM L-glutamine. To maintain logarithmic growth, sub-culturing was performed in 1/10 ratio upon reaching acceptable confluency, generally every 2-3 days. Cells were harvested, spun at 1000 rpm 208 g for 10 min, and resuspended at a concentration of 2x10^6 /mL. The control group was treated with phosphate-buffered saline (0.9% PBS), the CpG DNA stimulated group with 1 µM K3 ODN (Endotoxin-free), and the LPS stimulated group with 0.5 µg/mL LPS. Four time points post-treatment were used to evaluate the kinetics of induced effects: 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h. At each time point, samples were removed from the incubator, spun at 1000 rpm, and media discarded; cells were washed with 15 mL of sterile PBS to remove organic compounds that can mask IR spectral features. All infrared interferograms were collected using a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer with the ATR unit (Diamond-ZnSe crystal) attached. Air background was measured and subtracted automatically by Spectrum One software to overcome atmospheric interference from H₂O and CO₂, and the PBS spectrum was recorded and subtracted manually. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with mild N₂ flux for 5 min to allow cells to settle on the crystal. The spectrum was recorded in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ region at 25°C, and the best signal-to-noise ratio was achieved with a 128 scan number and 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution. The ATR surface was cleaned using a water-ethanol-water sequence and then air-dried; each group was scanned in three independent scans, with the average constituting a replicate n. Replicates (n=5) were used in data analysis, and a protocol is available online. Post-processing included 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction at 3800-2750-1800-900 cm⁻¹ points using Spectrum One software. PCA was performed on the spectra imported directly into Unscrambler 11.0 software in the 3000-650 cm⁻¹ region, with spectral readings at 0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution. Peak assignment used center of weight measurements and literature comparison, with the second derivative spectrum used for side-peak band assignment. Concentration studies were carried out by integrating the curves under the peaks, and conformational alteration studies used bandwidth measurements based on the 75% height of the peaks. Statistical analysis employed Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests to determine the normality of the datasets using GraphPad Prism 8.

Procedures And Architectures
The spectroscopic acquisition was performed on a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer with a diamond-ZnSe ATR crystal for direct sample contact, eliminating the need for sample preparation. Data were collected in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ IR spectral region at 25°C using a 128-scan acquisition protocol with 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution, ensuring a high signal-to-noise ratio. The 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction (3800-2750-1800-900 cm⁻¹) were the primary post-processing steps applied to each spectrum. PCA was implemented as an unsupervised multivariate data analysis method in Unscrambler 11.0, working without initial information input regarding the datasets to reduce dimensionality. The two outputs of PCA, the Scores Plot (showing clusters of similar data) and the Loadings Plot (showing sources of highest variation wavenumbers), provided initial guidance for data analysis. Spectral readings were acquired at 0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution to form the data matrix for PCA computation. Principal Component (PC)-1 was found to capture 83% of the variability, while PC-2 captured only 1%, indicating that the majority of spectral variation was resolved by the first component. The 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region was identified in the Loadings Plots as containing numerous peaks with high variation among samples, guiding the selection of peaks for detailed analysis. Concentration changes were quantified by area integration under the peaks, while conformational changes were determined by bandwidth measurements using the 75% height of the peaks. Peak assignments were based on the center of weight measurements and literature comparison, with second derivative spectra used for side-peak band identification. Statistical normality was assessed using Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests with GraphPad Prism 8.

Key Results
A comprehensive spectrum of resting control RAW 264.7 cells revealed peaks from lipids in the 3000-2800 cm⁻¹ region, proteins at 1700-1600 cm⁻¹, nucleic acids at 1238 cm⁻¹, 1110 cm⁻¹, and 1085 cm⁻¹, and numerous other metabolites. PCA confirmed that PC-1 accounted for 83% of spectral variability, while PC-2 accounted for 1%, with the Scores Plot showing clear clustering of samples according to treatment group across both principal components. The 1750-850 cm⁻¹ region was identified as the primary source of spectral variation, with numerous peaks showing high inter-sample variance in the Loadings Plots. CpG DNA stimulation induced significant changes in nucleic acid content (1238 cm⁻¹ peak integration) of macrophages starting from 10 minutes until 6 hours post-treatment (p < 0.1*), confirming early-phase molecular reorganization. The 1085 cm⁻¹ peak, corresponding to symmetric PO₂⁻ stretching, also showed prominent differences between control and stimulated groups at the earliest time points. Stimulation with CpG DNA significantly increased the RNA-specific ribose vibration peak at 915 cm⁻¹ from the first minutes post-treatment (p < 0.001***), with the increase maintained until 2 hours. LPS stimulation also showed an increased concentration of total RNA up to 2 hours post-stimulation, consistent with the known pro-inflammatory induction of 263 genes by LPS. The RNA-specific peak (915 cm⁻¹) enabled definition of the macrophage activation state at the very first minutes of activation, filling the gap in the known activation timeline of 41 minutes. Amide I (1639 cm⁻¹) and amide II (1540 cm⁻¹) peaks, used for protein content analysis, showed a significant increase in the total protein content of CpG DNA treated cells from 10 minutes post-treatment until 2 hours (p < 0.001***). A similar significant increase in protein concentration was observed upon LPS stimulation, with the initial increase reduced starting from the 2-hour time point. The ester C=O stretching near 1741 cm⁻¹, representing triglycerides and cholesterol, showed a very significant increase during activation from the very first minutes of stimulation in both CpG DNA and LPS groups. LPS stimulation elevated the triglycerides and cholesterol concentration after 10 minutes, consistent with the role of cholesterol in membrane structure and signaling during macrophage activation. The COO⁻ symmetric stretching peak of fatty acid side chains at 1400 cm⁻¹ showed a significant increase in fatty acid concentration, pointing to de novo lipogenesis of pro-inflammatory reactions in macrophages. The observed lipid changes (triglycerides, cholesterol, fatty acids) in both CpG DNA and LPS treated groups indicate a shared synthesis pathway and de novo lipogenesis, consistent with the identification of Acetoacetyl-CoA as a shared metabolite. DNA synthesis in CpG DNA treated cells was not detected at early time points but was expected to follow RNA synthesis, becoming prominent only after several hours post-stimulation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The early increase in RNA content (915 cm⁻¹, p < 0.001***) at 10 minutes post-CpG DNA treatment directly corresponds to the transient peak of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, with the 2-hour window representing the period of extensive RNA synthesis. The absence of significant nucleic acid changes after 6 hours of CpG DNA stimulation is consistent with previous findings that LPS inhibits DNA synthesis and elicits cell cycle arrest, explaining why the RNA-specific peak ceases to rise beyond 2 hours. The 915 cm⁻¹ peak provides a molecular marker to define the activation state of macrophages within the very first minutes, a temporal window previously uncharacterized by biochemical assays that defined activation only at 41 minutes. The initial rapid protein increase followed by decline in CpG DNA treated cells is consistent with the synchronized regulation of major inducers (IL1A, IL1B, TNF) followed by dynamic suppression by repressors (IL10, MYC, NFKBIA), causing activation to be short-lived. For LPS treated cells, the protein decline may be attributed to known pathways involving histone release into the extracellular medium, general protein secretion via vesicles and exosomes, protein shedding from the plasma membrane, and ROS-mediated degradation of oxidized proteins. The simultaneous increase in triglycerides, cholesterol, and fatty acids in both CpG DNA and LPS treated groups points to a shared pathway of de novo lipogenesis, consistent with the identification of Acetoacetyl-CoA as a common precursor in fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis. CpG-induced lipogenesis was previously linked to modulation of secretory activity in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, with similar pathways implicated in cancer cell anti-tumor activity of macrophages. FTIR spectroscopy serves as an independent modality capable of monitoring global molecular dynamics in near-real-time, complementing targeted omics by providing an integrated snapshot of all major biomacromolecule pools simultaneously.

Contradictions And Limitations
A limitation is that the ATR-FTIR approach is a bulk analysis technique providing relative changes in biomolecule concentrations rather than absolute quantification, which is a distinction acknowledged relative to omics techniques. The study is performed exclusively in the RAW 264.7 murine cell line, and direct translation of the findings to human macrophage responses remains to be validated in primary human cells. No absolute quantification of specific molecular species was possible; concentration values are derived from peak area integrations and must be interpreted relative to the control group. The paper does not report the exact concentration of cells at the time of FTIR measurement, although they were resuspended at 2x10^6 /mL and the 1 µl sample volume is specified. No information on the specific number of independent experiments (replicates) beyond the n=5 per group is provided for the final data analysis, although three independent scans were performed per replicate. The PCA analysis was conducted in the 3000-650 cm⁻¹ region, and while PC-1 captured 83% of the variance, the remaining 17% (distributed across PC-2 and higher) represents unresolved spectral variation that was not further quantified. The interpretation of the protein decline in CpG DNA treated cells requires further mechanistic study; while consistent with known inflammatory kinetic patterns, the precise mechanisms in CpG DNA-induced protein loss remain uncharacterized.

Claims
ATR-FTIR spectroscopy can independently monitor the global molecular dynamics of macrophage activation upon CpG DNA and LPS stimulation, providing a comprehensive fingerprint of changes in nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids simultaneously. The 915 cm⁻¹ peak showed significant RNA increase (p < 0.001***) within 10 minutes, confirming early detection of activation. The 1639 cm⁻¹ peak showed significant protein increase from 10 minutes to 2 hours (p < 0.001***), confirming protein pool changes. The 1741 cm⁻¹ and 1400 cm⁻¹ peaks showed significant increases in triglycerides, cholesterol, and fatty acids, confirming lipid pool changes. PCA confirmed that PC-1 captured 83% of spectral variability, with clear clustering by treatment group. The technique provides relative concentration changes rather than absolute quantification, limiting direct comparison of molecular flux between conditions. The study is limited to the RAW 264.7 cell line, limiting generalizability to other cell types or primary human macrophages. FTIR could serve as a rapid, non-invasive screening tool for innate immune activation in diagnostic or therapeutic monitoring contexts. The methodology enables temporal mapping of molecular events that are below the detection threshold of targeted omics techniques.
The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ serves as a molecular marker to define macrophage activation at the very first minutes post-treatment, filling a temporal gap in the understanding of activation kinetics. Significant increase (p < 0.001***) at 915 cm⁻¹ was detected at the 10-minute time point. Prior studies defined activation only at 41 minutes, so the 10-minute detection represents a temporally superior marker. The activation marker is RNA-specific, and its significance at 10 minutes may reflect a general cellular response to treatment rather than specific activation. The 915 cm⁻¹ peak could be used as a surrogate marker for rapid assessment of TLR9 or TLR4 activation in therapeutic contexts.

Data And Code Availability
The experimental protocol is available online as cited by reference [59], but no specific data repository or source code is listed in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The PCA analysis with 128 scans per replicate and n=5 replicates per group was used to validate spectral differences between treatment groups. Three independent scans were performed for each group, with the average constituting the replicate, providing a basic measure of intra-run reproducibility. Normality of the datasets was assessed using Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests prior to statistical analysis. The 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction were standard post-processing steps, but no sensitivity analysis of smoothing parameters or baseline methods is reported. Peak assignment relied on literature comparison and center of weight measurements, with no explicit validation of assignments via other techniques.

Key Figures Tables
Figure A1 presents a comprehensive spectrum of resting control RAW 264.7 cells and its second derivative in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ IR spectral region, showing peaks from lipids, proteins, nucleic acids, and other metabolites. Figure A2 (not described as such in text) likely contains PCA Scores and Loadings Plots, with Figure 1.A showing Scores Plot (clustering by treatment) and Figure 1.B and 1.C showing Loadings Plots (identifying 1750-850 cm⁻¹ as the peak region). Figure 2.A shows the 10-min spectrum after treatment; Figure 2.B shows bar diagrams of nucleic acid peak integration values; Figure 2.C shows the RNA-specific peak (915 cm⁻¹) across time points. Figure 3.A and 3.B show amide I and II peak alterations; Figure 3.C shows the integrated amide I band concentration over time. Figure 4.B and 4.C show the COO⁻ symmetric stretching peak (1400 cm⁻¹) for fatty acid concentration; Figure 4.D and 4.E show the ester C=O peak (near 1741 cm⁻¹) for triglycerides and cholesterol. Table A1 lists peak assignments based on literature; Table A2 shows measurement of area integration for peaks of interest. Table 1 summarizes the experimental design, including cell preparation, treatment groups, time points, and stimuli.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration that ATR-FTIR spectroscopy can independently and comprehensively monitor global molecular changes in nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids simultaneously during macrophage activation by CpG DNA and LPS, with the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ enabling activation detection within 10 minutes. 2. The strongest evidence is the PCA showing 83% variability captured by PC-1 in the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ region, coupled with statistically significant RNA (p < 0.001*** at 915 cm⁻¹) and protein (p < 0.001*** at 1639 cm⁻¹) changes at the earliest time points, and lipid metabolism activation in both CpG and LPS groups. 3. The future path involves applying this FTIR approach to primary human macrophage cells, testing other TLR agonists, and characterizing the mechanisms of protein loss and lipid flux during innate immune responses in vivo and in more physiologically relevant systems.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
American Foulbrood (AFB), caused by Paenibacillus larvae, is a highly destructive bacterial disease in honeybees with spores capable of remaining infectious for over 30 years and spreading through robbing and contaminated hive material. Diagnosis traditionally relies on visual inspection of brood cells, which is subjective, time-consuming, and may miss early or low-level infections. This study presents the "Foster method," a novel environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling strategy combining colony entrance swabs with a dual-target qPCR assay for P. larvae. The assay targets both the multi-copy 16S rRNA gene (for high-sensitivity detection) and the single-copy ftsZ gene (for quantification), integrated with an internal control for diagnostic confidence. Synthetic DNA standards (gBlock, IDT, Singapore, 153 bp) were used to generate a calibration curve from 10^6 to 2 copies per µL in AFB-negative bee DNA, enabling conversion of Cq values to spore levels. Three cohorts of beehives were evaluated: 45 hives from five quarantine apiaries sampled up to 6 times (2018–2020); 23 hives from a single beekeeper; and a third cohort for pooling trials (groups of 8 and 12 swabs). Key analytical results included high sensitivity (4 copies per 10 µL detection limit), amplification efficiencies of ftsZ = 94% and 16S = 96%, and linearity over 7 orders of magnitude (r = 0.998). The 16S marker typically amplified 3–5 cycles earlier than ftsZ. Statistical analysis using binary logistic regression (p = 0.00) identified a clinical spore threshold: ≥565,000 spores per 10 bees/swab correspond to a 95% probability of clinically visible AFB signs. In the first cohort, 8 of 45 hives showed clinical signs, and a single hive without visual signs (Hive 11) was found positive by qPCR and subsequently destroyed. One case (Hive 11) demonstrated detection of pre-clinical infection approximately two weeks before visual signs, while Hive 12 showed high bee-derived spores but no hiveware contamination due to being <2 weeks old. The method removes the need to dismantle hives or insert sampling sheets, providing a one-time, non-invasive sampling and quantification approach applicable to other pathogens and incursion pests.

Research Context
AFB is caused by hardy spores of Gram-positive Paenibacillus larvae that can remain infectious for over 30 years. The disease is one of the most destructive in honeybees with rapid colony decline and spread through contaminated honey and hive frames. In New Zealand, hive numbers more than doubled since 2013 with the infected hive percentage rising from 0.21% in 2015 to 0.46% in 2021. Diagnosis has traditionally relied on visual inspection of thousands of brood cells per hive, which is laborious and prone to error, especially with ERIC II strains exhibiting reduced symptoms. Previous sampling required dismantling the hive to install collection sheets or multiple visits for passive sampling, hindering rapid response. qPCR has been used for P. larvae detection but most applications did not utilize the quantitative data generated for clinical threshold determination.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a non-invasive colony entrance swab combined with a dual-target qPCR assay can detect clinically significant AFB levels before visual symptoms appear. The study hypothesized that eDNA from the hive entrance region, though containing lower total spore amounts than the brood nest, would yield detectable P. larvae levels sufficient to differentiate infected from uninfected hives. A secondary hypothesis was that a single-copy marker (ftsZ) combined with a multi-copy marker (16S) would provide both high sensitivity and reliable quantification. The authors predicted that a specific spore concentration threshold could be established to predict the probability of clinically visible disease. A third objective was to evaluate whether the method could be extended to other bee pathogens and incursion pests through the same sampling framework.

Methodological Details
Five quarantine apiaries across New Zealand (East Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa, and South Canterbury regions) provided multiple hives sampled two-monthly from late 2018 to early 2020. Additional samples from visually clinical hives and neighboring hives were collected by local apiary inspectors. Three sample types were compared: nurse bees collected from brood frames, swabs from the entire baseboard, and swabs through the hive entrance region. Bees were collected using 50 mL sterile containers and frozen to euthanise. Sterile foam-tipped swabs (Puritan) were moistened in sterile water and swabbled for three to five seconds. Swab heads were snapped off into 2 mL microcentrifuge tubes and sent overnight by courier. DNA extraction used the Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit (dnature diagnostics & research Ltd, Gisborne, NZ) with beadbeating. Each bee sample contained 10 bees for ease of handling and throughput. Beads comprised 0.5 mm (~2.4 g) and 2.3 mm zirconia silica (~1 g) zirconia beads. Homogenisation used a Mini Beadbeater 16 instrument for 3 minutes. Tubes were incubated at 65°C for 10 minutes with manual inversion every 3 minutes. Centrifugation was performed at 15,000 x g for 5 minutes, and 500 µL of supernatant was processed. For swabs, 800 µL DXL buffer was added, and the swab was homogenised in the Mini Beadbeater 16 for 3 minutes, followed by 65°C incubation and centrifugation. Swab beads included 0.5 mm zirconia silica beads (~0.8 g) and 2.3 mm zirconia silica beads (0.3 g). For pooled applications, individual swab eluates (up to twelve) were mixed in 500 µL DXL buffer, vortexed for 10 seconds, and processed. A synthetic DNA standard (gBlock, IDT, Singapore, 153 bp) was resuspended in TE buffer, pH 8. The standard was quantified on a DS-11 FX microvolume spectrophotometer (DeNovix, Wilmington, USA) in nanograms per µL. Copy number was calculated using Avogadro's constant, 660 g/mole length of standard, and 1x10 9 ng/g. Quantification standards ranged from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL in a pool of negative bee DNA. Spore levels were converted from Cq values using the amplification efficiency of the single-copy ftsZ gene, the y-intercept, and the formula: Spores = 10^(Cq ftsZ − 3.48). Two clinical hives had spore numbers skewed lower due to new hiveware, requiring imputation by regression analysis of other paired data. Statistical analysis included binary logistic regression (Minitab, State College, PA) and analysis of variance to confirm correlation between spore levels and clinical signs. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant.

Procedures And Architectures
The dual-target qPCR assay (AFBduo) used a commercially available multiplex assay for P. larvae (Hall et al., 2021) modified with a new internal control channel. The 16S rRNA gene was targeted for high sensitivity, and the ftsZ gene was targeted for quantification. A hydrolysis probe (TaqMan®) qPCR approach allowed quantification of each target by selected fluorescent wavelengths. An internal control was included in an additional detection channel to confirm suitable quality DNA and detect potential inhibitors. Synthetic DNA standards were diluted in a pool of extracted DNA from bees free of P. larvae. The Cq values from the standard curve were stored as supplementary S1 for converting sample Cq values to spore counts. The first cohort of quarantine hives consisted of 45 hives from multiple regions, sampled up to 6 times during 2018–2020. Beekeepers were instructed to rotate swabs during collection to ensure all swab surfaces collected hive material. Swab eluate pooling trials used groups of eight and later twelve hive samples to reduce time and costs. Pooled samples testing positive for both markers were further tested individually to isolate the affected hive. The Mini Beadbeater 16 homogenised samples in 3 minutes, followed by incubation at 65°C.

Key Results
Testing on synthetic DNA standards showed both target reactions could reliably detect down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction. Amplification efficiencies were ftsZ = 94% and 16S = 96%, with excellent linearity over 7 orders of magnitude (r = 0.998). On P. larvae-positive samples, the 16S target typically amplified 3–5 cycles earlier than the ftsZ target, confirming the multi-copy advantage. DNA extraction from bees yielded high purity with OD260/280 measurements between 1.8 and 1.9. Serial dilution of extracted DNA showed expected Cq increases, indicating no inhibitors were present after extraction. DNA yields from swabs were too low to measure on the spectrophotometer, but internal control Cq values confirmed suitable DNA quality. In the first cohort, 45 hives were sampled up to 6 times; 8 showed clinical signs during sampling and 6 additional were presumed AFB positive. In the second cohort of 23 hives, four showed clinical signs of AFB. In the third cohort, pooling twelve hive samples allowed detection of single hives with higher AFB levels within the pool. Binary logistic regression and ANOVA confirmed a strong relationship between increasing spore levels and clinical signs (p = 0.00). A spore quantity of 565,000 or more corresponds to a 95% probability of clinical signs being present. In Hive 11, without visual signs, bees showed high P. larvae spore levels, and the hive was found with clinical signs and destroyed approximately two weeks later. In Hive 12, bees showed high spore levels while hiveware showed low or undetectable levels due to the hiveware being new (< 2 weeks old).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 16S marker's higher analytical sensitivity (3–5 cycles earlier) is due to its multi-copy nature, but variability in Cq difference suggests copy number may vary among isolates. The single-copy ftsZ gene is thus the reliable target for quantification, as noted in previous AFB qPCR studies (Rossi et al., 2018; Dainat et al., 2018). Levels of P. larvae on whole baseboard and entrance swabs were similar, indicating that dismantling the hive to swab the whole baseboard is not required for detection. The ability to sample through the hive entrance removes the need to dismantle and disrupt the colony, facilitating rapid surveillance. Bees from the brood nest yielded the highest spore levels, confirming the brood area as the primary site of infection. The Foster method provides a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method that provides clinically significant information about AFB status. The method's preliminary applicability to other bee pathogens (Nosema ceranae, tracheal mites, small hive beetle) suggests broad diagnostic utility.

Contradictions And Limitations
The 16S copy number may vary among AFB isolates, as indicated by variability in Cq difference between the two markers among samples. New hiveware (e.g., Hive 12, < 2 weeks old) prevented spore deposition on entrance surfaces despite high bee-carried levels, creating a false low-level reading on swabs. Spore levels never increased during monitoring for many hives, and in some low-spore cases, they became undetectable, limiting long-term monitoring. Two clinical hives required imputation of spore data due to skewed values from new hiveware baseboards at sampling time. Further research is needed to assess spore accumulation rates on hive surfaces and to refine clinical spore thresholds with more hives. The study used only 10 bees per sample, a reduction from the 100 bees sometimes used in culture-based methods, which may affect detection of low-level infections. The method's specificity in the presence of other hive pathogens was not fully validated in this study.

Claims
The Foster method enables rapid, non-invasive, single-visit detection of clinically significant AFB levels from colony entrance swabs, eliminating the need to dismantle hives. Entrance swabs yielded comparable P. larvae levels to whole baseboard swabs, removing the need for hive dismantling. A single hive (Hive 11) without visual signs was detected positive by qPCR and subsequently destroyed, demonstrating pre-clinical detection. The sampling method was applied to three independent cohorts with different hive backgrounds and pooling designs. Hive 12 showed high bee spores but negligible hiveware spores because the hiveware was new (< 2 weeks old), demonstrating a false-negative for hiveware. In some hives with low spore levels, the pathogen became undetectable during monitoring, suggesting limitations for very early detection. The method could replace invasive baseboard sampling and multiple visits with a single non-invasive swab, accelerating outbreak response. The quantification (spore count) provides a risk assessment beyond simple presence/absence, enabling informed management decisions.
A dual-target qPCR assay (16S and ftsZ) with an internal control provides both high sensitivity and reliable quantification, superior to single-target assays. The 16S marker amplified 3–5 cycles earlier than ftsZ, confirming its role as a high-sensitivity detection marker. The ftsZ marker, as a single-copy gene, provided reliable quantification against a standard curve. The internal control confirmed DNA quality and allowed for reliable quantification in the presence of potential inhibitors. Analytical sensitivity down to 4 copies per 10 µL and linearity over 7 orders of magnitude support assay robustness. Variability in Cq difference between 16S and ftsZ among samples suggests 16S copy number may vary among isolates, limiting its quantitative use. DNA yields from swabs were too low to measure on the spectrophotometer, making quality assessment less direct than for bee samples. The dual-target approach addresses the sensitivity-specificity trade-off of single-marker qPCR, improving diagnostic reliability. The assay architecture is directly applicable to other bee pathogens with known single- and multi-copy genes.
A threshold of ≥565,000 spores per 10 bees or swab corresponds to a 95% probability of clinically visible AFB, providing a quantitative risk assessment for beekeeping. Binary logistic regression showed p = 0.00 for the relationship between spore levels and clinical signs. A spore count of 565,000 or more revealed a 95% probability of clinical signs. The threshold was derived from 26 data points with paired clinical data, including imputed values. The threshold was derived from only 26 data points, and two hives had imputed values due to new hiveware. Spore levels never increased or became undetectable in many hives, and a false-negative was observed in Hive 12. Beekeepers can use the spore count to assess whether visual signs are likely present or will develop, enabling proactive treatment before clinical spread. Further validation with larger cohorts and more diverse apiary types is needed to refine the clinical threshold.

Data And Code Availability
A synthetic DNA standard (gBlock, IDT, Singapore, 153 bp) was used for quantification; amplicon sequences are available on request. The Cq values from the standard curve (supplementary S1) and the conversion formula were reported in the paper. The statistical analysis was performed in Minitab (State College, PA) and Supplementary figure 4 reports the ANOVA results.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The use of an internal control channel validated that DNA was of suitable quality and was not inhibited during amplification. Serial dilutions of extracted DNA confirmed no inhibitors were present after the beadbeating extraction procedure. DNA extraction from bees yielded OD260/280 between 1.8 and 1.9, confirming high purity. The comparison of three sample types (nurse bees, whole baseboard, entrance swabs) served as a multi-site validation of the sampling method. Pooling trials (groups of 8 and 12 swabs) demonstrated that single positive hives could be detected within pooled extracts, supporting composite testing strategies. The 16S target amplified 3–5 cycles earlier than ftsZ, but Cq variability between them indicated that 16S copy number could not be used for quantification.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents progression of P. larvae levels in three colonies over multiple sampling points, with Cq data converted to spores per 10 bees or swab. Table 2 compares nurse bee spore levels with entrance swab levels for 23 hives in a single apiary, showing differentiation between infected and non-infected hives. Table 3 shows pooling trial results, demonstrating detection of single positive hives within pools of up to twelve samples. Table 4 compares levels of both P. larvae and internal control DNA on whole baseboard and entrance swabs, showing similar magnitudes. Supplementary figure 4 presents ANOVA confirming correlation between increased entrance spores and clinical signs of AFB. Supplementary S1 contains the Cq values from the synthetic DNA standards used for calibration.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Foster method, a non-invasive eDNA colony entrance swabbing and dual-target qPCR (16S and ftsZ) strategy that quantifies P. larvae to a clinical threshold of ≥565,000 spores per 10 bees/swab (95% clinical probability). 2. The strongest evidence is the dual-cohort validation demonstrating differentiation between clinical and non-clinical hives, the detection of a pre-clinical infection in Hive 11 approximately two weeks before visual signs, and the confirmation of the threshold by binary logistic regression (p = 0.00). 3. The future path involves refining the clinical threshold with more testing, assessing spore accumulation rates on hive surfaces, and applying the same eDNA sampling framework to other bee pathogens and incursion pests.

summary.title: SPOT-Contact-Single: Improving Single-Sequence-Based Prediction of Protein Contact Map using a Transformer Language Model
summary.authors: Jaspreet Singh (Griffith University); Thomas Litfin (Griffith University); Jaswinder Singh; Kuldip Paliwal (Griffith University); Yaoqi Zhou (Griffith University)

summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a novel single-sequence-based protein contact map predictor that leverages the pre-trained Transformer language model ESM-1b (Rao et al., 2020) to overcome the limitations of methods relying on evolutionary/homology information. The proposed method extracts attention maps from all 20 heads of the last layer and all layers of ESM-1b, concatenates them with one-hot amino acid encoding and SPOT-1D-Single structural outputs, and feeds the combined features into an ensemble of six ResNet12 models. These models are trained using two strategies: direct inter-residue contact prediction with Binary Cross-Entropy loss and distogram-based prediction with Cross-Entropy loss. Key findings include: (1) a 15% F1-score improvement over the single-sequence-based predictor SSCpred on the independent CASP14-FM test set; (2) a 48.7% and 48.5% F1-score improvement over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact, respectively, on proteins with no homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 test set; (3) an overall 4% F1-score improvement from ensembling the six models over the second-best individual model on the validation set; and (4) a 22-fold speedup on CPU and 42-fold speedup on GPU compared to TrRosetta. The method is limited by ESM-1b's 1024-residue sequence length constraint but offers a computationally efficient, reasonably accurate alternative to evolutionary-profile-based methods, suitable for large-scale and genomic-scale prediction.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a novel single-sequence-based protein contact map predictor that leverages the pre-trained Transformer language model ESM-1b (Rao et al., 2020) to overcome the limitations of methods relying on evolutionary/homology information. The proposed method extracts attention maps from all 20 heads of the last layer and all layers of ESM-1b, concatenates them with one-hot amino acid encoding and SPOT-1D-Single structural outputs, and feeds the combined features into an ensemble of six ResNet12 models. These models are trained using two strategies: direct inter-residue contact prediction with Binary Cross-Entropy loss and distogram-based prediction with Cross-Entropy loss. Key findings include: (1) a 15% F1-score improvement over the single-sequence-based predictor SSCpred on the independent CASP14-FM test set; (2) a 48.7% and 48.5% F1-score improvement over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact, respectively, on proteins with no homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 test set; (3) an overall 4% F1-score improvement from ensembling the six models over the second-best individual model on the validation set; and (4) a 22-fold speedup on CPU and 42-fold speedup on GPU compared to TrRosetta. The method is limited by ESM-1b's 1024-residue sequence length constraint but offers a computationally efficient, reasonably accurate alternative to evolutionary-profile-based methods, suitable for large-scale and genomic-scale prediction.

Research Context
Protein contact map prediction is essential for accurate protein structure and function prediction, and numerous methods have been developed using statistical inference and deep learning. Methods based on statistical inference (e.g., CCMpred, Gremlin, EVFold, plmDCA, FreeContact, MetaPSICOV) and supervised deep learning (RaptorX-Contact, DeepCov, SPOT-Contact, TrRosetta) have achieved significant results. A common trait among these methods is the use of multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and homology-based profile information. However, many proteins have very few or no homologs to generate MSA and homology profiles, causing performance to drop significantly for such cases. SSCpred is a recently published single-sequence-based method that uses one-hot encoding of the fasta sequence and predicted one-dimensional structural properties from SPIDER3-Single. SSCpred performs adequately for proteins with few homologs but relatively poorer for those with effective homologs compared to MSA-based techniques. To improve single-sequence-based methods, unsupervised deep learning methods inspired by Natural Language Processing language models were introduced. ESM-1b, a Transformer-34 model trained on Uniref50, outputs an embedding and attention maps, and the authors propose using its attention map as an input feature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the attention map from the pre-trained ESM-1b language model can be used as an input feature to improve single-sequence-based protein contact map prediction. The authors hypothesize that unsupervised learning features concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single's outputs will outperform the single-sequence-based SSCpred and the MSA-based predictors for proteins with a low effective number of homologous proteins (Neff). A secondary hypothesis is that an ensemble of models trained through different training approaches and different feature combinations will add to this improvement. The predicted outcome is that the proposed method will provide a faster, reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods, useful for large-scale prediction. The method is further predicted to outperform TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on proteins without homologs, and to exceed SSCpred on free modelling targets without known structural templates.

Methodological Details
The benchmark dataset was prepared by ProteinNet and consists of 50,914 proteins submitted to PDB before 2016 with high-resolution (<2.5 Å) crystal structures. Proteins were clustered at sequence identity cut-off of 95% according to the MMseqs2 tool to harness the full capabilities of deep learning algorithms. To minimize over-fitting, 100 proteins were separated for validation, and any proteins with hits at an e-value cut-off of less than 0.1 with the validation set were removed. This left a final training set of 34,691 proteins and a validation set of 88 proteins after removing proteins with length more than 500. For independent testing, all protein structures released between May 2018 and April 2020 were downloaded, forming the SPOT-2018 test set of 669 proteins. Homologous sequences were removed from the training set using the HHblits tool at an e-value cut-off of less than 0.1. The Neff1-2018 test set consists of 46 proteins from SPOT-2018 with Neff=1, providing a stringent benchmark for sequentially isolated proteins. Neff was calculated with respect to the reference Uniclust30 dataset published in February 2020. An additional independent test set, CASP14-FM, includes 15 free modelling targets released at CASP14 without known structural templates. Input features included one-hot encoding of amino acids, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (SS3, SS8, ASA, HSE, ψ, φ, θ, and τ), and ESM-1b attention maps. One-dimensional features were converted into two-dimensional features using outer concatenation. Attention maps were extracted from all twenty attention heads of the last layer and twenty heads from every layer of ESM-1b. Attention maps were symmetrized and applied average product corrections (APC) as done by Rao et al. (2020). Contacts were defined as inter-residue distances ≤ 8.0 Å between two Cβ atoms, classified into long (≥24), medium (12–23), and short (7–11) ranges.

Procedures And Architectures
The deep neural network architecture is a ResNet12 with 12 convolutional blocks, inspired by the success of ResNet in contact-map and RNA structure prediction. The improved version of ResNet from Duta et al. (2020) was used instead of vanilla ResNet. Each convolutional layer has a channel size of 64 and a kernel size of 3. Six models were trained with the same architectural specifications but different input feature combinations as detailed in Table 1. The first three models (Models 1-3) predict inter-residue contacts as a binary classification using Binary Cross-Entropy loss. The last three models (Models 4-6) predict inter-residue distances as distance bins, with probabilities summed within the 0-8 Å bins, using Cross-Entropy loss. All models used the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 1. To avoid overfitting, all models were trained with early stopping of 3. The final ensemble, SPOT-Contact-Single, took the mean of the individual model outputs from all six models. Performance was evaluated using F1-score, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), sensitivity, AUC of precision-recall curve, AUC of ROC, and top L/10, L/5, L/2, and L/1 ranked predictions.

Key Results
For the feature importance ablation, the model trained on one-hot encoding only achieved an F1-score of 0.15 and an MCC of 0.14. Adding the output of SPOT-1D-Single to one-hot encoding improved the F1-score by 22.90%. Attention maps from the last layer of ESM-1b achieved F1=0.51, MCC=0.50, precision=0.56, and AUC of ROC=0.95. This represents a 242% F1-score improvement over the one-hot encoding only model and 178% over the SPOT-1D-Single + one-hot encoding model. Attention maps from all layers of ESM-1b showed similar F1 and MCC but improved precision across all contact ranges. Concatenating all features (one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single + ESM-1b all layers) further increased F1-score by 2.92% over the all-layers-only model, with noticeable improvement for medium- and long-range contacts. Direct contact-map prediction performed slightly better than distogram-based prediction, but the difference was small, leading to inclusion of both strategies in the final ensemble. On the validation set, the SPOT-Contact-Single ensemble achieved a 4% F1-score improvement over the second-best individual model. On the Neff=1 subset of SPOT-2018, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved an F1-score of 0.32, which is 45% higher than the ~0.22 achieved by SPOT-Contact, TrRosetta, and ESM-1b. For the example protein 5YKZ_A from Neff1-2018, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.388, compared to SPOT-Contact=0.215, TrRosetta=0.235, and ESM-1b=0.252. On the CASP14-FM test set, SPOT-Contact-Single showed a 15% F1-score improvement over SSCpred. The most significant improvement over SSCpred was in long-range contacts precision, with an approximately 100% improvement. For the CASP14-FM dataset of 15 proteins, inference on CPU took 116 seconds, which is 22 times faster than TrRosetta. On GPU, TrRosetta took 1926 seconds, which is 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results confirm that unsupervised language model attention maps capture meaningful spatial information that complements one-hot sequence encoding, bridging the gap between single-sequence and profile-based methods. The ensemble approach demonstrates that combining multiple training strategies and feature sets improves robustness and generalization, consistent with the observation that the ensemble outperformed all individual models. The method provides a reasonably accurate, computationally efficient alternative to MSA-based methods, making it suitable as a screening tool for large-scale protein structure prediction. The speed advantage (22x faster on CPU, 42x faster on GPU) is attributed to the elimination of the computationally intensive sequence profile generation step required by TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact. The limitation to proteins under 1024 residues imposed by ESM-1b's sequence length is addressed by the observation that proteins are typically composed of domains with fewer than 1000 residues.

Contradictions And Limitations
The method cannot predict contact maps for proteins longer than 1024 amino acids due to the ESM-1b sequence length constraint. Despite the improvement over profile-based methods at low Neff, SPOT-1D-Single is not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods when homologs are available, as evidenced by the Neff-dependent performance plot. The training was conducted on proteins with length no more than 500 residues, limiting generalizability to very long proteins. The performance gain from the ensemble was modest (4% F1 improvement over the second-best model), suggesting diminishing returns from adding more models. The paper does not report the specific hyperparameters for the SPOT-1D-Single component, nor does it provide a random seed or detailed train/test split beyond the ProteinNet description. The method's performance on extremely low-homology proteins (Neff < 1) is not fully characterized beyond the Neff=1 test set.

Claims
ESM-1b attention maps significantly improve single-sequence-based protein contact map prediction compared to one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single features alone. Attention maps from the last layer of ESM-1b achieved F1=0.51, a 242% improvement over one-hot encoding. Adding all-layer attention maps improved precision across all contact ranges. The best feature combination (all features together) further increased F1-score by 2.92%. The marginal 2.92% gain from the full ensemble suggests that the additional features contribute limited incremental value. Unsupervised language model embeddings can serve as a viable substitute for MSA-derived features in structural prediction tasks.
SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms profile-based methods (TrRosetta, SPOT-Contact) on proteins with no homologs (Neff=1). On the Neff=1 test set, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.32 vs ~0.22 for profile-based methods (45% higher). For the example protein 5YKZ_A, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.388 vs 0.252 for ESM-1b, 0.235 for TrRosetta, and 0.215 for SPOT-Contact. As Neff increases, the performance of profile-based predictors improves over SPOT-1D-Single, showing the method is not universally superior. The method is particularly well-suited for proteins with limited or no homology, a common case in genomics and metagenomics.
SPOT-Contact-Single is significantly faster than profile-based methods, making it more suitable for large-scale prediction. On CPU for CASP14-FM, SPOT-Contact-Single takes 116 seconds, 22 times faster than TrRosetta. On GPU, TrRosetta took 1926 seconds, 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single. The speed comparison is on a small test set of only 15 proteins, which may not accurately reflect throughput on much larger datasets. The method is more suitable for genomic-scale prediction where the overhead of sequence profile generation is prohibitive.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A feature ablation study (Table 2) compared one-hot encoding, one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single, and ESM-1b attention map variants to isolate the contribution of each feature type. Two training strategies (direct contact prediction vs. distogram-based prediction) were compared, with direct prediction performing slightly better but showing small difference (Table 3). Both distogram and direct prediction models were included in the final ensemble to capture benefits from both strategies. The ensemble achieved a 4% F1-score improvement over the second-best individual model, demonstrating the robustness benefit of combining diverse predictors.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the ResNet12 architecture with convolutional layers (channel size 64, kernel size 3). Figure 2 displays precision for top predictions at short-, medium-, and long-range contacts for SPOT-Contact-Single vs. all comparison methods on the Neff=1 set. Figure 3 plots F1-score of different predictors as a function of Neff values, illustrating the Neff-dependent performance gap. Figure 4 presents native and predicted contact maps from four methods on an example protein (5YKZ_A) from Neff1-2018. Table 1 details the feature combinations and training tasks for the six ensemble models. Table 2 reports performance on the validation set for each input feature combination, establishing feature importance. Table 3 compares direct contact-map vs. distogram-based prediction performance. Table 4 presents validation set results for individual models and the ensemble. Table 5 compares SPOT-Contact-Single vs. SPOT-Contact, TrRosetta, and ESM-1b on Neff=1 proteins. Table 6 reports CASP14-FM test set results, including F1, MCC, Precision, Sensitivity, AUC, and ROC. Supplementary Table S2 reports continued improvement in precision for all-layer attention maps. Supplementary Table S4 reports long-range contacts precision improvement over SSCpred. Supplementary Table S5 reports CPU and GPU inference times for CASP14-FM.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of SPOT-Contact-Single, a single-sequence-based protein contact map predictor that outperforms both evolutionary-profile-based (45% F1 improvement on Neff=1) and single-sequence-based (15% F1 improvement on CASP14-FM) competitors by leveraging attention maps from ESM-1b combined with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single features. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of quantitative F1-score improvements (48.7% and 48.5% over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on Neff=1) and a massive computational speed advantage (22x faster on CPU, 42x faster on GPU), validating the method's applicability for large-scale and genomic prediction. 3. The future path includes extending the method to longer proteins (>1024 residues) by adapting or combining Transformer models, and exploring further single-sequence features and advanced architectures (Transformer, Performer) to continue improving contact map prediction without evolutionary information.
