The authors developed the package to address a critical gap: while integrating mathematical theory with empirical data is a fundamental driver of progress in the life sciences, the language of mathematical models can be inaccessible to empiricists, and equation-heavy papers are cited less often. Existing quantitative training in EEB has focused primarily on statistics or programming, with few advances in theoretical model pedagogy. The 11 apps were selected by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and commonly-used textbooks (Gotelli 2008; Begon and Townsend 2020). A core set of nine apps are available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. Apps range from single-model dynamics (e.g., abiotic resource competition) to multi-model suites (e.g., predator-prey dynamics including Lotka-Volterra, logistic growth extensions, and type II functional response). The UCLA and MU IRBs classified the surveys as exempt. The paper concludes that interactive tools provide a scalable entry point to theoretical insights for those without years of quantitative training. Unlike existing resources (Evo-Ed, HHMI BioInteractive, Populus), ecoevoapps is entirely open-source and written in R, making it accessible to the broader EEB community. Future releases will prioritize evolutionary biology and population genetics models.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package and web platform (https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io) that provides 11 interactive Shiny apps simulating fundamental ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB) models, alongside R functions for direct simulation and visualization. The authors developed the package to address a critical gap: while integrating mathematical theory with empirical data is a fundamental driver of progress in the life sciences, the language of mathematical models can be inaccessible to empiricists, and equation-heavy papers are cited less often. Existing quantitative training in EEB has focused primarily on statistics or programming, with few advances in theoretical model pedagogy. The 11 apps were selected by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and commonly-used textbooks (Gotelli 2008; Begon and Townsend 2020). A core set of nine apps are available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. Apps range from single-model dynamics (e.g., abiotic resource competition) to multi-model suites (e.g., predator-prey dynamics including Lotka-Volterra, logistic growth extensions, and type II functional response). Each app includes a description of model structure, parameter definitions, and references. Under the hood, the package provides run_ functions that take parameter vectors (params), initial populations (init), and time steps (time), returning dataframes for simulation, and plot_ functions that return ggplot2 objects. The shiny_ functions enable deployment from the R console or shinyapps.io, and model-specific vignettes (e.g., predator-prey-interactions) provide instructions for direct R simulation. A classroom evaluation of 51 UCLA upper-division ecology students used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition. The activity included ~15-minute video lectures followed by a guided worksheet. Students rated the apps on a 1-7 scale, and 40/51 (nearly 80%) reported the apps were moderately to very helpful (6 or 7). A parallel survey at the University of Missouri confirmed substantial gains in student confidence, especially among students with higher prior interest. The UCLA and MU IRBs classified the surveys as exempt. The paper concludes that interactive tools provide a scalable entry point to theoretical insights for those without years of quantitative training. Unlike existing resources (Evo-Ed, HHMI BioInteractive, Populus), ecoevoapps is entirely open-source and written in R, making it accessible to the broader EEB community. Future releases will prioritize evolutionary biology and population genetics models.

Research Context
Integrating mathematical theory with empirical observations and experiments is a fundamental driver of progress across the life sciences. In ecology and evolutionary biology, research that synthesizes data with mathematical models can enable generalization across systems and promote deeper conceptual understanding. Despite widespread agreement that more synergism between theoretical and empirical approaches in EEB can yield fruitful insights, numerous barriers limit such integration. One primary barrier is that the language of mathematical models and their analytical solutions may seem foreign to those coming from an empirical background. As a result, equation-heavy papers tend to be cited less often, and instructors of quantitative courses receive worse student evaluations than those who de-emphasize quantitative topics. While calls for increased quantitative training in EEB have mounted, they have focused primarily on statistical models or programming skills, with relatively few advances in the pedagogy of theoretical models. A growing body of research suggests that interactive tools allowing users to independently explore model structure and outcomes help increase student interest and understanding of quantitative concepts. Establishing a platform for interactive simulations of EEB models has the potential to facilitate communication and collaboration between theoretical and empirical researchers.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a collection of interactive Shiny apps simulating fundamental EEB models can facilitate communication, learning, and classroom instruction of theoretical concepts. The authors hypothesized that an open-source R package providing freely available interactive apps would bridge the gap between theoretical models and empirical practice, serving as a gateway for users to become familiar with coding and implementing theoretical models. A secondary hypothesis was that these apps could be deployed in large undergraduate classroom settings to enhance student understanding of specific model concepts. The expected outcome was that students using the apps would report moderate to high perceived helpfulness for understanding models as a whole and for specific topics. The package was designed to serve as a bridge to help users become familiar with coding and implementing theoretical models through a dual interface of interactive apps and R console functions. The apps were expected to provide the primary avenue through which most users would interact with the theoretical models, with the R functions serving as a gateway for more advanced users.

Methodological Details
At the heart of ecoevoapps are 11 interactive apps selected to be the primary avenue through which users interact with the models. The models were selected by surveying syllabi for undergraduate ecology courses and commonly-used textbooks, including Gotelli 2008 and Begon and Townsend 2020. Some apps implement the dynamics of one specific model, while other apps present several closely related models. A core set of nine apps are available in English, Spanish, and Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The apps are freely available online on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers, or can be launched locally from users' personal computers from the R console. To evaluate classroom value, 51 students used the shiny apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition in an upper-division Ecology course. The course was at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), with supplementary IRB documentation available. The learning activity included short (~15 minutes) video lectures presenting an overview of the model and the shiny app, followed by a worksheet navigating students through a guided exploration. After the activity, students rated on a scale of 1-7 the degree to which the apps helped them understand the model as a whole and specific associated topics. A parallel survey was conducted with students in a General Ecology course at the University of Missouri (MU). The surveys tracked individual students' interest and confidence in models before and after the activity. Classroom surveys were reviewed by the UCLA and MU Institutional Review Boards, which determined the studies to be exempt.

Procedures And Architectures
The shiny apps use functions in the ecoevoapps package to simulate and visualize model dynamics. Simulations are conducted by run_ functions, which take as input parameter values (params), initial population sizes (init), and the time steps (time) over which to run the model. The run_ functions return a dataframe of the population sizes for each species over the specified time series. For example, run_predprey_model() requires a parameter vector, a vector of initial population sizes, and time steps as inputs. The package includes a series of plotting functions prefixed plot_, which take as input the dataframe from the corresponding run_ function and return a ggplot2 object. The complete list of functions for simulating and plotting model dynamics is provided in Table 1. Each app includes a brief description of the model structure and history, a table with parameter definitions, and references to relevant literature. Users who wish to customize or deploy their own instance can use the vignette instructions, e.g., for hosting on institutional servers. Model-specific vignettes, such as vignette( The predator-prey dynamics app includes tabs for the classic Lotka-Volterra model, logistic growth in the prey, and type II functional response for the predator. The app is available online at a specific URL or can be deployed from the R command line with shiny_predprey(). For deployment, the package provides a series of functions with the prefix shiny_ that launch the apps from the R console. Users familiar with R can use the run_ and plot_ functions to conduct visualizations or analyses beyond those presented in the apps. summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the role of Cellular Communication Network Factor 2 (CCN2, also known as Connective Tissue Growth Factor, CTGF) in lymphangiogenesis and its intracellular signaling in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). While CCN2 is a well-characterized angiogenic factor in physiological and pathological angiogenesis, its role in lymphatic vessels remained largely unexplored. The authors first established that CCN2 dose-dependently upregulates LEC markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3) in primary cultured mouse LECs, with expression peaking at 100 ng/mL and decreasing at 200 ng/mL. Phospho-receptor tyrosine kinase array showed that CCN2 selectively increased EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylation while VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation remained unchanged, indicating that CCN2/VEGFR3 signaling is not activated upstream of ERK. The study then demonstrated that CCN2 significantly increases ERK phosphorylation (p<0.001) in LECs, whereas total ERK remains constant. siRNA knockdown of integrin av (Itgav) partially reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040), identifying integrin av as a key upstream mediator. CCN2 was found to weakly suppress LEC proliferation at 24 h (p=0.003 and 0.02) despite ERK activation, which was temporally transient (increasing up to 4 h, decreasing at 8 h). Immunoprecipitation revealed that CCN2 enhances the binding of ERK to DUSP6, and DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK at all time points (p<0.001, p=0.04, p=0.004), establishing DUSP6 as a negative modulator of ERK signaling. In vivo Matrigel plug assays using recombinant CCN2 (8.33 µg) confirmed increased Podoplanin-positive vessels and phospho-ERK/DUSP6 expression in Podoplanin-positive cells, demonstrating positive lymphangiogenic modulation. The discrepancy between in vitro proliferation suppression and in vivo promotion is attributed to extracellular matrix and matrix metalloproteinase effects in Matrigel. The authors conclude that CCN2 activates ERK via integrin av, and that DUSP6 mediates negative feedback on ERK, suggesting integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets in conditions such as oral squamous cell carcinoma where CCN2 is elevated.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the role of Cellular Communication Network Factor 2 (CCN2, also known as Connective Tissue Growth Factor, CTGF) in lymphangiogenesis and its intracellular signaling in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). While CCN2 is a well-characterized angiogenic factor in physiological and pathological angiogenesis, its role in lymphatic vessels remained largely unexplored. The authors first established that CCN2 dose-dependently upregulates LEC markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3) in primary cultured mouse LECs, with expression peaking at 100 ng/mL and decreasing at 200 ng/mL. Phospho-receptor tyrosine kinase array showed that CCN2 selectively increased EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylation while VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation remained unchanged, indicating that CCN2/VEGFR3 signaling is not activated upstream of ERK. The study then demonstrated that CCN2 significantly increases ERK phosphorylation (p<0.001) in LECs, whereas total ERK remains constant. siRNA knockdown of integrin av (Itgav) partially reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040), identifying integrin av as a key upstream mediator. Conversely, integrin a9 and b1 suppression did not mirror this effect, suggesting a specific role for integrin av. CCN2 was found to weakly suppress LEC proliferation at 24 h (p=0.003 and 0.02) despite ERK activation, which was temporally transient (increasing up to 4 h, decreasing at 8 h). Immunoprecipitation revealed that CCN2 enhances the binding of ERK to DUSP6, and DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK at all time points (p<0.001, p=0.04, p=0.004), establishing DUSP6 as a negative modulator of ERK signaling. In vivo Matrigel plug assays using recombinant CCN2 (8.33 µg) confirmed increased Podoplanin-positive vessels and phospho-ERK/DUSP6 expression in Podoplanin-positive cells, demonstrating positive lymphangiogenic modulation. The discrepancy between in vitro proliferation suppression and in vivo promotion is attributed to extracellular matrix and matrix metalloproteinase effects in Matrigel. The authors conclude that CCN2 activates ERK via integrin av, and that DUSP6 mediates negative feedback on ERK, suggesting integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets in conditions such as oral squamous cell carcinoma where CCN2 is elevated.

Research Context
CCN2 (CTGF) was originally isolated as a PDGF-like factor in HUVECs and belongs to the CCN family of matricellular proteins with six members. CCN2 has roles in development, tumorigenesis, fibrotic disease, and wound healing, and is a key regulator of physiologic and pathologic angiogenesis. CCN2 is highly expressed in coronary vessels and in the kidneys, lung, and liver vasculature, and promotes tumor angiogenesis. CCN2 activates MAPK pathways including p38, ERK, and JNK in vascular endothelial cells, either directly via surface receptors or indirectly via extracellular cofactors. Integrins are cell surface adhesion receptors that trigger intracellular signaling including ERK and MAPK pathways upon conformation change of the extracellular domain. Previous studies in renal, peritoneal dialysis-related, and liver fibrosis mouse models showed that CTGF enhanced lymphangiogenesis. CTGF is involved in fibrosis-associated renal lymphangiogenesis through interaction with VEGF-C, linking CCN2 to lymphangiogenesis in fibrous diseases. However, CCN2 signaling in LECs in lymphangiogenic signaling has not been elucidated prior to this study.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CCN2 exerts effects on lymphangiogenesis and what the intracellular signaling pathway is in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells. The authors hypothesized that CCN2-mediated lymphangiogenesis is regulated by intracellular signaling pathways, with ERK serving as a potential downstream mediator. It was further hypothesized that integrin receptors mediate the CCN2-ERK connection, given the known interaction between CCN2 and integrin avb3 in vascular endothelial cells. The study expected that CCN2-induced ERK activation would be counterbalanced by a negative regulatory mechanism, consistent with transient ERK phosphorylation observed in time-course experiments. The authors predicted that CCN2 would promote lymphangiogenesis in vivo, consistent with previous reports of CTGF enhancing lymphatic vessel formation in fibrosis models. The hypothesis was that DUSP6, a dual-specificity phosphatase predominant in LECs, would serve as the negative modulator of ERK signaling.

Methodological Details
Primary cultured LECs from C57BL/6 mice were obtained from CellBiologics (Chicago, IL, USA) and cultured in 0.1% gelatin-coated dishes at 37°C with 5% CO2 using EGM2 growth medium. Cells up to 6 passages were used in in vitro experiments, and proliferation was assessed by crystal violet staining on 24-well plates at 2 × 10^4 cells per well. LECs were treated with 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100, or 200 ng/mL of CCN2 for 3 hours for gene expression analysis by quantitative RT-PCR. For proliferation assays, cells were treated with 0, 10, 50, or 100 ng/mL of CCN2 for 24, 48, and 72 hours, with absorbance at 590 nm measured by SPARK 10M plate reader. 1.5 × 10^5 LECs were transfected with 25 pmol of target siRNA or non-target siRNA (MISSION siRNA universal control#1) using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX. For the phospho-RTK array, LECs were treated with 100 ng/mL of recombinant rat CTGF for 5 min, and 200 µg of total protein was incubated with the receptor-spotted membrane for 24 h. Western blot analysis used 5-20 µg protein samples, SDS-PAGE, PVDF membrane transfer, and primary antibodies incubated overnight at 4°C. Immunoprecipitation used 200 µg total protein incubated with anti-ERK (CST) or anti-DUSP6 (Abcam) at 4°C overnight with Protein A magnetic beads. In the in vivo Matrigel plug assay, male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice were used, and 450 µL of growth factor reduced Matrigel with 8.33 µg of recombinant rat CCN2 was injected subcutaneously (n=4; control n=3). Matrigel plugs were removed at day 7, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sections 4 µm thick were stained with hematoxylin-eosin. Immunohistochemistry used Alexa594 goat anti-Syrian hamster IgG, Alexa488 donkey anti-rat IgG, and Alexa488 donkey anti-rabbit IgG for staining. Morphology was observed using fluorescence microscope BZ-710X and confocal microscope LSM710 (Carl Zeiss, Tokyo, Japan). All experiments were performed more than three times except the RTK assay (n=2), with data expressed as mean ± standard error (S.E.). Statistical analysis used Student's t-test, one-way/repeated measures ANOVA, or two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni or Sidak multiple comparisons, significance at p < 0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
Gene expression of Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1, Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 was analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR using Purelink RNA purification kit, QuantiTect RT kit, TB Green Premix, and LightCycler96. The phospho-RTK array used a Proteome profiler mouse phospho-RTK array kit (R&D Systems) where 200 µg total protein was incubated with anti-phospho tyrosine kinase antibody. Integrin expression mRNA (Itgav, Itga9, Itga2b, Itgb1, Itgb2, Itgb3) was determined by quantitative RT-PCR to identify relevant integrin subtypes in LECs. SiRNA-mediated knockdown of integrin av, integrin a9, integrin b1, and DUSP6 was performed using Sidirect ver.2 design and Lipofectamine RNAiMAX transfection. Western blot signals were visualized using ECL Prime (GE Healthcare) and quantified with ImageQuant TL 8.1 software. Immunoprecipitation protocol involved incubation of cell lysates with anti-ERK or anti-DUSP6, addition of Protein A magnetic beads, 20-min incubation, five-fold washing, denaturation in 3×SDS Sample Buffer, and Western blotting. The Matrigel plug assay combined recombinant rat CCN2 with growth factor reduced Matrigel for subcutaneous back injection, followed by 7-day incubation before euthanization. Immunohistochemical staining in Matrigel plugs was performed with primary antibodies against Podoplanin, CD31, b3-Tubulin, ERK, and DUSP6, followed by fluorescent secondary antibody incubation.

Key Results
CCN2 increased expression of Lyve1, Podoplanin, and Prox1 in LECs in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, but at 200 ng/mL expression dramatically decreased. CCN2 increased expression of lymphangiogenic factors Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4, but did not affect Kdr expression. Phosphorylation of EGFR and EphB4 was increased by CCN2 (p<0.001), while VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations were unchanged. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased in response to CCN2 (p<0.001), whereas p38 MAPK, JNK, AKT, NFkB, Smad2, -3, and -1/5 were unchanged. Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2 treatment, confirming the effect is on phosphorylation rather than total protein. Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs, and their mRNA levels were increased by CCN2 stimulation. Knockdown of integrin av by siRNA partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK compared with non-target siRNA (p=0.0040). Knockdown of integrin a9 resulted in a slight increase of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK, and phospho-ERK was increased by suppression of integrin b1 (p=0.05) without CCN2 stimulation. CCN2-treated LECs showed suppressed cell growth at 24 h compared with 0 h (p=0.22, 0.92, >0.99) and compared with vehicle-treated LECs (p=0.003 and 0.02 for 50 and 100 ng/mL). Phospho-ERK was significantly increased at 15 min after CCN2 treatment, continued to increase up to 4 h, decreased at 8 h, and increased again after 48 h. Quantitative RT-PCR revealed Dusp1, -2, -4, -5, -6, -7, -8, -9, and -10 are expressed in LECs, with Dusp6 predominant and Dusp16 undetected. Immunoprecipitation showed that DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, and their interaction was enhanced by CCN2. In DUSP6 siRNA-transfected LECs, phospho-ERK levels were increased at 15 min (p<0.001), 4 h (p<0.001), 24 h (p=0.04), and 48 h (p=0.004) after CCN2 treatment. In Matrigel plug assays, the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased by exogenous CCN2, and blood vessels were macroscopically observed in CCN2 group but not control. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression in Podoplanin-positive cells were significantly increased in the CCN2 gel compared with the control gel (p<0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2 activates ERK signaling in LECs via integrin av, providing a mechanism for CCN2-mediated endothelial signaling independent of VEGFR3 activation. The temporal pattern of phospho-ERK (rising at 15 min, peaking at 4 h, dropping at 8 h) indicates a concomitant mechanism for suppressing ERK activation. DUSP6, being the predominant DUSP in LECs, functions as a negative modulator of ERK signaling by enhancing the ERK-DUSP6 interaction upon CCN2 stimulation. CCN2-mediated lymphangiogenesis is balanced by DUSP6-mediated negative feedback, preventing excessive ERK activation. The discrepancy between in vitro proliferation suppression and in vivo Matrigel promotion is likely due to extracellular matrix and matrix metalloproteinase effects, as CCN2-signaling is mediated by ECM and activated through proteolytic processing by MMP-2,3.

Contradictions And Limitations
CCN2 weakly suppressed LEC proliferation in vitro (p=0.003, 0.02) but promoted lymphangiogenesis in vivo in Matrigel assays, a discrepancy attributed to ECM and MMP effects in Matrigel. The study did not investigate the relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 (negative ERK regulators) and DUSP6 in LECs, limiting mechanistic understanding. The increase in phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation in integrin b1-suppressed LECs might be due to integrin a5 supplementation, but integrin a5 mRNA expression was not investigated. The RTK assay used only 100 ng/mL of CTGF for 5 min, which may not capture the full range of CCN2 effects. No in vivo data were provided for ERK and DUSP6 protein quantification beyond immunohistochemical localization in Matrigel plugs.

Claims
CCN2 activates ERK signaling in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells via integrin av. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased (p<0.001) in response to CCN2 in LECs. Knockdown of integrin av partially reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Itgav mRNA was predominantly expressed in LECs and increased by CCN2 stimulation. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations were unchanged, eliminating upstream receptor activation as the mechanism. Knockdown of integrin a9 only resulted in a slight increase of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Suppression of integrin b1 did not alter phospho-ERK levels upon CCN2 stimulation. Integrin av may be a druggable target to modulate CCN2-ERK signaling in lymphatic diseases. The CCN2-integrin av axis in LECs represents a specific lymphatic pathway distinct from known angiogenesis pathways.
CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo, but this effect is negatively regulated by DUSP6-mediated ERK dephosphorylation. In vivo Matrigel plug assays showed increased Podoplanin-positive vessels with CCN2. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 were significantly increased in Podoplanin-positive cells in CCN2 gels (p<0.05). DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK at multiple time points after CCN2 treatment (p<0.001, p=0.04, p=0.004). CCN2 enhances the binding of ERK to DUSP6 via immunoprecipitation. CCN2 weakly suppressed LEC proliferation in vitro (p=0.003, 0.02) despite ERK activation. The in vitro proliferation and in vivo Matrigel results may not be directly comparable. DUSP6 functions as a protective feedback loop against excessive CCN2-ERK activation in lymphatic vessels. Imbalance of the CCN2-ERK-DUSP6 axis may contribute to lymphangiomatous conditions.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Integrin knockdown experiments (av, a9, b1) demonstrated subtype-specific effects on CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Time-course analysis of phospho-ERK revealed a transient peak (4 h) followed by a decrease (8 h), suggesting feedback control. ERK was analyzed as both phospho-ERK and total ERK, with total ERK remaining constant across treatments. The Matrigel plug assay included both CCN2-supplemented (n=4) and PBS control (n=3) to validate the in vivo effect. DUSP6 knockdown was validated at four time points (15 min, 4 h, 24 h, 48 h) showing consistent increase in phospho-ERK.

Ethical Considerations
All experiments were performed in compliance with the relevant laws and institutional guidelines. The study was approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Fukuoka University with approval number: 2008024. Male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice were used and euthanized at 9 weeks of age.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows dose-dependent increase of Lyve1, Podoplanin, and Prox1 with CCN2, peaking at 100 ng/mL and decreasing at 200 ng/mL. Figure 1B displays CCN2-induced upregulation of Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 but no effect on Kdr expression. Figure 2A, 2B, and 2C demonstrate that phospho-ERK is significantly increased (p<0.001) by CCN2 while total ERK is unchanged. Figure 3A shows integrin mRNA expression; Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 increased with CCN2. Figure 3B shows siRNA knockdown of integrin av partially decreases CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Figure 3C shows integrin a9 knockdown results in slight phospho-ERK increase; Figure 3D shows integrin b1 suppression increases phospho-ERK (p=0.05) and blocks CCN2 effect. Figure 4A shows CCN2-suppressed LEC proliferation at 24 h (p=0.22, 0.92, >0.99 relative to 0 h; p=0.003, 0.02 relative to vehicle). Figure 4B presents the phospho-ERK time course showing rise at 15 min, peak at 4 h, decrease at 8 h, and late increase after 48 h. Figure 5A shows DUSP family expression in LECs; Dusp6 predominant, Dusp16 undetected. Figure 5B shows immunoprecipitation confirming DUSP6-ERK co-precipitation enhanced by CCN2. summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement, Priscilla S Redd, Chunwan Lu, Alyssa D Merting, Dakota B Poschel, Dafeng Yang, Gang Zhou, David H Munn, Kebin Liu
summary.field_subfield: Immunology/Cancer Immunology - Tumor Immunology and Immunotherapy
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental research article with mechanistic findings (in vitro, in vivo, scRNA-seq, flow cytometry, co-culture, myeloid depletion, and human clinical dataset validation)
summary.executive_summary: Tumor cell PD-L1 (tPD-L1) has traditionally been viewed as a direct checkpoint ligand that engages CTL PD-1 to inhibit CTL function, a paradigm that explains why PD-1 blockade works but fails to address how tPD-L1 differentially drives metastasis. This paper challenges that model, demonstrating that tPD-L1 exhibits no direct suppressive effect on CTL activation or lytic function when only tumor cells and tumor-specific CTLs are present. Instead, tPD-L1 targets PD-1 expressed on myeloid cells (mPD-1) in the lung metastatic niche. Upon tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1, SHP-2 activation is enhanced and pSTAT1 levels are diminished, suppressing type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. This repression downregulates the CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10, thereby impairing CTL recruitment to lung metastases and promoting metastatic growth in a CTL-dependent manner. The authors used 4T1 (triple-negative breast cancer) and CT26 (mismatch repair-proficient colorectal cancer) cell lines with PD-L1 knockout, in vitro CTL-tumor interaction assays using 2/20 CTLs, in vivo tail-vein metastasis models, single-cell RNA sequencing of ~7500 CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs, RAW264.7 macrophage co-cultures, clodronate liposome-mediated myeloid depletion, and a human patient scRNA-seq dataset of metastatic basal cell carcinoma before and after PD-1 blockade. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that PD-L1 loss preferentially remodeled myeloid cells rather than CTLs, with Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) upregulated as early as one day after injection. In vitro RAW264.7 co-culture confirmed that tPD-L1:mPD-1 engagement diminishes MHCII expression on both myeloid and tumor cells, while PD-1 loss in macrophages restores sensitivity to the TLR3 ligand poly(I:C) and enhances IFNβ production, revealing a negative feedback circuit where the PD-1/L1 axis attenuates the type I interferon signaling that induced it. Myeloid cell depletion abolished PD-L1-mediated metastasis, and human data showed PD-1 blockade releases myeloid differentiation restriction, enhances interferon signaling, and increases CTL-recruiting chemokines. The study identifies the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis as the critical mechanism controlling CTL infiltration in lung metastasis, explaining the durability of PD-1/L1 blockade in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Tumor cell PD-L1 (tPD-L1) has traditionally been viewed as a direct checkpoint ligand that engages CTL PD-1 to inhibit CTL function, a paradigm that explains why PD-1 blockade works but fails to address how tPD-L1 differentially drives metastasis. This paper challenges that model, demonstrating that tPD-L1 exhibits no direct suppressive effect on CTL activation or lytic function when only tumor cells and tumor-specific CTLs are present. Instead, tPD-L1 targets PD-1 expressed on myeloid cells (mPD-1) in the lung metastatic niche. Upon tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1, SHP-2 activation is enhanced and pSTAT1 levels are diminished, suppressing type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. This repression downregulates the CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10, thereby impairing CTL recruitment to lung metastases and promoting metastatic growth in a CTL-dependent manner. The authors used 4T1 (triple-negative breast cancer) and CT26 (mismatch repair-proficient colorectal cancer) cell lines with PD-L1 knockout, in vitro CTL-tumor interaction assays using 2/20 CTLs, in vivo tail-vein metastasis models, single-cell RNA sequencing of ~7500 CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs, RAW264.7 macrophage co-cultures, clodronate liposome-mediated myeloid depletion, and a human patient scRNA-seq dataset of metastatic basal cell carcinoma before and after PD-1 blockade. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that PD-L1 loss preferentially remodeled myeloid cells rather than CTLs, with Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) upregulated as early as one day after injection. In vitro RAW264.7 co-culture confirmed that tPD-L1:mPD-1 engagement diminishes MHCII expression on both myeloid and tumor cells, while PD-1 loss in macrophages restores sensitivity to the TLR3 ligand poly(I:C) and enhances IFNβ production, revealing a negative feedback circuit where the PD-1/L1 axis attenuates the type I interferon signaling that induced it. Myeloid cell depletion abolished PD-L1-mediated metastasis, and human data showed PD-1 blockade releases myeloid differentiation restriction, enhances interferon signaling, and increases CTL-recruiting chemokines. The study identifies the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis as the critical mechanism controlling CTL infiltration in lung metastasis, explaining the durability of PD-1/L1 blockade in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings.

Research Context
The prevailing paradigm holds that tumor-expressed PD-L1 binds CTL PD-1 to directly inhibit cytotoxic T lymphocyte activation and effector function via SHP-2 mediated dephosphorylation of TCR and CD28 signaling. While PD-1/L1 blockade is a cornerstone of immunotherapy, it is unclear how tPD-L1 differentially drives metastasis from the primary tumor site, given that metastases are the dominant cause of mortality. Emerging data suggests PD-1/L1 ICB response may depend on tumor anatomic sites and occur principally in metastatic sites rather than the primary tumor. Despite this, how non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression remains incompletely understood, leaving a mechanistic gap in the tPD-L1-mediated suppression model. Prior work has shown PD-1 expression in myeloid, dendritic, and tumor cells, but the role of mPD-1 in bridging tPD-L1 to CTL recruitment in metastasis has not been elucidated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether tPD-L1 exerts its anti-tumor effect through direct engagement of CTL PD-1 or through an intermediate cell population that mediates suppression of CTL recruitment. The authors hypothesize that tPD-L1 does not directly inhibit CTL activity but instead targets myeloid cell-expressed PD-1 (mPD-1) to suppress type I IFN expression and function, thereby impairing CTL recruitment to lung niche. A sub-hypothesis posits that a third factor, only present at the lung metastatic niche, is necessary for tPD-1 to exert its indirect protective role, and this factor is identified via RNA sequencing. The authors further hypothesize that mPD-1 engagement on RAW264.7 macrophages mediates attenuation of type I interferon signaling through SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1. The predicted outcome was that PD-L1 loss would increase CD3+ CTL infiltration in the lung but not the primary tumor, and that myeloid cell depletion would abolish PD-L1-mediated promotion of lung metastasis.

Methodological Details
The study utilized 4T1 (triple negative breast cancer, TNBC) and CT26 (mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer, MMRp CRC) murine cell lines, chosen to mimic clinically resistant breast and CRC models. PD-L1 was genetically ablated in both 4T1 and CT26 cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 to produce PD-L1 KO variants, with the resulting cell lines confirmed to express no PD-L2. In vitro CTL-tumor interaction assays employed the 2/20 tumor-specific CTL line, which recognizes the H2-L d-restricted AH1 epitope (residues 6-14) of gp70 endogenously expressed by 4T1 and CT26. The 2/20 CTL line was chosen because it exerts antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes and does not require differentiation from a naïve state, modeling effector CTL:tumor interaction with high fidelity. In vivo, PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 cells were injected into the right second mammary gland for orthotopic primary tumor models, while CT26 was injected into the right flank for subcutaneous tumors. Experimental metastasis models were established by lateral tail vein injection of WT or KO cells, with lungs harvested 24 hours later for gp70 colonization analysis and 14 days post-injection for metastasis analysis. For neutralization, 200 µg of anti-CD8α antibody (53-6.7) or isotype control (2A3) was injected i.v. every other day during the experiment. Single-cell RNA sequencing analyzed ~7500 CD45+ leukocytes isolated from 4T1-WT versus 4T1-PDL1-KO colonized lungs using Chromium Chip B (10x Genomics) and 3' Reagent Kit v3. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on lungs from mice injected with WT or KO cells, with RNA extracted using Direct-zol and sequenced by Novogene on the mm10 reference genome. Cell lines (4T1, CT26, RAW264.7, J774M, 293FT, CMS4-met) were obtained from ATCC or ThermoFisher, and the 2/20 CTL line was generated as previously described. Myeloid cell depletion was achieved in tumor-bearing mice via clodronate liposome injection, and tumor growth in the lungs was analyzed. In vitro co-cultures paired 4T1 WT or KO cells with RAW264.7 macrophages under cell-contact conditions, and PD-1 loss in RAW cells was generated using shRNA or lentivirus to target PD-1.

Procedures And Architectures
Gene knockout cell lines were generated by co-transfecting HEK293FT cells with pCMV-VSV-G, psPAX2, and lentiCRISPRv2 plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000 to produce CRISPR lentivirus. Tumor cells were transduced with lentivirus, selected with puromycin, and sorted for marker-negative cells using BD FACSARIA. In vitro CTL:tumor co-cultures were analyzed for antigen-specific cytotoxicity, with supernatant and cells harvested and stained with APC-AnnexinV and propidium iodide. Intracellular staining for pSTAT1 and surface antigens used the Cytofix/Cytoperm Plus kit, and samples were acquired on FACSCalibur with CellQuestPro or LSRFortessa with BD Diva 8.01. All flow cytometry data was analyzed with FlowJo v10.6.0, and statistical analysis was conducted using Prism8 with two-tailed Student's t-tests. scRNA-seq libraries were sequenced on Illumina NextSeq 500 with a protocol of 28 bp (Read 1), 8 bp (indexing), and 91 bp (RNA Read 2). Reads were mapped to the mm10 mouse genome using STAR aligner in the Cell Ranger 3.1.0 pipeline, yielding 30-39K reads per cell. Quality control extracted high-quality cells with 200 < feature count <4000, percent mitochondrial reads < 10, and >80% viable cells. Cells were clustered using the first fifty principal components, and myeloid and T cell clusters were reclustered using the top twenty principal components. Signature generation isolated genes whose expression increased by at least two-fold with a padj <0.05 after PD-L1 loss from bulk RNA-seq, and another two-fold increase after SHP099 treatment in myeloid cells. Human scRNA-seq analysis utilized the BMS038 dataset accessed from authors' processed files, pseudo-aligned with kallisto, and normalized counts generated following author's scripts. Batch effects in melanoma and basal cell carcinoma datasets were corrected by Harmony, and changes in resistant versus naïve cells were analyzed similarly. For in vivo metastasis, lungs were harvested, inflated with India ink, and quantified using IHC with CD3 staining analyzed by quPATH. Western blotting of homogenized lung lysates confirmed protein expression, with antibodies listed in Table S1, and IHC used 10% formalin fixation and paraffin embedding.

Key Results
No difference in primary tumor growth was observed between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 (Fig 2A) or CT26 (Fig 2E), supporting the in vitro finding that tPD-L1 confers no direct cytotoxic protection. Increased infiltration of CD3+ cells was observed in the lung after PD-L1 loss but not in the primary tumor (Fig 3A), indicating tPD-L1 blocked T cell infiltration at the metastatic site. No difference in initial tumor cell colonization (gp70 level) was seen one day after tail vein injection (Fig 3B), demonstrating PD-L1 does not enhance DTC seeding in the lung. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in RAGII-KO mice (Fig 3C), indicating tPD-L1 requires a functioning adaptive immune system to promote lung metastasis. Genetic ablation of MHC class I presentation and anti-CD8 T cell depletion revealed that tPD-L1 drove metastasis by suppressing CTL killing (Fig 2F, 3D). scRNA-seq of ~7500 cells in 4T1 WT versus KO colonized lungs identified differential expression in myeloid cells, not CTLs, with Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) upregulated as early as one day post-injection (Fig 5J-K). No change in bulk lung myeloid cell composition was observed by flow cytometry, but enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages (Fig 5E-F). Depletion of myeloid cells via clodronate liposomes diminished PD-L1 function in promoting tumor growth in the lungs, confirming myeloid cells bridge tPD-L1 to CTL suppression (Fig 6K-L). Human scRNA-seq of metastatic basal cell carcinoma before and after PD-1 blockade showed myeloid PHATE analysis revealed differentiation restriction released upon blockade, leading to enhanced IFN signaling, antigen presentation, and CTL-recruiting chemokine expression (Fig 7A-C). Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study uncouples the role of tPD-L1 at the metastatic site from its role at the primary tumor site, demonstrating that tPD-L1 binds mPD-1 to enforce an immunologically cold microenvironment in lung metastasis. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis is identified as the mechanism controlling CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis, providing a mechanistic basis for ICB efficacy in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. The finding that PD-1/L1 expression is induced by and then attenuates type I interferon signaling highlights a negative feedback circuit that may explain compensatory PD-L1 upregulation in interferon alpha therapies. The results suggest that the durable survival benefit of PD-1/L1 blockade arises from coordinated suppression of metastases rather than direct CTL re-activation at the primary tumor site. The demonstration that tPD-L1 controls CTL recruitment versus functionality provides a new framework for understanding the differential response of metastatic disease to ICB.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors explicitly note that the study exclusively analyzed lung metastases, which due to their location in barrier tissue, may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment that limits generalizability. The in vitro co-culture model using RAW264.7 macrophages, while mechanistically tractable, may not fully recapitulate the complexity of the in vivo lung metastatic niche. The human patient dataset is limited to metastatic basal cell carcinoma before and after PD-1 blockade, which may not generalize to all cancer types. The use of the 2/20 CTL line, while an effective effector model, represents a single antigen-specific population and may not capture the breadth of CTL infiltration. The study relies on the premise that mPD-1 is the primary myeloid PD-1 population, but the contribution of other myeloid subsets was not comprehensively interrogated.

Claims
tPD-L1 does not directly protect tumor cells from CTL cytotoxicity when only tumor cells and tumor-specific CTLs are present. No difference in primary tumor growth was observed between WT and KO 4T1 or CT26 cell lines in vivo. In vitro 2/20 CTL:4T1/CT26 co-culture experiments showed no direct PD-L1:PD-1 mediated inhibition of lysis. Loss of PD-L1 in tumor cells rendered them unable to engage CTL PD-1 because they express no PD-L2. The authors acknowledge the in vitro CTL model uses a single antigen-specific line (2/20), which may not fully represent the complexity of the in vivo CTL repertoire. The direct PD-L1:CTL PD-1 interaction model for tPD-L1 activity is insufficient to explain metastatic suppression, necessitating the inclusion of intermediate cell populations.
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis by binding to PD-1 on myeloid cells, suppressing type I IFN signaling and CXCL9/10 production, thereby impairing CTL recruitment. Increased CD3+ CTL infiltration in the lung after PD-L1 loss but not in the primary tumor confirms the effect is site-specific. MHC class I ablation and anti-CD8 T cell depletion abolished tPD-L1-mediated metastatic promotion, confirming CTL dependence. In vitro RAW264.7 co-culture demonstrated tPD-L1:mPD-1 engagement enhances SHP-2 activation and decreases pSTAT1, diminishing MHCII on myeloid and tumor cells. Myeloid cell depletion via clodronate liposomes abolished tPD-L1-mediated lung metastasis, confirming myeloid cells bridge tPD-L1 to CTL suppression. The in vitro RAW264.7 co-culture system is a simplified model and may not capture the full complexity of the in vivo lung myeloid microenvironment. This mechanistic finding provides a targetable pathway (mPD-1, STAT1, CXCL9/10) beyond the primary PD-1:PD-L1 axis for improving immunotherapy in metastatic disease.
The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis and underpins the efficacy of PD-1/L1 blockade in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. Human scRNA-seq of metastatic basal cell carcinoma showed PD-1 blockade releases myeloid differentiation restriction, enhances IFN signaling, and increases CTL-recruiting chemokines. Previous work confirmed type I interferon induces both PD-L1 and PD-1 in myeloid cells, with PD-L1 upregulated more rapidly. The authors cite multiple references (8-13) linking PD-1/L1 blockade to metastatic control as the driver of durable survival. The human dataset is limited to a single cancer type (basal cell carcinoma) before and after blockade, and the effect on CTL recruitment was not directly quantified in vivo in the human sample. This mechanistic link provides a physiological rationale for why PD-1/L1 blockade is effective in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings, potentially guiding the timing and combination of immunotherapy.

Data And Code Availability
The human patient scRNA-seq dataset for BMS038 was accessed from authors' processed files at https://github.com/riazn/bms038_analysis. The previously published PD-1 treatment response dataset (PRJEB23709) was accessed from EMBL and pseudo-aligned with kallisto. The authors do not explicitly mention a public repository for the main scRNA-seq or bulk RNA-seq data generated in this study.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Multiple in vivo metastasis models were used: primary orthotopic 4T1, CT26 subcutaneous, and tail-vein metastasis, with each confirming the site-specific effect. The CTL-dependence was confirmed through MHC class I ablation and antibody-mediated CD8 T cell depletion (200 µg anti-CD8α). In vitro co-culture experiments were conducted with both WT and KO tumor cells and WT and PD-1-KO macrophages, isolating the tPD-L1:mPD-1 interaction. The myeloid cell depletion via clodronate liposomes served as a functional ablation, confirming the requirement of myeloid cells for tPD-L1-mediated metastasis promotion. The in vitro model used the 2/20 CTL line which was validated to express antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes, eliminating the need for naïve T cell differentiation. Single-cell RNA sequencing quality was assured of ≥80% viable cells, with doublets removed by DoubletFinder and manual re-clustering.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the in vitro CTL-tumor interaction model with 2/20 CTLs recognizing gp70 on 4T1 and CT26. Figure 2A shows no difference in primary tumor growth between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 cells in the right second mammary gland. Figure 2E shows no difference in CT26 primary tumor growth at the site of injection. Figure 2F and Figure 3D show that tPD-L1 drove metastasis by suppressing killing by CTLs as revealed by MHC class I ablation and anti-CD8 T cell depletion. Figure 3A shows increased CD3+ cell infiltration in the lung after PD-L1 loss but not in the primary tumor. Figure 3B shows no difference in initial tumor cell colonization (gp70 level) one day after tail vein injection. Figure 3C shows equal metastasis between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 in RAGII-KO mice. Figure 4A shows the scRNA-seq UMAP of ~7500 CD45+ leukocytes from 4T1 WT versus KO colonized lungs. Figure 4B shows the clustering and population identification of CD45+ leukocytes. Figure 5E-F show no change in bulk lung myeloid cell composition but enhanced antigen presentation machinery in macrophages upon PD-L1 loss. Figure 5G-I show Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) as a marker for IFN-stimulated myeloid cells after tPD-L1 loss, with differential expression as early as one day post-injection. Figure 5L-M show the timeline of CTL infiltration after PD-L1 loss, with remodeling occurring before robust CTL infiltration. Figure 6A-B show enhanced myeloid cell surface PD-1 expression following tPD-L1 loss. Figure 6C shows RAW PD-1 upregulation in a cell-contact and IFNAR-dependent manner following 4T1 co-culture. Figure 6D-F show enhanced SHP-2 activation, decreased pSTAT1, and diminished MHCII on both 4T1 and RAW cells. Figure 6G shows elevated MHCII expression on CD45 negative stromal and tumor cells following loss of tPD-L1. Figure 6H-I show RAW PD-1 loss increased BST2 expression in response to poly(I:C) on both RAW and 4T1 cells. Figure 6J shows disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFNβ production. Figure 6K-L show myeloid cell depletion via clodronate liposomes abolished PD-L1 function in promoting lung metastasis. Figure 7A-C show human scRNA-seq of metastatic basal cell carcinoma before and after PD-1 blockade, with myeloid PHATE revealing differentiation restriction release.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the demonstration that tumor PD-L1 suppresses lung metastasis not by directly inhibiting CTL PD-1, but by engaging myeloid PD-1 to suppress type I IFN signaling and CXCL9/10, thereby impairing CTL recruitment in a CTL-dependent manner. The strongest evidence is the multiple convergent findings: in vitro RAW co-culture showing SHP-2 activation/pSTAT1 reduction, clodronate-mediated myeloid depletion abolishing tPD-L1-driven metastasis, and human scRNA-seq validating the myeloid-mediated mechanism in patient samples. The future path lies in targeting the tPD-L1/mPD-1 axis, STAT1 signaling, or CXCL9/10 expression to enhance CTL recruitment in metastases, and in testing this mechanistic framework in additional cancer types and neoadjuvant/adjuvant settings.

summary.title: Stem Cell Microarrays for Assessing Growth Factor Signaling in Engineered
summary.authors: Glycan Microenvironments (University of California San Diego); Austen L Michalak (University of California San Diego); Greg W Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kelsey A Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kamil Godula (University of California San Diego)
summary.field_subfield: Biomaterials / Stem Cell Biology
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a stem cell microarray platform integrating glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides, chemically crosslinked to adhesion proteins (gelatin) on polyacrylamide hydrogel substrates, to directly measure growth factor signaling activity in murine embryonic stem cells. The authors address the gap in structure-function analysis of ECM glycans, which are structurally complex and compositionally heterogeneous, making systematic profiling difficult. By arraying well-defined, synthetically modified heparin structures on hydrogel microarrays and seeding them with Exostosin 1-deficient murine ESCs (Ext1 -/-ESCs) that lack endogenous cell-surface HS, the platform isolates the effect of immobilized GAGs on FGF2-mediated MAPK (ERK1/2) activation. The key methodological innovation is the NHS-crosslinking of heparin to gelatin at low levels (~15% per chain), which retains ~40% FGF2 binding activity after 48 hours of ESC culture at 37°C/5% CO2 while preserving protein-binding specificity. Results demonstrate that FGF2 binds most strongly to fully sulfated heparin, and systematic desulfation of 6-O, 2-O, and N-sulfate groups results in progressive loss of binding activity, consistent with known requirements for FGF2/FGFR signaling. MAPK activation was quantified by measuring ERK1/2 phosphorylation ratios via immunofluorescence and microarray scanning. Ext1 -/-ESCs seeded at 40,000 cells/cm2 showed robust colony growth with no obvious differentiation. FGF2 stimulation (0.5 ng/mL, 15 min) produced dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation proportional to immobilized heparin concentration (0-500 g/mL), with NHS-crosslinked heparin providing 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding than non-covalently immobilized heparin. Soluble heparin (5 g/mL) restored MAPK activity as a positive control. The authors conclude that the platform enables rapid, multiplexed profiling of extracellular glycan activity in stem cell signaling, providing a tool to accelerate development of bioactive glycomaterials for regenerative therapies. The work is positioned within a broader context of emerging synthetic HS production technologies, building on prior work by Linhardt and Turnbull but extending to a spatial, arrayed hydrogel format with intact cellular signaling outputs.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a stem cell microarray platform integrating glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides, chemically crosslinked to adhesion proteins (gelatin) on polyacrylamide hydrogel substrates, to directly measure growth factor signaling activity in murine embryonic stem cells. The authors address the gap in structure-function analysis of ECM glycans, which are structurally complex and compositionally heterogeneous, making systematic profiling difficult. By arraying well-defined, synthetically modified heparin structures on hydrogel microarrays and seeding them with Exostosin 1-deficient murine ESCs (Ext1 -/-ESCs) that lack endogenous cell-surface HS, the platform isolates the effect of immobilized GAGs on FGF2-mediated MAPK (ERK1/2) activation. The key methodological innovation is the NHS-crosslinking of heparin to gelatin at low levels (~15% per chain), which retains ~40% FGF2 binding activity after 48 hours of ESC culture at 37°C/5% CO2 while preserving protein-binding specificity. Results demonstrate that FGF2 binds most strongly to fully sulfated heparin, and systematic desulfation of 6-O, 2-O, and N-sulfate groups results in progressive loss of binding activity, consistent with known requirements for FGF2/FGFR signaling. MAPK activation was quantified by measuring ERK1/2 phosphorylation ratios via immunofluorescence and microarray scanning. Ext1 -/-ESCs seeded at 40,000 cells/cm2 showed robust colony growth with no obvious differentiation. FGF2 stimulation (0.5 ng/mL, 15 min) produced dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation proportional to immobilized heparin concentration (0-500 g/mL), with NHS-crosslinked heparin providing 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding than non-covalently immobilized heparin. Soluble heparin (5 g/mL) restored MAPK activity as a positive control. The authors conclude that the platform enables rapid, multiplexed profiling of extracellular glycan activity in stem cell signaling, providing a tool to accelerate development of bioactive glycomaterials for regenerative therapies. The work is positioned within a broader context of emerging synthetic HS production technologies, building on prior work by Linhardt and Turnbull but extending to a spatial, arrayed hydrogel format with intact cellular signaling outputs.

Research Context
Extracellular glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) harbor binding sites for a range of growth factors and help establish gradients in the ECM and promote active signaling complexes. Their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make establishing structure-function relationships difficult for biomaterial development. Hydrogels decorated with peptides or proteins and supplemented with signaling molecules have enabled translation of stem cell regenerative capacity to clinical applications. Stem cell arrays have been particularly useful for examining ECM protein components in hydrogels, but extracellular glycans have been comparatively less explored. The compositional complexity of heparan sulfate (HS) made systematic structure-function analysis challenging for biomaterial integration. Recent advances in chemical, chemoenzymatic, and genetic engineering of HS biosynthetic pathways have produced well-defined HS structures.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether glycosaminoglycan polysaccharides can be arrayed on hydrogel substrates to directly measure their contribution to growth factor signaling in stem cells. The authors hypothesize that covalent immobilization of HS to gelatin via NHS-crosslinking will retain the protein-binding specificity of the glycans while increasing their stability in the hydrogel. It is predicted that FGF2 binding selectivity will be defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides on the array. The authors anticipate that a spatially isolated format will enable multiplexed analysis of a range of glycan structures while minimizing cellular crosstalk. A specific mechanistic prediction is that removal of 6-O, 2-O, and N-sulfate groups from HS will result in progressive loss of FGF2 binding activity. The platform is envisioned to enable systematic analysis of biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling and accelerate development of new bioactive glycomaterials.

Methodological Details
The substrate is a thin poly(acrylamide) hydrogel deposited on glass according to a method by Brafman et al. Gelatin (500 µg/mL) in PBS was loaded into the hydrogel in its dehydrated form to become entrapped within the crosslinked network. Heparin (12 kDa) was added in increasing concentrations from 50 to 750 g/mL as a model HS glycan. Heparin was crosslinked via NHS esters to solvent-exposed lysine residues in gelatin, activated by NHS in HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH = 7.4) with EDC at 4°C for 18 hours. The purified heparin-gelatin conjugate was analyzed by size exclusion on a PD10 column to remove small molecule reagents and byproducts. Crosslinking was targeted at ~15% carboxylic acid per chain to retain GAG in the hydrogel without compromising FGF2-binding ability. Cell culture was conducted at 37°C under 5% CO2 conditions. Slides were washed for 3 hours prior to staining with fluorescently labeled FGF2 (AlexaFluor 647) for imaging. FGF2 binding to heparin was selectively assessed using FGF2, the CS-specific antibody CS56, and the hyaluronic acid binding protein (HABP). Murine ESCs lacking Ext1 (Ext1 -/-ESCs), a glycosyl transferase responsible for HS assembly, were used to isolate arrayed GAG effects from endogenous cell-surface HS. Cells were seeded at 40,000 cells/cm2, producing consistent monolayers of Ext1 -/- ESCs that retained high Oct4 expression with no obvious Nestin-positive differentiation. The seeding density of 20,000 cells/cm2 produced slow growth and irregular colonies, while 100,000 cells/cm2 led to overgrowth and cell detachment. Cultivation proceeded for 24 hours in embryonic culture media supplemented with LIF and FBS, followed by 24 hours under serum-free conditions. For signaling, Ext1 -/-ESCs (40,000 cells/cm2) were grown for 48 hours under optimized culture and starvation conditions before stimulation. FGF2 (0.5 ng/mL) stimulation was applied for 15 min at 37°C in fresh serum-free media. Cells were fixed, permeabilized, and immunoassayed for Erk1/2 and pErk1/2 proteins. Soluble heparin (s-Hep, 5 g/mL) served as a positive control to restore MAPK activity in Ext1 -/-ESCs. ERK1/2 phosphorylation was quantified using ratios of pERK (green) to total ERK (red) signals. Fluorescence from the arrayed cells was detected using a microarray scanner and validated via fluorescence microscopy. ImageJ was used to confirm co-localization of pERK and ERK signals.

Procedures And Architectures
The platform generates hydrogel-based GAG microarrays by printing and physisorption of chemically crosslinked GAG-protein conjugates onto polyacrylamide hydrogel substrates. Gelatin was loaded in its dehydrated form, allowing the protein to enter and become entrapped within the crosslinked polymer network. Heparin was activated via NHS treatment in HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH = 7.4) with EDC at 4°C for 18 hours, then purified by size exclusion on a PD10 column. Crosslinking was targeted at ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain to promote GAG retention while maintaining GF-binding. Array substrates were prepared by depositing poly(acrylamide) hydrogel on glass, then spotted with a mixture of gelatin and crosslinked heparin. ESCs were seeded onto spots printed with gelatin (500 g/mL) and grown for 24 hours in embryonic culture media with LIF and FBS to establish colonies. The final 24 hours of culture were carried out under serum-free conditions to establish a signaling activity baseline. For the signaling assay, Ext1 -/-ESCs (40,000 cells/cm2) were grown on gelatin spots (500 g/mL) with or without NHS-crosslinked heparin (500 g/mL) for 48 hours. Cells were stimulated with FGF2 (0.5 ng/mL) for 15 min at 37°C, then fixed and permeabilized for immunofluorescence detection of ERK1/2 and pERK1/2. Fluorescence was detected using a microarray scanner, and the ratio of pERK to total ERK was quantified to measure signaling response. Soluble heparin (5 g/mL) was included as a positive control, benchmark, and to confirm that MAPK activity could be restored in Ext1 -/-ESCs. ERK1/2 protein levels were validated to be similar across all conditions, ensuring changes reflected phosphorylation rather than total protein expression. Fluorescence microscopy and ImageJ analysis confirmed co-localization of pERK and ERK signals, validating the quantification scheme.

Key Results
NHS-crosslinked heparin provided ~5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin on the array surface. After 48 hours of ESC culture at 37°C/5% CO2, ~40% of the FGF2 binding activity was retained on the NHS-crosslinked heparin arrays. FGF2 binding to heparin showed the greatest preference for fully sulfated heparin, followed by 2O- and 6O-sulfated heparin, respectively. Removal of 6-O, 2-O, and N-sulfate groups from heparin resulted in progressive loss of FGF2 binding activity. CS56 and HABP proteins exhibited high specificity for CS and HA, respectively, confirming the chemical integrity of the arrayed glycans. Only Ext1 -/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin showed a significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation. ERK1/2 protein levels were similar across all experimental conditions, indicating that differences in pERK reflected phosphorylation rather than total protein expression changes. Somewhat lower levels of MAPK activity were observed on the arrayed heparin compared to its soluble form, possibly due to limited FGFR accessibility. FGF2 stimulation of Ext1 -/-ESCs on gelatin spots containing increasing immobilized heparin (0-500 g/mL) showed a heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation. ERK1/2 phosphorylation was quantified as the ratio of pERK (green) to total ERK (red) fluorescence signals.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The NHS-crosslinking strategy preserves the protein-binding specificity of the GAGs while providing stability that non-covalent immobilization cannot sustain. The lower MAPK activity on the arrayed heparin compared to soluble form suggests that immobilization restricts FGFR accessibility to a subset of receptors at the cell-hydrogel interface. The platform demonstrates that a hydrogel-supported GAG microarray can directly capture and quantify FGF2-mediated signaling in live stem cells, validating the concept. The array offers a convenient platform to systematically analyze biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling, enabling a rapid structure-function approach. This platform can accelerate development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications by capitalizing on the expanding repertoire of synthetic, chemoenzymatic, and recombinant GAG structures.

Contradictions And Limitations
Only ~40% of the FGF2 binding activity was retained after 48 hours, indicating substantial loss of the immobilized heparin signal over time. Marked MAPK activity on arrayed heparin was somewhat lower than on soluble heparin, limiting direct comparison between immobilized and soluble forms. The limited accessibility of FGFRs at the point of cell contact with the array may constrain the maximal signaling output. Only the FGF2 growth factor was tested, limiting the scope of the platform to a single signaling pathway. Ext1 -/- murine ESCs were the only cell model used; the platform's generalizability to other cell types, species, or maturation stages is not demonstrated. The paper does not report N for independent experiments, p-values for statistical tests, or explicit quantification of the % loss after 48 hours. The crosslinking level of ~15% was targeted to avoid compromising FGF2-binding, but the exact tradeoff between retention and binding affinity is not fully quantified.

Claims
The NHS-crosslinking strategy provides stable GAG display on hydrogels that preserves protein-binding specificity while conferring retention during stem cell culture. NHS-crosslinked heparin provided 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal than non-covalently immobilized heparin. FGF2 binding was maintained on arrayed heparin after 48 hours of culture. Removal of sulfate groups resulted in progressive loss of activity consistent with known requirements, confirming specificity is maintained. Only ~40% binding activity was retained after 48 hours, representing a substantial degradation of the immobilized glycan. The platform can be extended to other GAGs and growth factors to build a comprehensive GAG-signaling atlas.
The hydrogel microarray platform can directly and multiplexedly profile FGF2-mediated MAPK signaling in live stem cells and is dose-responsive to heparin concentration. Ext1 -/-ESCs seeded at 40,000 cells/cm2 produced consistent monolayers showing ERK1/2 phosphorylation in response to FGF2. FGF2 stimulation (0.5 ng/mL, 15 min) produced dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation with immobilized heparin (0-500 g/mL). ERK1/2 protein levels were similar across all conditions, confirming changes are in phosphorylation, not total expression. MAPK activity on arrayed heparin was somewhat lower than on soluble heparin, indicating a potential dampening effect of immobilization. This enables rapid optimization of glycomaterials for stem cell differentiation and maturation by directly observing signaling outputs.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments used soluble heparin (5 g/mL) to confirm restoration of MAPK activity in Ext1 -/-ESCs as a positive benchmark. ERK1/2 protein levels were validated to be similar across all conditions, ensuring pERK/ERK ratios accurately reflect phosphorylation changes. Co-localization of pERK and ERK was confirmed via fluorescence microscopy and ImageJ analysis to validate the quantification scheme. Seeding densities were titrated from 20,000 to 100,000 cells/cm2 to optimize colony morphology and ERK1/2 signaling detectability. Glycan specificity was tested with CS56 and HABP antibodies to validate the chemical identity of immobilized heparin, CS, and HA.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the cellular microarray approach: (A) Gelatin hydrogels on acrylamide scaffold supporting ESC culture with GAGs; (B) Sulfation patterns of GAG classes. Figure 2 characterizes the hydrogel GAG arrays: (A) FGF2 binding to covalent vs. non-covalent heparin; (B) FGF2 retention after 48 hours; (C) GAG molecular recognition with FGF2, CS56, HABP on desulfated HS. Figure 3 shows ESC culture on the arrays: (A) Ext1 -/-ESCs at 40,000 cells/cm2 showing monolayer colonies; (B) Oct4 expression; (C) colony formation with 500 g/mL heparin under serum-free conditions. Figure 4 presents the on-array FGF2 signaling assay: (A) Ext1 -/-ESCs on gelatin with or without NHS-crosslinked heparin; (B) quantified ERK1/2 phosphorylation; (C) fluorescence microscopy images; (D) dose-response of ERK1/2 phosphorylation to 0-500 g/mL i-Hep. Figure S1 shows screening of surface passivation strategies for array construction. Figure S2 contains ImageJ analysis confirming co-localization of pERK and ERK.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform that combines covalently crosslinked GAG-protein conjugates with Exostosin 1-deficient ESCs to directly measure and multiplex FGF2-mediated signaling activity on arrayed GAGs. 2. The strongest evidence is the dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation in Ext1 -/-ESCs in response to 0-500 g/mL immobilized heparin, with NHS-crosslinking providing 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding while preserving desulfation-dependent specificity. 3. The future path lies in expanding the platform to additional GAGs and growth factors, and applying the systematic structure-function framework to the rapidly expanding repertoire of synthetic, chemoenzymatic, and recombinant GAG structures for bioactive glycomaterial design.
