summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal (University of Maryland); Priya Aggarwal (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology); Luiz Pessoa (University of Maryland); Anubha Gupta (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Neuroimaging / Deep Learning for Brain-Computer Interfaces
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a robust brain-state decoding framework using bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) networks applied to task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). The central challenge addressed is the inherent temporal latency and dynamics of the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response, which conventional unidirectional LSTMs—processing only past context—fail to fully capture. The authors propose that both past and future temporal information from fMRI time-series are crucial for accurate BOLD response representation, and their bi-LSTM architecture explicitly models these bidirectional dynamics without any manual time-delay adjustment. Validated on a working memory fMRI dataset including a 2-back and a 0-back task with four stimulus categories (tools, places, faces, body parts), the bi-LSTM outperformed the unidirectional LSTM by 18% in classification accuracy, achieving 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18. The study used 400 participants from the HCP 1200-subject data release, with 360 cortical regions of interest and 405 time-points per scan. The model architecture consisted of two hidden bi-LSTM layers with 256 hidden activations each, a fully-connected output layer with 9 neurons, dropout of 0.3, trained on a GTX 980 GPU with the ADAM optimizer for 100 epochs at a learning rate of 0.001 and batch size 32. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed. The paper also compares the bi-LSTM with a three-layer feed-forward neural network, demonstrating that temporal dependencies captured by recurrent architectures are essential for decoding. Key findings include that while the 'Others' class (fixation periods) remains the most misclassified, the bi-LSTM significantly reduces errors across all brain states compared to the unidirectional LSTM. The model occasionally confuses 'body' and 'tools' stimuli, suggesting specific cortical overlap. The authors conclude that bi-directional temporal modeling provides a principled, delay-free approach to capturing BOLD dynamics, with potential for further tuning of window size and overlap in future work.

claims.description: The bi-LSTM architecture outperforms the unidirectional LSTM in brain-state decoding by incorporating both past and future temporal context.
Temporal dependencies captured by recurrent networks are essential for accurate brain-state decoding, as evidenced by the superior performance of the LSTM over the feed-forward neural network.
The bi-LSTM does not require hard-coded time-delay adjustment for synchronization of stimuli and BOLD response, unlike previous works.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a robust brain-state decoding framework using bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) networks applied to task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). The central challenge addressed is the inherent temporal latency and dynamics of the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response, which conventional unidirectional LSTMs—processing only past context—fail to fully capture. The authors propose that both past and future temporal information from fMRI time-series are crucial for accurate BOLD response representation, and their bi-LSTM architecture explicitly models these bidirectional dynamics without any manual time-delay adjustment. Validated on a working memory fMRI dataset including a 2-back and a 0-back task with four stimulus categories (tools, places, faces, body parts), the bi-LSTM outperformed the unidirectional LSTM by 18% in classification accuracy, achieving 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18. The study used 400 participants from the HCP 1200-subject data release, with 360 cortical regions of interest and 405 time-points per scan. The model architecture consisted of two hidden bi-LSTM layers with 256 hidden activations each, a fully-connected output layer with 9 neurons, dropout of 0.3, trained on a GTX 980 GPU with the ADAM optimizer for 100 epochs at a learning rate of 0.001 and batch size 32. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed. The paper also compares the bi-LSTM with a three-layer feed-forward neural network, demonstrating that temporal dependencies captured by recurrent architectures are essential for decoding. Key findings include that while the 'Others' class (fixation periods) remains the most misclassified, the bi-LSTM significantly reduces errors across all brain states compared to the unidirectional LSTM. The model occasionally confuses 'body' and 'tools' stimuli, suggesting specific cortical overlap. The authors conclude that bi-directional temporal modeling provides a principled, delay-free approach to capturing BOLD dynamics, with potential for further tuning of window size and overlap in future work.

Research Context
Decoding brain states from underlying cognitive processes via learning discriminative feature representations has gained substantial interest in brain imaging studies. Particularly, there has been an impetus to encode the dynamics of brain functioning by analyzing temporal information available in fMRI data. Long short-term memory models possess a memory component and have been observed to perform well in applications with dynamic temporal behavior, including brain state decoding. Because of the dynamics and inherent latency in fMRI BOLD responses, future temporal context is crucial for accurate representation. However, future temporal context is neither encoded nor captured by the conventional unidirectional LSTM model. Conventional decoding methods involved massive univariate analysis measuring activity from thousands of brain locations, analyzing each separately, which does not integrate distributed overlapping information. Multivariate analysis takes into account brain activity at several locations simultaneously to integrate distributed but overlapping information across the spatial domain. During fMRI data acquisition, the ratio of oxygenated to de-oxygenated blood serves as the representative of underlying neuronal activation. Due to the time-lag observed in the peak of the BOLD response, it is typically not considered synchronized with the presentation of stimuli. Before training brain-state decoding models, each time point is typically adjusted according to the estimated delay of the BOLD signal, assuming all voxels have the same response delay. Recurrent Neural Networks, including LSTM models, have shown to perform better than conventional decoding models in characterizing dynamic fMRI information during both naturalistic and task conditions. Previous fMRI studies have used LSTM networks for integrating temporal information from the past, but not from the future.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether incorporating future temporal context via a bidirectional LSTM architecture improves brain-state decoding accuracy compared to a conventional unidirectional LSTM. The authors assert that because of the variations in latency of BOLD responses across time, temporal context from the future is also important for capturing the dynamics of BOLD response in order to generate accurate representations. The hypothesis is that a bidirectional LSTM architecture, which acquires information from both past and future time-instances, will outperform its unidirectional counterpart in predicting brain states. The bidirectional LSTM is expected to model the dynamics of the BOLD response without any hard-coded time-delay adjustment for synchronization of stimuli and BOLD response, unlike previous works. The prediction is that the two hidden activations of forward and reverse directions, when collated, build a superior memory of the model used to robustly predict brain states at every time instance. The experimental comparison also seeks to determine whether temporal dependencies, captured by recurrent architectures, add value over spatial-only features provided by a feed-forward neural network. The study explicitly aims to evaluate the bi-LSTM framework on the working memory task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project for validation. The predicted outcome is an increase in classification accuracy and a more balanced confusion matrix across all nine brain states when bidirectional temporal context is included.

Methodological Details
The study evaluated the bi-LSTM framework on task fMRI data of the working memory from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) data release. Participants performed a working memory task, indicating if the current stimulus matches with the one presented two stimuli before, called the 2-back task, or a control condition called 0-back. The working memory task from HCP also combines the category representation task, with participants presented with separate blocks of trials consisting of 4 different types of stimuli: tools, places, faces, and body parts. Stimuli blocks were separated with fixation periods. Data for two runs was available for each participant. Within each run, there were 8 task blocks for every task (2-back or 0-back) and stimuli (places, tools, faces, body) combination. Each task block lasted for 27.5 seconds, with 4 fixation blocks of 15 seconds each after two task blocks. Each scan resulted in a 405 time-points long sequence of fMRI volumes. N = 400 participants were randomly selected from the N = 1200 data release for the evaluation. The cortical parcellation method collated the individual voxels within each region by averaging to generate 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs). The region-averaged timeseries was used as the input feature vector for the temporal analysis. The generated 405 time-points sequence of 360 ROIs were structured in a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed to adjust for delay in the BOLD response in the bi-LSTM network. Each time-point in task blocks was marked as present in one of the brain states, and time instants belonging to fixation blocks were labeled as others, yielding a total of S = 9 brain states. The available preprocessed data contained field-map based distortion correction, functional to structural alignment, and intensity normalization. Motion-related variables (6 translation parameters and their derivatives) were regressed-out using 3dDeconvolve with the ortvec option in the AFNI software. Changes in low-frequency signals were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve with the polort option. Only cortical data, directly available in surface representation as a part of the HCP preprocessing pipeline, was used to evaluate the general brain-state decoding methodology.

Procedures And Architectures
The bi-LSTM architecture consisted of two hidden bi-LSTM layers, with each LSTM cell having 256 hidden activations to encode temporal dependencies. A schematic illustration of the bidirectional LSTM is provided in Fig. 1, showing it processes time-series data in both directions using separate hidden layers. The forward hidden activation h_t^l is computed using the standard LSTM transition equations, while the backward hidden activation h_t^l is calculated using future temporal dependency. The input to the subsequent layer is generated by combining both forward and backward hidden activations using a merging scheme. Three possible merging schemes were evaluated: vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise vector addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). The last layer of the bi-LSTM is followed by a fully-connected layer having S = 9 neurons and softmax activation, used to learn a mapping from feature representations to brain states. Input activations at time t were extracted from the 360 brain ROIs, and inputs to subsequent LSTM layers were the hidden activations of the previous layer. The proposed model was implemented in the Keras deep learning framework. The model was trained on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with a batch size of 32, using the ADAM optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001. The model was trained for 100 epochs with no early stopping performed. To prevent over-fitting, a dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers for training. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed, where N = 400 participants were divided into 10 parts, with 9 parts (N = 360 subjects) for model development and the remaining part (N = 40 subjects) held out for evaluation. The development set was randomly shuffled and split into 80-20 training-validation sets to tune hyperparameters and prevent over-fitting. The full-length training data was windowed into small overlapping sizes with window size w = 40 and an overlap of 10 points. Because the number of time-instances of class others was much larger than any other class, weights for the imbalanced classes were estimated using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine and applied during loss function calculation. The learning process, called Backpropagation through time (BPTT), estimates the parameters that allow data in the cells either to be retained or deleted. The transition equations involve the forget gate, input gate, cell activation, and hidden activation, with sigmoid activation for gating and softmax activation for the final classification. The unidirectional LSTM was built with the same specifications as in reference [12] for fair comparison. A three-layer feed-forward neural network (ff-NN) using ROIs at individual time points as features, discarding temporal dependencies, was also included for comparison.

Key Results
Mean normalised confusion matrices on the classification accuracy are illustrated in Fig. 2, comparing the miss-classifications of both LSTM and bi-LSTM-c. The overall accuracy of the unidirectional LSTM model was 0.66 ± 0.18. The classification accuracy of the bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM-c) was 0.84 ± 0.02, representing an 18% absolute improvement. For every brain-state, the LSTM model misclassified to a larger extent compared to the bi-LSTM-c model, although misclassification is highest for both models in the Others class. The second highest confusion, when participants were stimulated with faces and places, is with the task (0-back or 2-back), though the stimuli were detected correctly. The model also gets confused between the stimuli body and tools, indicating shared representation space. The bi-LSTM-c (vector concatenation) performed best among the merging schemes, with bi-LSTM-a (addition) and bi-LSTM-µ (averaging) yielding lower accuracy. The ff-NN, which used ROIs at individual time points discarding temporal dependencies, performed worse than both the LSTM and bi-LSTM, confirming the importance of temporal modeling. The improvement in accuracy from 0.66 to 0.84 (+0.18 absolute; approximately 27.3% relative) supports the hypothesis that bidirectional temporal context is critical.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The superior performance of the bi-LSTM supports the assertion that temporal context from future time-instances is essential for capturing the dynamics of BOLD response. The fact that the model works without any hard-coded delay adjustment emphasizes the availability of useful information in immediate future samples. The confusion between body and tools stimuli suggests that the model is learning representations that overlap across these categories, warranting further cortical region analysis. The 18% improvement over the unidirectional LSTM demonstrates the added value of bidirectional gating in capturing delayed BOLD dynamics. The method provides a principled approach to brain-state decoding that naturally accounts for BOLD latency without heuristic delay alignment. The findings imply that the temporal structure of fMRI data encodes complementary information in both past and future directions, both of which contribute to the representation of the underlying brain state.

Contradictions And Limitations
The misclassification is highest for both models in the Others class (fixation periods), indicating that the model still struggles to perfectly distinguish fixation from active task states. The model occasionally confuses body and tools stimuli, and the exact cortical regions responsible for this confusion remain to be studied. The class imbalance problem, although handled with Sklearn's compute_class_weight, still requires more sophisticated handling as the Others class frequency dominates. The window size was fixed at w = 40 with overlap of 10, but the authors note that future work may involve tuning the window size and overlap for time-series chunking. The inter-subject cross-validation framework limits the evaluation to the 400 selected HCP participants and does not account for inter-dataset generalization. No early stopping was performed, and the model was trained for a fixed 100 epochs, which may not be optimal for all data configurations. The study does not report performance across different brain regions or stimulus conditions separately beyond the aggregate accuracy.

Claims
The bi-LSTM architecture outperforms the unidirectional LSTM in brain-state decoding by incorporating both past and future temporal context. The bidirectional LSTM achieved accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional counterpart, an 18% absolute improvement. The confusion matrices in Fig. 2 show lower miss-classification rates for bi-LSTM-c across all brain states compared to the LSTM. The bi-LSTM-c (vector concatenation) outperformed addition and averaging merging schemes. The Others class (fixation periods) remains the most misclassified state for both models, indicating incomplete separation of task and non-task states. The model confuses body and tools stimuli, suggesting imperfect discrimination in specific regions. The bi-directional architecture provides a principled way to capture BOLD dynamics without heuristic delay adjustments. The results support the generalizability of the bi-LSTM approach to other brain-state decoding tasks.
Temporal dependencies captured by recurrent networks are essential for accurate brain-state decoding, as evidenced by the superior performance of the LSTM over the feed-forward neural network. The LSTM models outperformed the ff-NN, which used ROIs at individual time points and discarded temporal dependencies. Both the LSTM and bi-LSTM outperformed the ff-NN, demonstrating that temporal structure carries decoding-relevant information. The bi-LSTM improvement over the unidirectional LSTM (18%) is substantial, but the baseline LSTM still achieves 0.66 accuracy, suggesting spatial features also carry significant information. Future brain-decoding models should prioritize temporal modeling alongside spatial feature extraction. The spatial-temporal interplay in fMRI data requires multi-dimensional modeling approaches.
The bi-LSTM does not require hard-coded time-delay adjustment for synchronization of stimuli and BOLD response, unlike previous works. The authors explicitly state this framework does not require any time-delay adjustment unlike previous works. The bi-directional architecture naturally incorporates both past and future context, eliminating the need for a single heuristic delay estimate. While no explicit delay adjustment was performed, the authors acknowledge that latency variations still affect the BOLD response, and the model still makes errors on the Others class. The approach simplifies BCI pipeline development by removing the heuristic delay-estimation step. Further work could investigate whether different delay-free models (e.g., TCNs, transformers) offer comparable or better performance.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model was evaluated using three different merging schemes for forward and backward hidden activations: vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise vector addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). Vector concatenation was found to yield the best performance, as evidenced by the comparison of confusion matrices. A three-layer feed-forward neural network (ff-NN) served as an ablation model, using ROIs at individual time points without temporal dependencies, demonstrating that temporal modeling is crucial. The unidirectional LSTM served as a baseline, using the same specifications (2 hidden layers, 256 units each) to ensure a fair comparison. The model used inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation to ensure robustness across different participants. The development set was split into 80-20 training-validation sets for hyperparameter tuning, providing a separate validation set from the held-out test fold. The window size w = 40 with overlap of 10 was fixed, and future work may tune these parameters. Class imbalance was addressed using Sklearn's compute_class_weight, but the authors note that more sophisticated handling may still be needed.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 provides a schematic illustration of the Bi-directional LSTM, showing the separate forward and backward hidden layers and the merging of activations. Figure 2 illustrates the mean normalised confusion matrices for LSTM and bi-LSTM-c, comparing miss-classification patterns across all brain states. The confusion matrices reveal that the highest miss-classification is the Others class, and that body and tools stimuli are occasionally confused.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a bidirectional LSTM framework for brain-state decoding that incorporates both past and future fMRI temporal context, achieving 0.84 ± 0.02 accuracy on a 9-state working memory classification task. 2. The strongest evidence is the 18% absolute accuracy improvement of bi-LSTM-c over unidirectional LSTM, along with the ablation confirming that the ff-NN (discarding temporal dependencies) performs worse, and the fact that no heuristic BOLD delay adjustment is required. 3. Future work should involve tuning window size and overlap, developing more sophisticated class-imbalance handling, analyzing cortical regions engaged in body vs. tools discrimination, and extending to other brain-state decoding tasks.

summary.executive_summary:
This phylogenetic and comparative genomic study investigates the taxonomic relationships among the thermophilic, spore-forming genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus (all family Bacillaceae) using 113 publicly available whole-genome sequences plus one outgroup (114 total genomes). The authors constructed a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree based on 662 orthologous core genes identified via EDGAR 2.0, using Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 as the starting reference and Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T as the outgroup. Additionally, two-way average nucleotide identity (ANI) and average amino acid identity (AAI) similarity matrices were calculated using ani.rb and aai.rb scripts, with UPGMA dendrograms constructed via DendroUPGMA and visualized in Interactive Tree Of Life. The study also identified unique candidate genes using BLASTn with relaxed criteria (30% identity, bitscore 10, 1% overlap). 

The core gene ML tree partitions the genomes into two main clades: Clade I (87 genomes) containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, and Clade II (24 Anoxybacillus genomes) containing the majority of Anoxybacillus. Clade I is further subdivided into three distinct sub-clades, with the authors proposing the third sub-clade be elevated to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Specifically, two species in Clade I-c (A. tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies) are placed in Quasigeobacillus. The ANI and AAI values further support this, with Quasigeobacillus showing closer affinity to Parageobacillus than to the other three genera. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning across different methods and remain unresolved. The study also reconfirms the 2016 reclassification of G. galactosidasius and G. yumthangensis to Parageobacillus. The authors conclude that combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera is essential for accurate taxonomic delimitation, as single-genus analyses would obscure the incongruent placement of clade I-c genomes previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This phylogenetic and comparative genomic study investigates the taxonomic relationships among the thermophilic, spore-forming genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus (all family Bacillaceae) using 113 publicly available whole-genome sequences plus one outgroup (114 total genomes). The authors constructed a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree based on 662 orthologous core genes identified via EDGAR 2.0, using Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 as the starting reference and Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T as the outgroup. Additionally, two-way average nucleotide identity (ANI) and average amino acid identity (AAI) similarity matrices were calculated using ani.rb and aai.rb scripts, with UPGMA dendrograms constructed via DendroUPGMA and visualized in Interactive Tree Of Life. The study also identified unique candidate genes using BLASTn with relaxed criteria (30% identity, bitscore 10, 1% overlap). 

The core gene ML tree partitions the genomes into two main clades: Clade I (87 genomes) containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, and Clade II (24 Anoxybacillus genomes) containing the majority of Anoxybacillus. Clade I is further subdivided into three distinct sub-clades, with the authors proposing the third sub-clade be elevated to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Specifically, two species in Clade I-c (A. tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies) are placed in Quasigeobacillus. The ANI and AAI values further support this, with Quasigeobacillus showing closer affinity to Parageobacillus than to the other three genera. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning across different methods and remain unresolved. The study also reconfirms the 2016 reclassification of G. galactosidasius and G. yumthangensis to Parageobacillus. The authors conclude that combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera is essential for accurate taxonomic delimitation, as single-genus analyses would obscure the incongruent placement of clade I-c genomes previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus.

Research Context
For decades, DNA-DNA hybridization served as the gold standard for bacterial taxonomy, establishing species boundaries based on genomic similarity. 16S rRNA gene sequencing provided an alternative approach but suffers from low-resolution results in high sequence similarities among bacterial genera and species, limiting its usefulness for fine-scale classification. As an alternative to 16S rRNA, average nucleotide identity (ANI) values offer higher resolution for detecting relatedness among closely related bacterial genomes by comparing two sequences with BLAST. For comparisons between more distant genomes, average amino acid identity (AAI) is recommended because amino acid similarity is better conserved in homologous protein sequences than DNA. The genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus belong to the family Bacillaceae and are moderate thermophiles capable of spore formation for long-term survival. Anoxybacillus was proposed in 2000, Geobacillus in 2001, and Parageobacillus in 2016 through successive taxonomic revisions based on phylogenetic evidence and GC content. Prior to this study, these genera were often analyzed in isolation, raising questions about whether single-genus phylogenies accurately reflect inter-generic relationships.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is what are the phylogenomic relationships among the closely related thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus, and how do 7 newly isolated strains of these genera position within the established phylogeny. The authors hypothesize that the three genera are closely related and should be considered together in any phylogenetic or comparative genomic assessment to reveal true delimitation boundaries. They predict that the combined phylogenetic signals from the core gene tree, ANI dendrogram, and AAI dendrogram will consistently delineate the genera, but may also reveal incongruencies that single-genus analyses would mask. A specific hypothesis is that certain clades currently assigned to one genus may actually belong to a distinct, unrecognised taxonomic group, warranting the description of a new genus. The authors further test whether the two newly isolated strains from Australia can be assigned with confidence to existing genera or if they require new classification. The predicted outcome is a refined classification of these three genera, including the confirmation of prior reclassifications (e.g., G. galactosidasius) and the proposal of a new genus for unresolved clades.

Methodological Details
The study used a total of 113 genome assemblies from the RefSeq database, comprising 32 Anoxybacillus strains, 73 Geobacillus strains, and 8 Parageobacillus strains (one per validly described species). Additionally, 7 newly isolated strains from a study of thermophiles in Australia were included, bringing the total to 114 genomes including one outgroup. This group contained 31 chromosome-level assemblies, 33 scaffold genomes, and 49 genomes at the contig level. Anomalous genome assemblies with suppressed RefSeq status, including those identified as chimeric, contaminated, or frameshifted, were excluded from the study. The outgroup was selected as Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T, and the starting reference for core genome identification was Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2. During core gene discovery, five assemblies with relatively low numbers of CDS were excluded because they significantly reduced the number of core genes recognised, and one assembly was removed as an exact duplicate of another Anoxybacillus strain. The core gene set was identified using EDGAR 2.0, in which CDS from the starting reference were iteratively compared against all selected assemblies via BLAST to find orthologs. The obtained CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE, then used to build a maximum-likelihood tree with the FastTree software package. ANI and AAI values were calculated between all pairs of genomes using the ani.rb and aai.rb scripts from the enveomics package, with default parameters and 100 N bases inserted between contig boundaries for draft genomes. Similarity matrices from ANI and AAI were input to the DendroUPGMA web server using the unweighted pair group with arithmetic mean (UPGMA) clustering method to produce dendrograms. Trees were plotted using the web-based Interactive Tree Of Life tool. Genes unique to clade I-c were identified using BLASTn with relaxed filtering criteria: percentage identity 30%, bitscore 10, and percentage overlap of 1%. The BLASTn alignment used the CDS of Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 as a query against all assemblies in the NCBI RefSeq and nt databases. CDS found in all members of clade I-c and in no members of clades I-a, I-b, or II were considered unique to clade I-c. Methods were based on those used by Aliyu et al. (2016) for reassessment of the genus Geobacillus.

Procedures And Architectures
The study followed a stepwise bioinformatic workflow: first, core genes were identified from the bacterial genome group using EDGAR 2.0 to produce a common orthologous gene set. The genome of Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 served as the reference; all its CDS were compared against all other assemblies to identify orthologs, resulting in a core genome comprising the full set of CDS for which orthologs are present across all assemblies. Once core genes were identified, they were concatenated and aligned using the MUSCLE algorithm. The resulting multiple sequence alignment was used to construct a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree with the FastTree package. For the ANI and AAI calculations, all pairs of genomes were compared; the ani.rb script was used for ANI and the aai.rb script for AAI, both from the enveomics package. Draft genomes were processed by concatenating contigs with 100 N bases introduced between them before sequence comparison. The resulting similarity values were arranged into similarity matrices and processed through the DendroUPGMA web server using UPGMA clustering. For the visualization of all trees, the Interactive Tree Of Life web-based tool was used. The unique gene identification procedure used BLASTn alignment of Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 CDS against the entire NCBI RefSeq and nt databases with the specified relaxed criteria. GC content and genome size were calculated for all genomes, and the tree topology, GC contents, and ANI values were combined for taxonomic delimitation, following the protocol of Aliyu et al. (2016). The entire workflow was applied to the 114 genomes (113 + 1 outgroup) and the final results were tabulated across seven tables and three figures for comprehensive reporting.

Key Results
A total of thirty-two Anoxybacillus, seventy-three Geobacillus, eight Parageobacillus, and one Bacillus genome produced a core gene set of 662 orthologous genes per genome, used to construct the ML tree with 114 genomes. The core gene ML tree splits into three major groups: the outgroup, Clade I, and Clade II. Clade I consists of eighty-seven genomes, while Clade II consists of twenty-four Anoxybacillus genomes. Clade I is further partitioned into three sub-clades: Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade containing A. tepidamans and one genomospecies, which the authors propose as Quasigeobacillus. The ANI and AAI dendrograms (Figure 2 and Figure 3) reconstruct the same three-clade structure from the ML tree, confirming the partitioning of Clade I. Two-way ANI values between specific pairs are reported: Geobacillus sp. EFIL (97.99), Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3 (97.14), and Geobacillus sp. DSP4a (97.64), indicating they are within the common species threshold. The most distant ANI value was 95.03 and the corresponding AAI was 95.81, observed between Anoxybacillus sp. CHMUD and other genomes. A total of 6 CDS were found to be unique to clade I-c, present in all members of the clade and in no members of other clades. The mean ANI and AAI values suggest that the candidate new genus (Quasigeobacillus) is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus than to the other existing three genera. GC content also suggests a closer affinity of the new genus to Parageobacillus (Table 2). The structure of all three phylogenetic trees (core gene ML, ANI UPGMA, AAI UPGMA) reaffirms the distinctiveness of the two species in clade I-c with respect to the three existing genera. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning among the trees produced by differing methods and could not be clearly resolved. The data agrees with the prior conclusion that G. galactosidasius and G. yumthangensis should be reclassified as Parageobacillus, and the study follows this classification.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary theoretical implication is that combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera is essential for accurate taxonomic delimitation; individual-genus analyses would obscure the incongruent placement of genomes that bridge genera. When genus designation for new strains is determined without broader phylogenetic assessment, the designation can become incongruent with the phylogeny of the underlying complete set of available genomes. For example, the genomes of clade I-c were previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus, but when the two genera are considered together, clade I-c is seen to be outside of either, justifying the new genus. The study demonstrates that genomic proximity (ANI/AAI) alone may be insufficient for genus delimitation, as the three genera are so closely related that thresholds between them are blurred without core-gene phylogenetic context. The proposal of Quasigeobacillus extends the taxonomic framework of the Bacillaceae, incorporating previously unresolved genomes into a formally defined genus that reflects true evolutionary relationships.

Contradictions And Limitations
Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning among the three tree types, and their affinities remain unresolved. The study was not certified by peer review (preprint version), and all conclusions should be treated as preliminary until formal publication. Only 113 available genomes were used, representing a snapshot of the extant genome assemblies and not necessarily a complete sampling of the genetic diversity in these genera. A genome sequence for Geobacillus zalihae was available in GenBank, but the name has not been validly published, limiting its use in formal taxonomy. The reliance on the EDGAR 2.0 tool and a single starting reference (G. thermodenitrificans) for core gene identification introduces potential bias compared to orthogonal methods. The outgroup was chosen based on established relationships, but an alternative outgroup could potentially yield a different tree topology.

Claims
The genomes in clade I-c of the combined Anoxybacillus-Geobacillus-Parageobacillus phylogeny constitute a distinct taxonomic unit that should be elevated to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., rather than being assigned to existing genera. The core gene ML tree, ANI dendrogram, and AAI dendrogram all consistently group the two species of clade I-c together and apart from the three existing genera. A total of 6 CDS were found unique to clade I-c, supporting the hypothesis of a distinct evolutionary lineage. The mean ANI and AAI values position the new genus closer to Parageobacillus than to Geobacillus or Anoxybacillus, supporting a paraphyletic relationship with Parageobacillus. GC content also supports the closer affinity of clade I-c to Parageobacillus. An alternative approach could be to merge the two species with Parageobacillus, but the authors note this would then support merging Parageobacillus with Geobacillus, undermining the tripartite genus structure. Two species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) still cannot be resolved into any of the four genera, leaving a gap in the classification scheme. The creation of Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. provides a formally recognized taxonomic home for genomes previously misclassified, improving the accuracy of genomic affinity assignments. The study highlights that taxonomies based on individual genus boundaries are prone to error when closely related genera are not considered simultaneously.
Combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera is essential for accurate taxonomic delimitation and assignment of new genomes to genera. Clade I-c genomes were previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus in single-genus analyses but fell outside both genera in the combined analysis. The three-clade structure was consistently recovered by all three methods (ML tree, ANI, AAI), increasing confidence in the combined signal. The study explicitly states that without broader phylogenetic assessment, genus designation for new strains can become incongruent with the underlying phylogeny. The two unresolved species (A. vitaminiphilus, A. amylolyticus) show that even with combined analysis, some genomes remain unassignable. Future taxonomic revisions should adopt a combined-genus approach rather than single-genus workflows to prevent misclassification. This paradigm shift has implications for how all bacterial genomes of related genera are curated and taxonomically assigned.
The 2016 reclassification of Geobacillus galactosidasius and Geobacillus yumthangensis to Parageobacillus is confirmed by the combined phylogenomic data. The data from the present study agrees with the conclusion that these two should belong to Parageobacillus. The authors state they are following this reclassification for the taxonomy used in this study. No direct contradictory evidence is presented within the paper for this reclassification. This reconfirmation solidifies the current taxonomic arrangement of the Bacillaceae thermophile genera.

Data And Code Availability
Genomes were obtained from the RefSeq database. The ani.rb and aai.rb Ruby scripts are publicly available in the enveomics package. The core gene discovery, ML tree construction, and ANI/AAI workflows use publicly available bioinformatic tools (EDGAR 2.0, FastTree, MUSCLE, DendroUPGMA, Interactive Tree Of Life). The genome assemblies used are listed in Supplementary Table S1, and excluded assemblies in Supplementary Table S2.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Five assemblies with relatively low numbers of CDS were excluded during core gene identification because they significantly reduced the number of core genes recognised. One Anoxybacillus Suryakundensis strain was removed as it was an exact duplicate of another assembly. Anomalous genome assemblies with suppressed RefSeq status (chimeric, contaminated, frameshifted) were excluded from the analysis. Two-way ANI and AAI similarity matrices were calculated between all pairs of genomes to ensure robustness of the UPGMA dendrograms. The relaxed BLASTn criteria (30% identity, bitscore 10, 1% overlap) were applied to identify unique clade I-c genes against the entire RefSeq and nt databases.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the core gene maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree with 114 genomes, illustrating the outgroup, clade I, and clade II. Figure 2 shows the UPGMA dendrogram of two-way ANI values calculated between all genome pairs for 114 genomes. Figure 3 shows the UPGMA dendrogram of two-way AAI values calculated between all genome pairs for 114 genomes. Table 3 presents the two-way ANI and AAI values between specific genome pairs, including those for the candidate new genus and key Geobacillus strains. Table 4 lists the 6 CDS unique to clade I-c with their names, descriptions, and products. Table 5 presents the DNA sequences for each of the 6 unique clade I-c CDS. Table 6 shows the BLASTn alignment results of these 6 CDS against all members of clade I-c. Table 7 shows the best BLAST hits for each of the 6 unique CDS. Table 1 presents the mean ANI and AAI values separating the candidate new genus from the members of the existing three genera. Table 2 presents genome characteristics including GC content (%) for the analyzed genomes. Supplementary Table S1 lists all genome assemblies included in the core gene analysis. Supplementary Table S2 lists the assemblies removed during the core gene discovery process.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the demonstration that combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera is essential for accurate taxonomic delimitation, revealing that clade I-c genomes previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus actually form a distinct taxonomic unit that warrants the description of Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. The strongest evidence is the consistent recovery of the same three-clade structure across three independent genomic metrics (core gene ML tree, ANI UPGMA, and AAI UPGMA), supported by 6 unique CDS for clade I-c and specific ANI/AAI values that position the new genus closer to Parageobacillus. The future path involves formal description of Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., continued genomic sampling of these three genera to resolve the unresolved A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, and adoption of a multi-genus phylogenomic workflow for bacterial taxonomic assignment.

summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal; Cinthia R Millan; Samantha I Zangari; Samantha Avila; Dewight Williams; Tarjani M Thaker; Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.field_subfield: Structural biology; ABC transporter regulation; Cryo-EM

summary.executive_summary: This study reports the first structural determination of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae glutathione transporter Ycf1 in an ordered regulatory domain state. Using cryo-EM, the authors determined two inward-facing conformations (IFwide at 3.4Å and IFnarrow at 4.0Å) of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1. The most striking finding is that the intrinsically disordered R-domain (residues 901-935), which was previously unassigned in sequence and unmodeled in other ABCC structures, is in a partially ordered helical conformation (residues 920-929) and is phosphorylated at three specific sites: S908, T911, and S914. The R-domain encircles NBD1 and is stabilized by extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts along a basic groove of NBD1, the intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain. The interactions are maintained between both conformations, with the R-domain/NBD1 complex related by rigid-body movements relative to NBD2. A rearrangement within the R-domain (angle change of 7.5º) correlates with the transition to the narrow conformation, where ATP binding sites are occluded. Biochemical data from ATPase assays show that dephosphorylation via lambda phosphatase drastically reduces ATPase activity, and that GSSG stimulates activity at physiologically relevant µM concentrations. The hydrophobic surface burying (~1530 Å² in IFnarrow and ~1338 Å² in IFwide) provides a large thermodynamic driving force for R-domain engagement. These findings challenge the prevailing model that the R-domain must be fully released between NBDs upon phosphorylation, and instead propose that phosphorylated engagement with NBD1/lasso represents a stimulatory architecture. The authors also identify a negative regulatory phosphosite at S251 in the lasso domain and note that the NBD1 architecture bears striking similarity to clinically relevant CFTR mutations and lumacaftor binding. The structures provide a general mechanism for ABCC transporter regulation that may be applicable beyond Ycf1.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the first structural determination of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae glutathione transporter Ycf1 in an ordered regulatory domain state. Using cryo-EM, the authors determined two inward-facing conformations (IFwide at 3.4Å and IFnarrow at 4.0Å) of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1. The most striking finding is that the intrinsically disordered R-domain (residues 901-935), which was previously unassigned in sequence and unmodeled in other ABCC structures, is in a partially ordered helical conformation (residues 920-929) and is phosphorylated at three specific sites: S908, T911, and S914. The R-domain encircles NBD1 and is stabilized by extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts along a basic groove of NBD1, the intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain. The interactions are maintained between both conformations, with the R-domain/NBD1 complex related by rigid-body movements relative to NBD2. A rearrangement within the R-domain (angle change of 7.5º) correlates with the transition to the narrow conformation, where ATP binding sites are occluded. Biochemical data from ATPase assays show that dephosphorylation via lambda phosphatase drastically reduces ATPase activity, and that GSSG stimulates activity at physiologically relevant µM concentrations. The hydrophobic surface burying (~1530 Å² in IFnarrow and ~1338 Å² in IFwide) provides a large thermodynamic driving force for R-domain engagement. These findings challenge the prevailing model that the R-domain must be fully released between NBDs upon phosphorylation, and instead propose that phosphorylated engagement with NBD1/lasso represents a stimulatory architecture. The authors also identify a negative regulatory phosphosite at S251 in the lasso domain and note that the NBD1 architecture bears striking similarity to clinically relevant CFTR mutations and lumacaftor binding. The structures provide a general mechanism for ABCC transporter regulation that may be applicable beyond Ycf1.

Research Context
Ycf1 transports the tripeptide glutathione into vacuoles to maintain redox balance and detoxify heavy metals. Ycf1 also functions as a major redox sink, sequestering oxidized glutathione in the cytoplasm. Approximately half of all human ABC transporters are phosphorylated, suggesting post-translational tuning of transport function. The R-domain was experimentally confirmed to have as low as 5% helical content by CD and proteolysis. Cryo-EM structures of human CFTR and Ycf1 revealed a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned sequence for phosphorylation sites. To date, no structure of an intact R-domain with the NBDs has been determined in any state.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how R-domain phosphorylation regulates the structural and functional properties of Ycf1. The authors hypothesized that phosphorylation of the R-domain induces structural reorganization and is required for maximal ATPase activity. They predicted that phosphorylation would promote electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions between the R-domain, NBD1, and the lasso domain. The hypothesis was that the R-domain would transition from a disordered state to an ordered, bound conformation upon phosphorylation. They further hypothesized that dephosphorylation would abolish the regulatory architecture and reduce ATPase rates. A complementary hypothesis was that the lasso domain phosphorylation at S251 could negatively regulate transport through electrostatic repulsion.

Methodological Details
S. cerevisiae Ycf1 was codon-optimized and expressed in the DSY-5 yeast strain. Two forms were purified: wild-type Ycf1 and the NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. Two inward-facing conformations were determined to 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution by cryo-EM. The R-domain spans residues 901-935 with a helical segment at residues 920-929. Phosphorylation was assigned to S908, T911, and S914 based on electron density and mass spectrometry. E1435Q showed reduced ATPase activity with a Vmax of 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg. ATPase assays used 6.45 µg protein in a mix with 20 mM Tris-HCl, 10 mM MgCl₂, and 1 mM PEP. Substrate-stimulated ATPase with GSSG was measured at 30ºC with NADPH-coupled enzyme assay. Dephosphorylation was achieved by treating purified Ycf1 with lambda phosphatase for 45 min at 4ºC. Limited proteolysis was performed with trypsin at concentrations from 0.5 to 15 µg/mL for 30 min on ice. Evolutionary coupling analysis identified 13,723 sequences from the Uniref90 database. Cryo-EM processing used RELION 3.0, 3.1, MotionCor2, and CTFFIND4.1 for drift correction and CTF estimation. Particle picking was manual and reference-free 2D classification was used for automated picking. A 15º degree angular search was used for automatic particle picking in the E1435Q dataset. LC-MS/MS with Scaffold Q+S v4.11.1 quantified phosphorylation with Bayesian statistics.

Procedures And Architectures
Ycf1 was cloned into p423_GAL1 with N-terminal Flag and C-terminal 10X His tags. Primary culture was grown for 24 hours at 30°C in SC-His media, followed by 16 hours induction with galactose. Protein purification involved lysis in buffer with 300 mM NaCl and protease inhibitors. E1435Q mutant was selected because it yielded homogeneous particles suitable for structural determination. Cryo-EM maps were processed in RELION and cisTEM, producing maps at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution. Initial model building used the SWISS-MODEL server with 6jb1 as a template. Refinement included real-space refinement in Phenix, map sharpening/blurring in CCP-EM, and geometry optimization in Modrefiner. Isolde was used to optimize model-to-map fit, and Molprobity was applied for geometry validation. Secondary structure restraints and evolutionary couplings guided the model building process. ATPase rates were monitored by NADH consumption at 340 nm every minute for 30-45 minutes. Nonlinear regression with Michaelis-Menten equation was performed in GraphPad Prism 9. In-gel phosphoprotein staining used Pro-Q Diamond on 10% SDS-PAGE gels. Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 served as a loading control on parallel SDS-PAGE gels.

Key Results
Two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 were determined at 3.4Å (IFwide) and 4.0Å (IFnarrow). The E1435Q mutant showed substantially lowered ATPase activity with Vmax of 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg. The R-domain spanning residues 901-935 was visualized as partially ordered with a helix at residues 920-929. Phosphorylation was confirmed at S908, T911, and S914 by both electron density and mass spectrometry. The R-domain encircles NBD1 in both states and is stabilized by extensive contacts along a basic groove of NBD1. Three distinct hydrophobic surface burying sites were identified: site 1 (I621, L802, I902, I904), site 2 (F917, I1123, L1120), and site 3 (L912, I915, I1154). A total of ~1530 Å² of surface area was buried in IFnarrow and ~1338 Å² in IFwide along the R-domain/NBD1 interface. Specifically between NBD1 and the R-domain, ~523 Å² was buried in IFnarrow and ~480 Å² in IFwide. The angle between residues G913, G918, and G932 changed from 130º in IFwide to 137.5º in IFnarrow. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed a drastic reduction in ATPase activity compared to the phosphorylated form. In-gel phosphostaining and LC-MS/MS confirmed phosphorylation at all three sites in both WT and E1435Q. S908 was found to be part of the RRAS motif and adopt a conformation similar to PKA-bound phosphomimetic peptide. GSSG stimulated ATPase activity at physiologically relevant µM concentrations. Limited trypsin proteolysis showed a more complete digestion of dephosphorylated Ycf1, indicating increased protease accessibility.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The ordered, phosphorylated R-domain architecture represents a stimulatory conformation that drives association with NBD1. The R-domain acts as a regulatory 'clutch' that engages the motor upon phosphorylation but does not perform work itself. The S251 phosphosite in the lasso domain could disrupt R-domain interactions via electrostatic repulsion, explaining its inhibitory role. The structures challenge the model of CFTR activation depending on R-domain release between NBDs. The NBD1 architecture bears striking similarity to clinically relevant CFTR mutations, particularly delF506 at Ycf1 F713. The binding site of lumacaftor is located near the R-domain/NBD1 interface, suggesting the region is a hotspot for allosteric modulation. The general binding mechanism may apply to other ABC transporters with long phosphorylated unstructured domains.

Contradictions And Limitations
NBD2, the ATP-hydrolyzing NBD, was the less ordered domain and its density was weaker in both structures. A third state, IFtransition, was insufficiently detailed to enable model building and is described as having predominant disorder. No structure of an intact R-domain with NBDs has been determined in any state prior to this work. The paper does not resolve the full sequence assignment of the R-domain, only the highly conserved helical segment. The ATPase assay was performed in a reconstituted system rather than in vivo, limiting direct cellular context. The dephosphorylation model acknowledges that phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility, complicating interpretation of proteolysis data.

Claims
Phosphorylation of the Ycf1 R-domain induces a partially ordered helical conformation that promotes engagement with NBD1 and the lasso domain. The R-domain is visualized as helical at residues 920-929 in both structures. Mass spectrometry confirmed phosphorylation at S908, T911, and S914 in both WT and E1435Q. Hydrophobic surface burial reaches ~1530 Å² in IFnarrow. The R-domain remains partially disordered at residues 901-919 and 930-935. Previous cryo-EM structures of CFTR and Ycf1 showed a mostly disordered R-domain. This ordered architecture provides a defined binding site that could be used for allosteric modulation of ABCC transporters. The regulatory mechanism may be conserved across the ABCC subfamily.
The R-domain-NBD1 interaction network is a major driver of ATPase activity and is required for proper Ycf1 function. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed a drastic reduction in ATPase activity. S908 and T911 Ycf1 mutants showed deficient cadmium detoxification in yeast cells. Hydrophobic interactions bury ~523 Å² specifically between NBD1 and the R-domain in IFnarrow. The structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. The R-domain contacts are nearly constant between IFwide and IFnarrow states. Loss-of-single-phosphate robustness in Ycf1 is explained by the multiple-contact architecture. The requirement for an intact lasso domain for activity is consistent with structural findings.
Lasso domain phosphorylation at S251 provides a plausible negative regulatory mechanism through electrostatic repulsion of R-domain phosphates. S251 is accessible to the surface and poised to disrupt R-domain interactions. The lasso domain is adjacent to the R-domain and shares a conserved phosphorylation site. The authors do not observe phosphorylation at S251 in their structures. S251 is the equivalent of T249 in the Ycf1 homolog MRP1. The clustering of R-domain and lasso domain provides a mechanistic basis for bidirectional regulation by phosphorylation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The E1435Q Walker B mutant was used as a comparator; it yielded homogeneous particles but had reduced ATPase activity (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg). Dephosphorylation with lambda phosphatase confirmed the regulatory role of R-domain phosphates through reduced ATPase activity and altered proteolysis. Limited trypsin proteolysis showed increased protease accessibility in the dephosphorylated state. Evolutionary coupling analysis with 13,723 sequences validated secondary structure assignments and supported the R-domain helix model. The IFtransition state was insufficiently resolved for model building, highlighting the importance of the E1435Q mutant for structural trapping.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-C displays the 3.4Å and 4.0Å cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 in IFwide and IFnarrow conformations. Figure 1D quantifies the reduced ATPase activity of E1435Q Ycf1 (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg). Figure 1F shows GSSG-stimulated ATPase activity at µM concentrations. Figure 2A-D illustrates the extensive contacts between the R-domain and NBD1/lasso domain. Figure 2E-F shows the electron density for phosphorylation at S908, T911, and S914, with mass spectrometry confirmation. Figure 3 detailes the three hydrophobic surface burying sites and the total buried surface area in each conformation. Figure 4 shows the R-domain angle change and the occlusion of the NBD1 ATP binding site in IFnarrow. Figure S1 displays the purification scheme and gels of WT and E1435Q Ycf1. Figure S2 shows the cryo-EM data processing workflow and final EM map quality. Figure S7 compares Ycf1 R-domain features with CFTR, including C-terminal helix alignment and evolutionary coupling. Figure S8 compares substrate-bound and substrate-free states of MRP1. Table S2 reports mass spectrometry quantification of phosphorylation at S908, T911, and S914.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first structural determination of an ordered R-domain in endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 at 3.4Å and 4.0Å, revealing a regulatory architecture driven by S908, T911, and S914 phosphorylation. 2. The strongest evidence is the combined cryo-EM structures showing ~1530 Å² of hydrophobic surface burying, three distinct hydrophobic contact sites, and the dramatic ATPase activity reduction upon dephosphorylation. 3. The future path involves investigating the generalizability of the R-domain regulatory model to other ABCC transporters and exploring the full sequence-specific effects of R-domain mutations in both yeast and human systems.

summary.title: Influence of plant growth regulators and nitrogen sources on the production and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk
summary.authors: Leone Campos Rocha, Fábio Andrade, Teixeira 2, Márcio Dos, Santos Pedreira, Daniela Deitos Fries, Giovanna Evely, Leite Costa, Ana Cláudia, Maia Soares, Daniel Lucas, Santos Dias, Abdias José De Figueiredo, Angel Amaral, Seixas 4, Camile Carvalho Pacheco
summary.field_subfield: Agronomy: Pasture management and plant physiology
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental research with greenhouse and field component
summary.executive_summary:
This study evaluated the combined effects of plant growth regulator (PGR) seed treatment and nitrogen fertilization on the growth and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. Using a 2 x 4 factorial completely randomized design at the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB) in Itapetinga - BA, Brazil, the authors applied two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) and four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL/kg) composed of auxin (0.05 mg/L), cytokinin (0.09 mg/L), and gibberellin (0.05 mg/L). Four nitrogen fertilization methods (no, soil, foliar, and multiple: soil + foliar) were also evaluated. Germination and initial growth were monitored in a greenhouse under a 12h photoperiod at 28ºC using hermetic storage in a Mangelsdorf chamber; dry mass production, leaf number, tiller count, and chlorophyll/carotenoid contents were recorded over two 28-day periods following a 15 cm standardization cut at 30 days after sowing.

PGR treatment significantly improved germination (quadratic effect) and root dry mass, with optimal levels of 10.3 mL/kg for germination and 12.8 mL/kg for root mass. Coated seeds outperformed conventional seeds at low PGR levels, while a significant interaction between seed type and PGR was observed only for leaf and pseudostem dry mass, where coated seeds excelled at 8.85 and 9.57 mL/kg, respectively. Conventional seeds required higher PGR levels (15.5 and 18.1 mL/kg) to achieve comparable mass. Nitrogen fertilization was critical: soil N-fertilization increased dry mass of all structures and root volume, and the combination of PGR with soil fertilization yielded the highest dry mass. Notably, PGR increased root dry mass only under multiple fertilization; for other fertilization regimes, PGR had no effect. For pigments, PGR significantly increased chlorophyll a, while foliar N increased chlorophyll a, b, and total chlorophyll, though no exclusive foliar effect was observed. The authors attribute these findings to altered hormonal signaling (auxin/gibberellin antagonism, cytokinin/auxin interaction), auxin-mediated rhizogenesis via PIN proteins, and increased photosynthetic capacity driven by elevated chlorophyll a and nitrogen supply. The study positions PGR as a key tool for accelerating pasture establishment under adverse climatic conditions.
