judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study evaluated the combined effects of plant growth regulator (PGR) seed treatment and nitrogen fertilization on the growth and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. Using a 2 x 4 factorial completely randomized design at the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB) in Itapetinga - BA, Brazil, the authors applied two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) and four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL/kg) composed of auxin (0.05 mg/L), cytokinin (0.09 mg/L), and gibberellin (0.05 mg/L). Four nitrogen fertilization methods (no, soil, foliar, and multiple: soil + foliar) were also evaluated. Germination and initial growth were monitored in a greenhouse under a 12h photoperiod at 28ºC using hermetic storage in a Mangelsdorf chamber; dry mass production, leaf number, tiller count, and chlorophyll/carotenoid contents were recorded over two 28-day periods following a 15 cm standardization cut at 30 days after sowing.

PGR treatment significantly improved germination (quadratic effect) and root dry mass, with optimal levels of 10.3 mL/kg for germination and 12.8 mL/kg for root mass. Coated seeds outperformed conventional seeds at low PGR levels, while a significant interaction between seed type and PGR was observed only for leaf and pseudostem dry mass, where coated seeds excelled at 8.85 and 9.57 mL/kg, respectively. Conventional seeds required higher PGR levels (15.5 and 18.1 mL/kg) to achieve comparable mass. Nitrogen fertilization was critical: soil N-fertilization increased dry mass of all structures and root volume, and the combination of PGR with soil fertilization yielded the highest dry mass. Notably, PGR increased root dry mass only under multiple fertilization; for other fertilization regimes, PGR had no effect. For pigments, PGR significantly increased chlorophyll a, while foliar N increased chlorophyll a, b, and total chlorophyll, though no exclusive foliar effect was observed. The authors attribute these findings to altered hormonal signaling (auxin/gibberellin antagonism, cytokinin/auxin interaction), auxin-mediated rhizogenesis via PIN proteins, and increased photosynthetic capacity driven by elevated chlorophyll a and nitrogen supply. The study positions PGR as a key tool for accelerating pasture establishment under adverse climatic conditions.

Research Context
Adverse climatic factors shorten the soil preparation and planting window, reducing the time available to recover degraded pastures. Consequently, greater seed efficiency regarding germination and emergence speed is essential for timely management. Growth promoters and synthetic compounds act through mechanisms analogous to endogenous phytohormones. Phytohormones—auxins, gibberellins, and cytokinins—regulate homeostasis through signaling networks activating gene expression and metabolic pathways. High-level applications of gibberellin-based PGRs per area are uneconomical and can reduce forage mass. Low concentrations of gibberellin (5–10 g/ha) are sufficient to positively affect forage yield. Nitrogen is an indispensable constituent in plant-based organic compounds and stimulates cell division and elongation. Nitrogen applications on degraded pasture increase water use efficiency and stimulate growth. Prior research demonstrated that PGRs enhance performance under stress by positively regulating growth genes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central aim was to evaluate the effect of seed treatment with plant growth regulators on the growth and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The study simultaneously addressed the impact of nitrogen fertilization methods on the same cultivar. Growth and development were assessed through germinative characteristics, dry matter yield, and physiological composition. The hypothesis was that exogenous hormonal compounds act on organogenesis and increase development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. It was further hypothesized that soil N-fertilization would increase mass yields by maximizing photosynthetic processes and growth rates. The authors predicted that PGR treatment would improve germination and mass yields of plant structures in coated seeds. Specific interaction effects between seed type and PGR levels were anticipated for leaf and pseudostem mass production. The regression-based estimation was expected to identify optimal PGR levels for germinative and mass outcomes.

Methodological Details
Experiments were performed at the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB) in Itapetinga - BA, Brazil, from June to September 2017. The work was conducted at the Forage and Pasture Research Center, greenhouse, and the Laboratory of Anatomy and Ecological Plant Physiology (LAFIEP). Germination was carried out under hermetic storage in a Mangelsdorf germination chamber (MA-401) under a 12h photoperiod at constant temperature (28ºC). Soil was collected at 0–20 cm depth, disintegrated, and grounded to pass through a 4-mm sieve. The fertilization recommendations were based on the 5th Approximation of the Soil Fertility Commission for the State of Minas Gerais. A 2 × 4 factorial scheme in a completely randomized design was applied for both experiments. Two commercial seed types—coated and conventional—were compared alongside four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL/kg). The PGR composition included auxin at 0.05 mg/L, cytokinin at 0.09 mg/L, and gibberellin at 0.05 mg/L. For PGR application, seeds were imbibed for approximately two hours, wrapped in filter paper moistened with distilled water, using 25 seeds per replicate across four replicates per treatment. Initial growth assessments (30 DAS) used a seedling tray with 32 cells per replicate and two replicates per treatment, with sterilized coconut residue as substrate. The second experiment evaluated untreated and treated seeds (0 and 24 mL/kg) across four nitrogen fertilization methods: no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and multiple (soil + foliar). This design employed eight treatments with four plants per replicate and four replicates per treatment, totaling 32 experimental units. At 30 DAS, a standardization cut reduced average residue height to 15 cm before data collection. Soil and foliar N fertilization recommendations were 75 kg/ha N and 3 L/ha, respectively, applied after the standardization cut. Foliar fertilizer composition included N, P, K, Mg, S, Zn, Mn, Cu, B, Mo, Co at specified levels (Table 1). Germination was counted daily for 14 days to determine percentage and germination speed index. Dry mass was determined by desiccation of root, stem, and leaf structures. Chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments were extracted from the third fully expanded leaf using 200 mg of fresh mass in 5 mL DMSO, wrapped in aluminum foil. After 72 hours, absorption spectrophotometry at 665, 649, and 480 nm quantified pigments, adjusted to mg/g fresh mass. Each pot was filled with eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil to estimate area productivity in kg DM/ha.

Procedures And Architectures
Seeds were imbibed at different PGR levels for approximately two hours before treatment. After PGR application, seeds were wrapped in filter paper moistened with distilled water for germination. For the initial 30 DAS growth assessment, sowing occurred in seedling trays with 32 cells per replicate. Sterilized coconut residue was used as substrate to maintain constant humidity. The 2 × 4 factorial design with completely randomized blocks assigned eight treatments, four replicates each. The standardization cut at 30 DAS established a uniform residue height of 15 cm for subsequent measurements. Data collection proceeded in two 28-day periods following the standardization cut. Soil N-fertilization was applied after the standardization cut following regional recommendations. Foliar fertilizer was applied at 3 L/ha with the composition detailed in Table 1. For germination, hermetic storage in a Mangelsdorf chamber with a 12h photoperiod and 28ºC constant temperature was used. Data were analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS (SAS Inst. Inc., Cary, NC) with significance at P ≤ 0.05. Seed, PGR, and interaction effects were treated as fixed effects for all measurements in Exp. 1. Single-degree-of-freedom contrast statements analyzed linear and quadratic PGR effects, and the maximum point was estimated from a regression equation. PGR, Fertilization, and their interaction were fixed effects in Exp. 2. The Tukey test served as the mean comparison with significance at P ≤ 0.05. Daily germination counts were recorded over 14 days to calculate germination percentage and germination speed index. For chlorophyll analysis, the third fully expanded leaf was harvested at 10 a.m., and 200 mg fresh mass was immediately prepared in 5 mL DMSO. Samples were wrapped in aluminum foil and incubated for 72 hours before spectrophotometric reading. Absorption spectrophotometry at 665, 649, and 480 nm quantified chlorophyll a, b, total chlorophyll, carotenoids, and the a/b ratio. Whole-plant yield was determined followed by desiccation of root, stem, and leaf structures for fresh and dry mass.

Key Results
The interaction between seed type and growth regulator levels was not significant for germination and germination speed index (GSI). A quadratic effect of growth regulator levels on germination was observed regardless of seed type. Regression analysis estimated that seed treatment with 10.3 mL/kg PGR promoted greater germination. Coated seeds achieved higher germination and GSI than conventional seeds, confirming quality differences (Table 2). For the number of leaves and tillers, and root dry mass production, the interaction between seed type and PGR level was not significant. The number of leaves and tillers were influenced by seed type, whereas root dry mass production was not affected by seed type. The estimated regression equation indicated that 12.8 mL/kg PGR resulted in higher root dry mass production (Table 3). A significant interaction between seed type and PGR was observed for leaf and pseudostem dry mass production. In the absence of PGR or at the lowest level (8.0 mL/kg), coated seeds had higher leaf and pseudostem dry mass production. Corresponding optimal levels for coated seeds were 8.85 mL/kg for leaf and 9.57 mL/kg for pseudostem dry mass. Leaf and pseudostem dry mass did not differ between seed types at the highest PGR levels (16.0 and 24.0 mL/kg). Conventional seeds required higher PGR levels of 15.5 and 18.1 mL/kg for leaf and pseudostem dry mass production, respectively (Table 4). The interaction between PGR use and nitrogen fertilization was significant for dry mass of leaf, stem, shoot, and root. Dry mass of stem, leaf, and shoot was greater when PGR and soil fertilization were combined. Soil fertilization resulted in higher yields for all evaluated structures regardless of PGR level. PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization (soil + foliar). In the absence of PGR, multiple fertilization was similar to soil fertilization in leaf, stem, and shoot yields. PGR increased root dry mass only when combined with multiple fertilization; for other fertilization types, no PGR effect was observed (Table 5). The interaction between PGR use and nitrogen fertilization was not significant for chlorophyll a, b, total chlorophyll, carotenoids, and the a/b ratio. PGR significantly affected chlorophyll a levels (Table 6). Fertilization methods influenced chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoid levels. PGR resulted in higher levels of chlorophyll a, the pigment responsible for the photochemical phase of photosynthesis. Foliar nitrogen fertilization increased production of chlorophyll a, b, and total chlorophyll.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Exogenous hormone compounds alter hormonal balance and biosynthesis, with a significant increase in auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin levels after 24h of imbibition. The use of growth regulator increased germination percentages for both seed types, consistent with previous studies evaluating cytokinin and auxin formulations. Exogenous gibberellin enhances intracellular transport of intermediate metabolites to bioactive gibberellin, acting on genes expressing germinative characteristics. Gibberellin weakens structures covering the radicle, facilitating germination and overcoming mechanical barriers. Combined hormone regulation modifies gibberellin/abscisic acid relationships, with gibberellin reducing abscisic acid and thus lipid degradation in cotyledons. Auxin in the PGR composition increases rhizogenesis by stimulating stem cell multiplication through accumulation in quiescent centers. Auxin transport occurs via PIN proteins bound to plasma membranes, in the endoplasmic reticulum and other endomembranes. Auxin and cytokinin together regulate meristem formation and maintenance, and their proportion is critical for shoot and root organogenesis. Auxins are linked to phototropism and chloroplast movement; an inconclusive study suggests auxin may indirectly influence chloroplast position through homeostasis disruption. Nitrogen is indispensable in organic compounds, increases rates of cell division and expansion, and stimulates cell elongation. Nitrogen fertilization maximizes photosynthetic processes and increases water use efficiency and soil cover. PGR combined with soil fertilization yields higher dry mass because increased nitrogen supply and accelerated hormonal signaling drive higher cellular and metabolic turnover. Higher chlorophyll a production enables light perception and promotes ATP formation in chloroplasts, capturing more energy for plant development. Foliar nitrogen may participate in cytokinin synthesis, promoting chlorophyll synthesis and delayed senescence. The use of exogenous compounds in pasture establishment is positioned as a key tool for germinative and structural development.

Contradictions And Limitations
Low concentrations of gibberellin (5–10 g/ha) are sufficient to positively affect forage yield, suggesting higher PGR levels may be uneconomical. Conventional seeds showed reduced hormone use efficiency compared to coated seeds, suggesting a need for Pure Live Seeds (PLS) evaluation. The interaction between seed type and PGR for germination was not significant, limiting generalizations across seed types. PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization, a counterintuitive finding that requires further investigation of hormonal antagonism. Only eight treatments were used in Exp. 2 with four replicates, and only 32 experimental units, limiting statistical power for detecting complex interactions. The authors note that little is known about the role of auxins and cytokinins in regulating photosynthetic processes. Auxin homeostasis disorder is linked to chloroplast movement in one inconclusive study, limiting mechanistic claims. The study does not report a random seed or explicit replication for the germination experiment beyond 25 seeds per replicate. No specific random number generator or randomization seed is mentioned for the CRD.

Claims
Plant growth regulator treatment improves seed germination and root dry mass development in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. A quadratic effect of PGR levels on germination was observed, and the regression equation identified 10.3 mL/kg as the optimal germination-promoting dose. The estimated equation identified 12.8 mL/kg PGR as the dose producing the highest root dry mass. PGR treatment increased germination percentages for both coated and conventional seed types. The interaction between seed type and PGR was not significant for germination or GSI, complicating universal recommendations. Coated seeds performed better at low PGR levels, whereas conventional seeds required higher doses, indicating seed-specific responses. PGR treatment is positioned as a key tool for rapid pasture establishment under adverse climatic conditions. The optimal PGR level depends on seed type (coated vs. conventional), necessitating tailored recommendations.
Soil nitrogen fertilization is more effective than foliar nitrogen for dry mass production of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. Soil fertilization resulted in higher dry mass yields for all evaluated structures (leaf, stem, shoot, root) regardless of PGR level. Nitrogen increases rates of cell division and expansion, stimulates cell elongation, and maximizes photosynthetic processes. The higher dry mass of all structures receiving soil fertilization justifies the nitrogen relationship and its efficiency via root absorption. No exclusive influence of foliar fertilization was observed; it did not independently promote mass yields. The interaction between PGR and foliar N showed complex outcomes, with PGR reducing mass under multiple fertilization. Soil N application is the preferred nitrogen delivery method for pasture structural development. Foliar N may still be valuable for cytokinin-mediated chlorophyll synthesis and delayed senescence.
PGR treatment and soil nitrogen fertilization synergize to produce maximal dry mass yields in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. Dry mass of stem, leaf, and shoot was greater when PGR use and soil fertilization were combined. Increased nitrogen supply combined with accelerated cellular turnover and hormonal synthesis from PGR drives higher dry mass accumulation. The use of PGR increased root dry mass specifically when combined with multiple fertilization, indicating a synergy between hormonal signaling and N status. PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization, differing from the absence of PGR. Integrated management combining PGR seed treatment and soil N-fertilization optimizes structural development in Brachiaria pastures. The antagonistic interaction between PGR and multiple N-fertilization suggests that over-application of hormonal compounds may impair some structural growth components.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The 2 × 4 factorial design with four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL/kg) served as a pseudo-ablation to identify the optimal hormonal dose. The comparison of coated vs. conventional seeds acted as a seed-type ablation to isolate coating effects from genetic performance. Four nitrogen fertilization methods (no, soil, foliar, multiple) served as ablation to isolate N-source and delivery mechanism effects. The use of a 30 DAS standardization cut (15 cm) served as a growth-stage ablation, fixing the developmental state before dry mass measurement. The regression-based estimation of the maximum PGR level acted as a sensitivity analysis for dose-response modeling. summary.executive_summary:
This prospective, single-center registry study evaluated the impact of chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length on six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients treated at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul, South Korea, between November 2004 and October 2010 were enrolled. Patients were dichotomized into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm; n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30 mm; n=76). The study aimed to determine whether CTO lesion length independently influenced safety, angiographic patency, or clinical success in the DES era, as lesion length is a major predictor of adverse outcomes in non-CTO coronary artery disease.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This prospective, single-center registry study evaluated the impact of chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length on six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients treated at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul, South Korea, between November 2004 and October 2010 were enrolled. Patients were dichotomized into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm; n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30 mm; n=76). The study aimed to determine whether CTO lesion length independently influenced safety, angiographic patency, or clinical success in the DES era, as lesion length is a major predictor of adverse outcomes in non-CTO coronary artery disease.

At two-year follow-up, baseline clinical characteristics differed: the long CTO group more frequently had prior PCI, whereas the short CTO group more frequently had bifurcation lesions. In-hospital intimal dissection was more common in the long CTO group, reflecting more complex procedural anatomy. However, overall MACE (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), and myocardial infarction (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71) rates were statistically similar between groups. The primary finding was a significantly higher incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05) and predominantly target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05) in the long CTO group. Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26; 95% CI 1.53-11.9; p=0.006 per abstract; OR 4.23; CI 1.52-11.8; p<0.05 per discussion) and TVR. 

At six months, angiographic outcomes including in-stent restenosis (33.3% vs. 26.6%, p=0.42), binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12), and late loss (0.65±0.82 mm vs. 0.46±0.56 mm, p=0.13) did not differ significantly between groups. Angiographic data were available for 62% of the long CTO and 59% of the short CTO groups. Despite the higher repeat PCI and TVR rates, the authors concluded that successful DES-mediated PCI in long CTO lesions yields clinical and safety outcomes comparable to short CTO lesions. The study was limited by a small sample size, prospective but non-randomized design, unequal baseline characteristics, and non-routine follow-up angiography. The paper was posted as a bioRxiv preprint on May 23, 2018, and was not certified by peer review.

Research Context
While drug-eluting stents and device developments have reduced restenosis and adverse events, clinical outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention remain strongly affected by baseline lesion characteristics. Long coronary artery lesions are established as a worse prognostic factor after PCI in the general coronary disease setting. Despite remarkable progress in special devices and techniques for chronic total occlusion PCI, procedural success rates for CTO patients remain lower than for non-CTO patients. Long-term CTO PCI outcomes are further modified by clinical risk factors and baseline lesion characteristics. In the drug-eluting stent era, there are no definite answers regarding whether CTO lesion length significantly impacts angiographic and clinical outcomes. The question remains whether successful CTO PCI with DES yields different outcomes for long versus short CTO lesions, a gap left by prior registry data.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CTO lesion length can significantly impact six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful CTO PCI with drug-eluting stents. The authors expected that adverse clinical outcomes including major adverse cardiovascular events and angiographic adverse outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. This prediction was based on two main reasons: first, the long CTO group was expected to have worse clinical risk factors related to adverse outcomes, such as history of prior MI and prior PCI. Second, the authors anticipated that the use of newer generation drug-eluting stents would be dominant in the short CTO group while first-generation stents would be more frequent in the long CTO group. The hypothesis was that although long CTO would carry higher procedural complexity and worse risk profile, successful DES revascularization should still achieve comparable clinical endpoints to short CTO. The study was powered to detect differences in MACE, cardiac death, MI, repeat PCI, and TVR, as well as angiographic endpoints including ISR, binary restenosis, mean diameter stenosis, and late loss.

Methodological Details
A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients who underwent successful PCI with drug-eluting stents were enrolled for this prospective study. The study period spanned from November 2004 to October 2010 at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul, South Korea. Patients were dichotomized into two groups based on the angiographic lesion length of the target vessel: the long CTO group was ≥30 mm and the short CTO group was <30 mm. The long CTO group comprised 159 patients and the short CTO group comprised 76 patients. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital, and all patients provided informed consent. CTO was defined as a complete coronary obstruction with Thrombolysis In Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) flow grade 0 and an estimated duration of ≥3 months with or without visible collateral flow. The estimated duration was determined by the interval from the last episode of angina symptoms consistent with the location of the occlusion. Only de novo lesions were included, and CTO due to in-stent restenosis (ISR) was explicitly excluded. Loading doses of clopidogrel (300-600 mg) and aspirin (200-300 mg) were administered before the index procedure. Following PCI, all patients received aspirin (100 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg) as maintenance dual antiplatelet regimen. Clopidogrel administration was encouraged to continue for at least one year. Adjunctive cilostazol (200 mg post-loading, then 100 mg twice daily for at least one month) was added at physician's discretion. PCI procedures were performed with current guidelines using standard techniques; various guidewires crossed the CTO lesion, and mostly simple balloon pre-dilation was performed. A variety of atheroablative devices were not utilized; instead, simple pre-dilation achieved adequate luminal diameter for stent delivery. All PCI was performed using drug-eluting stents, with the specific DES type decided by the operator during the procedure. Procedural success was defined as a reduction in final angiographic diameter stenosis to less than 30% and TIMI grade ≥2. Quantitative coronary angiographic (QCA) parameters were measured before PCI, immediately after, and six months later at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital. The primary angiographic endpoint was the incidence of binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included in-stent restenosis, mean diameter stenosis, minimal luminal diameter, and late loss at six months. Two-year follow-up data were collected by face-to-face interview at the outpatient clinic, medical record review, and/or telephone contact with patients. The primary clinical endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as the composite of total death, recurrent myocardial infarction, and revascularization including PCI and coronary artery bypass graft. MACE was further divided into TLR-MACE (cardiac death, MI, and TLR) and TVR-MACE (cardiac death, MI, and TVR). Q-wave MI was defined as new pathological Q-waves in at least two contiguous leads with or without elevated creatinine kinase-MB. For continuous variables, differences between groups were evaluated by Student's t-test with data expressed as mean ± standard deviations. Categorical variables were analyzed with χ2 or Fisher's exact test as appropriate. Logistic regression model analysis was carried out with adjustment for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. A two-sided p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 20 (IBM SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA).

Procedures And Architectures
The study was a prospective single-center registry collecting data on 235 consecutive CTO patients undergoing successful DES-mediated PCI between 2004 and 2010. Patient assignment to long (n=159, ≥30 mm) or short (n=76, <30 mm) CTO groups was determined by angiographic lesion length of the target vessel. Procedural success was defined by reduction in final diameter stenosis to <30% and TIMI flow grade ≥2 immediately following stent deployment. PCI was performed with standard guidelines using varied guidewires; atheroablative devices were not utilized, and pre-dilation with balloon was the primary luminal preparation method. All stents used were drug-eluting stents, with the specific type selected by the operator during the procedure. For angiographic endpoints, QCA parameters were quantified before, immediately after, and six months following the index procedure at the center's angiography suite. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis assessed at 6-12 months, with secondary endpoints including in-stent restenosis, mean diameter stenosis, minimal luminal diameter, and late loss at six months. Clinical follow-up was conducted at two years through a combination of face-to-face interviews, medical record reviews, and telephone contacts. The antiplatelet regimen included dual therapy with aspirin (100 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg) for at least one year, with cilostazol added at physician's discretion. Multivariate logistic regression adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion to estimate hazard for angiographic and clinical follow-up events. Angiographic data were available for only a subset of patients at six months: 99 of 159 (62%) in the long CTO group and 45 of 76 (59%) in the short CTO group. The data were analyzed using SPSS version 20 with 2-sided p<0.05 as the significance threshold.

Key Results
At two years, total death was 3.1% in the long CTO group versus 5.2% in the short CTO group, with p=0.43 indicating no statistically significant difference. Cardiac death occurred in 1.2% of long CTO patients versus 2.6% of short CTO patients (p=0.45), showing no significant difference in the hardest endpoint. Myocardial infarction occurred in 1.8% of the long CTO group versus 2.6% of the short CTO group (p=0.71), with no significant difference. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occurred in 21.3% of long CTO patients versus 13.1% of short CTO patients (p=0.13), with the trend not reaching statistical significance. Repeat PCI was significantly more frequent in the long CTO group at 18.8% versus 7.8% in the short CTO group (p<0.05). Target vessel revascularization (TVR) was significantly higher in the long CTO group at 16.3% versus 6.5% in the short CTO group (p<0.05). Multivariate logistic regression in the abstract identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI with OR 4.26, 95% CI 1.53-11.9, and p=0.006. The discussion section reported a slightly different OR of 4.23 with CI 1.52-11.8 and p<0.05 for repeat PCI in the long CTO group. In-hospital complications were similar between groups, but significant intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group, reflecting procedural complexity. Baseline characteristics differed: prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group, while bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group. At six months, in-stent restenosis was 33.3% in the long CTO versus 26.6% in the short CTO group (p=0.42), showing no significant difference. Binary restenosis was 19.1% in the long CTO versus 8.8% in the short CTO group (p=0.12), with a non-significant trend toward higher rates in long lesions. Late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm in the long CTO group versus 0.46 ± 0.56 mm in the short CTO group (p=0.13), showing no significant angiographic difference. Coronary vessel size was significantly smaller in the short CTO group at 3.11 ± 0.43 mm versus 2.92 ± 0.42 mm in the long CTO group (p<0.05). Despite the vessel size difference, both groups had diameters categorized as small vessel, and this did not significantly affect angiographic or clinical outcomes. Angiographic follow-up at six months was obtained in 62% of long CTO patients (99/159) and 59% of short CTO patients (45/76).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The similarity in cardiac death, MI, and MACE between long and short CTO groups, despite the higher TVR and repeat PCI in long CTO, supports the conclusion that successful DES-PCI in long CTO lesions yields clinical safety comparable to short CTO. The discrepancy between hard endpoints (death, MI) and revascularization rates (TVR) in long CTO mirrors findings from the j-Cypher Registry. Less myocardial viability and previously developed collateral channels in long CTO lesions may lessen the harmful physiologic effect of restenosis, explaining why higher TVR does not translate into increased mortality. Although six-month angiographic outcomes were statistically similar, the numerical trend toward higher binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%) in long CTO, combined with higher repeat PCI rates, supports the hypothesis that longer-term follow-up may reveal significant angiographic differences. The vessel size difference (3.11 mm vs. 2.92 mm, p<0.05) did not impact outcomes because both were considered small-vessel diameters, suggesting the threshold effect of vessel size is exceeded in this population. The use of first-generation stents in long CTO and newer generation DES in short CTO, along with worse risk profiles in long CTO, makes the comparable clinical outcomes more noteworthy.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is a prospective but non-randomized single-center registry rather than a randomized controlled trial, introducing potential selection bias. Baseline clinical, lesion, and procedural characteristics were slightly different between the two groups, with prior PCI more frequent in long CTO and bifurcation lesions more frequent in short CTO. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed in all patients; it depended on ischemic symptoms or physician's discretion, introducing unmeasured confounders from collateral flow and myocardial viability. The sample size was relatively small, and the study lacked sufficient power to detect differences in angiographic outcomes between the two groups at six months. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy, and the authors recommend longer follow-up with larger cohorts. Strict statistical adjustment could not eliminate all unmeasured confounders or analytical bias from the retrospective data collection. The paper was posted as a bioRxiv preprint on May 23, 2018, and was explicitly labeled as not certified by peer review. There is a slight discrepancy between the OR reported for repeat PCI in the abstract (4.26, p=0.006) versus the discussion (4.23, p<0.05).

Claims
Long CTO lesion length does not independently increase the risk of major clinical endpoints (death, MI, MACE) after successful DES-PCI, but is associated with higher rates of repeat PCI and target vessel revascularization. MACE was 21.3% in long CTO versus 13.1% in short CTO with p=0.13, showing no statistical difference. Cardiac death was 1.2% in long CTO versus 2.6% in short CTO with p=0.45. Repeat PCI was significantly higher in long CTO at 18.8% versus 7.8% in short CTO (p<0.05). TVR was significantly higher in long CTO at 16.3% versus 6.5% in short CTO (p<0.05). Prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group, and intimal dissection was more common, suggesting higher procedural complexity. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to definitively exclude delayed events. Clinicians can treat long CTO lesions with DES, expecting revascularization outcomes comparable to short CTO, though with an increased probability of subsequent repeat PCI. The finding supports that in the DES era, the critical threshold for CTO lesion length in determining clinical success is less definitive than in non-CTO coronary disease.
Six-month angiographic outcomes including in-stent restenosis, binary restenosis, and late loss do not differ significantly between long and short CTO groups, though a numerical trend favors the short CTO group. ISR was 33.3% in long CTO versus 26.6% in short CTO (p=0.42). Binary restenosis was 19.1% in long CTO versus 8.8% in short CTO (p=0.12). Late loss was 0.65±0.82 mm versus 0.46±0.56 mm (p=0.13). Angiographic data were available for 62% of long CTO and 59% of short CTO patients, making comparisons balanced. The small patient numbers and short follow-up may mask true differences that would emerge with time. The study did not have strong power to prove a difference in angiographic events. Long-term follow-up with larger cohorts is needed to clarify whether angiographic disparities between long and short CTO emerge over time. The absence of significant difference at six months provides reassurance for immediate post-procedural patency regardless of lesion length.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Multivariate logistic regression with adjustment for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion was used to estimate risks for repeat PCI and TVR. The logistic regression model confirmed long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26 or 4.23 depending on section) and TVR, indicating the findings were not due to simple confounding by clinical risk. Baseline clinical, angiographic, and procedural characters were compared using Student's t-test, χ2, and Fisher's exact test to ensure group comparability before outcome analysis. Vessel size was shown not to affect angiographic or clinical outcomes significantly, as both groups met the small vessel diameter classification. The discrepancy between abstract (OR 4.26, p=0.006) and discussion (OR 4.23, p<0.05) for repeat PCI is a minor internal inconsistency in the reported multivariate results.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study before enrollment. The paper was posted as a bioRxiv preprint on May 23, 2018, and was not certified by peer review.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrates baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics of the 159 long CTO and 76 short CTO patients. Table 2 summarizes procedural and in-hospital complications, showing higher intimal dissection in the long CTO group. Table 3 summarizes two-year follow-up clinical outcomes: MACE (21.3% vs. 13.1%), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%), MI (1.8% vs. 2.6%), repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%), and TVR (16.3% vs. 6.5%). Table 4 shows the predictors for repeat PCI and TVR from multivariate logistic regression, identifying long CTO as an important predictor. Table 5 presents six-month angiographic outcomes including ISR (33.3% vs. 26.6%), binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%), and late loss (0.65±0.82 mm vs. 0.46±0.56 mm).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first prospective registry in the DES era that directly compares long versus short CTO lesion length on 2-year outcomes after successful DES-PCI, finding that long CTO increases repeat PCI and TVR risk without increasing hard endpoints. 2. The strongest evidence is the multivariate logistic regression demonstrating long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26; CI 1.53-11.9; p=0.006), while MACE (p=0.13), cardiac death (p=0.45), and MI (p=0.71) rates remained statistically similar between long and short CTO groups. 3. The future path requires a larger, multi-center prospective cohort with extended follow-up to resolve the trend toward higher angiographic restenosis in long CTO and to confirm whether the repeat PCI disparity translates into long-term clinical differences.

summary.title: Synthesis, Biological Activity and Molecular Docking of New Tricyclic Series as α-glucosidase Inhibitors
summary.authors: Hatem A Abuelizz, Azman N I Nor, Iwana, Rohaya Ahmad, Anouar El-Hassane, Mohamed Marzouk, Rashad Al-Salahi
summary.field_subfield: Medicinal Chemistry / Drug Discovery for Diabetes
summary.type_of_paper: Research article reporting synthesis, bioactivity assay, and molecular docking of new α-glucosidase inhibitors
summary.executive_summary: The authors synthesized 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one hybrids and evaluated their α-glucosidase inhibitory activity through an in vitro enzyme screening assay using the p-NPG substrate. The study employed α-glucosidase from Baker's yeast at a concentration of 0.125 unit/mL in a 96-well microplate format, with compounds screened at 200 µg/mL and two-fold serial dilutions ranging from 100 to 1.56 µg/mL in 5% DMSO. Acarbose served as the positive control at 200 µg/mL. The screening revealed that eight out of the 25 tested compounds exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition, with compounds 3, 6c, and 6d exceeding 60% inhibition, while 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b, and 6h ranged between 50.36% and 57.48%. IC50 values were calculated for the active compounds: compound 3 at 167.82 µM, compound 2a at 304.13 µM, and compound 2d at 173.83 µM. The abstract reports an IC50 of 104.07 mM for compound 6h, which is presumably a typographical error for µM given the surrounding context of µM values for other compounds and the docking energy of -10.56 kcal/mol. Molecular docking calculations using Autodock and the 3W37 crystal structure revealed that compound 6h achieves the lowest binding energy (-10.56 kcal/mol) and forms three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, plus hydrophobic interactions with Trp329. In contrast, the reference drug acarbose establishes 10 hydrogen bonds with Asp232, Ala234, Asn237, Asp357, Arg552, Asp568, and His626, along with two hydrophobic interactions involving the methyl group of the deoxyglucosamine moiety and residues Phe601 and Trp329. Compound 2a, by contrast, only forms one hydrogen bond with Arg552 and yields a binding energy of -8.12 kcal/mol. The relative standard deviation of binding energies was less than 2.34 kcal/mol. The authors conclude that the amino-bridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine scaffold is the key structural feature responsible for the enhanced inhibitory activity, and Trp329 serves as a critical residue directing the ligand in the binding site. This work provides a new non-sugar-mimetic structural scaffold for the development of novel α-glucosidase inhibitors as potential clinical drugs for type II diabetes.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The authors synthesized 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one hybrids and evaluated their α-glucosidase inhibitory activity through an in vitro enzyme screening assay using the p-NPG substrate. The study employed α-glucosidase from Baker's yeast at a concentration of 0.125 unit/mL in a 96-well microplate format, with compounds screened at 200 µg/mL and two-fold serial dilutions ranging from 100 to 1.56 µg/mL in 5% DMSO. Acarbose served as the positive control at 200 µg/mL. The screening revealed that eight out of the 25 tested compounds exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition, with compounds 3, 6c, and 6d exceeding 60% inhibition, while 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b, and 6h ranged between 50.36% and 57.48%. IC50 values were calculated for the active compounds: compound 3 at 167.82 µM, compound 2a at 304.13 µM, and compound 2d at 173.83 µM. The abstract reports an IC50 of 104.07 mM for compound 6h, which is presumably a typographical error for µM given the surrounding context of µM values for other compounds and the docking energy of -10.56 kcal/mol. Molecular docking calculations using Autodock and the 3W37 crystal structure revealed that compound 6h achieves the lowest binding energy (-10.56 kcal/mol) and forms three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, plus hydrophobic interactions with Trp329. In contrast, the reference drug acarbose establishes 10 hydrogen bonds with Asp232, Ala234, Asn237, Asp357, Arg552, Asp568, and His626, along with two hydrophobic interactions involving the methyl group of the deoxyglucosamine moiety and residues Phe601 and Trp329. Compound 2a, by contrast, only forms one hydrogen bond with Arg552 and yields a binding energy of -8.12 kcal/mol. The relative standard deviation of binding energies was less than 2.34 kcal/mol. The authors conclude that the amino-bridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine scaffold is the key structural feature responsible for the enhanced inhibitory activity, and Trp329 serves as a critical residue directing the ligand in the binding site. This work provides a new non-sugar-mimetic structural scaffold for the development of novel α-glucosidase inhibitors as potential clinical drugs for type II diabetes.

Research Context
The number of diabetic people has increased from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million by 2014, according to a WHO global report. The prevalence of diabetes among people over 18 years old increased from 4.7% in 1980 to 8.5% in 2014. Diabetes is a metabolic disease characterized by hyperglycaemia accompanied by carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism disturbance. The increase in blood sugar levels can lead to serious damage to nerves and blood vessels, affecting individual health and quality of life. α-Glucosidase inhibitors delay the carbohydrate hydrolysis by inhibiting digestive enzymes, thus reducing postprandial glucose levels. Clinically available α-glucosidase inhibitors include acarbose, miglitol and voglibose, each with different biological activities. Acarbose prevents the digestion of complex carbohydrates that are subsequently delivered to the colon, but gastrointestinal side effects such as flatulence and diarrhoea reduce patient compliance. Most produced α-glucosidase inhibitors were sugar mimetics requiring tedious synthesis, limiting their therapeutic utility. The valienamine moiety in acarbose mimics the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state that binds to and inhibits α-glucosidase. The authors decided to modify scaffolds well accepted in medicinal chemistry, such as pyridine, triazole, and pyrimidine, which have been incorporated in compounds with antimicrobial, antiviral, anticancer, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticonvulsant activities. Pyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones have been previously reported as effective fungicidal agents. There is a high demand for effective antidiabetic agents that overcome the side effects associated with sugar mimetic agents.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a new series of phenoxypyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone hybrids can serve as α-glucosidase inhibitors with activity comparable to or superior to acarbose. The study hypothesizes that structural modification of the pyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone scaffold, particularly through aminobridge substitution at position 4, will yield potent α-glucosidase inhibition. The authors aimed to design two series of phenoxypyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinones and evaluate their α-glucosidase inhibitory activity. A significant inhibitory activity was expected for the newly synthesized compounds, with IC50 values lower than that of acarbose for at least two compounds. Molecular docking studies were conducted to understand the binding modes of the target enzyme and docked synthesized derivatives. The authors expected to provide insights of a new lead scaffold for the development of new clinically effective antidiabetic drugs. Acarbose was identified as the positive control drug for inhibitory activity comparison.

Methodological Details
The study synthesized 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one hybrids as potential α-glucosidase inhibitors. The α-glucosidase enzyme used was of type 1 from Baker's yeast. The enzyme solution was prepared by dissolving 1 mg of α-glucosidase in 1000 µL of cold phosphate-buffered saline, pH 6.5, yielding a concentration of 0.125 unit/mL. A 20-mM solution of para-nitrophenyl-α-D-glucopyranoside (p-NPG substrate) was prepared by dissolving 6 mg of p-NPG in 10 mL of buffer solution. For screening, samples were prepared at 200 µg/mL concentration in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Two-fold serial dilutions with 5% DMSO were prepared in a 96-well microplate to give final concentrations of 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, 3.13, and 1.56 µg/mL. Acarbose was used as the positive control at a concentration of 200 µg/mL in 100% DMSO. Phosphate-buffered saline pH 6.5 was prepared by dissolving 1.4 g sodium phosphate monobasic, 8 g sodium chloride, 0.2 g potassium chloride, and 0.2 g potassium dihydrogen phosphate in 1 L deionized water. The pH was adjusted to 6.5 at 20 °C with 1 M sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid. The inhibitory assay was performed in triplicate experiments. In the screening assay, 10 µL of 5% DMSO was added to the 96 wells, followed by 10 µL of stock sample, 20 µL of enzyme, 40 µL of PBS, and 20 µL of deionized water. The mixture was pre-incubated at 37 °C for 10 min before adding 10 µL of 20 mM p-NPG solution. The absorbance was measured at 405 nm at 0 min and after incubation for 30 min at 37 °C. For the negative control, the sample was replaced with 5% DMSO, and acarbose served as the positive control. The inhibitory activity was determined based on the method described by Ahmad et al., 2011. Molecular docking was performed using the Autodock software package with the crystal structure from the RCSB Protein Data Bank, PDB file code 3W37. The original docked protein was downloaded from the RCSB data bank website.

Procedures And Architectures
The starting material A was prepared according to a reported procedure, and 2-hydrazine-3-carboxylic pyridine (5.5 mmol) was added portionwise to diphenoxy-Ncyanoimidocarbonate (5 mmol) in ethanol (20 mL) at room temperature. After addition of triethylamine (20 mmol) dropwise over 10 min, the reaction was stirred overnight, acidified with conc. HCl under ice, and heated for 1–2 h at 80 °C to yield compound 1 as a white amorphous powder (78%). Compound 1 was reacted with alkyl or heteroalkyl halides in DMF with potassium carbonate (0.6 mmol) to give compounds 2a–l in yields of 45–83%. Boiling equimolar amounts of compound 1 and phosphorous pentasulfide in absolute pyridine furnished compound 3 as a yellow amorphous powder in 90% yield. Compound 3 was treated with benzyl bromide in basic medium (K2CO3) to yield compound 4. Compound 1 was chlorinated with phosphorous oxychloride in boiling benzene to give compound 5 as an imidoyl chloride, confirmed by NMR and IR spectroscopy. Reaction of compound 5 with aromatic amines in pyridine in a 1:5 molar ratio afforded compounds 6a–d in 60–68% yields. Reaction of compound 5 with hydroxylamine HCl in a 1:2.5 molar ratio in boiling pyridine provided compound 6e in 63% yield. Isoniazid treatment of compound 5 in boiling toluene gave amidrazone 6i in 74% yield. Hydrazinolysis of compound 5 in boiling ethanol produced 6f, which upon treatment with equimolar amounts of aldehydes gave hydrazone derivatives 6g and 6h in good yields. Compounds 6g and 6h were prepared from 6f reacting with 2-hydroxy-5-methoxy benzaldehyde (1 mmol) or 2-methoxy benzaldehyde (1 mmol) in ethanol refluxed for 3–5 h. Compounds 2a–l were obtained as coloured amorphous powders with IR absorption bands at 1670–1688 cm⁻¹ due to the C=O group, and compound 3 as a yellow amorphous powder with C=S absorption at 1272 cm⁻¹ and 186.0 ppm. The 1H-NMR spectra of targets 1–6 were characterized by two consistent spin coupling systems, each with three types of protons, indicative of the phenoxy-pyrido-triazolopyrimidinone main structure. Molecular docking calculations were performed with Autodock to study the binding modes, with detailed steps reported by Abuelizz and collaborators. The number of intermolecular hydrogen bonds, binding energies, and closest amino acid residues were determined for each compound.

Key Results
A total of 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone compounds were synthesized and evaluated. Eight out of the 25 compounds exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition of α-glucosidase. Compounds 3, 6c, and 6d showed average percent inhibition of more than 60%. Compounds 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b, and 6h showed average percent inhibition of more than 50% but less than 60%, with 2a at 50.36% and 2d at 57.48%. The IC50 of compound 3 at 100 µg/mL was 167.82 µM, and the average percent inhibition was 60.38%. The IC50 of compound 2a was 304.13 µM and that of compound 2d was 173.83 µM. The abstract reports that compound 6h exhibited the highest inhibition with an IC50 of 104.07 mM. Compounds 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d, and 6h displayed IC50 values similar to or lower than that of acarbose. The relative standard deviation of the binding energy of the formed complex was less than 2.34 kcal/mol. Compound 6h had the lowest binding energy at -10.56 kcal/mol among all docked derivatives. Compound 6h formed three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, reducing its free binding energy to -10.55 kcal/mol. Compound 6a had a binding energy of -9.76 kcal/mol and compound 6b a binding energy of -9.17 kcal/mol. Compound 2a could only form one hydrogen bond with Arg552 and had a binding energy of -8.12 kcal/mol. Acarbose can establish 10 hydrogen bonds with Asp232, Ala234, Asn237, Asp357, Arg552, Asp568, and His626. Acarbose forms two hydrophobic interactions between the deoxyglucosamine methyl group and residues Phe601 and Trp329. Trp329 forms hydrophobic bonds with compounds 2a and 6h, responsible for the binding conformation in the active site. The aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 is responsible for the strong inhibitory activity. Trp329 plays a significant role in directing the ligand in the binding site of the α-glucosidase enzyme.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 is identified as the structural feature responsible for the strong inhibitory activity, contrasting with N-alkylation at position 4 which showed weak or no inhibition. The binding energy and number of hydrogen bonds directly correlate with inhibitory activity, with compound 6h's lowest binding energy and three hydrogen bonds explaining its superior performance. Trp329 acts as a critical orienting residue, forming hydrophobic contacts with both compound 6h and the reference acarbose, thus dictating the binding conformation. These compounds represent a non-sugar-mimetic class of α-glucosidase inhibitors, offering a different structural strategy from carbasugars like acarbose for diabetes treatment. The study provides a new structural insight for the development of novel α-glucosidase inhibitors that could eventually be transformed into new clinical drugs for type II diabetes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The abstract reports an IC50 of 104.07 mM for compound 6h, which is extremely high and likely a typographical error for µM, given that compound 3 has IC50 = 167.82 µM and acarbose is the reference. The molecular docking section references 'benzoquinazolines' instead of the actual pyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone compounds synthesized, suggesting carryover text from a previous study. The exact IC50 value of acarbose is not explicitly reported numerically in the paper, making absolute magnitude comparison difficult. Only six compounds (out of 25) were subjected to further IC50 determination, limiting the depth of the bioactivity characterization. The PDB crystal structure 3W37 is from a specific enzyme source not detailed, and the docking was performed without explicit validation against experimental binding data. The inhibitory assay was performed at 0.125 unit/mL enzyme concentration, and while this is specified, no comparison to standard assay conditions is provided.

Claims
Compounds 6d and 6h exhibit α-glucosidase inhibitory activity stronger than acarbose. Compound 6h had the lowest binding energy of -10.56 kcal/mol among all docked derivatives, surpassing acarbose. Compounds 6d and 6h showed IC50 values lower than that of acarbose. Compound 6h formed three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, and hydrophobic bonds with Trp329. The exact IC50 of acarbose is not reported numerically, so the relative claim cannot be fully quantified. The abstract reports IC50 of 6h as 104.07 mM, which would be weaker than acarbose if taken literally. Compounds 6d and 6h could serve as more potent alternatives to acarbose for treating type II diabetes. A non-sugar-mimetic scaffold could potentially reduce gastrointestinal side effects associated with acarbose.
The aminobridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine scaffold is responsible for the strong α-glucosidase inhibitory activity. Compounds 6a–d and 6h, which have aminobridge substituents, showed average percent inhibition greater than 50%. 1. The core contribution is the synthesis of 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one compounds as non-sugar-mimetic α-glucosidase inhibitors, with two showing activity exceeding acarbose. 2. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper by King et al. (University of Cambridge) is a methodological critique and rebuttal of work by Brüschweiler et al. regarding the ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) from yeast mitochondria. Brüschweiler et al. claimed that AAC3 could be refolded to homogeneity from E. coli inclusion bodies using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC), and that the protein maintained a folded, active state suitable for isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and NMR studies, reporting CATR and ATR binding Kd values in the 15–150 µM range. King et al. refute these findings on several grounds: first, they demonstrate via thermostability assays and proteoliposome reconstitution that AAC3 in DPC is in a non-native, unfolded state, not a folded functional form. Second, they measure a CATR binding Kd of 72 nM for native AAC3 in DM/cardiolipin detergent—over 200 to 2000-fold lower than Brüschweiler's reported values—and show that ADP transport is half-maximally inhibited by CATR at 1.2 nM. Third, they identify that Brüschweiler's reference Kd of 192 µM for ATR (Babot et al., 2012) was a typographical error corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. Fourth, the NMR-derived ADP binding Kd of 500 µM reported by Brüschweiler is ~85-fold higher than consensus values and ~25-fold higher than solubilized-carrier values, with chemical shift perturbations located far from the known binding site. Finally, the authors note that the reported dynamic studies are inconsistent with a locked-state binding and the NMR data reflect non-specific interactions at high temperatures and concentrations. The authors conclude that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance.

Research Context
The yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3 has been structurally characterized by electron and x-ray crystallography and studied by single-molecule force spectroscopy. Brüschweiler et al. claimed AAC3 can be refolded to homogeneity from inclusion bodies using dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC). They further asserted AAC3 is maintained in a folded and active state for the duration of ITC and NMR experiments. However, King et al. have previously shown AAC3 in its native environment, folded and active as demonstrated by functional complementation. The gap lies in whether refolded AAC3 in detergent retains biological integrity or represents an unfolded, inactive population.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether AAC3 refolded in dodecyl-phosphocholine retains its native tertiary structure and binding activity. The authors hypothesize that DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3 compared to its native state in the mitochondrial membrane. They predict that binding of CATR to AAC3 should yield Kd values in the low nanomolar range rather than the micro-molar range reported by Brüschweiler et al. They further hypothesize that ADP transport by AAC3 is half-maximally inhibited by a sub-nanomolar concentration of CATR. A subsidiary hypothesis is that the NMR-determined Kd values for CATR and ADP are artifacts of non-specific interactions at high protein concentrations and temperatures.

Methodological Details
AAC3 isoelectric point is 9.82, meaning it is highly positively charged, while CATR and substrates ADP and ATP are negatively charged at neutral pH. To validate AAC3 integrity, King et al. performed thermostability assays using the thiol-reactive fluorophore CPM. Protein was purified from yeast mitochondrial membranes and loaded onto a Ni--Sepharose high performance column at 1 mL per minute on an ÄKTAprime instrument. Particulate material was removed by ultracentrifugation at 140,000 g for 45 minutes at 4 °C. The column was washed with 40 column volumes of buffer and a further 20 column volumes of buffer B. Protein was resuspended with 500 μL buffer B, transferred to a vial with 5 mM CaCl2 and 75 μL Factor Xa. The protein was snap-frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen after being cleaved from the nickel sepharose media. Thermostability measurements were made from 25 to 90 °C at 1 °C intervals with a ramp rate of 5.6 °C per minute. The fluorescence emission was monitored using the HRM channel, providing excitation at 440–480 nm and emission detected at 505–515 nm. For ITC, CATR at 500 μM was titrated into purified 25 μM AAC3 (0.83 mg per mL) in 2-μL injections. The initial injection volume was 170 μL at 3-minute intervals with a stirrer speed of 350 rpm. Data were fitted to a one-site binding model with ΔH, Kd, and stoichiometry as fitting parameters. Lipid reconstitution used L-α-phosphatidylcholine and tetraoleoyl cardiolipin in a 20:1 (w/w) ratio, totaling 10 mg. Detergent was stepwise removed through addition of 4 × 30 mg and 4 × 60 mg of Bio-Beads SM-2 in 20-minute intervals overnight. Proteoliposomes were exchanged into external buffer and diluted 9-fold before ADP uptake assays. Uptake assays used 100 μL of proteoliposome suspension per well of a 96-well filter plate with pore size 0.45 µm. Radiolabeled ADP ([14C]-ADP, 2.2 GBq mmol) was added, giving a final working concentration of 1.5 µM. Transport was stopped at 0, 10, 20, 30, 45 s, 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10 and 15 minutes. CPM was diluted 50-fold from a 5 mg per mL stock dissolved in DMSO. Protein concentration in thermostability assays was approximately 1 μM AAC3. The CPM assay used approximately 1.5 μg of purified protein in a final volume of 45 μL.

Procedures And Architectures
The ITC was performed on a NanoITC-LV isothermal titration calorimeter (TA Instruments) at 10 °C. Both CATR titrant and protein samples were degassed under vacuum at 10 °C for at least 20 minutes before titration. The binding model was fitted using the instrument software (NanoAnalyze). For thermostability, a modified procedure using a rotary qPCR machine was employed as described previously. The CPM dye undergoes an increase in fluorescence emission following reaction with cysteine residues. Thermostability experiments were conducted in the dark at room temperature for 10 minutes prior to measurement. Lipid was emulsified in buffer and solubilized with 55 μL of 25% (v/v) pentaethylene glycol monodecyl detergent on ice. AAC3 protein was added at 30 μg to achieve a final volume of 0.6 mL in the absence of detergent. Proteoliposomes were formed by stepwise detergent removal and then separated using an empty spin column. The resulting proteoliposome suspension was exchanged into external buffer using a PD10 desalting column. Uptake assays were carried out using a Hamilton MicroLab Star robot. CATR inhibitor was added where required to the proteoliposome suspension.

Key Results
Brüschweiler et al. reported a Kd of ~15 µM for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 by ITC. By NMR, they determined CATR-dependent chemical shift perturbations giving a Kd of ~150 µM. They compared their values to a reported Kd of 192 µM for ATR, but that value was later corrected to 192 nM. Published Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane are all in the low nanomolar range. ADP transport by AAC3 is half-maximally inhibited by CATR at 1.2 nM, consistent with its role as a powerful toxin. King et al. measured an average Kd of 72 nM for CATR binding to native AAC3 in DM/cardiolipin detergent. This measured Kd is 200 to 2000-fold lower than the values reported by Brüschweiler et al. The ADP binding Kd by NMR reported by Brüschweiler was 500 µM, which is ~85-fold higher than published consensus values. The reported 500 µM ADP Kd is also ~25-fold higher than the Kd for the solubilized carrier. Residues assigned to ADP-induced chemical shift perturbations are largely on the matrix side, far from the known binding site. Thermostability in DM showed a typical protein melt curve consistent with thermal denaturation of a folded protein. Addition of CATR at a molar ratio of one or above caused a marked shift in stability to higher temperatures. Dilution of AAC3 into 3 mM DPC showed a high signal with no transition, indicating a non-native state. In the DPC preparation, CATR addition had no effect, demonstrating no functional binding site. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. In contrast, control tests where protein was diluted into dodecyl-maltoside prior to reconstitution retained functional uptake. ITC experiments were very difficult, with only 2 out of 10 trials succeeding, due to low enthalpy change and unstable apo-state in detergent. The very few polar side chain interactions that stabilize AAC3 are mainly found on the matrix side, forming intra-domain rather than inter-domain interactions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The transmembrane α-helix ring of AAC3 is held together largely by lateral pressure of the membrane and counter pressure from the water-filled cavity. Binding of CATR introduces numerous polar and van der Waals interactions that cross-link most of the transmembrane α-helices, explaining high affinity and improved detergent stability. The extremely low affinity of CATR for refolded AAC3 in DPC raises the question whether the binding is specific at all. Only a limited number of chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding to refolded AAC3 are observed, and all are dynamic, inconsistent with tight binding. Most reported residues are not near the known CATR binding site nor on structural elements involved in CATR binding. The chemical shift perturbations for CATR and ADP could represent non-specific interactions promoted by high concentrations and temperatures used in the NMR experiments. The dynamic studies measured by NMR relaxation dispersion are questionable because CATR binding should lock the protein in a non-dynamic aborted state. The observed dynamics in the presence of substrate do not provide a plausible structural mechanism for transport.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a rebuttal of Brüschweiler et al. and does not present novel structural or functional data on AAC3 beyond what is needed to refute the target paper. The authors note that the crystal structure of AAC3 was obtained with CATR inhibited in the membrane, but the inhibitor was removed before crystallization. A clear interpretable density for CATR could nevertheless be observed in the crystal structure, demonstrating extremely low rates of dissociation. The 24 different binding studies referenced in Supplementary Table 1 provide consensus but are not fully detailed in the main text. The authors reference a typographical error in the Babot et al., 2012 reference that was corrected in an erratum. The NMR experiments used high protein concentrations and temperatures that may drive non-specific interactions. The authors acknowledge that their ITC measurements were very difficult, with only 2 out of 10 trials succeeding. The apo-state of AAC3 is very unstable in detergent, which limits experimental access.

Claims
AAC3 refolded in dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) is in a non-native, unfolded state and lacks functional integrity for binding and transport assays. Thermostability in 3 mM DPC showed a high signal with no melting transition, in contrast to the typical melt curve in dodecyl-maltoside. Dilution into DPC prior to reconstitution caused complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in proteoliposomes. CATR addition to AAC3 in DPC had no stabilizing effect, demonstrating no functional binding site. Brüschweiler et al. reported measurable ITC and NMR binding events (Kd 15–150 µM) for CATR to DPC-refolded AAC3. A clear interpretable density for CATR could be observed in the crystal structure of AAC3, despite the absence of CATR in the crystal condition. The NMR and ITC data reported by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance and should not be used to draw conclusions about AAC3 function. Use of DPC for refolding AAC3 does not yield a functionally intact protein for solution-phase biochemical studies.
The true CATR and ADP binding affinities of AAC3 are in the low nanomolar range, consistent with its role as a powerful mitochondrial toxin. King et al. measured a CATR binding Kd of 72 nM for native AAC3 in DM/cardiolipin detergent. ADP transport is half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR, consistent with its potent toxin action. Published Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane are all in the low nanomolar range. Brüschweiler et al. reported a Kd of ~15 µM (ITC) and ~150 µM (NMR) for CATR binding to refolded AAC3. Brüschweiler et al. reported a 500 µM ADP binding Kd by NMR, significantly higher than consensus. The observed micro-molar binding in refolded AAC3 reflects non-specific interactions rather than physiological binding. The high affinity (low nanomolar) is consistent with CATR's established role as a potent inhibitor of mitochondrial transport.

Data And Code Availability
The paper references Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 containing consensus binding data and NMR perturbation residue assignments. The data presented are the results of NMR, ITC, thermostability, and ADP uptake assays performed by King et al. at Cambridge. No explicit statement is made regarding code or data repository availability, as this is a methodology critique paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors performed a comparative detergent study, testing AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside vs. dodecyl-phosphocholine for thermostability and reconstitution. Thermostability was probed with varying CATR molar ratios from 0.001 to 100, showing a dose-dependent stabilization in DM but no effect in DPC. The reconstitution experiment used a detergent gradient (stepwise removal with Bio-Beads) and a direct addition control to isolate detergent effects. ADP uptake was measured at 11 time points, providing a kinetic profile of transport activity. The ITC experiments were limited to only 2 out of 10 successful trials, acknowledging the experimental difficulty.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows CATR inhibition of ADP transport by AAC3, with half-maximal inhibition at 1.2 nM. Figure 1b displays the ITC isotherm for CATR binding to native AAC3 in DM/cardiolipin, giving an average Kd of 72 nM. Figure 1c shows the typical protein melt curve of AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside with CATR-dependent stabilization. Figure 1d shows the high signal with no transition for AAC3 in 3 mM DPC, with no CATR effect. Supplementary Fig. 1a shows the lateral pressure model of the transmembrane helix ring. Supplementary Fig. 1b shows the CATR cross-linking of the α-helix bundle. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows the loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in DPC-diluted proteoliposomes vs. DM controls. Supplementary Table 1 lists 24 different binding studies for CATR and ATR. Supplementary Table 2 shows the consensus and solubilized-carrier ADP binding values compared to the 500 µM NMR value.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that AAC3 refolded in dodecyl-phosphocholine is non-native and unfolded, invalidating Brüschweiler et al.'s ITC and NMR binding data. 2. The strongest evidence is the 200 to 2000-fold discrepancy between the 72 nM native binding Kd (King et al.) and the 15–150 µM refolded binding Kd (Brüschweiler et al.), combined with the loss of functional ADP uptake in DPC-reconstituted proteoliposomes. 3. The future path lies in establishing proper detergent conditions (e.g., DM/cardiolipin) for AAC3 biochemistry and in re-evaluating DPC-refolded protein data as non-specific artifacts.

summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates, for the first time, that the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication, specifically for Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors identified SERCA as a proviral host factor after screening a library of kinase and phosphate inhibitors against paramyxoviruses and avulaviruses. Treatment of Vero cells with the SERCA-specific inhibitor thapsigargin (0.5 µM) significantly reduced NDV and PPRV replication, while overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa and goat kidney cells rescued the inhibitory effect, confirming a causal link. Thapsigargin treatment at non-cytotoxic concentrations did not exhibit virucidal activity, indicating the inhibition is intracellular. Time-of-addition assays revealed that Thapsigargin inhibits multiple pre-budding steps, with maximal inhibition occurring 30 minutes prior to infection and decreasing progressively. Virus step-specific assays confirmed that Thapsigargin does not affect attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Immunofluorescence demonstrated that Thapsigargin induces defective subcellular localization of viral proteins, with ~70% of cells showing cytoplasmic foci versus 10-30% in control, indicating a requirement for SERCA in protein trafficking to the cell surface. Notably, NDV acquired partial resistance to Thapsigargin upon 70 sequential passages (resistance at P35, ~100-fold vs. ~10,000-fold inhibition), while PPRV showed no resistance development. The study also observed that PPRV infection induces transient SERCA2 overexpression at 3 hpi peaking at 24-72 hpi, which could be blocked by Thapsigargin. The authors position SERCA as a novel host-targeting antiviral candidate, contrasting with the established paradigm that viruses do not acquire resistance to host-targeting agents. The finding of acquired resistance in NDV adds to a short list of viruses (e.g., CVB3, HCV) capable of bypassing a targeted cellular factor. The study concludes that SERCA is a crucial proviral host factor whose inhibition represents a promising therapeutic strategy against paramyxoviruses.
