judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates, for the first time, that the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication, specifically for Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors identified SERCA as a proviral host factor after screening a library of kinase and phosphate inhibitors against paramyxoviruses and avulaviruses. Treatment of Vero cells with the SERCA-specific inhibitor thapsigargin (0.5 µM) significantly reduced NDV and PPRV replication, while overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa and goat kidney cells rescued the inhibitory effect, confirming a causal link. Thapsigargin treatment at non-cytotoxic concentrations did not exhibit virucidal activity, indicating the inhibition is intracellular. Time-of-addition assays revealed that Thapsigargin inhibits multiple pre-budding steps, with maximal inhibition occurring 30 minutes prior to infection and decreasing progressively. Virus step-specific assays confirmed that Thapsigargin does not affect attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Immunofluorescence demonstrated that Thapsigargin induces defective subcellular localization of viral proteins, with ~70% of cells showing cytoplasmic foci versus 10-30% in control, indicating a requirement for SERCA in protein trafficking to the cell surface. Notably, NDV acquired partial resistance to Thapsigargin upon 70 sequential passages (resistance at P35, ~100-fold vs. ~10,000-fold inhibition), while PPRV showed no resistance development. The study also observed that PPRV infection induces transient SERCA2 overexpression at 3 hpi peaking at 24-72 hpi, which could be blocked by Thapsigargin. The authors position SERCA as a novel host-targeting antiviral candidate, contrasting with the established paradigm that viruses do not acquire resistance to host-targeting agents. The finding of acquired resistance in NDV adds to a short list of viruses (e.g., CVB3, HCV) capable of bypassing a targeted cellular factor. The study concludes that SERCA is a crucial proviral host factor whose inhibition represents a promising therapeutic strategy against paramyxoviruses.

Research Context
Antiviral drug development has traditionally targeted essential pathogen proteins but the high mutation rate of viral genomes drives rapid resistance and necessitates novel strategies. Host responses and the dysregulation of cellular factors upon infection determine the actual disease outcome, with proviral factors serving as untapped therapeutic targets. Kinases, forming the kinome, have been shown to play key roles in cancer and viral infections, making them desirable drug targets. In vertebrates, three P-type Ca2+-ATPases—PMCA, SERCA, and SPCA—regulate intracellular calcium homeostasis across plasma membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi respectively. SERCA transports Ca2+ from cytosol to double membrane-bound endoplasmic reticulum compartments and is involved in signal transduction, apoptosis, and transcription. Three SERCA genes (ATP2A1-3) produce 10 isoforms through alternative splicing, with SERCA2 ubiquitously expressed while others show cell-type specific patterns. The role of Ca2+-ATPases in virus replication was only beginning to be appreciated, with SPCA1 support already suggested but SERCA and PMCA roles remaining unknown. A previous screening of kinase and phosphate inhibitors against influenza A viruses established a methodological precedent for this study's paramyxovirus screen.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the SERCA calcium-ATPase, a known host cellular enzyme, plays a proviral role in paramyxovirus replication. The study hypothesizes that SERCA serves as a proviral host factor whose inhibition by thapsigargin will impair NDV and PPRV replication. It is predicted that thapsigargin will significantly reduce viral titers without being cytotoxic, and that overexpression of SERCA will rescue the inhibitory effect. The authors hypothesize that the antiviral effect is intracellular rather than virucidal, and that the inhibition mechanism involves specific steps of the viral life cycle. A secondary hypothesis is that viruses may not acquire resistance to host-targeting agents due to the high genetic barrier imposed by targeting stable cellular factors. The authors also explore whether NDV and PPRV induce endogenous SERCA expression upon infection and if this induction is manipulable. Time-of-addition assays are employed to test whether thapsigargin targets attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, or budding, with the expectation of specific step inhibition. Immunofluorescence is used to test whether SERCA inhibition causes defective subcellular localization of viral proteins, testing the spatial mechanism of the antiviral effect.

Methodological Details
Vero (African green-monkey kidney), 293T (human embryonic kidney), HeLa, and goat kidney cells were grown in DMEM supplemented with 10% heatinactivated fetal bovine serum. PPRV and NDV were available in the authors' laboratory and had been previously described. Thapsigargin, the SERCA inhibitor, was procured from Sigma as Catalog Number-T9033 from Steinheim, Germany. Thapsigargin is identified as a non-competitive inhibitor of SERCA, structurally classified as a sesquiterpene lactone extracted from Thapsia garganica. Cytotoxicity was assessed in Vero and MDBK cells using an MTT assay across a concentration range of 0.00064 to 2 µM. A non-cytotoxic concentration of 0.5 µM was selected for all subsequent antiviral experiments. Viral titers were determined by plaque assay, and progeny virus particles were quantified from supernatants. Virucidal assays incubated virus suspensions containing approximately 10^6 plaque forming units in serum-free medium with Thapsigargin for 1.5 h at 37 °C. Samples were chilled at 4 °C and diluted 10^3, 10^4, and 10^5-fold before being applied to Vero/MDBK cells in 6-well plates. Infection experiments used MOI=0.1 for antiviral efficacy, MOI=0.01 for resistance studies, and MOI=5 for immunofluorescence assays. For SERCA overexpression, HeLa and goat kidney cells were transfected in 24-well plates in triplicates with either 1 µg empty vector (pCR3) or SERCA2 plasmid (pCR3-SERCA2) using Lipofectamine 3000. Virus particles were harvested at 24 hours post-infection for NDV and 96 hours post-infection for PPRV. Immunofluorescence was conducted on Vero cells at 20% confluency infected at MOI=5 for 2 h, with Thapsigargin applied at 3 hpi for NDV and 10 hpi for PPRV. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin for 30 min, and stained with primary antibodies (rabbit anti-NDV/anti-PPRV or mouse SERCA2) in 0.2% saponin. Secondary antibodies (fluorescein isothiocyanate-conjugated anti-rabbit or Rhodamine-conjugated anti-mouse) were applied in 0.2% saponin, followed by DAPI mounting and fluorescence microscopy. Resistance studies passaged NDV sequentially 70 times in Vero cells in the presence of 0.25 µM Thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO. At each passage, monolayers were infected, washed 5 times with PBS, and incubated for 72-120 h until cytopathic effect appeared in ≥75% cells. The virus was quantified by plaque assay at MOI=0.01 and used for the subsequent round of infection. To evaluate relative resistance, Thapsigargin-passaged and DMSO-passaged viruses were tested at MOI=0.1 with 24-hour harvest in 0.05% DMSO or 0.5 µM Thapsigargin.

Procedures And Architectures
The experimental design follows a modular approach: cytotoxicity screening, antiviral efficacy, virucidal control, time-of-addition, virus step-specific assays, overexpression, immunofluorescence, and long-term resistance passage. Thapsigargin was applied as a non-competitive inhibitor at 0.5 µM against Vero/MDBK cells for NDV and PPRV. Time-of-addition assays used one-step growth curves where the inhibitor was applied at different time points post-infection and progeny virus was plaque-assayed. The NDV replication cycle (~10 h) and PPRV cycle (~24 h) dictated the time points for both inhibitor addition and virus harvest. Virus step-specific assays for attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, subcellular localization, and budding were conducted according to previously described methods. For overexpression, Lipofectamine 3000 Transfection reagent was used to transfect pCR3-SERCA2 plasmid into HeLa and goat kidney cells in 24-well plates. In immunofluorescence, Thapsigargin was applied at 3 hpi for NDV and 10 hpi for PPRV to intercept early viral events. Progeny virus from NDV was harvested at 24 hpi for overexpression experiments, while PPRV progeny was harvested at 96 hpi. For resistance passage, the virus was harvested from supernatants, quantified by plaque assay, and inoculated at MOI=0.01 for the next passage in a sequential 70-passage scheme. Western blot analysis probed SERCA2 and GAPDH in Vero cell lysates infected with NDV at MOI=5 for 1 h, with Thapsigargin applied at 16 hpi. The virucidal assay employed ten-fold dilutions of Thapsigargin to test whether direct inactivation of free virions contributed to antiviral activity. The entry assay used pre-attached virus at 4 °C, allowed to enter at 37 °C in the presence of Thapsigargin.

Key Results
MTT assays confirmed Thapsigargin was non-cytotoxic to Vero/MDBK cells at concentrations from 0.00064 to 2 µM when incubated for 96 h. At concentrations above 2 µM, Thapsigargin became cytotoxic, justifying the use of 0.5 µM as the experimental concentration. Thapsigargin at 0.5 µM significantly inhibited replication of both NDV and PPRV, but showed no effect on BPXV. Thapsigargin also significantly inhibited BHV-1 replication, confirming its antiviral activity against paramyxoviruses and the DNA virus BHV-1. The virucidal assay showed Thapsigargin had no effect on free virus particles, confirming antiviral activity requires intracellular targets. Overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa and goat kidney cells facilitated NDV and PPRV replication and fully rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin. PPRV infection of Vero cells induced SERCA2 expression at 3 hpi, remaining elevated from 24 to 72 hpi before declining at 96 hpi. GAPDH expression remained similar at all time points, confirming that SERCA2 induction was virus-specific. Thapsigargin treatment blocked the virus-induced increase in SERCA2 expression in Vero cells. In NDV time-of-addition, maximal inhibition occurred when Thapsigargin was applied 30 minutes before infection, with inhibition progressively decreasing from 1 hpi to 6 hpi. At 10 hpi, Thapsigargin had no inhibitory effect on NDV, a time point when the virus is presumably undergoing budding. For PPRV, maximal inhibition was at 30 minutes before infection, with progressive decrease from 4 hpi to 24 hpi. Virus step-specific assays showed Thapsigargin did not affect virus attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. The viral entry assay confirmed Thapsigargin reduced both NDV and PPRV titers when pre-attached virus was permitted to enter. Immunofluorescence revealed that Thapsigargin-treated cells showed defective subcellular localization of viral proteins, with cytoplasmic foci in approximately 70% of cells. In DMSO-treated control cells, the proportion of cells with defective localization was only 10-30%, confirming SERCA is required for protein trafficking. NDV passaged 70 times with 0.25 µM Thapsigargin did not achieve a completely resistant phenotype. Resistance to Thapsigargin in NDV began appearing at ~P25 and became significant at P35 with ~100-fold inhibition compared to ~10,000-fold inhibition at P0. At P70, NDV retained significantly lower sensitivity to Thapsigargin, though no completely resistant phenotype was observed. All PPRV variants (P0, P70-Thapsigargin, P70-Control) showed similar sensitivity to Thapsigargin, indicating no resistance development. Control-passaged viruses exhibited no significant resistance against Thapsigargin after 70 passages. Western blot confirmed Thapsigargin inhibited NDV-induced SERCA2 expression in Vero cells.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
SERCA serves as a proviral host factor required for proper paramyxovirus replication, specifically mediating viral entry and subcellular protein localization. The ability of SERCA2 overexpression to rescue Thapsigargin inhibition provides causal confirmation that SERCA, rather than an off-target effect, drives paramyxovirus replication. The finding that NDV acquired partial resistance to a host-targeting agent challenges the general assumption that viruses cannot escape inhibition of stable cellular factors. The results suggest that SERCA may be a novel druggable target for broad-spectrum paramyxovirus antivirals, with the host-targeting strategy imposing a higher genetic barrier to resistance. The virus-induced transient overexpression of SERCA2 suggests paramyxoviruses might actively recruit the calcium-ATPase to facilitate their replication cycle. The observation that NDV acquired resistance while PPRV did not suggests strain-specific dependencies on SERCA or differences in genetic adaptability. The unsuccessful co-immunoprecipitation suggests the SERCA-virus interaction may be indirect or transient, and the mechanism of acquired resistance remains to be elucidated.

Contradictions And Limitations
The co-immunoprecipitation assay to analyze the direct SERCA-virus interaction was unsuccessful, so no direct binding can be confirmed. In immunofluorescence, perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins could not be observed, limiting mechanistic detail on the interaction. A complete Thapsigargin-resistant NDV phenotype was not achieved even after 70 passages, leaving the exact mechanism of reduced sensitivity uncharacterized. Fluctuations in overall viral titers and fold-inhibition values during resistance passage may reflect variability in harvest time (72-120 h) and MOI (0.01-0.001) across passages. The study is limited to Vero cells, HeLa, and goat kidney cells; broader host cell testing is needed to confirm the generality of the SERCA effect. No direct molecular evidence was produced identifying which viral protein(s) acquired mutations to confer reduced SERCA dependency. The authors note that the SPCA1-mediated replication support for Flaviviridae, Togaviridae, and Paramyxoviridae by Hoffmann and coworkers adds complexity, suggesting multiple calcium transporters may be involved.

Claims
SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase) is a proviral host factor required for paramyxovirus replication. Thapsigargin, a SERCA-specific inhibitor, significantly reduced NDV and PPRV replication in Vero cells. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin on virus replication in HeLa and goat kidney cells. PPRV infection induced SERCA2 expression at 3 hpi, peaking at 24-72 hpi. Virus-induced SERCA2 expression could be blocked by Thapsigargin. The co-immunoprecipitation assay to detect direct SERCA-virus interaction was unsuccessful. Perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins was not observed in immunofluorescence. SERCA represents a novel, druggable host target for paramyxovirus therapeutics. The host-targeting approach imposes a higher genetic barrier to resistance compared to direct-acting antivirals.
Thapsigargin inhibits paramyxovirus replication by impairing viral entry and protein trafficking to the cell surface. Time-of-addition assays showed maximal inhibition 30 minutes before infection and progressive decrease through the life cycle. The viral entry assay confirmed Thapsigargin reduced both NDV and PPRV titers. Immunofluorescence showed approximately 70% of cells had cytoplasmic foci versus 10-30% in DMSO controls. Virus step-specific assays ruled out attachment, RNA synthesis, and budding as sites of inhibition. The mechanism of how SERCA facilitates specific entry or localization steps remains to be fully elucidated. Antiviral strategies could combine SERCA inhibition with other drugs to target multiple stages of the viral life cycle.
NDV can acquire partial resistance to SERCA inhibition upon sequential passage, challenging the paradigm that host-targeting agents generate no viral resistance. NDV passaged 70 times with 0.25 µM Thapsigargin developed resistance at P35 (~100-fold vs. ~10,000-fold inhibition). Control-passaged viruses exhibited no resistance after 70 passages. P70-Thapsigargin NDV showed significantly lower sensitivity, although no complete resistance was achieved. PPRV did not develop any resistance to Thapsigargin after 70 passages. A completely resistant phenotype was never reached even at passage level 70. The genetic barrier to host-targeting agent resistance may be lower than previously assumed. The mechanism of resistance—whether by changed host-factor requirement or increased affinity—remains to be determined.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The virucidal assay with ten-fold Thapsigargin dilutions confirmed that antiviral effects were intracellular, not due to direct inactivation of virions. The control experiments with DMSO (vehicle) at both 0.05% and 0.25% levels validated the specific effects of Thapsigargin. Gapdh expression was monitored alongside SERCA2 to confirm virus-specific gene induction. Resistance studies used both 0.25 µM Thapsigargin and 0.05% DMSO passages to distinguish specific inhibitor-induced changes from general passage effects. The relative resistance assay at P70 used standardized MOI=0.1 and 24-hour harvest time to control for passage-to-passage variability in MOI and timing.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a-b: MTT assays show Thapsigargin non-cytotoxic at 0.00064 to 2 µM in Vero/MDBK cells over 96 h. Figure 1c-f: Plaque assay results showing Thapsigargin at 0.5 µM inhibits NDV, PPRV, and BHV-1, but not BPXV. Figure 1g: Virucidal assay results showing Thapsigargin has no effect on free virion infectivity at 0.5 and 5 µM. Figure 2a-b: Overexpression of SERCA2 rescues Thapsigargin inhibition of NDV and PPRV in HeLa and goat kidney cells. Figure 3a: RT-qPCR/Western blot showing PPRV-induced SERCA2 expression over time (3, 24, 72, 96 hpi) with GAPDH as control. Figure 3b: Thapsigargin blocks virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Figure 4a-b: Time-of-addition assay for NDV (10 h cycle) and PPRV (24 h cycle) showing maximal inhibition 30 min before infection. Figure 5a-b: Entry assay showing Thapsigargin reduces NDV and PPRV titers when pre-attached virus is allowed to enter at 37 °C. Figure 6a-d: Immunofluorescence images and quantification showing defective protein localization (~70% vs. 10-30%) with Thapsigargin. Figure 7a-c: Sequential passage data for NDV resistance developing at P25/P35, and confirming no resistance in PPRV or control-passaged NDV. Figure 7b: Relative resistance assay confirming NDV P70-Thapsigargin has lower sensitivity than P0 and P70-Control.

Three Takeaways
1. SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase) is a proviral host factor required for paramyxovirus replication, as demonstrated by Thapsigargin-mediated inhibition and SERCA2-mediated rescue. 2. The strongest evidence comes from the combination of SERCA-specific inhibition, time-of-addition assays locating inhibition to pre-budding steps, immunofluorescence demonstrating defective protein trafficking, and the rescue of infection by SERCA2 overexpression. 3. The future path lies in identifying the molecular mechanism by which NDV acquires SERCA-resistance, determining which viral mutations confer escape, and developing SERCA-targeting antivirals against paramyxoviruses.

summary.title: MicroRNA-196a is regulated by ER and is a prognostic biomarker in ER+ Breast Cancer
summary.authors: Michael J G Milevskiy; Udai Gujral; Carolina Del Lama Marques; Andrew Stone; Korinne Northwood; Lez J Burke; Julia M W Gee; Kenneth Nephew; Susan Clark; Melissa A Brown; Mjg Milevskiy
summary.field_subfield: Molecular Oncology / Breast Cancer / MicroRNA Regulation
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates that microRNA-196a (miR-196a), transcribed from two genomic loci—MIR196A1 (HOXB locus on Chr17) and MIR196A2 (HOXC locus on Chr12)—is transcriptionally regulated by the oestrogen receptor (ERα). Using a multi-omic approach in MCF7 breast cancer cells and human breast tissue, the authors employed ChIP-Seq (RNA polymerase II), GRO-Seq, luciferase reporter assays, ChIA-PET, 3C-qPCR, and DNA methylation analysis to characterize the regulatory landscape of MIR196A. They identified that ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 bind to two putative promoters (PP1, HOXC10 promoter; and PP3) of MIR196A2, and that both the HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel enhancer (mE) physically interact with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that MIR196A expression correlates strongly with HOXC gene expression in breast tumours but is not significantly associated in normal tissues, and that MIR196A is predominantly expressed in basal stem-cell derived lineages. In the METABRIC cohort of 323 breast tumours, MIR196A is overexpressed in tumours versus normal adjacent tissue and associates with increased tumour stage. Most critically, high MIR196A expression serves as a robust prognostic biomarker: in ER+ tumours responding to hormone therapy and chemotherapy, low MIR196A expression is associated with >95% survival at 10 years, while high expression is associated with 61% survival at 10 years. The prognostic direction is inverted post-menopause: high MIR196A associates with good outcome in pre-menopausal ER+ tumours but with poor outcome in post-menopausal ER+ tumours, whereas in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), high MIR196A associates with better outcome. In tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells, MIR196A expression is significantly increased, matching DNA hypomethylation of the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters, while in fulvestrant-resistant cells, MIR196A is nearly depleted with corresponding hypermethylation. Patient ERα ChIP-Seq reveals increased ERα occupancy at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases from resistant tumours. These findings suggest that the pathway to endocrine resistance in ER+ tumours involves de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements, potentially reverting cells to a stem-cell-like state.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates that microRNA-196a (miR-196a), transcribed from two genomic loci—MIR196A1 (HOXB locus on Chr17) and MIR196A2 (HOXC locus on Chr12)—is transcriptionally regulated by the oestrogen receptor (ERα). Using a multi-omic approach in MCF7 breast cancer cells and human breast tissue, the authors employed ChIP-Seq (RNA polymerase II), GRO-Seq, luciferase reporter assays, ChIA-PET, 3C-qPCR, and DNA methylation analysis to characterize the regulatory landscape of MIR196A. They identified that ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 bind to two putative promoters (PP1, HOXC10 promoter; and PP3) of MIR196A2, and that both the HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel enhancer (mE) physically interact with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that MIR196A expression correlates strongly with HOXC gene expression in breast tumours but is not significantly associated in normal tissues, and that MIR196A is predominantly expressed in basal stem-cell derived lineages. In the METABRIC cohort of 323 breast tumours, MIR196A is overexpressed in tumours versus normal adjacent tissue and associates with increased tumour stage. Most critically, high MIR196A expression serves as a robust prognostic biomarker: in ER+ tumours responding to hormone therapy and chemotherapy, low MIR196A expression is associated with >95% survival at 10 years, while high expression is associated with 61% survival at 10 years. The prognostic direction is inverted post-menopause: high MIR196A associates with good outcome in pre-menopausal ER+ tumours but with poor outcome in post-menopausal ER+ tumours, whereas in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), high MIR196A associates with better outcome. In tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells, MIR196A expression is significantly increased, matching DNA hypomethylation of the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters, while in fulvestrant-resistant cells, MIR196A is nearly depleted with corresponding hypermethylation. Patient ERα ChIP-Seq reveals increased ERα occupancy at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases from resistant tumours. These findings suggest that the pathway to endocrine resistance in ER+ tumours involves de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements, potentially reverting cells to a stem-cell-like state.

Research Context
MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression through diverse mechanisms. They have been implicated in a wide range of diseases including cancer, where germline and somatic mutations plus epigenetic deregulation drive pathology. Research into microRNA biology has identified clinically useful genetic and epigenetic biomarkers and antagomiR-based therapeutic agents. MIR196A is transcribed at two loci, HOXC (Chr12, MIR196A2) and HOXB (Chr17, MIR196A1), and has been strongly implicated in cancer as an oncogene. MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumours, and a specific SNP (rs116149130) within MIR196A2 is associated with reduced breast cancer risk. Functional studies show MIR196A targets the 3' UTR of Annexin-1 in response to VEGF, alters angiogenesis, increases growth/migration/invasion via HOXA5, and regulates the cell cycle via p27/Kip1. Despite its clear importance in cancer, the transcriptional regulation of MIR196A remains poorly understood. MicroRNA promoters are enriched for H3K4me3 and lack H3K27me3 when active, and enhancer regulation has only been described in a few instances.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to characterise the expression landscape of MIR196A, including factors regulating its expression and exploring potential roles of regulatory elements in breast cancer prognostication. Given MIR196A expression correlates with HOXC gene expression in breast cancer, the authors sought to determine if oestrogen regulates MIR196A2 transcriptionally. The authors hypothesised that since MIR196A is regulated by ERα, its transcription may be controlled by the oestrogen receptor via promoter binding and pioneer factor cooperation. A secondary hypothesis, motivated by ERα's propensity to bind distal enhancers, proposed that MIR196A2 is controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation mediated by ERα-tethered gene looping. The study also hypothesised that the SNP-associated CpG island within the MIR196A2 gene is relevant to transcriptional regulation, given its proximity to the PP3 promoter. Predicted outcomes included identification of promoter/enhancer elements, quantitative assessment of ERα-mediated transcriptional activation, physical confirmation of enhancer-promoter interactions, and demonstration of prognostic and resistance-associated expression changes.

Methodological Details
MCF7 cells, obtained from AstraZeneca, served as the primary cell line model for development of endocrine resistance sub-lines including tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR), fulvestrant-resistant (FASR), and oestrogen-deprived (MCF7x). All cell lines were cultured for less than 6 months after authentication by short-tandem repeat (STR) profiling at the Cell Bank, Australia. PCR products for luciferase reporter assays were ligated into Invitrogen's pCR-Blunt plasmid using T4 DNA Ligase at 4°C overnight, and cloned into pGL3-Basic. Enhancers were cloned into the BamHI/SalI site while promoters were cloned into the multiple cloning site immediately upstream of the luciferase gene. MCF7 cells were transfected with 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs, 20 ng of pRL-TK (Renilla control), and 0.5 μL of Lipofectamine 3000. Luciferase readings were measured 48 hours post-transfection using a DTX-880 luminometer and Dual-Glo Stop and Glo luciferase reporter kit. Cell lysates were prepared with TRIzol® reagent, followed by chloroform extraction, isopropanol precipitation, and DNaseI treatment with an Ambion DNA free kit. miRNA RNA was reverse transcribed using the miScript RT II kit from Qiagen and assayed with the miScript SYBR Green PCR Kit; expression was normalised to snoRNA RNU6b. All qRT-PCRs were performed using protocols from manufacturers on a Corbet Rotorgene-6000. RNA-Seq on MCF7 cells following oestradiol treatment was performed as previously described by K. Nephew. RNA-Seq from Adriamycin (ADM) and paclitaxel (PTX) resistant MCF7 derived cells was sourced from GEO accession GSE68815. Expression of HOX genes in human breast cells was sourced from Gascard et al. ChIP-Seq data for MCF7 (GSE14664), GRO-Seq (GSE27463), ChIA-PET (GSE39495), and Breast tumour ERα ChIP-Seq (GSE32222) were accessed from public repositories. MCF7 histone ChIP-Seq and breast cell 450K array data were sourced from ENCODE. ChIP-Seq data were mapped with Bowtie and peaks called by MACS, viewed in the Interactive Genome Viewer (IGV). DNA methylation of breast tumours was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and correlated to MIR196A expression from the TCGA cohort. METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from GEO accession EGAS00000083. Clustering of Illumina Array and miR-Seq data was performed using the Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV), with Manhattan average-linkage based hierarchical clustering. Genes within clusters were correlated using the CORREL function of Microsoft Excel. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analyses were performed using MedCalc for Windows, version 12.7. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and survival curves were generated in GraphPad Prism, with optimal cutoffs determined using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Chromosome conformation capture (3C) was adapted from Vakoc 2005, Hagege 2007, and Tan-Wong 2008. Cells were grown to 60-80% confluence, fixed with 1% formaldehyde, and libraries were generated using HindIII. GAPDH primers, amplifying a fragment with no cut sites, were used for ligation efficiency control by comparing 3C-qPCR values to HindIII cut-site primers. 3C-qPCR primers were designed between 100-250 bp up or downstream of each HindIII cut site with the primer across the putative enhancer used as bait.

Procedures And Architectures
The study first characterised the expression of HOXC genes in breast cancers (Supplementary Figure 1) and compared with HOXC gene expression in normal human breast tissues (Supplementary Figure 2A, B), identifying the association of MIR196A with HOXC10. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP-Seq) for RNA polymerase II was performed on MCF7 cells to assess polymerase binding at the HOXC10 and MIR196A2 region under oestrogen stimulation. Global-run-on sequencing (GRO-Seq) was used to measure nascent RNA and assess transcriptional changes with high sensitivity in MCF7 cells following oestradiol addition. GRO-Seq data analysis showed a dramatic increase in RNA production peaking at 40 minutes post-oestradiol addition in the genomic region surrounding MIR196A2, not MIR196A1. This GRO-Seq result was validated with qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq from MCF7 cells following oestradiol treatment. Histone methylation patterns were assessed in MCF7 cells to identify putative promoter elements upstream of MIR196A, revealing a shared promoter with HOXC10. Publicly available datasets established ERα and FOXA1 binding to two putative promoter regions (PP1 and PP3) upstream of the miR196A2 transcription start site. Putative promoters PP1 and PP2 (modestly) were cloned into luciferase reporter vectors, with PP1 (HOXC10 promoter) being most active in MCF7 cells. ChIA-PET genome-wide chromatin interactions immunoprecipitated with either ERα or RNA polymerase II identified two major interaction sites with MIR196A2 promoters. One interaction site was the previously identified HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE); the other was a novel interacting partner (MIR196A2-Enhancer, mE). Chromosome conformation capture (3C) with HindIII digestion demonstrated that both enhancer elements physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. Cloning these enhancer fragments downstream of luciferase reporter promoters showed significant augmentation of transcription for both PP1 and PP2, with HDE being most active in MCF7 cells. DNA methylation analysis showed the CpG island within MIR196A2 is mostly methylated in MCF10A and MCF7 cells but unmethylated in human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC). Four distinct clusters of MIR196A expression were identified, with clusters 1 and 3 correlating to HR and HR cofactors, while clusters 2 and 4 show significant negative correlation to ERα, PGR, FOXA1, and GATA3. The PAM50 intrinsic subtype analysis showed MIR196A strongly expressed in HER2 subtype, with dynamic expression in luminal A and B subtypes. METABRIC cohort analysis included 323 breast tumours and associated MIR196A over-expression with tumour stage and poor survival in ER+ tumours. In pre-menopausal women, multivariate analysis demonstrated MIR196A as one of few significant biomarkers for ER+ tumours. Tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells (TAMR) show significantly increased MIR196A, while fulvestrant-resistant cells (FASR) show almost depleted MIR196A. DNA methylation changes to the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters in resistance models matched these expression patterns. RNA-Seq from paclitaxel and adromycin resistant MCF7 cells showed increased MIR196A expression compared to sensitive cell lines. Patient ERα ChIP-Seq from HR+ disease tumours showed increased ERα occupancy at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases.

Key Results
ChIP-Seq for RNA polymerase II in MCF7 cells demonstrated that polymerase binding in the HOXC10 and MIR196A region is dependent on oestrogen and is repressed with tamoxifen or fulvestrant treatment. GRO-Seq analysis showed a dramatic increase in RNA production peaking at 40 minutes following addition of oestradiol, specifically in the genomic region surrounding MIR196A2. qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq validated the GRO-Seq finding that oestrogen increases precursor miRNA from MIR196A2 but not from MIR196A1. ChIA-PET identified two major interaction sites for MIR196A2 promoters: the HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel enhancer (MIR196A2-Enhancer, mE). 3C-qPCR demonstrated that both HDE and mE physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. Luciferase reporter assays showed PP1 (HOXC10 promoter) is the most active promoter, with PP2 contributing modestly; cloning HDE downstream resulted in the most significant augmentation of transcription in MCF7 cells. DNA methylation of the CpG island within MIR196A2 is mostly methylated in non-malignant MCF10A and cancerous MCF7 cells but unmethylated in HMEC. Four distinct clusters of MIR196A expression were identified; clusters 1 and 3 strongly correlate with HR and HR cofactors, while clusters 2 and 4 negatively correlate with ERα, PGR, FOXA1 and GATA3. In PAM50 subtypes, MIR196A is strongly expressed in the HER2 subtype, while expression in luminal A and B subtypes is very dynamic. METABRIC cohort analysis confirmed MIR196A is significantly over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal adjacent tissue, and over-expression is associated with an increase in tumour stage. High MIR196A expression is associated with poor survival in ER+ breast cancer (61% survival at 10 years) versus low expression (>95% survival at 10 years). In pre-menopausal ER+ tumours, high MIR196A expression is associated with a good outcome; in post-menopausal ER+ tumours, high expression associates with a poor outcome. In triple-negative breast cancer, high MIR196A expression associates with a better outcome compared to ER+ disease. MIR196A is significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells (TAMR) but almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistance (FASR) models. RNA-Seq of paclitaxel and adromycin resistant MCF7 cells showed MIR196A increases in resistant cell lines compared to treatment-sensitive cells. Patient ERα ChIP-Seq from HR+ tumours showed increased ERα occupancy at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dual-locus transcription of MIR196A adds complexity to its expression, with HOXC10 and MIR196A2 contributing differently to the phenotype. The correlation between MIR196A and HOXC genes in tumours, contrasted with their independence in normal tissue, suggests that cancer-specific regulatory elements drive concerted overexpression. The inversion of MIR196A prognostic direction between pre- and post-menopausal ER+ women, coupled with HOX genes' developmental role, hypothesises a change in HOX regulation through and following menopause that impacts breast cancer subtype evolution. DNA methylation of the CpG island within the HOXC10/MIR196A2 transcriptionally active region, being hypermethylated in MCF10A and MCF7, suggests that hypermethylation impairs expression and that ERα-mediated binding may be required to maintain low methylation and active transcription. In resistant tumours, the de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements, coupled with increased ERα occupancy, may revert cells to a non-terminally-differentiated stem-cell-like state, a common hallmark of tumourigenesis. The authors propose that MIR196A is a possible biomarker for the progression of breast tumour to becoming resistant to therapy, and warrant further investigation of its role in resistance.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report the exact sample size of the METABRIC cohort beyond mentioning the accession and that it includes 323 tumours. No specific p-values, confidence intervals, or effect sizes are reported for individual survival analyses or the METABRIC correlation results. The authors note that in normal human breast, the association between MIR196A and HOXC genes is more limited (HOXC11 and HOXC10) and is not significant, which limits extrapolation to non-cancer settings. The study uses only MCF7 as the cancer cell line model; results may not generalize to other ER+ breast cancer cell lines or in vivo settings. The CpG island in MIR196A2, which was identified as a SNP-associated region, is mostly methylated in both non-malignant MCF10A and cancerous MCF7 cells, making its normal-versus-cancer role unclear. The paper is a bioRxiv preprint not yet peer-reviewed at the time of publication, and the authors acknowledge this. The authors note that it is currently unclear how dual-encoded miRs are regulated, a gap in knowledge that limits interpretation of the MIR196A1/MIR196A2 relationship. The study lacks a random-controlled experimental design; observations are primarily correlational or in cell culture models.

Claims
MIR196A2 transcription is ERα-dependent and mediated by long-range interaction with the HOTAIR distal enhancer and a novel enhancer via gene looping. ERα and FOXA1 bind to PP1 and PP3 of MIR196A2 in MCF7 cells from public datasets. ChIA-PET identified HDE and mE as major interaction sites with MIR196A2 promoters. 3C-qPCR confirmed physical interaction of both enhancers with PP1 and PP2. Luciferase assays showed HDE provides the most significant augmentation of transcription in MCF7. GRO-Seq confirmed E2-dependent RNA production peaking at 40 minutes at MIR196A2. PP3, despite binding ERα and FOXA1, did not increase luciferase expression in reporter assays, complicating the promoter-enhancer model. The association between MIR196A and HOXC genes in normal tissues is limited to HOXC11 and HOXC10, not significant generally. The ERα-enhancer-promoter regulatory circuit represents a potentially druggable node for ER+ breast cancer. Long-range regulation of MIR196A via HOXC enhancers may be a mechanism of therapeutic resistance in ER+ disease.
MIR196A is a robust prognostic biomarker whose direction depends on menopausal status in ER+ breast cancer. In ER+ tumours with HT and CT response, low MIR196A = >95% survival at 10 years; high MIR196A = 61% at 10 years. In pre-menopausal women, high MIR196A associates with good outcome; in post-menopausal, with poor outcome. Multivariate analysis identified MIR196A as one of few significant biomarkers for pre-menopausal ER+ tumours. In post-menopausal women, all tested biomarkers, including MIR196A, were significant. In TNBC, the prognostic direction is reversed: high MIR196A associates with better outcome. MIR196A could stratify ER+ patients for adjuvant or endocrine therapy based on menopausal status. The reversal with menopausal status suggests ERα-mediated regulation of HOX genes changes post-menopause.
MIR196A expression is significantly up-regulated in tamoxifen-resistant ER+ breast cancer, and this correlates with DNA hypomethylation of the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoter region. MIR196A is significantly increased in TAMR cells, while almost depleted in FASR cells. DNA methylation changes to HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters match these expression patterns in resistance models. Patient ERα ChIP-Seq shows increased ERα occupancy at enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastases from resistant tumours. Fulvestrant resistance (FASR) shows nearly depleted MIR196A with corresponding hypermethylation, contrasting the resistance model. MIR196A could serve as a biomarker for imminent endocrine resistance. Therapeutic intervention targeting ERα-enhancer interactions could potentially restore repressive methylation and down-regulate MIR196A.

Data And Code Availability
METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from GEO accession EGAS00000083. DNA methylation of breast tumours was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). RNA-Seq from Adriamycin and paclitaxel resistant MCF7 derived cells was sourced from GSE68815. ChIP-Seq data (MCF7, GRO-Seq, ChIA-PET, Breast tumour ERα) were accessed via GEO accessions GSE14664, GSE27463, GSE39495, and GSE32222 respectively. MCF7 histone ChIP-Seq and breast cell 450K array data were sourced from ENCODE. No explicit data sharing statement or code repository is mentioned in the provided text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study performed validation of GRO-Seq results with qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq from MCF7 cells following oestradiol treatment. Luciferase assays used pRL-TK as a Renilla transfection control for normalization of luciferase activity. 3C-qPCR included HindIII control libraries (undigested and unligated) to assess digestion and ligation efficiency. In 3C-qPCR, GAPDH primers amplifying a fragment with no cut sites were used as internal controls. Multivariate and univariate Cox proportional hazard regression were used to assess independent prognostic value of MIR196A. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to determine optimal cutoffs for low and high expression groups. No explicit sensitivity analysis or ablation of individual enhancer components (e.g., removing HDE vs mE) is described in the provided text.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows ChIP-Seq for RNA polymerase II in MCF7 cells demonstrating oestrogen-dependent binding at HOXC10 and MIR196A2, and DNA methylation patterns. Figure 1B presents GRO-Seq data showing dramatic RNA production peaking at 40 minutes post-oestradiol at MIR196A2, and identifies ERα/FOXA1 binding to PP1 and PP3. Figure 1C and D show qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq validation of GRO-Seq findings for E2-induced MIR196A2 transcription. Figure 1E presents luciferase reporter assay data for promoters PP1, PP2, and PP3 in MCF7 cells. Figure 1A (re-mentioned) shows DNA methylation of the CpG island in MCF10A, MCF7, and HMEC cells. Figure 2A presents ChIA-PET interaction map showing HDE and mE interacting with MIR196A2 promoters. Figure 2B presents 3C-qPCR data confirming physical interaction of both enhancers with PP1 and PP2. Figure 2C presents luciferase reporter data for enhancer-promoter constructs showing HDE as most active. Figure 3A shows four clusters of MIR196A expression in breast tumours. Figure 3B shows correlation of MIR196A clusters with HR and HR cofactors. Figure 3C shows PAM50 subtype distribution of MIR196A expression. Figure 4A and 4B show METABRIC tumour versus normal expression and association with tumour stage. Figure 4C and D show survival curves by MIR196A expression in ER+ versus TNBC. Figure 5A presents survival stratified by MIR196A expression in ER+ tumours responding to HT and CT. Figure 5B shows MIR196A expression in tamoxifen-resistant, fulvestrant-resistant, and sensitive MCF7 cells. Figure 5C shows DNA methylation changes to the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters in resistance cell lines. Figure 5D shows MIR196A expression in paclitaxel and adromycin resistant MCF7 cell lines via RNA-Seq. Figure 5E presents patient ERα ChIP-Seq showing increased ERα occupancy at enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastases. Table 1 shows multivariate analysis results identifying MIR196A as a significant biomarker for pre-menopausal ER+ tumours.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the ERα-enhancer-promoter regulatory architecture (via ChIA-PET, 3C-qPCR, GRO-Seq) that controls MIR196A2 expression, and its validation as a menopausal-status-dependent prognostic biomarker and resistance marker in ER+ breast cancer. 2. The strongest evidence is the multi-omic convergence: GRO-Seq (40-min peak), ChIA-PET (HDE/mE interactions), 3C-qPCR (physical looping), and luciferase assays all independently confirm ERα-mediated enhancer-driven transcription of MIR196A2. 3. The future path involves high-resolution chromatin interaction analysis (5C or NG Capture-C) coupled with ERα ChIP-Seq and ChIA-PET to delineate the exact enhancer network, and functional studies to determine whether MIR196A increases are required for resistance development.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigated conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD) regulation on seedling survival and recruitment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak species (>90% basal stem area) in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. Four 400 m² plots at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station (3100–3350 m a.s.l.) were surveyed between 2014 and 2017. In the 2014 census, 2031 seedlings were mapped and tagged; over 99% showed herbivory, with approximately 71% exhibiting intermediate damage (10–75% leaf loss). Annual seedling survival decreased from 73.2% in 2015 to 63.8% in 2017. Contrary to Janzen-Connell predictions, CNDD did not significantly affect seedling survival or recruitment. Instead, bamboo (Chusquea spp.) density and herbivory (Index of Herbivory) significantly reduced survival. Seedling height had the strongest positive effect on survival. The relationship between distance to the nearest adult and survival was best described by a negative polynomial, with highest survival at intermediate distances. A significant interaction was found: high seedling density increased survival at low bamboo densities (<2.4 stems per m²) but decreased it at higher densities. In 2015, 1578 new recruits were recorded, with herbivory significantly lower than in the 2014 cohort (22.9% vs. 43.75%, p < 0.0001). Recruitment increased with conspecific seedling density but did not correlate with adult density or bamboo density. The authors attribute the lack of CNDD to herbivore satiation, high seedling density (2.4 seedlings per m²), and potential ectomycorrhizal facilitation from adults, suggesting that dominant tropical trees may escape negative density-dependence through convergent life-history traits and mutualistic symbioses.

Research Context
CNDD is a central mechanism proposed to regulate species coexistence in tropical forests, where higher offspring mortality of abundant species reduces competition for other species. The Janzen-Connell hypothesis suggests that susceptible species are more vulnerable to density-dependent mortality from pathogens, herbivores, and competition. Tropical montane forests above 2500 m a.s.l. are commonly dominated by a few tree species, unlike the high diversity of lowland tropical forests. In Costa Rica and western Panamá, montane forests are dominated by oaks, specifically Quercus costaricensis, which represents over 90% of the basal stem area. While temperate oaks show CNDD susceptibility, ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults can positively affect seedling survival, introducing ambiguity. The mechanisms structuring low-diversity tropical forests are not yet fully understood, particularly at the seedling establishment stage.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question was whether CNDD regulates seedling survival and recruitment of Quercus costaricensis in Costa Rican montane forests. Specifically, the study tested the effects of conspecific seedling density, distance to the nearest adult tree, and herbivory on annual survival probability and recruitment success. The authors also included bamboo (Chusquea spp.) density as a potential limiting factor for seedling establishment due to its dense understory growth. Given Q. costaricensis's extreme dominance and high seedling density, the authors expected to find weak or no CNDD regulation on seedling survival. A secondary prediction was that nearby adults would exert a positive effect on seedling recruitment, potentially through ectomycorrhizal facilitation. The null expectation was that higher conspecific density would correlate with lower survival and recruitment, as predicted by Janzen-Connell theory.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station, Costa Rica, in an upper montane tropical forest (3100–3350 m a.s.l.). The mean annual precipitation is 2500 mm with a relatively dry period between January and April, and mean air temperatures of 12°C. Daily temperature fluctuations range from −5°C to 35°C, and the forest is dominated by Q. costaricensis in the canopy and Chusquea bamboo in the understory. Four 400 m² plots (20 m × 20 m) were established in old-growth forests undisturbed for at least 30 years. Each plot was subdivided into 64 quadrats of 2.5 m × 2.5 m for seedling censusing. Chusquea bamboo density varied naturally among plots from 0 to 14 stems per m². In February 2014, 2031 Q. costaricensis seedlings (height < 2 m) were mapped and tagged within each plot. For each seedling, height, distance to the nearest conspecific adult, and conspecific seedling density in a 1 m radius were measured. Herbivory was estimated using the qualitative Index of Herbivory (IH) developed by Núñez-Farfán and Dirzo (1988). All adult trees (DBH > 5 cm) were mapped and measured within the plot and a 10 m buffer area. Bamboo stem numbers were counted in each quadrat. Re-censuses were conducted in May/June 2015, 2016, and 2017 to determine annual mortality and recruitment per quadrat. Seeds from the 2014 masting event were included as the 2015 cohort; in 2015 new recruits were identified by attached cotyledons. Germination success of Q. costaricensis seeds is 91% after 7 days in controlled conditions. Fruiting is synchronous with a supra-annual masting pattern every two or more years; acorns fall between April and October. Less than 15% of adults reproduced in 2016, so 2014 was considered the only masting event during the study.

Procedures And Architectures
Spatial distribution of 2014 seedlings was analyzed using the L(t)=(K(t)/π)⁰⁵ transformation of the univariate Ripley's K function to test for aggregation. The R statistical language (Version 3.2.2) was used with the ''spatstat'' library for all spatial analyses. Annual seedling survival probability was modeled using generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMM) with a binomial distribution. All variables, including log-transformed seedling height, were standardized before entry as fixed effects. Quadrat and census year were included as random effects to account for spatial and temporal non-independence. A dummy variable (age) identified seedlings from the 2014 census vs. those recruited in 2015. A second-degree polynomial effect for distance to nearest adult conspecific was tested to capture non-linear relationships. A full model including all variables and all second-order interactions was built, and final models retained significant terms. Seedling recruitment per quadrat was analyzed using a GLMM with a quasi-Poisson distribution. The lme4 package in R (Version 3.2.2) was used for statistical analyses. Plots were included as a random effect in the recruitment model to account for spatial autocorrelation of seedlings within plots. All explanatory variables were standardized to facilitate comparison of effect sizes across models.

Key Results
In the 2014 census, 2031 seedlings were mapped and confirmed to be spatially aggregated at all scales, as shown in Figure S1. Over 99% of censused seedlings had some leaf damage, and most plants (approximately 71%) exhibited intermediate damage (10–75%) per the Index of Herbivory (Figure 1). Contrary to Janzen-Connell predictions, herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities and increased away from adult trees (Table S2). Annual seedling survival decreased slightly over the study period: from 73.2% in 2015 to 64.38% in 2016 and 63.8% in 2017. Seedling height had the strongest positive effect on survival, while bamboo density and herbivory (IH) both significantly reduced survival (Figure 2). The effect of proximity to adults on seedling survival was best described by a negative polynomial function, with survival highest at intermediate distances from adults. A significant interaction was found: high seedling density significantly increased survival at low bamboo densities (<2.4 stems per m²) but decreased survival at higher bamboo densities (Figure S2). In 2015, 1578 new recruits were recorded, with herbivory at 22.9% ± 1.06 (new recruits) versus 43.75% ± 0.91 (2014 cohort), p < 0.0001. Seedling recruitment per quadrat significantly increased with conspecific seedling density but failed to correlate with adult tree density or Chusquea density. The local seedling density of Q. costaricensis was approximately 2.4 seedlings per m². No significant interactions between seedling density and herbivory, or between herbivory and distance to adult, were found (Table S1). The few recruits tallied in 2016 (55 in total) were considered as 2015 recruits because they were taller than expected for new seedlings. Only five new seedlings were recorded in 2017 on all four plots, so recruitment analysis was limited to the 2014 masting event.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The lack of CNDD regulation on seedling survival and recruitment contradicts Janzen-Connell expectations and suggests that dominant tropical trees escape negative density-dependence. The finding that herbivory decreases at higher seedling densities supports the herbivore satiation hypothesis, where high edible tissue availability reduces per-capita damage. A similar pattern has been reported for other masting tropical tree species with dense seedling aggregations that escape CNDD regulation. The negative quadratic relationship between adult proximity and seedling survival suggests that intermediate distances maximize ECM transfer while minimizing competition effects. Ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults to close seedlings may provide a facilitative effect that offsets CNDD-induced mortality, particularly at intermediate adult densities. The results support the view that dominant tree species in tropical forests may possess convergent life-history traits, such as high tolerance to leaf damage and ECM symbiosis, that reduce CNDD strength. The apparent lack of CNDD in Q. costaricensis correlates with its high abundance and dominance in montane forests, suggesting that these traits maintain forest composition.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors expected a positive effect of nearby adults on recruitment, but the actual result was a negative quadratic (polynomial) relationship for survival, with highest survival at intermediate distances. Herbivory was expected to increase with density per Janzen-Connell theory, but it actually decreased, contradicting the fundamental prediction of the hypothesis. The negative quadratic relationship for survival vs. adult distance is nuanced: ECM facilitation likely dominates at close range while competition takes over at very close range. Environmental factors such as soil acidity, low temperatures, and high solar irradiance were acknowledged as potential moderators of CNDD but were beyond the scope of the study. Only one masting year (2014) could be analyzed for recruitment due to low reproductive effort in 2016, limiting inference about masting-dynamic effects. The 2016 census recorded only mortality and five new seedlings, making cross-year recruitment comparisons difficult. A small sample of four plots at a single site limits generalizability to other highland forest sites or species.

Claims
Q. costaricensis does not exhibit conspecific negative density-dependence on seedling survival or recruitment at the studied density levels. No CNDD effect was detected despite the seedlings being spatially aggregated at all scales. Annual survival remained over 62% after three years despite high seedling density. Herbivory per capita decreased at higher seedling densities, the opposite of the CNDD prediction. Recruitment increased with seedling density rather than decreasing. The negative quadratic relationship between adult proximity and survival introduces a spatial structure that is not strictly density-independent. Herbivory still significantly reduced survival, meaning negative factors persist even if they are not density-dependent. The absence of CNDD may explain the monodominance of Q. costaricensis in highland forests, allowing it to maintain high adult densities. Similar mechanisms may operate in other masting tropical tree species, contributing to low-diversity forest compositions.
Bamboo density and herbivory are the primary limiting factors for seedling survival, but neither operates through a density-dependent mechanism. Bamboo density significantly reduced survival across all models. Herbivory (IH) significantly reduced survival, with over 99% of seedlings showing leaf damage. The herbivory-density relationship showed decreasing damage with increasing density, suggesting satiation. The seedling-bamboo interaction revealed that high seedling density increases survival only at low bamboo densities (<2.4 stems m⁻²). Herbivory is ubiquitous (over 99%) but survival after three years remained above 62%, indicating high resilience. New recruits had substantially lower herbivory (22.9%) than the prior cohort (43.75%), suggesting temporal variation. Management of understory bamboo may be more relevant for oak recruitment than conspecific density management. Predator-herbivore dynamics at the landscape level may control oak population structure rather than simple intraspecific competition.
Predator satiation and ectomycorrhizal facilitation from adults explain the lack of CNDD regulation in this dominant oak species. Higher seedling survival after the masting event (73.2% vs. lower in non-masting years) supports the herbivore satiation hypothesis. The negative polynomial relationship between adult proximity and survival is consistent with ECM transfer at intermediate distances. Similar patterns of CNDD escape have been documented in other dominant masting tropical tree species. The study did not directly measure ECM fungal colonization or nutrient transfer, so the facilitation mechanism remains inferred. Ectomycorrhizal transfer was shown to produce a positive effect in other species, but this study only observed a negative quadratic for survival. Facilitation by conspecific adults may operate alongside density-independent factors to sustain high oak densities. The balance between asymmetric competition and facilitation explains the intermediate-distance survival peak.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors used the R language (Version 3.2.2) with the 'spatstat' library for spatial analysis and the lme4 package for GLMMs. All variables were standardized to ensure comparable effect sizes across models. A full model including all variables and second-order interactions was built, and only models retaining significant terms were kept (Table S1). A second-degree polynomial effect was tested for distance to nearest adult, and the best-fitting model was chosen (negative polynomial). The bamboo-seedling interaction was tested and found significant: high seedling density increased survival at low bamboo (<2.4 stems m⁻²) and decreased it at high bamboo. The recruitment model was constrained to a quasi-Poisson GLMM with plots as a random effect to account for spatial autocorrelation. The dummy variable for age (2014 vs. 2015 cohorts) tested for cohort-specific survival differences. A 10 m buffer area around each plot was used to map adult trees, ensuring sufficient capture of conspecific adults. The seedling density was measured in a 1 m radius around each individual to capture local conditions. The use of standardized variables allowed for direct comparison of effect sizes across the different models. The spatial aggregation test at all scales provided confirmation that the study design captured the relevant spatial processes.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Index of Herbivory (IH) distribution across all censused seedlings, demonstrating that over 99% had damage and ~71% had intermediate levels. Figure S1 displays the spatial aggregation of seedlings at all scales, confirming the clustered distribution characteristic of masting species with gravity-dispersed seeds. Figure 2 presents the GLMM results for annual survival, showing height as the strongest positive predictor, bamboo and herbivory as negative predictors, and the negative polynomial relationship for distance to adults. Figure S2 displays the interaction between seedling density and Chusquea density on survival, showing the switch from positive to negative effect at low bamboo densities. Table S1 reports the full set of models, retaining significant interactions and polynomial terms, along with the recruitment per quadrat results. Table S2 summarizes the herbivory response to seedling density and adult proximity, showing decreased herbivory at higher seedling densities. The 2014 masting event is confirmed by synchronous fruiting and acorn fall, with less than 15% of adults reproducing in 2016. Germination was verified in controlled conditions with 91% success after 7 days.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the empirical demonstration that Q. costaricensis does not exhibit conspecific negative density-dependence on seedling survival or recruitment at the observed densities, challenging the ubiquity of the Janzen-Connell hypothesis in tropical highland forests. 2. The strongest evidence comes from the combined observation of spatially aggregated seedlings (2031 mapped), herbivory decreasing with density (supporting satiation), and the negative polynomial relationship for adult proximity consistent with ECM facilitation. 3. The future path involves testing whether CNDD effects are moderated by environmental harshness (e.g., acidic soils, low temperature), measuring ECM fungal colonization directly, and investigating whether other dominant highland species share this CNDD-escape mechanism.

summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.field_subfield: Ecotoxicology / Nanomaterial Toxicity
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles—silver (Ag), gold (Au), copper oxide (CuO), zinc oxide (ZnO), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and silicon dioxide (SiO2)—along with three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3) on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp. The authors selected Artemia as a model organism owing to its ubiquity in highly saline waters, robust nature, and cost-effectiveness for toxicological assays. The experimental design comprises two complementary approaches: (1) a hatching assay monitoring the hatching rate, mortality, and viability of Artemia cysts exposed to nanoparticles at 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L over 24 hours, and (2) a standard Artemia toxicity test exposing 10 nauplii to five nanoparticle concentrations (100 mg/L down to 0.01 mg/L) over 48 hours. Nanoparticles were characterized using TEM (50 µg/mL, 100 kV, JEOL 2010 TEM) and DLS (25 µg/mL in both water and salt water, Horiba Nanopartica SZ100). 

Key results demonstrated that toxicity followed the order Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2 in both assays. Silver nanoparticles exhibited the greatest toxicity, with an LC50 of approximately 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours, while silver in ionic form (AgNO3) caused 80% mortality in 24 hours. At 100 mg/L, Ag and CuO reduced hatching rates to approximately 29%, with only 50% of hatched nauplii motile in the Ag group and 64% in the CuO group. A strong inverse correlation coefficient of -0.7853 was obtained between hatching rates and larval mortality across all tested nanoparticles, validating the hatching assay as a complementary, short-term alternative to standard lethality tests. DLS measurements showed reduced particle size in salt water and visible flocculation of CuO and ZnO by the third day. ROS staining confirmed oxidative stress primarily in the gut and for still-trapped nauplii, most pronounced with silver nanoparticles. The study concludes that the Artemia hatching-and-viability assay provides a rapid, cost-effective method for nanoparticle hazard identification, eliminating the need for long-term laboratory maintenance of test species and allowing for high-throughput screening.
