judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles—silver (Ag), gold (Au), copper oxide (CuO), zinc oxide (ZnO), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and silicon dioxide (SiO2)—along with three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3) on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp. The authors selected Artemia as a model organism owing to its ubiquity in highly saline waters, robust nature, and cost-effectiveness for toxicological assays. The experimental design comprises two complementary approaches: (1) a hatching assay monitoring the hatching rate, mortality, and viability of Artemia cysts exposed to nanoparticles at 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L over 24 hours, and (2) a standard Artemia toxicity test exposing 10 nauplii to five nanoparticle concentrations (100 mg/L down to 0.01 mg/L) over 48 hours. Nanoparticles were characterized using TEM (50 µg/mL, 100 kV, JEOL 2010 TEM) and DLS (25 µg/mL in both water and salt water, Horiba Nanopartica SZ100). 

Key results demonstrated that toxicity followed the order Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2 in both assays. Silver nanoparticles exhibited the greatest toxicity, with an LC50 of approximately 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours, while silver in ionic form (AgNO3) caused 80% mortality in 24 hours. At 100 mg/L, Ag and CuO reduced hatching rates to approximately 29%, with only 50% of hatched nauplii motile in the Ag group and 64% in the CuO group. A strong inverse correlation coefficient of -0.7853 was obtained between hatching rates and larval mortality across all tested nanoparticles, validating the hatching assay as a complementary, short-term alternative to standard lethality tests. DLS measurements showed reduced particle size in salt water and visible flocculation of CuO and ZnO by the third day. ROS staining confirmed oxidative stress primarily in the gut and for still-trapped nauplii, most pronounced with silver nanoparticles. The study concludes that the Artemia hatching-and-viability assay provides a rapid, cost-effective method for nanoparticle hazard identification, eliminating the need for long-term laboratory maintenance of test species and allowing for high-throughput screening.

Research Context
Nanomaterials with their expanding diversity and unique properties pose risks to the environment and human health. A dearth of information exists on the impact or risk of nanoscale objects to ecosystems. Increasing nanomaterial utility means enhanced exposure of ecosystems to unknown risks. Release into the environment may begin with production, during applications, by weathering, and finally wastes. Nanomaterials behave differently from bulk due to unique physicochemical properties. Information on the predictability of nanoparticle behavior is almost negligible. Limited information exists on bioavailability, biopersistence, and behavior under pH and salinity variations. Hazard identification is an essential step for risk assessment of nanomaterials. Aquatic systems are the inevitable receptacles for materials released into the environment. Many ecotoxicity assays have been tested for nanomaterials in bacteria, fishes, copepods, and Daphnia. Artemia is a non-selective filter feeder available worldwide in highly saline waters. Due to ubiquitous distribution, robust nature, and cost-effective culture, Artemia make a good model for toxicological assays. Early developmental stages of Artemia are highly vulnerable to many test materials. Few studies report nanomaterial toxicity using Artemia sp, with most carried out in newly hatched nauplii. Hatching of hydrated cysts has not been used as a toxicity end point except in a single study. Earlier studies had shown sensitivity of hatching rate of Artemia to metals. This paper studies acute toxicity of four metal oxide and two metal nanoparticles on nauplii and hatching of cysts. Mortality and hatching rates serve as end points respectively for the nauplii and hatching tests. The authors hypothesize that both tests show a good inverse correlation in sensitivity, implying another bioassay for hazard assessment.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether engineered nanoparticles and soluble salts exhibit acute toxicity on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp. The study aims to estimate the order of toxicity among six engineered nanoparticles and three soluble salts. The physiochemical properties of nanoparticles are estimated in both normal and marine water to understand behavior. The hypothesis is that hatching rate and larval mortality will show inverse correlation in sensitivity to nanoparticles. The authors predict that Ag and CuO nanoparticles, being metal-based, will show higher toxicity than oxide and silica counterparts. The study further tests whether ionic forms (solubilized salts) contribute to nanoparticle toxicity. Oxidative stress is tested as a potential mechanism for nanoparticle-induced toxicity in nauplii. A second hypothesis is that particles that reduce hatching rate will show increased mortality in the standard toxicity test. The study aims to establish Artemia hatching rate as a valid, rapid pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity. The authors seek to determine if nanoparticles remain stable in seawater conditions during the exposure period. The comparison aims to determine if the hatching assay is a statistically valid alternative or complement to the standard test. The ultimate goal is to provide a simple, efficient method for hazard identification of nanomaterials.

Methodological Details
Six engineered nanoparticles were tested: Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, and SiO2, alongside three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3). Nanoparticles were obtained from the NANOVALID consortium: SiO2 from Nanologica AB, Ag from Colorobbia, Au from INMETRO, CuO from Intrinsiq Materials, and ZnO from Nanogate. TiO2 nanoparticles were synthesized in-house using an existing protocol. SiO2, TiO2, CuO, and ZnO suspension was made at 2 mg/mL. Ag nanoparticles were prepared as 4% suspension with PVP as a stabilizing agent. Au nanoparticles were in water at 0.006%. The suspension was sonicated at ~30W with 50% pulse for 10 minutes. All nanoparticles were characterized in the NANOVALID consortium via TEM and DLS in round robin manner. TEM studies used a 50 µg/mL nanoparticle suspension applied to formvar-coated copper grids. TEM was performed on JEOL 2010 TEM at 100 kV using 20 µ aperture, capturing ~10 images per grid. Images were analyzed with GATAN software for size determination. DLS measurements used a 25 µg/mL suspension in milliQ water and salt water, analyzed thrice for three days. DLS was performed on the Horiba Nanopartica SZ100 system. Data was represented as mean ± SEM. For every 1 L culture, 1.0 g of Artemia cysts (San Francisco Bay strain) were used. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water under aeration for 45 minutes. Cysts were bleached in 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes. Bleached eggs were washed six times with distilled water and allowed to hatch in 25% salt water (pH 8.0). Temperature was maintained at 28°C, the optimum for hatching. Aeration was continuous; light was continuous for 24 hours. Nanoparticles were added at concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L for the hatching test. Three aliquots of 100 µL were taken from each flask for counting under a stereo-microscope. Hatched Artemia (immotile vs. motile), umbrella stage, and unhatched cyst were counted after 24 hours. The experiment was repeated six times with average and SEM calculated. In the toxicity test, 10 nauplii were transferred to six well plates. Particle concentrations were 100 mg/L, 10 mg/L, 1 mg/L, 0.1 mg/L, and 0.01 mg/L. Viability was counted at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. Mortality was the endpoint, recorded as cessation of swimming or movement. LD50 was calculated using Graphpad software quickcalcs module. Oxidative stress was assessed with 10 µM DCFDA, a chemiluminescent probe reacting with ROS. Fluorescence was imaged using a Zeiss Axiovert imager. Hatching validity criterion: low mortality in control. Toxicity validity criterion: mortality below 10% in 24 hr period. Correlation test performed using online software and Microsoft Excel. Artemia were not fed during the toxicity test period. Hatching rate expressed as percent of total fully hatched Artemia vs. total in aliquot.

Procedures And Architectures
Nanoparticle suspensions were prepared by diluting the stock concentrations in salt water (NaCl) for various studies. The hatching assay exposed Artemia cysts to nanoparticles at 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L in filtered sterile salt water with continuous aeration. Continuous aeration kept nanoparticles in suspension throughout the 24-hour hatching period. After 24 hours, three 100 µL aliquots were taken from each flask, thoroughly mixed, and counted under a stereo-microscope. The standard toxicity test followed the Artemia Reference Centre (ARC) protocol, exposing hatched nauplii to nanoparticle suspensions for up to 48 hours. Viability was recorded every 6 hours for the first 24 hours, then up to 48 hours. In the toxicity test, 10 nauplii were transferred to six-well plates per concentration. The larval toxicity test monitored sedimentation and flocculation of nanoparticles by 48 hours. Particle accumulation in the gut of Artemia was observed by the end of 24 hours. For oxidative stress, nauplii exposed to DCFDA were imaged in a Zeiss Axiovert imager to detect ROS fluorescence. Correlation analysis was performed using online software for correlation coefficient and comparing data in Microsoft Excel. The paired T test was used to compare hatching rate with viability mean values (P=0.683). The pH of salt water was monitored and remained around 6.3–6.5 up to 48 hours. To confirm whether toxicity was due to ionic forms, nanoparticle suspension was centrifuged and resuspended in brine solution. Resuspended particles remained as nanoparticles even after 72 hours in high salinity water. Nanoparticles suspended in Milli Q water and 25% NaCl solution were measured up to 48 hours to track dispersion pattern changes.

Key Results
Control Artemia showed a hatching rate of 74% ± 5.5 and 97% viability. Nanoparticles reduced hatching rate in concentration-dependent manner, with Ag and CuO having the highest effect. At 100 mg/L, Ag and CuO reduced hatching rate to about 29%, with 50% motile and viable in Ag and 64% in CuO. At 10 mg/L, Ag hatching rate remained lower, but viability was good at 85%. In CuO, hatching rate was low with better viability around 64%. With silver nitrate or PVP-capped silver, hatching slightly improved to 33% and 41%, respectively. Gold, silicon, titanium, copper, and zinc oxide nanoparticles yielded hatching rates around 50–60% at 100 mg/L compared to control. ZnO nanoparticles at 100 mg/L yielded a hatching rate of 60%, but cysts tended to clump together. TiO2 at 100 mg/L yielded hatching rate of 41.50% with 67.8% viability. TiO2 at 10 mg/L yielded hatching rate of 54% with ~90% viability. SiO2 at 10 mg/L showed hatching rate and viability equivalent to controls. The order of toxicity for nanoparticles was estimated as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. Silver in ionic form (AgNO3) killed 80% of nauplii in 24 hours. Other nanoparticles were nontoxic initially but after 30 hours showed concentration-dependent mortality. A strong inverse correlation coefficient of -0.7853 was found between hatching rates and larval mortality across all nanoparticles. The paired T test comparing hatching rate to viability showed no statistically significant difference (P = 0.683). DLS showed reduced size in salt water; TiO2, CuO, ZnO showed higher DLS values, while Au and SiO2 showed lesser values compared to water. Visible flocculation was observed in CuO and ZnO nanoparticles, with very high DLS values corroborating the flocculent. On the third day, Ag, TiO2, and SiO2 showed higher aggregate sizes in salt water, while CuO and ZnO showed visible flocculation and sedimentation. Particles remained stable in seawater up to one week, though ionic or dissolved components may settle. ROS staining confirmed stress in a few still-trapped nauplii and the gut of dead nauplii, most pronounced with Ag. Nauplii exposed to Ag showed highest ROS and superoxide staining, followed by TiO2 and SiO2. Nauplii exposed to other nanoparticles showed accumulation in the gut but no ROS or superoxide staining.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The strong correlation between hatching rate and larval mortality suggests hatching can serve as a complementary toxicity endpoint. Toxicity of Ag and CuO nanoparticles could be due to ionic forms, though centrifugation confirmed particle-mediated toxicity. Even when ionic silver precipitates in high salinity, it still affects hatching and subsequent viability. Silicon nanoparticles at low concentration were conducive to hatching, showing better hatching than control. The gut accumulation of nanoparticles suggests gut clogging as a mechanism for mortality in non-ionic particle exposures. The hatching assay provides a rapid, cost-effective, short-term alternative that eliminates the need for laboratory maintenance of test species. Cysts available in enormous quantities as batch cut down on variability. With strictly laid out protocol and test conditions, this assay can be adopted for nanomaterial hazard identification and high-throughput methods. Artemia's capacity to maintain homeostasis in variable salt concentrations makes it a suitable model for nanoparticle behavior and ecotoxicity. The hatching assay could be used as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity prior to in vivo validation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The hatching test used only two concentrations (100 and 10 mg/L), limiting the precision of dose-response characterization compared to the five-concentration toxicity test. The study was conducted with only one strain of Artemia (San Francisco Bay strain), limiting generalizability to other strains. The toxicity test was conducted only at 24 and 48 hours, potentially missing chronic or late-onset effects. The authors acknowledge that sedimentation of nanoparticle suspensions may vary for different particles, potentially confounding exposure. Theionic or dissolved component of particles may settle down, although the hatching test uses continuous aeration to mitigate this. The study was conducted as a preprint (May 25, 2018) and may not have undergone full peer-review at the time of writing. The hatching assay was validated with only 6 replicates, which may have limited statistical power for some comparisons. The authors state that hatching rate equals toxicity of the test compound, but the physiological mechanism connecting the two is not fully elucidated.

Claims
The Artemia hatching rate assay is a valid and complementary endpoint for nanoparticle acute toxicity assessment, showing strong inverse correlation with larval mortality. A correlation coefficient of -0.7853 was obtained between hatching rates and larval mortality across all nanoparticles. Particles that reduced hatching rate showed an increase in mortality in the ARC test. The hatching assay eliminated the need for laboratory maintenance of test species. Cysts available in batch cut down on variability. The correlation was based on only two concentrations in the hatching assay vs. five in the toxicity test. Hatching rate and mortality were correlated across only six nanoparticle types, limiting generalizability. The assay could be adopted for nanomaterial hazard identification and high-throughput methods. The hatching assay could serve as a pre-screening test prior to in vivo toxicity validation.
Silver nanoparticles exhibit the highest acute toxicity among the tested engineered nanoparticles in both hatching and larval viability assays. The LC50 of Ag nanoparticles was approximately 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. At 100 mg/L, Ag and CuO reduced hatching to 29%, the highest effect among all tested nanoparticles. Ag was ranked highest in toxicity in the standard Artemia toxicity test. Staining confirmed ROS and gut accumulation most pronounced with silver. At 10 mg/L, Ag hatching rate remained lower but viability was good at 85%. Silver in ionic form caused 80% mortality in 24 hours, suggesting the ionic component may contribute significantly to toxicity. Ag nanoparticles pose a primary risk among the tested nanomaterials in aquatic environments.
Nanoparticle dispersion and physiochemical behavior change significantly in high salinity conditions, affecting bioavailability and observed toxicity. DLS showed reduced size in salt water for all nanoparticles. CuO and ZnO showed visible flocculation and higher DLS values in salt water by the third day. Ag, TiO2, and SiO2 showed higher aggregate sizes in salt water on the third day. Ionic or dissolved components may precipitate over time in high salinity water. The pH of salt water remained stable at 6.3–6.5 up to 48 hours. Particles remained stable in seawater up to one week, according to the authors. No apparent change in aggregation or dispersion was noted in TEM studies, suggesting DLS may overestimate flocculation. The behavior of nanoparticles in salt water may not be fully predicted from water-only characterization.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The hatching study was conducted six times with average and SEM calculated for each sample to ensure reproducibility. The toxicity test was repeated for each nanoparticle concentration at 100, 10, 1, 0.1, and 0.01 mg/L. Particle accumulation in the gut was observed by the end of 24 hours to verify exposure. DLS measurements were taken up to 48 hours to track changes in dispersion pattern over time. A control (unexposed) Artemia culture was maintained for comparison, showing 74% ± 5.5 hatching rate. The validity criterion for the toxicity test was mortality below 10% in the 24 hr control period. The correlation test was performed for both sets of data using online software and Microsoft Excel. The paired T test compared hatching rate with viability at P = 0.683 to check for statistical equivalence. Nanoparticle suspension was centrifuged and resuspended in brine solution to confirm particle-mediated toxicity. Continuous aeration in the hatching test kept particles in suspension, reducing confounding effects of sedimentation. The study was repeated six times for hatching rate measurements, with average and SEM reported. DLS measurements were analyzed thrice for three days, represented as mean ± SEM.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows TEM studies of nanoparticles at 50 µg/mL, demonstrating no apparent change in aggregation or dispersion between water and salt water. Figure 2 presents DLS values for nanoparticles in water and salt water, showing reduced size in salt water and higher DLS values for TiO2, CuO, and ZnO. Figure 3 displays hatching rate and viability versus nanoparticle concentration (100 mg/L and 10 mg/L) for all six nanoparticles.
